parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student places cubes of starch–agar, stained blue-black with iodine, into amylase solution at five temperatures and times how long each cube takes to lose its blue-black colour. She writes her results in her notebook as: "20 degrees took 340 seconds, 30 degrees took 190 seconds, 40 degrees took 95 seconds, 50 degrees took 160 seconds, 60 degrees took 500 seconds".
Describe how she should set out these results in a table.
parts.answer: two columns (or rows): first 'temperature / °C' (independent variable), second 'time / s'; units only in the headings; numbers only in the body, in increasing order of temperature
parts.working: B1 independent variable (temperature) in first column; B1 headings with units (temperature / °C, time / s); B1 no units in the body of the table / all five results entered correctly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student records the time taken for an enzyme reaction to finish at three concentrations of enzyme: 1 % – 125 s; 2 % – 80 s; 4 % – 50 s. Calculate the rate of reaction for each concentration using rate = 1000 ÷ time. Give each answer to one decimal place.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thermometer is marked in 1 °C divisions with a small mark halfway between each. At the start of an experiment the liquid level is at the halfway mark between 23 °C and 24 °C. At the end it is exactly on 31 °C. State both readings and calculate the temperature change.
parts.answer: start 23.5 °C; end 31.0 °C; change 7.5 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert 2.4 dm³ into cm³.
parts.answer: 2400 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 0.085 g into mg.
parts.answer: 85 mg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert 560 mm into cm.
parts.answer: 56 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three repeat readings for the time taken for a leaf disc to float were 42 s, 46 s and 61 s. Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean of the other readings.
parts.answer: anomalous 61 s; mean 44 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why carrying out repeats is useful.
parts.answer: allows anomalous results to be identified (and a mean calculated)
parts.working: B1. Do not credit 'makes it accurate'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A potato cylinder had a mass of 2.40 g before and 2.13 g after soaking in a sugar solution for 30 minutes. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to two significant figures and show whether it is a gain or a loss.
parts.answer: −11 % (a loss)

practice.stem:
Time for a cut piece of beetroot to release enough pigment to colour the water a set shade:
temperature / °C | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
time / s | 70 | 48 | 32 | 15 | 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which variable should be plotted on the x-axis and why.
parts.answer: temperature, because it is the independent variable (the one the student changed)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the change between 30 °C and 40 °C is linear, estimate the time at 35 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two things a student should do when plotting this graph so that it gains full marks.
parts.answer: linear scales using more than half the grid; axes labelled with units; points plotted accurately as small crosses; join points with ruled straight lines or a smooth curve; do not extrapolate beyond 20 °C or 60 °C
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of Hydrilla pondweed is placed in hydrogencarbonate solution under a lamp. The gas given off is collected in an inverted syringe. In 5 minutes, 3.6 cm³ of gas is collected. Calculate the rate of gas production in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 0.72 cm³ per min

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lamp is moved further away and 1.5 cm³ is collected in 5 minutes. Calculate the percentage decrease in rate. Give your answer to two significant figures.

practice.stem:
A student measured the time taken for milk to clear at different temperatures in an experiment using a protease. The rate of reaction was calculated as 1000 ÷ time (in arbitrary units).
Temperature (°C): 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Time to clear (s): 84, 52, 33, 41, 118.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 19.2 (arbitrary units)
parts.working: 1 mark: correct method, 1000 ÷ 52. 1 mark: 19.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the temperature at which the rate of reaction is highest.
parts.answer: 40 °C (time to clear is shortest, 33 s)
parts.working: 1 mark: 40 °C has the shortest time, so the highest rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate falls between 40 °C and 60 °C.
parts.answer: Above the optimum, the enzyme's active site changes shape (the enzyme is denatured), so fewer substrate molecules fit and the rate falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: the enzyme denatures / active site changes shape. 1 mark: fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, so the rate falls.

practice.stem: Seeds were sown in three trays and the number that germinated was counted: tray 1: 14 of 20 seeds; tray 2: 18 of 25 seeds; tray 3: 9 of 30 seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of seeds that germinated in each tray.
parts.answer: Tray 1: 70 %; tray 2: 72 %; tray 3: 30 %
parts.working: 1 mark: method (germinated ÷ sown × 100). 1 mark: all three values correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the overall percentage of seeds that germinated, using the total number of seeds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the overall percentage should be calculated from the total seeds rather than by averaging the three percentages.
parts.answer: Each tray has a different number of seeds, so the average of the percentages gives equal weight to each tray, which is not correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: trays have different numbers of seeds, so the percentages must be weighted (use totals).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has a 1.0 mol per dm³ sucrose solution and distilled water. He needs 20 cm³ of each of the concentrations 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mol per dm³. Calculate the volumes of sucrose solution and distilled water for 0.2 and for 0.6 mol per dm³.
parts.answer: 0.2: 4 cm³ sucrose + 16 cm³ water; 0.6: 12 cm³ sucrose + 8 cm³ water
parts.working: B1 each pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the piece of apparatus he should use to measure these volumes and explain your choice.
parts.answer: a graduated syringe (or 10 cm³ / 25 cm³ measuring cylinder) – measures small volumes precisely (a beaker is not precise)
parts.working: B1 syringe / small measuring cylinder; B1 precise / small graduations.

practice.stem:
Students measured the lengths of 36 earthworms collected from a school garden and grouped them:
length / mm | 40–59 | 60–79 | 80–99 | 100–119 | 120–139
number of earthworms | 3 | 8 | 13 | 9 | 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of earthworms in the 100–119 mm class.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these data should be shown as a histogram rather than a line graph.
parts.answer: length is continuous data grouped into classes; each class is a range, so bars of equal width that touch are used (a line graph is for showing how one variable changes with another)
parts.working: B1 continuous data in classes; B1 frequency of each class shown by touching bars.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the modal class.

practice.stem:
A student heats standard glucose solutions with Benedict's solution in a boiling water-bath and records the time for the first colour change from blue.
glucose concentration / % | 0.5 | 1.0 | 2.0
time / s | 240 | 120 | 60
A fruit-juice sample took 90 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the pattern in the results (time × concentration is constant) to estimate the glucose concentration of the fruit juice. Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.working: M1 time × concentration = 120; M1/A1 120 ÷ 90 = 1.3 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is better to estimate the concentration from a graph drawn through all the standard results than from one pair of standards.
parts.answer: the graph uses all the data, so the estimate is more reliable / reduces the effect of an error in one reading

practice.stem: A mould colony growing on agar was measured at intervals. Diameter of the colony: 2 h: 5 mm; 3 h: 12 mm; 4 h: 30 mm. At 1 h the colony diameter was 2 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of growth, in mm per hour, between 2 h and 4 h.
parts.answer: 12.5 mm per hour
parts.working: 1 mark: increase = 30 − 5 = 25 mm. 1 mark: 25 ÷ 2 h = 12.5 mm per hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the time interval in which the colony grew fastest.
parts.answer: Between 3 h and 4 h (18 mm in 1 h)
parts.working: 1 mark: 3–4 h increase of 18 mm is the largest (1–2 h gives 3 mm; 2–3 h gives 7 mm).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate of growth increases over time.
parts.answer: The colony grows by repeated cell division, so the number of growing cells increases over time and the growth becomes faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeated division increases the number of cells.

practice.stem: A student measured the length of a plant stem (y, in mm) at different times (x, in days). The points were: (10, 4.1), (20, 8.3), (30, 12.0), (40, 15.9), (50, 27.5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous point.
parts.working: 1 mark: it does not follow the pattern of the other four points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line between (10, 4.1) and (40, 15.9). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.39 mm per day

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the anomalous point should not be included when drawing the line of best fit.
parts.answer: It is an outlier that does not fit the trend; including it would distort the line and the calculated gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: an anomaly that would distort the line of best fit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of sucrose concentration on the change in mass of cylinders of radish (mooli). You have a radish, a cork borer, a scalpel, a ruler, a balance, sucrose solutions of 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mol per dm³, boiling tubes and paper towels.
parts.answer: Cut equal cylinders, blot and weigh, place in each concentration for a fixed time, blot and reweigh, calculate % change; repeat; control size, volume, time, temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: use cork borer and scalpel to cut cylinders of the same diameter and length (e.g. 30 mm); remove skin / same part of radish; blot and weigh each cylinder before; place in same volume of each concentration (five concentrations); leave for the same time (e.g. 30 min) at the same temperature; remove, blot in the same way and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass; repeat with three cylinders per concentration and find mean; safety: cut away from fingers on a tile.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an investigation to find the effect of pH on the activity of amylase. You are provided with: starch solution, amylase solution, buffer solutions of pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, iodine solution, a spotting tile, test-tubes, syringes, a stop-clock and a thermostatically controlled water-bath.
Your plan should include what you would measure, the variables you would control and how you would make your results reliable.
parts.answer: Mix fixed volumes of starch, buffer and amylase at each pH at 37 °C; test a drop with iodine every 30 s; record time until iodine stays orange-brown; repeat three times; control temperature, volumes, concentrations
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: independent variable pH using at least five buffers (4–9); same volume of buffer added to starch; same volume and concentration of starch; same volume and concentration of amylase; temperature kept constant with thermostatically controlled water-bath (e.g. 37 °C); solutions equilibrated to temperature before mixing; sample a drop onto iodine on the tile at regular intervals (e.g. every 30 s); record time until no blue-black colour (starch gone); rate = 1 ÷ time; repeat each pH at least three times and calculate a mean; control with boiled amylase; safety: eye protection with iodine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis of Hydrilla. You may use a lamp, a metre rule, a beaker, sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, a stop-clock and any other normal apparatus.
parts.answer: Hydrilla in hydrogencarbonate solution; lamp at five distances; acclimatise 5 min; count bubbles per minute or collect gas volume; heat shield; control temperature, CO₂, same piece of plant; repeat
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: place same piece of Hydrilla in a beaker / test-tube of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution; vary distance of lamp (at least five distances, e.g. 10–50 cm) measured with metre rule; allow time to adjust (e.g. 5 min) at each distance; count bubbles in a fixed time or collect gas in a syringe / measuring cylinder; keep temperature constant (heat filter / water bath / LED lamp); same concentration of hydrogencarbonate (CO₂ supply); darken the room so only the lamp gives light; repeat and calculate mean; safety: keep water away from mains lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the leaf area of a leafy shoot affects the rate of water loss (transpiration). A leafy shoot can be placed in a water bath and its water loss measured over time.
parts.answer: Independent variable: leaf area, changed by removing leaves so that 25 %, 50 % and 100 % of the leaf area remains. Dependent variable: volume of water lost (or the distance a bubble moves in a potometer) in a set time. Control: temperature, light, humidity, air movement and the number of leaves kept the same. Method: cut shoots under water, seal the apparatus, set up each shoot, wait 5 minutes, then record the reading every 5 minutes for 30 minutes. Repeat three times and calculate a mean rate. Safety: avoid spills near electrical equipment and dry the bench.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the heart rate of Daphnia (water flea), a small crustacean whose heart can be seen through its transparent body under a microscope.
parts.answer: Independent variable: temperature of the water, set using ice and warm water (e.g. 5 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C, 35 °C). Dependent variable: heart beats counted in 10 seconds. Control: same individual or similar sized Daphnia, same volume of water, same time for acclimatising. Method: place a Daphnia in a depression slide with water at the set temperature, wait 2 minutes, count beats for 10 s, repeat three times and calculate beats per minute. Ethics: handle carefully, return the Daphnia to the pond water after use, and do not heat the water above 35 °C.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether woodlice prefer damp or dry conditions. Use a choice chamber with two halves.
parts.answer: Independent variable: humidity, one half damp (moist paper) and the other dry. Dependent variable: number of woodlice in each half after a set time (e.g. every 2 minutes for 10 minutes). Control: same number and size of woodlice, same temperature and light, same time of day, and the chamber left in the dark. Method: place 10 woodlice in the centre, record numbers in each half at each interval, repeat with new woodlice at least three times, and calculate the mean. Safety/ethics: return the woodlice to their habitat after the experiment and wash hands.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of salt solution affects the germination of mung bean seeds (Vigna radiata).
parts.answer: Independent variable: concentration of sodium chloride solution (0, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 mol per dm³ or equivalent). Dependent variable: percentage of seeds germinated after five days (a seed is counted as germinated when the radicle is at least 2 mm long). Control: same number of seeds per dish, same volume of solution, same temperature and light, same seed batch and dish type. Method: place 20 seeds on filter paper in each dish, add 10 cm³ of solution, keep in the same place, add water to keep moist, repeat three times. Accuracy: measure the radicle with a ruler and calculate the mean percentage germinated.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the pH of water affects the growth of duckweed (Lemna), a small floating plant.
parts.answer: Independent variable: pH of the water, adjusted with dilute acid or alkali (e.g. pH 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10). Dependent variable: number of fronds (leaves) after seven days. Control: same volume of water, same number of starting fronds, same light and temperature, same container and nutrient solution. Method: add 10 fronds to each container, check and adjust pH each day with a pH meter or universal indicator, repeat three times, and count the fronds at the end. Safety: wear gloves when using acid or alkali and wash hands afterwards; do not release duckweed into the environment.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the colour of light affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed, measured by counting the bubbles of oxygen released.
parts.answer: Independent variable: colour of light (red, green, blue, white) obtained with coloured filters. Dependent variable: number of bubbles of oxygen per minute. Control: same light intensity (same distance from the lamp), same temperature, same length and species of pondweed, same volume of water, and the same time allowed for the plant to adjust. Method: place the shoot in water, put the filter in front of the lamp, wait 2 minutes, count bubbles for 1 minute, repeat each colour three times. Safety: keep lamp and water apart to avoid electric shock; allow the lamp to cool.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the amount of soil water affects the height of cress seedlings after seven days.
parts.answer: Independent variable: volume of water added to each pot (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 cm³ per day). Dependent variable: height of the seedlings after seven days, measured with a ruler from soil level to tip. Control: same type and number of seeds, same soil mass and type, same light, temperature and pot size. Method: sow 10 seeds in each pot, water daily with the set volume, measure the height of each seedling, calculate the mean height per pot, and repeat three times. Accuracy: measure the tallest and shortest plants and calculate the mean; avoid overwatering that drowns seedlings.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how exercise affects pulse rate. Use step-ups on a bench as the exercise.
parts.answer: Independent variable: number of step-ups (e.g. 0, 20, 40 steps). Dependent variable: pulse rate (beats per minute) measured on the wrist after resting for 2 minutes. Control: same person and same step height, same type of exercise, same time allowed for rest between each trial. Method: measure resting pulse, complete the step-ups at the same speed, count the pulse for 15 seconds immediately, multiply by four, repeat each step count with rest, and calculate the mean. Safety: stop if the participant feels unwell, use a sturdy bench, and have a chair nearby.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the rate of anaerobic respiration of yeast. You may use any normal laboratory apparatus.
parts.answer: Yeast + glucose suspension in tubes in water-baths at 20–60 °C, oil layer, count bubbles or measure gas volume in a gas syringe/ inverted cylinder over a fixed time; acclimatise; repeat; control yeast mass, glucose volume and concentration
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: independent variable temperature, at least five values (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C); thermostatically controlled water-baths; same mass / volume of yeast suspension; same volume and concentration of glucose; layer of oil / boiled glucose solution to keep conditions anaerobic; allow mixture to reach temperature before starting; measure volume of CO₂ (gas syringe / upturned measuring cylinder) or count bubbles over a fixed time (e.g. 5 min); calculate rate; repeat at least three times and calculate mean; control with no yeast / boiled yeast; safety: care with hot water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of air movement (wind speed) on the rate of water loss from a leafy shoot. You may use a cut leafy shoot, an electric fan, a balance, a tube of water, oil and any other normal laboratory apparatus.
parts.answer: Shoot in water tube with oil layer on a balance; fan at different distances; measure mass loss over fixed time; same shoot or similar shoots; control light, temperature, humidity; repeat
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: shoot cut under water and placed in tube of water; oil layer to stop evaporation from the water surface; weigh apparatus at start; vary wind speed by placing fan at five distances (e.g. 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 cm) or fan speed settings, plus a no-fan control; measure mass after a fixed time (e.g. 30 min); calculate mass loss per hour; same shoot / shoots with similar leaf area; keep light intensity, temperature and humidity constant; repeat and calculate mean; safety: keep water away from the fan's electrics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the surface area to volume ratio of agar cubes affects the rate at which a substance diffuses into them. The cubes are soaked in a dilute sodium hydroxide solution containing phenolphthalein, which turns pink in alkali.
parts.answer: Use cubes of 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm side length, and measure the time taken for the pink colour to reach the centre of each cube. Keep the concentration, volume and temperature of the solution the same, and cut all cubes from one block. Repeat each size three times, cut each cube in half, and measure the depth of pink diffusion. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio for each size and plot the rate or depth against the ratio. Safety: wear gloves and eye protection when handling sodium hydroxide, and wipe up spills at once.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the age of a leaf affects the rate of photosynthesis, using the leaf disc method. Leaf discs are cut and placed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution under a light.
parts.answer: Independent variable: age of the leaves (young, mature, old, taken from the same plant). Dependent variable: time taken for a set number of discs to float to the surface, or number of discs floating after a set time. Control: same size and number of discs, same concentration of hydrogencarbonate solution, same light intensity and temperature, same volume of solution. Method: cut 10 discs from each leaf age avoiding the midrib, use a syringe to remove air, place in solution under the lamp, record the time when half the discs float, repeat three times. Safety: keep lamp away from water and avoid spilling solution.
parts.working: Mark points (6 marks): 1 independent variable and how it is changed (range and intervals); 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 control variables named and how they are kept the same; 1 method in ordered steps including repeats and a control; 1 apparatus, measurements and how results are recorded/averaged; 1 safety or accuracy point (e.g. ethical care of living organisms, lamp heat, sterile technique).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four rules for making a good biological drawing of a specimen.
parts.answer: draw large (fill most of the space); use clear, continuous lines with a sharp pencil; no shading or colouring; correct proportions; label lines ruled, touching the structure, without arrowheads
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's drawing of a pollen grain is 36 mm across. The actual pollen grain is 0.024 mm across. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
parts.working: 1 mark: the sizes are in the same unit (0.024 mm); magnification = image size ÷ actual size. 1 mark: 36 ÷ 0.024 = 1500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student adds shading to a biological drawing of a leaf section to make it look more realistic. Explain why this is not allowed.
parts.answer: Shading hides the detail and does not show the structure clearly; a biological drawing must show only what is seen, using clear unshaded lines.
parts.working: 1 mark: shading hides detail. 1 mark: a drawing must show what is seen clearly with lines only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a student should draw only the structures that are actually seen in the specimen, and not what she expects to see.
parts.answer: A biological drawing is a record of observations; drawing expected features would make the drawing inaccurate and would mislead others.
parts.working: 1 mark: a drawing must record observations. 1 mark: drawing expected features is inaccurate/misleading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why a biological drawing should be made from the real specimen, not copied from a textbook.
parts.answer: A drawing made from the real specimen records the features of that specimen, including any variation or damage, and shows the student's own observations.
parts.working: 1 mark: it records the actual specimen and observations. 1 mark: textbook copies do not show the student's observations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two things that should be shown on a biological drawing, other than the specimen itself.
parts.answer: Any two: a title; the magnification or scale; labels; the type of view (for example transverse section).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct item.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A guava cut in half across its middle shows a thin skin, a thick layer of firm flesh and a central pulpy region containing about 150 small, hard seeds. A tomato cut in the same way shows a thin skin, thinner flesh and three chambers of jelly, each containing about 20 flat seeds attached to a central column.
State one similarity and two differences between the two fruits, using comparative language.
parts.answer: similarity: both have a thin skin / both have seeds inside the fruit; differences: guava has more seeds than the tomato; guava has thicker flesh; guava seeds are in one central region whereas tomato seeds are in three chambers; tomato seeds are flatter
parts.working: B1 similarity; B1 each difference (max 2); differences must compare both fruits (not colour or overall size).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student is asked to draw one cell from a slide of onion epidermis seen under high power. State three structures that should be drawn and labelled.
parts.answer: cell wall; cytoplasm; nucleus (also cell membrane closely against the wall; vacuole)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student's drawing of the cell is 60 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 0.3 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
parts.working: B1 60 ÷ 0.3 = ×200 (both lengths in mm).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A specimen is 4.0 mm long. The student's drawing of it is 60 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
parts.working: 1 mark: method (60 ÷ 4.0). 1 mark: ×15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A structure in the specimen is 0.5 mm long. Calculate its length in the drawing.
parts.answer: 7.5 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the magnification should be written on the drawing.
parts.answer: So that readers know the actual size of the specimen from the drawing.
parts.working: 1 mark: gives the size scale for the reader.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student labels a drawing of a cross-section of a stem. Her labels are written at an angle, the label lines cross each other, and some label lines do not touch the structure they name. Identify three errors and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: Errors: labels not horizontal (should be written horizontally); label lines crossing (should not cross); label lines not touching the structure (should touch it).
parts.working: 1 mark for each error identified with a correct correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student is drawing a dicot root cross-section. Explain why the outline of the specimen should be drawn as a single, continuous line, and why the drawing should be made in pencil.
parts.answer: A continuous line shows the real outline of the specimen. Pencil can be erased and lines can be made clear without spreading ink; a sharp pencil gives fine, accurate lines.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous line shows the real outline. 1 mark: pencil can be corrected/erased. 1 mark: fine accurate lines are possible with a sharp pencil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student is asked to draw a cell from a prepared slide. Explain why she should draw only one cell in detail, rather than drawing several cells together in outline.
parts.answer: Drawing one cell in detail allows the structures to be shown clearly and accurately at the same magnification; a group of cells in outline would not show detail well.
parts.working: 1 mark: one cell allows clear, accurate detail. 1 mark: several cells in outline would not show structures clearly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A teacher describes a student's drawing of a leaf: the outline is made of several short, overlapping sketchy lines; the veins are shaded in dark pencil; the drawing is 3 cm long on a page with a box 12 cm long; two label lines end in arrowheads and one label line crosses another.
Identify four errors and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: sketchy lines – use single continuous lines; shading – show veins as lines with no shading; too small – draw large to fill most of the box; arrowheads – label lines should be ruled and end on the structure without arrowheads; crossing label lines – label lines must not cross
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four errors with corrections.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the width of a cell under the microscope using an eyepiece graticule. The cell spans 12 graticule divisions and each division is 5 µm at this magnification. Calculate the width of the cell in µm. Then explain how a stage micrometer is used to calibrate the graticule.
parts.answer: 60 µm. A stage micrometer (a slide with a scale of known length) is placed on the stage and the graticule divisions are matched to known lengths on it, so each division's real length at that magnification is found.
parts.working: 1 mark: 12 × 5 = 60 µm. 1 mark: correct unit. 1 mark: stage micrometer is placed on the stage. 1 mark: divisions matched to known lengths to calibrate.

practice.stem: A teacher assesses a student's drawing of a leaf section. The drawing has no title and no magnification, the label lines do not touch the structures they name, and the cells are coloured in with felt-tip pens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four errors and explain why each reduces the quality of the drawing.
parts.answer: Errors: no title (the reader cannot tell what the drawing shows); no magnification or scale (the actual size cannot be found); label lines that do not touch the structures (the reader cannot tell which part is labelled); cells coloured in with felt-tip pen (colour and heavy marks hide detail; drawings should use clean, unshaded pencil lines).
parts.working: 1 mark for each error identified with a valid reason, up to 4.

practice.stem: A student places 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide in each of five test-tubes at 30 °C. She adds 1 g, 2 g, 3 g, 4 g or 5 g of chopped liver and measures the height of froth (oxygen bubbles) after 2 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: independent: mass of liver; dependent: height of froth
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that the student has kept constant.
parts.answer: volume of hydrogen peroxide; temperature; time (2 minutes)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other variable that should be controlled.
parts.answer: concentration of hydrogen peroxide / size of liver pieces (surface area) / diameter of test-tubes

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates the effect of the amount of fertiliser on the height of maize seedlings. State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: amount of fertiliser added. Dependent: height of the seedlings.
parts.working: 1 mark for the independent variable. 1 mark for the dependent variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests the effect of temperature on the rate at which yeast produces gas. State two variables that the student should keep the same.
parts.answer: Any two: volume and concentration of the sugar solution; mass of yeast; volume of water; time of measurement.
parts.working: 1 mark for each suitable control variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways a student can make sure the dependent variable is measured fairly.
parts.answer: Any two: use the same method and equipment for each measurement; measure at the same time after the start of the test; use the same person to take readings; take repeats and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible method, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student changes the temperature of water in an experiment and keeps the volume of water the same. State which quantity is the independent variable, and explain why the volume of water is a control variable.
parts.answer: Independent variable: temperature. The volume of water is a control variable because it is kept the same, so it cannot affect the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature is the independent variable. 1 mark: the volume is kept constant so it is a fair test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation of catalase activity, one tube contains liver that has been boiled and cooled. Explain why this tube is included.
parts.answer: it is a control; it shows that the bubbles in the other tubes are due to the active enzyme (boiling denatures catalase) and not some other factor
parts.working: B1 control / comparison; B1 shows the result is due to enzyme activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an osmosis experiment using potato cylinders in different salt solutions, explain why all cylinders must be cut to the same length and diameter.
parts.answer: so they have the same surface area (and mass / volume); surface area affects the rate of water movement, so comparisons are fair
parts.working: B1 same surface area; B1 surface area affects rate of osmosis / fair test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the enzyme and substrate solutions in an enzyme experiment are placed in the water-bath separately for 5 minutes before mixing.
parts.answer: so both reach the required temperature before the reaction starts; otherwise the reaction would begin at a different temperature
parts.working: B1 reach the set temperature; B1 reaction occurs at the intended temperature from the start.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests an antibacterial soap by spreading bacteria on agar plates. One plate is treated with the soap and a second plate is treated with sterile water. Explain why the second plate is needed.
parts.answer: It is the control: if the bacteria grow equally on both plates, the soap is not having an effect. Comparing the two shows whether any difference in growth is due to the soap rather than to other factors, such as the agar or the technique.
parts.working: 1 mark: a control is needed to compare with the soap plate. 1 mark: any difference is due to the soap. 1 mark: rules out other causes such as contamination or the water itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the same batch of seeds should be used for every treatment in an investigation of germination.
parts.answer: Different batches may differ in age, size or genetic variation, which would affect germination and so make the results unreliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: batches vary in quality or genetic make-up. 1 mark: this would affect germination and the results would not be a fair test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a control variable and a control experiment.
parts.answer: A control variable is a factor that is kept the same in all parts of the investigation, so that it cannot affect the results. A control experiment is a set-up that does not receive the treatment being tested (e.g. a tube with water in place of the enzyme solution), so that any change can be compared with it.
parts.working: 1 mark: control variable is kept constant. 1 mark: control experiment has no treatment for comparison. 1 mark: both help make the test fair/valid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the terms 'reliable' and 'valid' when describing the results of an investigation.
parts.answer: Reliable: results are consistent and can be repeated when the investigation is done again, usually shown by similar repeats. Valid: the investigation measures what it was designed to measure and the test is fair (only the independent variable is changed).
parts.working: 1 mark: reliable means repeatable/consistent. 1 mark: valid means it tests what it was intended to test. 1 mark: a fair test keeps all other variables constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the activity of pectinase in releasing juice from chopped apple. He leaves beakers of apple pulp and enzyme on a laboratory bench, beside a sunny window, and in a refrigerator for 20 minutes, then filters the juice. Identify two weaknesses in how the independent variable was controlled and describe how to improve each.
parts.answer: only three temperatures and they are not known – use at least five set temperatures measured with a thermometer; temperatures are not kept constant (sunlight varies) – use thermostatically controlled water-baths; enzyme and pulp not at temperature before mixing – equilibrate separately first
parts.working: Two weaknesses with matching improvement (2 × 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis by moving a lamp to different distances from a pondweed in one window area. Identify a confounding variable in this investigation, explain how it affects the validity of the results, and suggest how it could be controlled.
parts.answer: Confounding variable: the temperature of the water changes as the lamp is moved, because the lamp gives out heat. This would change the rate of photosynthesis as well as the light intensity, so the results would not show the effect of light alone. Control by using a water bath or a heat-filter/cool the water and measuring the temperature at each distance.
parts.working: 1 mark: a confounding variable named (temperature from the lamp). 1 mark: explains that it changes the rate, so results are not valid. 1 mark: a control experiment or measurement of temperature. 1 mark: a method to keep temperature constant (heat filter/water bath).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses five concentrations of a solution. Explain why it is important to include a concentration of zero, and why the range of concentrations should be wide enough to show a clear trend.
parts.answer: A concentration of zero gives a baseline or control to compare the other results with. A wide range of concentrations gives enough data points to show the trend clearly and to find where the effect changes (for example the point at which it stops).
parts.working: 1 mark: zero gives a control/baseline. 1 mark: a wide range shows the trend. 1 mark: data points allow clear comparison. 1 mark: range gives information about where the effect changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses only three seedlings for each treatment in a growth experiment. Explain why a sample of 20 seedlings would give more reliable results.
parts.answer: A larger sample is less affected by individual variation (one unusually large or small seedling), so the mean is more representative of the whole population. The student can also identify and check anomalous results more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger sample reduces the effect of individual variation. 1 mark: the mean is more representative. 1 mark: anomalies are easier to identify.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State one hazard and a precaution for each of these steps in food tests:
(i) heating Benedict's solution in a water-bath
(ii) cutting a potato with a scalpel
parts.answer: (i) hot liquid may spit / scald – use a water-bath (not a direct flame), wear eye protection, use a test-tube holder; (ii) scalpel may cut fingers – cut on a tile, cut away from the body
parts.working: B1 hazard and B1 precaution for each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Students heat a solution in a boiling tube over a Bunsen burner. State one hazard and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: the hot liquid or glass may cause burns, or the liquid may spit. Precaution: point the open end of the tube away from people and use a test-tube holder; do not heat above the required temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct hazard. 1 mark for a suitable precaution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a student should wear safety goggles when cutting plant material with a scalpel.
parts.answer: Pieces of plant material or the blade can fly off or slip, which could injure the eyes.
parts.working: 1 mark: material or blade may slip or fly. 1 mark: eyes could be injured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student leaves a potato cylinder in a solution for a shorter time than planned. Explain the effect on the reliability of the results.
parts.answer: The cylinder would not reach equilibrium, so the mass change would not show the true effect of the solution; results would be different from other trials and so would be less reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: not enough time to reach equilibrium. 1 mark: results are inconsistent, so less reliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an experiment on vitamin C in fruit juices, a student adds juice drop by drop to a blue indicator (DCPIP) until the blue colour just disappears. Identify one source of error in judging the end point and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: difficult to judge exactly when the colour disappears (subjective); compare against a colourless standard / white background / use a colorimeter
parts.working: B1 error; B1 matching improvement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why drops from a pipette may give inaccurate volumes and how this could be improved.
parts.answer: drop size varies; use a burette or graduated syringe to measure volume
parts.working: B1 error; B1 improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student counts oxygen bubbles released from pondweed each minute. Explain why counting bubbles may give unreliable results, and describe a better method of measuring the gas produced.
parts.answer: bubbles are not all the same size; some may be missed if they come fast; collect the gas in a gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder and measure its volume
parts.working: B1 bubbles vary in size; B1 difficult to count fast bubbles accurately; B1 measure volume of gas (syringe / capillary tube / measuring cylinder).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before weighing a sample, a student checks an electronic balance and it shows 0.02 g with nothing on the pan. Explain the effect of this on the results, and suggest how the student could correct it.
parts.answer: The balance has a zero error, so every reading is 0.02 g too high (or the mass is overestimated). The student can either tare (zero) the balance before weighing, or subtract 0.02 g from every reading.
parts.working: 1 mark: a systematic error - all masses too high by 0.02 g. 1 mark: the student must tare/zero the balance before use. 1 mark: or correct each reading by subtracting 0.02 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student times a reaction with a stopwatch that she starts and stops by hand. Identify a source of error and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Source of error: human reaction time means the timer starts late and stops late, giving a result that is too long or too short. Improvement: use a data logger or video recording; or have the timing done by two people and average.
parts.working: 1 mark: human reaction time as the source of error. 1 mark: explains the effect on the result. 1 mark: a sensible improvement (data logger, video, or repeated timing by different people).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's repeat results show large scatter. Suggest two reasons for the scatter and one way to improve the investigation.
parts.answer: Reasons: uneven sample material (e.g. different sizes of potato or leaf); inconsistent timing or measurement; unnoticed changes in temperature. Improvement: use a larger number of repeats; use samples of a standard size; use a method that is consistent for every trial.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason (up to 2). 1 mark for a valid improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests the bacteria on agar plates. Explain why the lids should be kept closed and why the plates should be disposed of by autoclaving or with disinfectant rather than in the bin.
parts.answer: Keeping the lids closed stops contamination from the air and stops harmful microorganisms being released. Autoclaving or disinfecting kills the bacteria, so that they cannot spread to other people or the environment.
parts.working: 1 mark: lids closed prevents contamination/escape. 1 mark: disinfecting or autoclaving kills microorganisms. 1 mark: prevents spread to people or the environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student estimates the area of a leaf by drawing around it on centimetre-square graph paper and counting squares. Suggest one improvement to make the estimate more accurate, and explain why.
parts.answer: Count partly covered squares by estimating half-squares, or count only squares more than half covered, which reduces the error; alternatively, use a larger number of squares or a smaller grid so the outline is followed more closely.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid improvement (partial squares counted as halves/ majority rule, or a finer grid). 1 mark: explanation of how this reduces error. 1 mark: a reason why counting is an estimate and the outline is approximate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured the change in mass of potato cylinders after 20 minutes in salt solutions. She blotted some cylinders firmly and others lightly, and timed using the classroom wall clock, starting the cylinders one after the other. Identify two sources of error and suggest how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: inconsistent blotting leaves different amounts of surface water – blot each cylinder the same way (e.g. roll once on paper towel); cylinders were in solution for different times – start each at a timed interval with a stop-clock and remove each after exactly 20 min
parts.working: Two errors each with matching improvement (2 × 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each concentration should be tested with at least three cylinders.
parts.answer: allows anomalous results to be identified and a mean to be calculated

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an enzyme investigation, a lamp is used to heat a water bath. The lamp is moved closer to the water bath for some trials. Identify one variable that is not controlled, explain how it could affect the results and suggest two improvements.
parts.answer: Uncontrolled variable: temperature of the water bath, which rises as the lamp moves closer, so the enzyme activity changes for reasons other than the variable under test. Improvements: use a thermostatically controlled water bath; measure the temperature of the water at the start of each trial and check it stays constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: names the uncontrolled variable (temperature). 1 mark: explains the effect on enzyme rate. 1 mark: a suitable improvement (thermostatic water bath). 1 mark: measure/check temperature during trials.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a systematic error and a random error. Give one example of each in an experiment that measures the volume of a liquid.
parts.answer: A systematic error affects every reading in the same direction (e.g. a measuring cylinder whose scale starts 0.5 cm³ above zero, so every volume is too high). A random error varies unpredictably between readings (e.g. the bottom of the meniscus judged slightly differently each time).
parts.working: 1 mark: systematic error is consistent/one direction. 1 mark: random error is unpredictable. 1 mark: a valid systematic example. 1 mark: a valid random example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses one timed trial at each temperature to find the optimum temperature for an enzyme using a milk-clearing method. Evaluate the method and suggest two improvements.
parts.answer: The method uses a single trial at each temperature, so there is no way to show whether results are reliable or to spot anomalies; a single reading may be chance. Improvements: repeat each temperature three times and calculate the mean; use a water bath with a thermometer to hold the temperature steady and narrow the temperature range around the optimum.
parts.working: 1 mark: one trial is not reliable. 1 mark: repeats are needed to find a mean / spot anomalies. 1 mark: use a thermostatic water bath. 1 mark: narrow the range near the optimum.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the most suitable apparatus to measure:
(i) 7.5 cm³ of enzyme solution
(ii) the temperature of a water-bath
(iii) the length of a leaf
parts.answer: (i) 10 cm³ syringe or 10 cm³ measuring cylinder; (ii) thermometer; (iii) ruler (in mm)
parts.working: B1 each. Do not accept a beaker for (i).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student needs to measure 6.0 cm³ of enzyme solution accurately. Name the most suitable apparatus and explain why a measuring cylinder is less accurate for this volume.
parts.answer: A 10 cm³ syringe or measured pipette; a measuring cylinder has a larger scale division and a larger meniscus error at this small volume.
parts.working: 1 mark: a 10 cm³ syringe or measuring pipette. 1 mark: the measuring cylinder has larger divisions so a small volume is read less accurately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electronic balance shows 12.37 g. State the reading to 1 decimal place, and state the precision of this balance.
parts.answer: 12.4 g; the balance reads to 0.01 g.
parts.working: 1 mark: 12.4 g. 1 mark: precision of 0.01 g (two decimal places).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student observes a colour change when iodine solution is added to a starch solution. Explain how the student should record this observation.
parts.answer: The student should write a clear description of the colour before and after (e.g. brown/orange to blue-black), using the same words each time, rather than writing an interpretation.
parts.working: 1 mark: describe the colour before and after. 1 mark: record descriptive observations, not conclusions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a light microscope with an eyepiece graticule. State what the graticule is and what it is used for.
parts.answer: The graticule is a transparent scale placed in the eyepiece; it is used to measure the size of objects seen under the microscope.
parts.working: 1 mark: a scale in the eyepiece. 1 mark: used to measure the size of objects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thermometer reads 36.4 °C. State the quantity measured, the unit, and the number of decimal places the reading should be recorded to.
parts.answer: Temperature, measured in degrees Celsius (°C), recorded to 1 decimal place (as the scale allows).
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature in °C. 1 mark: 1 decimal place consistent with the scale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student places a paper disc soaked in a garlic extract on an agar plate of bacteria. After 2 days a clear zone forms around the disc. She measures the clear zone as 14 mm across in one direction and 16 mm across at right angles. Calculate the mean diameter and then the area of the clear zone, using area = πr². Give the area to the nearest mm².
parts.answer: mean diameter 15 mm; area 177 mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student measured two diameters at right angles.
parts.answer: the clear zone may not be a perfect circle, so a mean is more representative

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures a leaf with a ruler marked in millimetres and records 12.3 cm. Give the uncertainty in this measurement and explain why the uncertainty is needed.
parts.answer: ± 0.05 cm (half of the smallest division of 1 mm, which is 0.5 mm = 0.05 cm). The uncertainty shows the range within which the true value lies.
parts.working: 1 mark: ± 0.05 cm (half of 1 mm). 1 mark: uncertainty shows the precision of the reading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student reads the volume collected in a gas syringe as 30 cm³. Explain how she should read the scale to avoid error.
parts.answer: She should read the scale at eye level with the plunger's edge (or the top of the gas column) to avoid parallax error. She should wait until the reading has stopped changing before reading, and record it to the nearest division.
parts.working: 1 mark: eye level (no parallax). 1 mark: wait until the reading is steady. 1 mark: read to the nearest division on the scale.

practice.stem: A student estimates the number of daisies in a field by looking across it, and records 'about 300 daisies'. She does not use quadrats or any sampling method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this estimate is less reliable than one made by counting daisies in randomly placed quadrats.
parts.answer: The estimate is subjective and varies between people and between days, depending on what each person looks at. Quadrats sample a known area at random, so the number per square metre can be averaged and scaled up to the whole field.
parts.working: 1 mark: an estimate by eye is subjective and varies between observers. 1 mark: random quadrats give a measurable sample that can be averaged and scaled up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures 25 cm³ of water using a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder. Explain why the student should read the volume to the nearest 0.5 cm³ and not to the nearest whole cm³.
parts.answer: The scale on a 50 cm³ cylinder is marked in 1 cm³ divisions, so the reading can be estimated to the nearest 0.5 cm³ (half a division); reading to 1 cm³ would ignore the precision of the scale.
parts.working: 1 mark: the scale is marked in 1 cm³ so half-divisions can be estimated. 1 mark: this uses the full precision of the apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two sources of human error when measuring the length of a leaf with a ruler.
parts.answer: Any two: the ruler is not lined up with the base of the leaf (zero not at the edge); parallax, when the eye is not directly above the scale; judging the tip of the leaf differently each time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid source of human error, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student records a reaction time from a digital stop-clock as 63.47 s. Explain why it is better to record this as 63 s.
parts.answer: human reaction time when starting and stopping the clock is much larger than 0.01 s, so the extra decimal places are not meaningful

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a 10 cm³ measuring cylinder is better than a 100 cm³ measuring cylinder for measuring 8 cm³ of liquid.
parts.answer: the 10 cm³ cylinder has smaller graduations (e.g. 0.2 cm³ instead of 1 cm³), so the reading is more precise; the error is a smaller fraction of the volume measured
parts.working: B1 smaller divisions / finer scale; B1 more precise / smaller percentage error.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When reading a measuring cylinder, state where the student should look and which part of the liquid surface should be read.
parts.answer: eye level with the liquid surface; read the bottom of the meniscus
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of a good results table for an experiment that measures the time taken for a reaction at five temperatures, with three repeats each.
parts.answer: The table has a clear title; headings with units in every column (e.g. Temperature / °C, Time / s); the independent variable in the first column; repeats in separate columns; a mean column; values recorded to a consistent number of decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three features: title; units in headings; independent variable first; repeats recorded; means calculated; consistent decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student estimates the pH of a solution by comparing the colour of universal indicator with a colour chart. Discuss how the subjective nature of colour matching affects the reliability of the result, and suggest one way to improve it.
parts.answer: Colour judgement varies between people and under different lighting, so two students may decide on different pH values; the result is therefore not very reliable. Improvement: use a pH meter with a digital reading, or use a colour comparison under the same light by several students and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: colour judgement varies between people. 1 mark: lighting changes the colour seen. 1 mark: result is not reliable. 1 mark: a valid improvement (pH meter; several judges; standard lighting).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the structure in the human reproductive systems that:
(i) produces sperm
(ii) carries sperm from the testis to the urethra
(iii) secretes fluid containing nutrients for sperm (name one gland)
(iv) releases eggs
(v) is where the fetus develops
parts.answer: (i) testis; (ii) sperm duct; (iii) prostate gland (accept seminal vesicle); (iv) ovary; (v) uterus
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the human male, which tube carries both urine and semen out of the body (at different times)?
A sperm duct
B urethra
C ureter
D oviduct
parts.answer: B urethra
parts.working: The urethra runs through the penis and carries urine from the bladder and semen during ejaculation. The ureter (C) carries urine from kidney to bladder only; the sperm duct (A) carries sperm only.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each structure in the male reproductive system.
(i) scrotum (ii) sperm duct (iii) prostate gland (iv) penis
parts.answer: (i) holds the testes outside the body (at a lower temperature) (ii) carries sperm from the testis to the urethra (iii) produces fluid that is added to sperm to make semen (iv) passes semen into the vagina during sexual intercourse (and urine out)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the structures, in order, through which an egg cell passes from where it is released to where an embryo implants.
parts.answer: ovary → oviduct → uterus
parts.working: B1 oviduct; B1 uterus (in correct order after ovary).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where sperm are deposited during sexual intercourse.
parts.answer: the vagina (near the cervix)
parts.working: B1 vagina.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the ring of muscle at the lower end of the uterus.
parts.answer: cervix
parts.working: B1 cervix.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the function of each part of a human egg cell.
(i) jelly coat (ii) cytoplasm (iii) nucleus
parts.answer: (i) protects the egg / changes after fertilisation so that only one sperm can enter (ii) contains energy stores for the early embryo (iii) contains the genetic material (23 chromosomes) from the mother
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where egg cells are produced.
parts.answer: the ovaries
parts.working: B1 ovary.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where does fertilisation normally take place in humans?
A cervix
B ovary
C oviduct
D uterus
parts.answer: C oviduct
parts.working: Sperm meet the egg in the oviduct (fallopian tube); the embryo then moves to the uterus to implant. D is the main distractor: the uterus is where implantation, not fertilisation, occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a sperm cell is adapted for its function.
parts.answer: Flagellum for swimming; many mitochondria to release energy (by respiration) for movement; acrosome containing enzymes to digest through the jelly coat of the egg; haploid nucleus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three features with function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways an egg cell is adapted for its function.
parts.answer: Energy stores (cytoplasm with nutrients) for the early embryo; jelly coat that changes after fertilisation so only one sperm can enter; haploid nucleus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the structures that sperm pass through from where they are made to where fertilisation takes place.
parts.answer: testis → sperm duct → urethra → (vagina) → cervix → uterus → oviduct
parts.working: 3 marks for all in correct order; 2 marks for one error; 1 mark for two errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of the cervix during birth.
parts.answer: It dilates / widens to let the baby pass from the uterus into the vagina.
parts.working: B1 dilates / widens.

practice.stem:
A fertility clinic tested semen samples from two men.
Man A: 60 million sperm per cm³, volume 3.0 cm³
Man B: 4 million sperm per cm³, volume 2.5 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of sperm in one sample for each man. Give your answers in millions.
parts.answer: man A 180 million; man B 10 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more sperm there are in man A's sample.
parts.answer: 18 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only one sperm fertilises an egg. Suggest why man B is less likely to father a child.
parts.answer: Most sperm die or are lost on the way through the uterus and oviducts and only a few reach the egg; with a low count it is likely that none reach the egg; many sperm may be needed to break through the layers around the egg.
parts.working: B1 most sperm do not reach the oviduct / die on the way; B1 fewer sperm → lower chance any reach / penetrate the egg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a vasectomy, a small section of each sperm duct is cut and the ends are tied. Explain why the man can no longer father children.
parts.answer: Sperm made in the testes cannot pass along the sperm ducts to the urethra, so the semen contains no sperm and no egg can be fertilised.
parts.working: B1 sperm cannot leave the testes / reach the urethra; B1 no sperm in semen so no fertilisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After a vasectomy, the man still produces semen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Most of the fluid in semen comes from glands such as the prostate gland, which join the pathway after the cut, so fluid is still released.
parts.working: B1 fluid made by prostate gland (and other glands); B1 these add fluid beyond / below the cut point.

practice.stem: A student looked at a stained sample of bull semen with a microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The image of one whole sperm measured 55 mm long at a magnification of ×1000. Calculate the actual length of the sperm in µm.
parts.answer: 55 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student counted the sperm in five squares of a counting slide: 12, 15, 9, 14, 10. Calculate the mean number per square.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted sperm in five squares instead of one.
parts.answer: The sperm are not spread evenly, so a mean of several squares is more representative / reliable.
parts.working: B1 more representative / reliable mean.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one feature of the sperm that the student would see that helps it swim to the egg.
parts.answer: a long flagellum (tail)
parts.working: B1 flagellum.

practice.stem: A human egg cell has a diameter of 0.12 mm. The head of a human sperm cell is 5 µm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the egg diameter into micrometres (µm).
parts.answer: 120 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the diameter of the egg is than the length of the sperm head.
parts.answer: 24 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why an egg is so much larger than a sperm, and why millions of sperm are released but only one egg each month.
parts.answer: The egg contains energy stores / nutrients for the zygote and early embryo; sperm are small so they can swim; most sperm die or do not reach the oviduct, so many are needed to make it likely that one fertilises the egg.
parts.working: 1 mark each: egg stores food / energy for embryo; sperm small and mobile; many sperm lost / long journey, so large numbers increase chance of fertilisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly compares a human sperm cell with a human egg cell?
A sperm: large, has energy stores, not able to move; egg: small, able to swim
B sperm: small, able to swim using a flagellum, few energy stores; egg: large, not able to swim, has energy stores in its cytoplasm
C sperm: small, 46 chromosomes; egg: large, 23 chromosomes
D sperm: small, able to swim, many energy stores; egg: large, able to swim, few energy stores
parts.answer: B sperm: small, able to swim using a flagellum, few energy stores; egg: large, not able to swim, has energy stores in its cytoplasm
parts.working: A sperm is small and motile (flagellum) with little cytoplasm; an egg is much larger, not motile, with energy stores. Both gametes have 23 chromosomes, so C is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some infections can scar and block both oviducts. Explain why a woman with blocked oviducts may be unable to become pregnant, even though she ovulates normally.
parts.answer: Sperm cannot travel up the oviduct to reach the egg, and the egg cannot pass along the oviduct; fertilisation normally takes place in the oviduct, so no zygote forms (and an embryo could not reach the uterus).
parts.working: B1 sperm cannot reach the egg; B1 fertilisation normally in oviduct; B1 egg / embryo cannot reach uterus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In in vitro fertilisation (IVF), eggs are collected directly from the ovaries and mixed with sperm in a dish. Embryos are then placed in the uterus. Explain why IVF can help this woman.
parts.answer: IVF bypasses the oviducts: fertilisation happens outside the body, and the embryo is put directly into the uterus, where it can implant.
parts.working: B1 oviducts not needed / bypassed; B1 embryo placed in uterus to implant.

practice.stem: In this question, assume that a sperm swims at 3 mm per minute and must travel 180 mm from the cervix to an egg in the oviduct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for a sperm to swim from the cervix to the egg, in minutes.
parts.answer: 60 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the roles of the mitochondria and the flagellum of a sperm cell.
parts.answer: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration for swimming; the flagellum is a whip-like tail that uses this energy to beat and drive the sperm forward.
parts.working: B1 mitochondria: energy release by respiration for swimming; B1 flagellum: whip-like tail that moves the sperm forward.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After one sperm enters the egg, the jelly coat changes. Explain why this is important.
parts.answer: It stops any other sperm entering the egg, so only one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus and the zygote has the correct number of chromosomes (46).
parts.working: B1 prevents more sperm entering; B1 so zygote has correct chromosome number / only one set from father.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?
A anther
B ovary
C sepal
D stigma
parts.answer: A anther
parts.working: Pollen (containing the male gametes) is made in the anthers. The stigma (D) receives pollen; it does not produce it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the part of an insect-pollinated flower that has each function.
(i) sticky surface that receives pollen
(ii) contains the ovules
(iii) brightly coloured to attract insects
(iv) stalk that holds the anther up
(v) protects the flower while it is a bud
parts.answer: (i) stigma; (ii) ovary; (iii) petal; (iv) filament; (v) sepal
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is pollination?
A the fusion of a male nucleus with a female nucleus
B the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma
C the growth of a pollen tube down the style
D the release of seeds from a fruit
parts.answer: B the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma
parts.working: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. A is fertilisation, which happens later, after the pollen tube (C) reaches the ovule.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each part of a flower.
(i) sepal (ii) petal (iii) filament (iv) ovule
parts.answer: (i) protects the flower when it is a bud (ii) attracts insects (for pollination) (iii) holds up / supports the anther (iv) contains the female gamete (egg cell nucleus); becomes the seed after fertilisation
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which the pollen of a wind-pollinated flower differs from the pollen of an insect-pollinated flower.
parts.answer: Wind pollen is smaller and lighter; it is smooth (not sticky or spiky).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two comparative points (smaller/lighter; smooth, not sticky or spiky).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each difference helps wind pollination.
parts.answer: Small, light grains are carried further by air currents; smooth, non-sticky grains do not clump together and are easily released and blown away from the anther.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a linked explanation: size/weight → carried far by the wind; smooth, not sticky → not clumped, released easily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Wheat is wind-pollinated and mustard is insect-pollinated. Describe four ways in which a wheat flower differs from a mustard flower.
parts.answer: Wheat: small, dull / green petals or none (mustard: large, bright yellow petals); no scent or nectar (mustard has scent and nectar); anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments (mustard: anthers inside); large feathery stigmas outside the flower (mustard: small sticky stigma inside); large amounts of small, light, smooth pollen (mustard: less pollen, larger / sticky or spiky grains).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparative differences; each must refer to both flowers or be clearly comparative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a wind-pollinated plant produces far more pollen than an insect-pollinated plant.
parts.answer: Pollen transfer by wind is random / much pollen does not land on a stigma, so more is needed to make pollination likely.
parts.working: B1 wind transfer is random / wasteful.

practice.stem:
Pollen grains grow a pollen tube when they germinate. A student placed pollen from a single flower species in drops of sucrose solution on microscope slides. After 2 hours, she examined 50 grains in each drop and counted how many had grown a pollen tube.
sucrose concentration / %: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30
number of grains germinated (out of 50): 3, 14, 31, 38, 22, 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of pollen grains that germinated in 15 % and in 30 % sucrose solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of sucrose concentration on pollen germination shown by these results.
parts.answer: Germination increases from 0 % to 15 % sucrose, is highest at 15 %, and decreases from 15 % to 30 %.
parts.working: B1 increase to a maximum at 15 %; B1 decrease above 15 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature; time before counting; species / source of pollen; volume of sucrose solution; number of grains counted.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted 50 grains in each solution instead of 5.
parts.answer: A larger sample is more representative / reduces the effect of a few unusual grains.
parts.working: B1 representative sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row shows features of a typical wind-pollinated flower?
A stigma: feathery, outside flower; petals: small and green; nectar: absent
B stigma: small and sticky, inside flower; petals: large and bright; nectar: present
C stigma: feathery, outside flower; petals: large and bright; nectar: present
D stigma: small and sticky, inside flower; petals: small and green; nectar: absent
parts.answer: A stigma: feathery, outside flower; petals: small and green; nectar: absent
parts.working: Wind-pollinated flowers have large feathery stigmas that catch pollen from the air and no need to attract insects. B describes an insect-pollinated flower.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why do insect-pollinated flowers usually produce nectar?
A To keep the stigma moist so that pollen can germinate
B To attract insects, which feed on it and carry pollen from flower to flower
C To make the pollen grains heavier so that they fall onto the stigma
D To provide food for the developing embryo inside the seed
parts.answer: B To attract insects, which feed on it and carry pollen from flower to flower
parts.working: Nectar is a sugary reward that attracts insects, which brush against the anthers and carry pollen to other flowers. A and C are not functions of nectar (the stigma is not kept moist by nectar and the pollen weight is unchanged); D confuses nectar with stored food in the seed.

practice.stem: Two chilli plants, X and Y, are growing in a garden. Plant X has flowers 1 and 2. Plant Y has flowers 3 and 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each transfer of pollen, state whether it is self-pollination or cross-pollination.
(i) from the anther of flower 1 to the stigma of flower 1
(ii) from the anther of flower 1 to the stigma of flower 2
(iii) from the anther of flower 2 to the stigma of flower 3
(iv) from the anther of flower 3 to the stigma of flower 4
parts.answer: (i) self (ii) self (iii) cross (iv) self
parts.working: 1 mark each. Flowers 1 and 2 are on the same plant, so (ii) is self-pollination; (iii) is between different plants, so cross-pollination; flowers 3 and 4 are on the same plant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of the offspring produced after cross-pollination that is less likely after self-pollination.
parts.answer: More genetic variation among the offspring.
parts.working: B1 more variation / new combinations of alleles.

practice.stem:
In spring, many people in Islamabad suffer from allergies caused by pollen from paper mulberry trees. The number of pollen grains per m³ of air was recorded each day for one week.
Day: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
Pollen grains per m³: 3200, 4500, 7800, 6100, 1200, 900, 5300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean daily pollen count for the week.
parts.answer: 4143 grains per m³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rain fell on day 5 and day 6. Suggest why the pollen counts were low on these days.
parts.answer: Rain washes pollen out of the air / wet anthers do not release pollen and pollen is not carried far by wind.
parts.working: B1 rain removes pollen from air; B1 wet pollen / anthers not released or not blown.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The paper mulberry tree is wind-pollinated. Explain why wind-pollinated plants release such large numbers of pollen grains.
parts.answer: Pollen is carried randomly by the wind and most grains never land on a stigma of the same species; producing huge numbers makes it likely that some will reach a stigma.
parts.working: B1 transfer by wind is random / most pollen wasted; B1 increases chance some reaches a stigma.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination.
parts.answer: Self-pollination: transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination: transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.
parts.working: B1 self – same flower / same plant; B1 cross – different plant of same species.
