parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage, to a species, of cross-pollination compared with self-pollination.
parts.answer: Advantage: more genetic variation in offspring, so the species is more likely to adapt to environmental change / disease. Disadvantage: depends on pollinators or wind, so pollination may fail if pollinators are scarce or plants are far apart.
parts.working: B1 advantage with reason (variation → adaptation); B1 disadvantage with reason (relies on external agent / plants close together).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mango farmers in Multan have reported fewer flies and bees visiting their trees after heavy insecticide spraying. Suggest how this could affect the mango harvest.
parts.answer: Fewer insects → less pollination of flowers; fewer ovules fertilised, so fewer fruits / lower yield.
parts.working: B1 less pollination; B1 fewer fruits / seeds formed (lower yield).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some flowers, the anthers release their pollen several days before the stigma of the same flower is ready to receive pollen. Suggest and explain the advantage of this to the species.
parts.answer: It prevents self-pollination within the same flower, so pollen must come from another plant (cross-pollination); this increases genetic variation in the offspring, so the species is more likely to survive changes in the environment / new diseases.
parts.working: B1 prevents / reduces self-pollination; B1 promotes cross-pollination; B1 more variation → better chance of adapting / surviving environmental change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage to a plant of depending only on cross-pollination.
parts.answer: If pollinators are scarce or there are no other plants of the species nearby, no seeds are produced.
parts.working: B1 depends on pollinators / other plants being present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Date palms have separate male trees and female trees. In date orchards in Sindh, farmers climb female trees and tie strands of male flowers among the female flowers. Name this process and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: Hand pollination (artificial pollination). Each tree has flowers of one sex only, so pollen must reach the female flowers from a male tree; wind alone is unreliable and the farmer plants few male trees, so tying male flowers among the female ones makes sure that pollen reaches the stigmas.
parts.working: B1 (artificial / hand) pollination; B1 pollen must come from a different (male) tree / cross-pollination needed; B1 ensures pollen reaches stigmas so more fruits / dates form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why farmers grow only a few male trees in an orchard.
parts.answer: Male trees do not produce fruit; one male tree can provide enough pollen for many female trees, so more space is used for fruit-bearing trees.
parts.working: B1 male trees produce no dates / one male supplies many females.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what develops from the ovary of a date flower after fertilisation.
parts.answer: the fruit (the date)
parts.working: B1 fruit.

practice.stem:
A student studied 150 flowers on mustard plants in a field near Faisalabad. 50 flowers were left open, 50 were covered with fine mesh bags that kept out insects, and 50 were bagged and then hand-pollinated with a brush. The number of flowers that formed fruits was counted.
Open: 48
Bagged: 6
Bagged and hand-pollinated: 45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of flowers that formed fruits in each group.
parts.answer: open 96 %; bagged 12 %; bagged and hand-pollinated 90 %
parts.working: M1 number ÷ 50 × 100; A1 all three correct (96, 12, 90).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the results show about how this plant is normally pollinated.
parts.answer: It is mainly pollinated by insects (animals): when insects were kept out, very few fruits formed.
parts.working: B1 insect pollinated; B1 bagged flowers formed far fewer fruits (12 % compared with 96 %).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the third group, bagged and hand-pollinated, was included.
parts.answer: To show that the bag itself did not stop fruit forming (for example by changing temperature or damaging the flower); when pollen was supplied, fruits formed, so the lack of pollen was the cause.
parts.working: B1 control for effect of the bag; B1 shows lack of pollination (not the bag) caused low fruit set.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a few fruits still formed in the bagged group.
parts.answer: Some self-pollination occurred within the bag (or pollen got in / tiny insects got through the mesh).
parts.working: B1 self-pollination / some pollen entered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the main sex hormone secreted by:
(i) the testes
(ii) the ovaries (name two)
parts.answer: (i) testosterone; (ii) oestrogen and progesterone
parts.working: 1 mark for (i); 1 mark each for oestrogen and progesterone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two secondary sexual characteristics that develop in boys at puberty.
parts.answer: Any two: growth of facial / body / pubic hair; deepening of the voice; growth of muscles; growth of penis and testes; sperm production starts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone causes the development of breasts and the widening of the hips in girls at puberty?
A testosterone
B oestrogen
C insulin
D adrenaline
parts.answer: B oestrogen
parts.working: Oestrogen from the ovaries controls the female secondary sexual characteristics. Testosterone (A) controls the male ones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three secondary sexual characteristics that develop in girls during puberty.
parts.answer: Any three: breasts develop; hips widen; pubic and underarm hair grows; menstrual cycle begins; more fat deposited under the skin.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes oestrogen.
parts.answer: the ovary
parts.working: B1 ovary.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table for a typical 28-day menstrual cycle.
Days 1–5: ______
Days 6–13: the lining of the uterus ______
Day 14 (about): ______
Days 15–28: the lining of the uterus is ______
parts.answer: Days 1–5: menstruation (the uterus lining breaks down and is lost); days 6–13: thickens / repairs; day 14: ovulation (an egg is released from an ovary); days 15–28: maintained (kept thick, ready for implantation)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone maintains the thickened lining of the uterus in the second half of the menstrual cycle?
A FSH
B LH
C oestrogen
D progesterone
parts.answer: D progesterone
parts.working: Progesterone maintains the uterine lining after ovulation. Oestrogen (C) is the main distractor: it causes the lining to build up / repair in the first half of the cycle.

practice.stem:
The concentrations of hormones in a woman's blood were measured during one 28-day menstrual cycle.
FSH: rises from day 1, peaks at day 13, then falls.
Oestrogen: low during menstruation (days 1–5), rises to a peak on day 12, then falls.
LH: low except for a sharp peak on days 13–14.
Progesterone: low until day 14, rises to a peak on day 21, then falls to a low level by day 28.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the day on which ovulation is most likely to have happened. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Day 14; LH concentration peaks on day 13–14 and a surge of LH causes ovulation.
parts.working: B1 day 14 (accept 13–15); B1 LH peak / surge triggers ovulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the roles of FSH and oestrogen in the first half of the cycle.
parts.answer: FSH (from the pituitary gland) stimulates a follicle / egg to develop in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen secretion; oestrogen causes the uterus lining to thicken / repair.
parts.working: 1 mark each: FSH – follicle / egg development; FSH stimulates oestrogen production; oestrogen – builds up uterus lining (also: high oestrogen triggers LH surge).

practice.stem:
The concentration of progesterone in a woman's blood was measured during one 28-day cycle (arbitrary units).
Day: 1, 7, 14, 21, 28
Progesterone: 1, 1, 2, 15, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the day on which progesterone concentration was highest.
parts.answer: day 21
parts.working: B1 day 21.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes progesterone in this cycle.
parts.answer: the ovary
parts.working: B1 ovary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the role of progesterone in the second half of the cycle.
parts.answer: It maintains the thick lining of the uterus (keeps it ready for an embryo to implant) and inhibits the release of FSH and LH.
parts.working: B1 maintains uterus lining; B1 inhibits FSH / LH (prevents another ovulation).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what happens to the uterus lining after day 25 if no embryo implants.
parts.answer: Progesterone concentration falls, so the uterus lining is no longer maintained; it breaks down and is lost in menstruation.
parts.working: B1 progesterone falls; B1 lining breaks down → menstruation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the hormone secreted by the testes and state one secondary sexual characteristic it causes in boys.
parts.answer: Testosterone; any one: growth of facial / body / pubic hair; voice deepens; muscles develop; growth of penis and testes; shoulders broaden.
parts.working: B1 testosterone; B1 any one characteristic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 16-year-old boy's testes produce very little testosterone because of a medical condition. Suggest two ways in which his development would differ from that of other boys of the same age.
parts.answer: Any two: little facial or body hair; voice does not deepen; less muscle development; reproductive organs stay small / no sperm production.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how doctors could treat this condition.
parts.answer: Give him testosterone (hormone treatment, e.g. injections).
parts.working: B1 testosterone / hormone replacement.

practice.stem:
A school nurse asked ten Year 11 students, who agreed to take part anonymously, the age at which their menstrual cycle started.
Ages / years: 11.5, 12.0, 12.5, 13.0, 12.0, 11.0, 13.5, 12.5, 12.0, 14.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean age at which menstruation started for this group.
parts.answer: 12.4 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of the ages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the hormone that causes the development of the uterus lining during each cycle after puberty.
parts.answer: oestrogen
parts.working: B1 oestrogen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the results from ten students may not represent all girls in the city.
parts.answer: The sample is very small / from one school only.
parts.working: B1 small sample / not random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the table for the four hormones of the menstrual cycle. For each hormone state where it is made and one role.
FSH; LH; oestrogen; progesterone
parts.answer:
FSH – pituitary gland – stimulates a follicle (egg) to develop in the ovary / stimulates oestrogen secretion.
LH – pituitary gland – causes ovulation.
Oestrogen – ovary – causes the uterus lining to thicken (repair).
Progesterone – ovary – maintains the uterus lining.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hormone with both site and role correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why menstruation begins at the end of a cycle in which the egg is not fertilised.
parts.answer: Progesterone concentration falls; the uterus lining is no longer maintained, so it breaks down and is lost.
parts.working: B1 progesterone falls; B1 lining not maintained / breaks down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why menstruation does not occur during pregnancy.
parts.answer: Progesterone stays high; it is secreted (first by the ovary and later) by the placenta, so the lining is maintained.
parts.working: B1 progesterone remains high; B1 secreted by placenta / lining maintained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the role of LH in the menstrual cycle.
parts.answer: It causes ovulation (release of an egg from the ovary).
parts.working: B1 triggers ovulation.

practice.stem: A woman recorded the length of five of her menstrual cycles: 27, 29, 28, 30 and 26 days. Assume ovulation happens 14 days before the start of the next menstruation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean cycle length.
parts.answer: 28 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another woman has a regular cycle of 31 days. Using the information given, calculate on which day of her cycle ovulation is likely to occur.
parts.answer: Day 17

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why cycle lengths vary from month to month.
parts.answer: Hormone concentrations vary / affected by stress, illness, diet or exercise.
parts.working: Any one sensible suggestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row shows the hormone that triggers ovulation and the gland that secretes it?
A FSH, ovary
B LH, pituitary gland
C progesterone, ovary
D oestrogen, pituitary gland
parts.answer: B LH, pituitary gland
parts.working: A surge of LH from the pituitary gland causes the egg to be released. FSH (A) is also from the pituitary, not the ovary, and stimulates follicle development; progesterone maintains the uterus lining.

practice.stem:
A woman recorded her body temperature every morning before getting up.
Days 10–14: 36.4, 36.3, 36.4, 36.5, 36.4 °C
Day 15: 36.4 °C; day 16: 36.7 °C
Days 17–21: 36.8, 36.9, 36.8, 36.7, 36.8 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean temperature for days 10–14 and for days 17–21, and the difference between them.
parts.answer: 36.40 °C; 36.80 °C; difference 0.40 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Progesterone causes a small rise in body temperature. Use this information to suggest on which day ovulation took place. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: About day 15 (accept day 14 or 15): the temperature rises on day 16, after the progesterone rise that follows ovulation, so ovulation happened just before the rise.
parts.working: B1 day 15 (accept 14–15); B1 temperature rise follows ovulation as progesterone increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why recording temperature alone cannot be used to predict the day of ovulation in advance.
parts.answer: The temperature rises only after ovulation has happened (and illness or room temperature can also change body temperature).
parts.working: B1 rise happens after ovulation / other factors affect temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During pregnancy the concentration of progesterone stays high. Explain how this prevents menstruation.
parts.answer: Progesterone maintains the thick uterus lining, so it does not break down; menstruation only happens when progesterone falls.
parts.working: B1 progesterone maintains lining; B1 lining not lost because progesterone does not fall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pregnant woman does not ovulate.
parts.answer: High progesterone (and oestrogen) inhibits the secretion of FSH and LH by the pituitary gland, so no new follicles develop and no LH surge triggers ovulation.
parts.working: B1 FSH / LH inhibited; B1 no follicle development / no LH surge so no ovulation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organ that takes over the secretion of progesterone later in pregnancy.
parts.answer: the placenta
parts.working: B1 placenta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens after a pollen grain lands on the stigma, up to the formation of a seed.
parts.answer: A pollen tube grows out of the pollen grain, down through the style to the ovary; it enters an ovule; the male nucleus fuses with the female nucleus in the ovule (fertilisation); the ovule develops into a seed (and the ovary into a fruit).
parts.working: 1 mark each: pollen tube grows; down the style; enters ovule / reaches ovary; nuclei fuse (fertilisation); ovule becomes seed / ovary becomes fruit (any four).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After fertilisation in a flower, state what each structure becomes or what happens to it.
(i) ovule (ii) ovary (iii) petals
parts.answer: (i) seed (ii) fruit (iii) wither and fall off
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is formed when the male nucleus fuses with the female nucleus.
parts.answer: a zygote
parts.working: B1 zygote.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three environmental conditions needed for seeds to germinate.
parts.answer: water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why seeds need water to germinate.
parts.answer: Water makes the seed swell and split the seed coat, and it activates enzymes that break down the stored food so it can be used for growth.
parts.working: B1 activates enzymes / allows reactions; B1 swelling / splits coat / transport of food in solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define fertilisation.
parts.answer: The fusion of the nuclei of a male gamete and a female gamete.
parts.working: B1 fusion of gamete nuclei.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a flowering plant, name the structure that carries the male nucleus from the pollen grain to the ovule.
parts.answer: the pollen tube
parts.working: B1 pollen tube.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the flower in which the female gamete is found.
parts.answer: the ovule (inside the ovary)
parts.working: B1 ovule.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.

After pollination, a pollen grain on the ______ grows a tube down through the ______ to the ovary. A male ______ travels down the tube and fuses with a female nucleus inside an ______. This is called ______. The ovule then develops into a ______.
parts.answer: stigma; style; nucleus (gamete); ovule; fertilisation; seed
parts.working: 1 mark for each gap.

practice.stem:
A student set up four tubes, each with 30 moong (mung bean) seeds, and left them for 5 days.
A: damp cotton wool, air, 25 °C — 27 seeds germinated
B: dry cotton wool, air, 25 °C — 0 germinated
C: seeds under boiled and cooled water covered by oil, 25 °C — 0 germinated
D: damp cotton wool, air, 4 °C in a refrigerator — 2 germinated

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination in tube A and in tube D. Give your answer for tube D to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three conditions needed for germination that are shown by these results. Use the tubes to explain your answer.
parts.answer: Water – compare A with B (no water, no germination); oxygen – compare A with C (no oxygen, no germination); suitable / warm temperature – compare A with D (cold, very little germination).
parts.working: 1 mark each condition with the correct comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the water in tube C was boiled and then covered with a layer of oil.
parts.answer: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen; oil stops oxygen from the air dissolving back in.
parts.working: B1 both ideas.

practice.stem:
Groups of 50 wheat seeds were kept on damp paper at different temperatures for 7 days. The percentage that germinated was recorded.
Temperature / °C: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
Germination / %: 6, 30, 64, 84, 92, 80, 40, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for germination from these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of seeds out of 50 that germinated at 15 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of increasing temperature from 5 °C to 25 °C.
parts.answer: Germination increases because enzymes in the seed work faster at higher temperatures (more kinetic energy, more collisions), so stored food is broken down faster for growth.
parts.working: B1 more germination with data; B1 enzyme activity increases / more kinetic energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why germination was so low at 40 °C.
parts.answer: The enzymes are denatured at high temperature (active site changes shape), so the stored food cannot be broken down and the embryo cannot grow.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured; B1 food reserves not digested / no energy or materials for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A seed bank stores seeds of many crop varieties for many years. The seeds are dried and kept in sealed containers at about −18 °C. Explain why the seeds do not germinate during storage.
parts.answer: There is very little water, so enzymes cannot work and food stores are not mobilised; the very low temperature slows / stops enzyme activity; the sealed container limits oxygen (and stops water entering).
parts.working: B1 lack of water; B1 low temperature – enzymes inactive; B1 sealed / little oxygen (no respiration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the seeds are not simply stored at room temperature.
parts.answer: At room temperature respiration continues slowly and uses up stored food, and fungi may grow, so the seeds would lose viability / die sooner.
parts.working: B1 respiration uses up food stores / enzymes active; B1 seeds die / lose ability to germinate (or fungal decay).

practice.stem: A student wanted to find out whether mung bean seeds need light to germinate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should set up the experiment so that the only difference between the dishes is the light.
parts.answer: Use two identical dishes with the same number (e.g. 20) of the same type of mung beans on cotton wool soaked with the same volume of water; keep both at the same temperature; put one in light and cover the other with a box / put it in a dark cupboard at the same temperature.
parts.working: B1 same number and type of seeds; B1 same water / cotton wool; B1 same temperature, only light differs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After 4 days, 18 out of 20 seeds had germinated in the light and 19 out of 20 in the dark. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: Light is not needed for germination of mung beans.
parts.working: B1 light not needed / no effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The seedlings in the dark were taller and yellow. Suggest why they were yellow.
parts.answer: No chlorophyll was made in the dark.
parts.working: B1 no chlorophyll (light needed to make it).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one way to improve the reliability of the results.
parts.answer: Use more seeds / repeat with more dishes and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 more seeds or repeats.

practice.stem: 20 dry chickpea seeds had a mass of 6.0 g. After soaking in water for 12 hours their mass was 10.5 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the use of the water absorbed by the seeds during germination.
parts.answer: Any two: activates enzymes; allows enzymes to digest stored starch/protein; transports dissolved food to the growing embryo; makes cells swell / bursts seed coat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The soaked chickpeas were then kept in a sealed jar with no air. Predict whether they would germinate, and explain.
parts.answer: No (or very few): there is no oxygen for aerobic respiration, so not enough energy is released for growth.
parts.working: B1 no germination; B1 oxygen needed for respiration / energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of temperature on the germination of radish seeds.
parts.answer: Place equal numbers (e.g. 20) of radish seeds on damp cotton wool in Petri dishes; keep dishes at five temperatures (e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 °C) in incubators; same volume of water, same seed type/age, same light; count the number germinated (radicle visible) after a fixed time (e.g. 3 days) and calculate %; repeat with three dishes per temperature and find mean; wash hands after handling seeds.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: 1. at least five temperatures; 2. how temperature is controlled (incubators / thermostatically controlled); 3. same number of seeds per dish (≥ 10); 4. how germination is judged (radicle emerges) and measured (count / % after fixed time); 5. two controlled variables with method (same volume of water, same seed variety / age, same light, same time); 6. repeats and means; 7. keep cotton wool damp / supply oxygen (lid with air gap); 8. relevant safety (seeds may be treated with fungicide – wear gloves / wash hands).

practice.stem:
40 radish seeds were placed on damp cotton wool at 22 °C. The total number of seeds that had germinated was counted each day.
Day: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total germinated: 0, 4, 15, 28, 34, 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final percentage germination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of seeds that germinated on day 4 only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Half of the seeds that eventually germinated had germinated by a certain day. Between which two days was this?
parts.answer: Between day 3 and day 4 (half of 36 is 18; 15 by day 3, 28 by day 4).
parts.working: M1 half of 36 = 18; A1 between day 3 and day 4.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why 4 of the seeds did not germinate.
parts.answer: Any two: the embryo was dead or damaged; seed was dormant; seed was infected by fungus; seed coat was too hard / impermeable to water; not enough water reached that seed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: In this question, a pollen tube grows down a style 9.0 mm long at a steady rate of 1.2 mm per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the pollen tube to reach the ovule. Give your answer in hours and minutes.
parts.answer: 7 hours 30 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens when the pollen tube reaches the ovule.
parts.answer: The tube enters the ovule (through a small hole); the male nucleus passes from the tube into the ovule; it fuses with the female nucleus (egg cell) – fertilisation – forming a zygote.
parts.working: B1 tube enters ovule; B1 male nucleus moves into ovule; B1 fuses with female nucleus / fertilisation / zygote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the pollen tube grows more slowly on a cold day.
parts.answer: Enzyme activity / respiration in the tube is slower at low temperature.
parts.working: B1 slower enzyme reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer in Punjab sowed maize seeds, then heavy rain flooded the field for four days. Very few seeds germinated. Explain why.
parts.answer: Water filled the air spaces in the soil, so little oxygen reached the seeds; germinating seeds need oxygen for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth; without enough energy the embryo could not grow (and may have died from anaerobic respiration products).
parts.working: B1 waterlogging removes air / oxygen; B1 oxygen needed for aerobic respiration; B1 energy needed for germination / growth (anaerobic respiration insufficient).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seeds sown too deep in dry, compacted soil also often fail to grow into seedlings. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Any two: food stores run out before the shoot reaches light to photosynthesise; little oxygen in compacted soil; dry soil supplies too little water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Bean seeds were germinated in soil in light. Every 2 days, 10 seedlings were dried in an oven and weighed.
Day: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Dry mass of 10 seedlings / g: 2.40, 2.30, 2.15, 2.10, 2.35, 2.80

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass between day 0 and day 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dry mass decreased during the first 6 days.
parts.answer: Stored food in the seed was broken down and used in respiration to release energy for growth; carbon dioxide and water were lost, so dry mass fell; no photosynthesis yet.
parts.working: B1 stored food used in respiration; B1 no photosynthesis yet / CO₂ lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dry mass increased after day 6.
parts.answer: The leaves had grown above the soil and turned green, so the seedlings photosynthesised faster than they respired, making new organic substances.
parts.working: B1 leaves / photosynthesis begin; B1 photosynthesis > respiration so organic matter gained.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why dry mass rather than fresh mass was measured.
parts.answer: Fresh mass changes greatly with the water content (seeds absorb water), so it does not show the amount of organic material.
parts.working: B1 water content varies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of asexual reproduction?
A a bee carrying pollen between sunflowers
B a potato plant growing new plants from tubers
C a frog laying eggs that are fertilised in water
D a wheat plant producing grain after pollination
parts.answer: B a potato plant growing new plants from tubers
parts.working: Tubers grow into new plants that are genetically identical to the parent, without gametes. A, C and D all involve gametes (sexual reproduction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define asexual reproduction.
parts.answer: A process resulting in the production of genetically identical offspring from one parent (no gametes / no fertilisation).
parts.working: B1 one parent; B1 genetically identical offspring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of asexual reproduction to a plant species.
parts.answer: Advantage: fast / no pollinator or mate needed / all offspring suited to the same environment. Disadvantage: no genetic variation, so all may be killed by a disease or change in environment; overcrowding / competition near parent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the offspring produced by asexual reproduction?
A They are genetically identical to each other and to the parent.
B They have genes from two parents.
C They are formed by the fusion of gametes.
D They show more variation than offspring from sexual reproduction.
parts.answer: A They are genetically identical to each other and to the parent.
parts.working: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gametes, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and each other. B and C describe sexual reproduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each example is asexual or sexual reproduction.
(i) a bacterium dividing into two
(ii) new garlic plants growing from the cloves of one bulb
(iii) a mango tree growing from a seed
(iv) new ginger shoots growing from pieces of an underground stem (rhizome)
parts.answer: (i) asexual (ii) asexual (iii) sexual (iv) asexual
parts.working: 1 mark each. The seed (iii) forms after fertilisation of an ovule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define sexual reproduction.
parts.answer: A process involving the fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote, producing offspring that are genetically different from each other.
parts.working: B1 fusion of nuclei of (male and female) gametes / forms zygote; B1 offspring genetically different.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of sexual reproduction to a species.
parts.answer: Any two: produces genetic variation; species can adapt to changes in the environment / more likely to survive new diseases; seeds can be dispersed to new areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of sexual reproduction.
parts.answer: Any two: two parents are needed (finding a mate / pollinator); slower; more energy used (e.g. making flowers, nectar, many gametes); good combinations of features may be lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A farmer grows bananas from suckers, which are new shoots that grow from the base of one parent plant. All the banana plants on the farm came from one original plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all the banana plants in the plantation are genetically identical.
parts.answer: They are produced asexually from one parent (by mitosis), so there is no fusion of gametes and no variation.
parts.working: B1 asexual / from one parent; B1 mitosis / no gametes, so same genes / alleles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a fungal disease could destroy the whole plantation.
parts.answer: No genetic variation, so if one plant is susceptible all are; no plant has resistance alleles, so the disease spreads to every plant.
parts.working: B1 no variation / all have same alleles; B1 none resistant, so all infected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way the farmer could reduce this risk.
parts.answer: Grow several different varieties / grow plants from seed (sexual reproduction) / mix with other crops.
parts.working: Any one sensible.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements describe sexual reproduction?
1 The offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
2 The nuclei of two gametes fuse.
3 The zygote has a haploid nucleus.
4 The offspring show genetic variation.
A 1 and 3
B 2 and 3
C 2 and 4
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: C 2 and 4
parts.working: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of two haploid gamete nuclei to form a diploid zygote, giving variation. Statement 3 is false (the zygote is diploid), so B and D are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dog has 78 chromosomes in each body cell. State the number of chromosomes in (i) a dog sperm cell and (ii) a dog zygote.
parts.working: B1 39 (haploid); B1 78 (diploid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why gametes must have half the number of chromosomes of body cells.
parts.answer: When two gametes fuse at fertilisation their nuclei combine; if gametes were not haploid the chromosome number would double each generation; haploid gametes give a diploid zygote with the normal number.
parts.working: B1 two gametes fuse / nuclei combine; B1 keeps chromosome number constant (diploid zygote) between generations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sugarcane farmers in Pakistan usually plant pieces of stem, called setts, instead of seeds. Give two advantages to the farmer of growing sugarcane from setts.
parts.answer: Any two: all plants are genetically identical to a high-yielding parent, so the crop is uniform and keeps the good features; plants grow faster / establish more quickly than from seed; no pollination needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plant breeders who want to produce a new variety of sugarcane that resists a disease use sexual reproduction. Explain why.
parts.answer: Sexual reproduction mixes genetic material from two parents, giving offspring with new combinations of features (variation); breeders can select individuals that resist the disease; asexual reproduction only produces copies with no new features.
parts.working: B1 two parents / fusion of gametes; B1 variation / new combinations; B1 allows selection of resistant plants (asexual gives only clones).

practice.stem:
A student took five stem cuttings from one money plant and stood them in jars of water on a windowsill. After 14 days she counted the roots on each cutting.
Number of roots: 8, 11, 9, 12, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of roots per cutting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is sexual or asexual reproduction. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Asexual: only one parent is involved and no gametes fuse.
parts.working: B1 asexual; B1 one parent / no gametes / no fertilisation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using cuttings from one parent plant is useful when testing the effect of a rooting powder on root growth.
parts.answer: All the cuttings are genetically identical, so genetic differences cannot affect the results; any difference is due to the rooting powder (fair test).
parts.working: B1 genetically identical; B1 removes genetic variation as a variable / fairer comparison.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one variable, other than the type of plant, that should be kept the same for all cuttings.
parts.answer: Any one: length of cutting / number of leaves; volume of water; temperature; light; time.
parts.working: B1 any valid variable.

practice.stem: In summer, female aphids reproduce asexually. Assume that each aphid produces 4 daughters every week and that no aphids die, so the population is multiplied by 5 every week. A cotton plant starts with 1 aphid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of aphids after 3 weeks and after 4 weeks.
parts.answer: 3 weeks: 125; 4 weeks: 625

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why asexual reproduction is an advantage to aphids in summer.
parts.answer: Plenty of food and good conditions; asexual reproduction is fast (no mate needed), so the population can grow quickly and exploit the food; offspring suited to the same conditions as the parent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why aphids reproduce sexually in autumn.
parts.answer: Sexual reproduction produces genetic variation; some offspring (eggs) may survive the changing / cold winter conditions or new diseases.
parts.working: B1 variation; B1 better chance of some surviving changing conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of statements are both advantages to a species of sexual reproduction rather than asexual reproduction?
1 It produces offspring with genetic variation.
2 Only one parent is needed.
3 The species is more likely to survive a change in the environment.
4 Large numbers of offspring are produced quickly.
A 1 and 2
B 1 and 3
C 2 and 4
D 3 and 4
parts.answer: B 1 and 3
parts.working: Variation (1) means some individuals may survive new diseases or conditions (3). Needing one parent (2) and rapid production of many offspring (4) are advantages of asexual reproduction.

practice.stem: A small number of yeast cells were added to fruit juice at 5000 cells per cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of yeast cells per cm³ after 9 hours, assuming the number doubles every 90 minutes and no cells die.
parts.answer: 320000 cells per cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Yeast cells reproduce by budding, a type of asexual reproduction. Explain one advantage of this to yeast growing in sugary fruit juice.
parts.answer: It is fast and needs only one parent, so the yeast can quickly increase its population and use the food source before competitors.
parts.working: B1 rapid / one parent / no need to find a mate; B1 can exploit the food quickly / colonise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the population would not keep doubling for several days.
parts.answer: The sugar would be used up and waste products such as ethanol would build up, so the cells would stop dividing or die.
parts.working: B1 food / sugar runs out; B1 toxic waste (ethanol) accumulates / limited space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identical twins form when a zygote divides into two cells that separate and each develops into a baby. Explain why identical twins are genetically identical.
parts.answer: Both come from the same zygote, formed by one sperm and one egg; the cells divide by mitosis, which produces genetically identical cells.
parts.working: B1 from one zygote / same sperm and egg; B1 mitosis gives identical copies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says, 'Identical twins are produced by asexual reproduction.' Explain why this is not correct.
parts.answer: The zygote was formed by sexual reproduction – fusion of gametes from two parents; the twins differ genetically from both parents, whereas asexual offspring are identical to their single parent.
parts.working: B1 zygote formed by fusion of gametes / two parents; B1 twins are not identical to the parents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Non-identical twins form when two eggs are each fertilised by a different sperm. Explain why non-identical twins are no more similar genetically than ordinary brothers and sisters.
parts.answer: Each twin comes from a different egg and sperm, each with a different combination of alleles.
parts.working: B1 different gametes / different combination of genes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cheetahs have very little genetic variation; individuals are nearly as alike genetically as identical twins. Suggest why a new disease is a greater threat to cheetahs than to a species with more variation.
parts.answer: If all individuals are genetically similar, any individual that is susceptible means that all are likely to be susceptible; there are unlikely to be any individuals with alleles giving resistance; so the disease could kill most of the population.
parts.working: B1 little variation / all similar; B1 no resistant individuals likely; B1 whole population could be wiped out (species could become extinct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Zoos sometimes move male cheetahs between zoos in different countries for breeding. Explain how this helps to conserve the species.
parts.answer: It allows breeding between less closely related animals, so sexual reproduction combines more different alleles, increasing genetic variation in the offspring.
parts.working: B1 unrelated / different populations; B1 increases variation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the amniotic fluid.
parts.answer: Protects the fetus from mechanical shock / bumps (cushioning).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the umbilical cord.
parts.answer: It contains blood vessels (umbilical artery and vein) that carry blood between the fetus and the placenta.
parts.working: B1 contains blood vessels; B1 links fetus to placenta / carries blood both ways.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the structure in which a fertilised egg implants.
parts.answer: Uterus (lining)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these stages in the correct order, starting with fertilisation.
implantation in the lining of the uterus; fetus with recognisable organs; fertilisation in the oviduct; zygote divides to form a ball of cells (embryo)
parts.answer: fertilisation in the oviduct → zygote divides to form a ball of cells (embryo) → implantation in the lining of the uterus → fetus with recognisable organs
parts.working: 2 marks for correct order; 1 mark if one pair reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by implantation.
parts.answer: The embryo (ball of cells) sinks into / attaches to the lining of the uterus.
parts.working: B1 embryo embeds in uterus lining.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fetus does not use its lungs for gas exchange. State how the fetus obtains oxygen.
parts.answer: Oxygen diffuses from the mother's blood into the fetal blood across the placenta and is carried to the fetus in the umbilical cord.
parts.working: B1 from mother's blood by diffusion across placenta; B1 carried through umbilical cord.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other substances, apart from oxygen, that pass from the mother to the fetus.
parts.answer: Any two: glucose; amino acids; water; mineral ions (e.g. iron, calcium); vitamins; fatty acids; antibodies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the waste gas that passes from the fetus to the mother.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) The placenta is attached to the wall of the uterus.
(ii) The blood of the mother flows directly into the fetus.
(iii) Urea passes from the fetus to the mother across the placenta.
(iv) The amniotic fluid supports and protects the fetus.
parts.answer: (i) true (ii) false (iii) true (iv) true
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three substances that pass from the mother's blood to the fetus across the placenta.
parts.answer: Any three: oxygen; glucose; amino acids; water; ions / minerals; antibodies; vitamins.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two waste substances that pass from the fetus to the mother.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide and urea.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some harmful substances and pathogens can also cross the placenta. Give one example.
parts.answer: Any one: nicotine; alcohol; some drugs; rubella virus; HIV.
parts.working: Any one.

practice.stem:
A study compared the birth mass of babies born to mothers who smoked during pregnancy with those born to mothers who did not.
mean birth mass, non-smokers: 3.42 kg
mean birth mass, smokers: 3.15 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the mean birth mass of babies of smokers is lower than that of babies of non-smokers. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how smoking during pregnancy could cause lower birth mass.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin, so the mother's blood carries less oxygen; less oxygen crosses the placenta to the fetus; less aerobic respiration / energy for growth; nicotine crosses the placenta (and narrows blood vessels).
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: carbon monoxide; binds haemoglobin / less oxygen carried; less oxygen to fetus; less respiration for growth; nicotine / toxins cross placenta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rubella (German measles) is a mild illness in adults, but if a woman catches it early in pregnancy the virus can damage the developing fetus. Explain how the virus reaches the fetus.
parts.answer: The virus is carried in the mother's blood and can cross the placenta into the fetal blood (then travels through the umbilical cord).
parts.working: B1 virus in mother's blood; B1 crosses the placenta.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many countries vaccinate girls against rubella before they are old enough to become pregnant. Explain how this protects babies born later.
parts.answer: Vaccination gives the girl active immunity: she makes antibodies and memory cells; if she meets the virus while pregnant, the virus is destroyed quickly before it can infect her and cross the placenta.
parts.working: B1 makes antibodies / memory cells; B1 long-term immunity; B1 virus destroyed before it reaches fetus.

practice.stem:
The volume of amniotic fluid around a fetus at different weeks of pregnancy:
Week: 10, 20, 30, 34, 38, 40
Volume / cm³: 30, 350, 800, 1000, 900, 800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the volume of amniotic fluid changes during pregnancy.
parts.answer: It increases rapidly from 30 cm³ at week 10 to a maximum of 1000 cm³ at week 34, then decreases to 800 cm³ at week 40.
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 peak 1000 cm³ at week 34; B1 then decreases, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in volume between week 34 and week 40.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two functions of the amniotic fluid.
parts.answer: Any two: protects the fetus from bumps / shocks (cushions); supports the fetus; allows the fetus to move; keeps temperature steady.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Doctors advise pregnant women in Australia not to drink any alcohol. Explain how alcohol in the mother's blood can affect the fetus.
parts.answer: Alcohol is a small molecule that diffuses across the placenta into the fetal blood; it can damage the developing organs (especially the brain) and slow growth, giving a low birth mass.
parts.working: B1 crosses placenta; B1 enters fetal blood; B1 harms development / brain / growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other substance that can cross the placenta and harm the fetus.
parts.answer: Any one: nicotine; carbon monoxide; some medicinal drugs; heroin.
parts.working: B1 any valid substance (not a pathogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pregnant women are advised to eat foods rich in iron. Explain why extra iron is needed during pregnancy.
parts.answer: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin for the fetus's developing red blood cells and for the mother's increased volume of blood.
parts.working: B1 haemoglobin / red blood cells; B1 for fetus and mother's extra blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why extra calcium is also needed.
parts.answer: For the development of the fetus's bones and teeth.
parts.working: B1 bones / teeth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a balanced diet with enough protein is especially important during pregnancy.
parts.answer: Protein provides amino acids for growth of the fetus (making new cells and tissues) and of the placenta and uterus.
parts.working: B1 amino acids for growth / new cells; B1 of fetus (or placenta).

practice.stem: A fetus had a mass of 1.2 kg at week 28 of pregnancy and 3.3 kg at birth in week 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in mass of the fetus per week between week 28 and week 40, in grams per week.
parts.answer: 175 g per week

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of the placenta is adapted for efficient exchange of substances.
parts.answer: Large surface area (villi); thin barrier between the blood of mother and fetus so short diffusion distance; rich blood supply on both sides keeps concentration gradients high.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three features linked to function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that the blood of the mother and the fetus do not mix.
parts.answer: Mother's higher blood pressure could damage fetal vessels / the blood groups may be different and could clump / protects fetus from some toxins and pathogens.
parts.working: Any one.

practice.stem: Near the end of pregnancy, about 500 cm³ of the mother's blood flows through the placenta every minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of mother's blood that flows through the placenta in one day, in dm³.
parts.answer: 720 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this large blood flow helps the fetus to obtain enough oxygen and glucose.
parts.answer: Fresh maternal blood keeps bringing a high concentration of oxygen and glucose, while the fetal blood flow carries them away; this maintains steep concentration gradients across the placenta, so diffusion is fast.
parts.working: B1 maternal blood brings high concentrations; B1 fetal blood removes them; B1 steep gradient maintained so rapid diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one structural feature of the placenta that also increases the rate of exchange.
parts.answer: Many villi giving a large surface area / thin barrier between the two bloods.
parts.working: B1 large surface area (villi) or thin walls.

practice.stem:
Concentrations of four substances in the blood on each side of a placenta (arbitrary units):
Oxygen: maternal 12, fetal 6
Glucose: maternal 5.0, fetal 3.5
Urea: maternal 2.0, fetal 3.0
Carbon dioxide: maternal 5, fetal 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to explain the direction in which each substance moves across the placenta.
parts.answer: Oxygen: higher in maternal blood, so diffuses into fetal blood. Glucose: higher in maternal blood, so moves into fetal blood. Urea: higher in fetal blood, so diffuses into maternal blood. Carbon dioxide: higher in fetal blood, so diffuses into maternal blood.
parts.working: 1 mark per substance, each linked to the concentration gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the placenta keeps the two blood supplies separate.
parts.answer: Any two: the mother's blood pressure is higher and could damage the fetal blood vessels; blood groups may be incompatible, causing clotting / agglutination; reduces transfer of some pathogens and toxins.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A student modelled the amniotic fluid. Raw eggs were sealed in plastic bags, either dry or completely filled with water, and dropped onto a hard floor from different heights. Five eggs of each type were dropped from each height.
Height / cm: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
Eggs broken, dry bag: 0, 2, 4, 5, 5
Eggs broken, water-filled bag: 0, 0, 0, 1, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total percentage of eggs broken for each type of bag over all the heights.
parts.answer: dry bag 64 %; water bag 12 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the model shows about the function of the amniotic fluid.
parts.answer: Fluid around the egg absorbed the force of the impact, so far fewer eggs broke; similarly amniotic fluid cushions the fetus and protects it from bumps.
parts.working: B1 water absorbs / spreads impact (fewer broken); B1 amniotic fluid protects fetus from mechanical shock.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two ways in which the model is not like a real fetus in the uterus.
parts.answer: Any two: the fetus is also protected by the mother's body wall / uterus muscle / amniotic sac; the fetus is alive and can move; the egg shell is not like fetal tissue; the drops are much harder than knocks to a pregnant woman.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way of making the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Use more eggs at each height / repeat and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 more repeats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some antibodies in the mother's blood cross the placenta into the fetus. Name the type of immunity this gives the baby.
parts.answer: passive immunity
parts.working: B1 passive (natural) immunity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this immunity is useful to a newborn baby, but only lasts a few months.
parts.answer: The baby's immune system has not yet met many pathogens, so the mother's antibodies protect it immediately against diseases the mother is immune to; the antibodies are not made by the baby and no memory cells are formed, so they are broken down and not replaced.
parts.working: B1 immediate protection while baby's own immune system develops; B1 antibodies are from the mother / baby makes no memory cells; B1 antibodies broken down and not replaced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other way in which a baby can receive antibodies from its mother after birth.
parts.answer: In breast milk.
parts.working: B1 breast milk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: HIV is a sexually transmitted infection. State what is meant by a sexually transmitted infection.
parts.answer: An infection that is passed on through sexual contact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways, other than sexual contact, in which HIV can be transmitted.
parts.answer: Any two: sharing needles (e.g. drug users); transfusion of infected blood; from mother to baby across the placenta, at birth or in breast milk.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways of controlling the spread of HIV.
parts.answer: Any two: use condoms; screen blood donations; do not share needles / use sterile needles; HIV testing and treatment; education.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes HIV infection.
parts.answer: a virus
parts.working: B1 virus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the disease that HIV infection may lead to.
parts.answer: AIDS
parts.working: B1 AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one body fluid through which HIV can be passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Any one: blood; semen; vaginal fluid; breast milk.
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether HIV can be passed on in each of these ways. Answer yes or no.
(i) sharing a needle to inject drugs
(ii) a mosquito bite
(iii) from a mother to her baby during birth
(iv) shaking hands
(v) receiving a transfusion of blood that has not been screened
parts.answer: (i) yes (ii) no (iii) yes (iv) no (v) yes
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient with HIV asks a doctor for antibiotics. Explain why antibiotics will not cure HIV.
parts.answer: HIV is a virus; antibiotics only kill bacteria (or stop their growth) and do not affect viruses.
parts.working: B1 HIV is a virus; B1 antibiotics do not affect viruses / only work on bacteria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: There is no cure for HIV, but antiretroviral drugs can be taken. Suggest one benefit of taking these drugs every day.
parts.answer: They slow down the reproduction of the virus, so the person stays healthy for longer / is less likely to develop AIDS / less likely to pass HIV on.
parts.working: B1 any valid benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) HIV is a bacterium.
(ii) AIDS can develop in a person infected with HIV.
(iii) HIV can be passed on in breast milk.
(iv) HIV infection can be cured with antibiotics.
parts.answer: (i) false (ii) true (iii) true (iv) false
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using a condom during sexual intercourse reduces the spread of sexually transmitted infections.
parts.answer: It acts as a barrier, preventing the exchange of body fluids (semen, vaginal fluid) that contain the pathogens.
parts.working: B1 barrier; B1 prevents contact with / exchange of body fluids containing pathogens.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two other ways in which the spread of HIV can be controlled in a country.
parts.answer: Any two: screening donated blood; using sterile / single-use needles and syringes; testing people and treating those infected; education about how HIV is spread; limiting the number of sexual partners; treating infected pregnant women.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Estimated number of new HIV infections per year in one country:
2010: 14 000
2015: 20 000
2020: 25 000
2023: 26 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in new infections per year between 2010 and 2023. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in the data after 2015.
parts.answer: New infections continued to rise, but the increase slowed (5000 from 2015 to 2020, then only 1000 from 2020 to 2023).
parts.working: B1 still increasing; B1 rate of increase slowing, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two measures the government could take to reduce the number of new infections.
parts.answer: Any two: free testing and treatment; education campaigns; providing condoms; needle-exchange programmes / single-use syringes in clinics; screening all blood donations; treating pregnant women with HIV.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An outbreak of HIV occurred among children in one district. Investigators found that some clinics had reused the same syringes and needles on many patients. Explain how this spread HIV.
parts.answer: Blood containing HIV from an infected patient remained in / on the syringe or needle; when it was used on the next patient, the virus entered their blood directly.
parts.working: B1 infected blood left on needle / syringe; B1 enters bloodstream of next patient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two actions that health authorities could take to prevent this happening again.
parts.answer: Any two: use only single-use / auto-disable syringes; train and inspect clinic staff; safe disposal in sharps boxes; sterilise reusable equipment properly; test and treat children and families affected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a bacterium. State how gonorrhoea can be treated.
parts.answer: with antibiotics
parts.working: B1 antibiotics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some strains of the bacterium that causes gonorrhoea are now resistant to several antibiotics. Explain why this makes it more important to prevent its spread.
parts.answer: Resistant infections are difficult or impossible to treat with the usual antibiotics, so infected people may stay ill or suffer complications and continue to spread it; prevention avoids the need for treatment.
parts.working: B1 harder to treat / antibiotics ineffective; B1 infection lasts longer / spreads further, so prevention needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a person can be infected with an STI and pass it on without knowing.
parts.answer: Many STIs cause few or no symptoms for a long time.
parts.working: B1 no / few symptoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all blood donated to a blood bank is tested for HIV before it is used.
parts.answer: Blood from an infected donor contains HIV; a transfusion puts the blood directly into the patient's bloodstream, so the patient would be infected.
parts.working: B1 infected blood contains virus; B1 transfused directly into patient's blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nurses wear gloves when taking blood and put used needles into a puncture-proof sharps box. Explain how each precaution reduces the risk of HIV infection.
parts.answer: Gloves stop infected blood touching cuts in the nurse's skin; the sharps box prevents needlestick injuries that could inject infected blood.
parts.working: B1 gloves – barrier to blood entering cuts; B1 sharps box – prevents needle injuries / reuse.

practice.stem:
The number of lymphocytes in the blood of a person infected with HIV was measured when the infection was first diagnosed and again six years later, before treatment began.
at diagnosis: 1050 lymphocytes per mm³
six years later: 340 lymphocytes per mm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the lymphocyte count. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person with a very low lymphocyte count often suffers from other infections, such as tuberculosis.
parts.answer: HIV infects and destroys lymphocytes; fewer lymphocytes means fewer antibodies are produced; so the body cannot fight pathogens and other infections develop (AIDS).
parts.working: 1 mark each: HIV destroys lymphocytes; fewer antibodies made; immune system weakened / pathogens not destroyed, so opportunistic infections.

practice.stem: HIV infects and destroys some types of lymphocyte. A person's lymphocyte count fell from 1000 per mm³ to 200 per mm³ over 8 years without treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean decrease in lymphocyte count per year.
parts.answer: 100 per mm³ per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: The person felt healthy for most of the 8 years. Explain why it is important for people who may have been exposed to HIV to be tested, even if they feel well.
parts.answer: HIV may cause no symptoms for many years, but the virus is present in body fluids, so the person can pass it on without knowing; testing allows them to start treatment early to slow damage to the immune system and to take precautions to protect others.
parts.working: B1 no symptoms for years; B1 can still transmit HIV; B1 early treatment / prevent spread.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person with a lymphocyte count of 200 per mm³ is likely to develop serious infections such as tuberculosis.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes make antibodies; with very few lymphocytes the immune system cannot make enough antibodies to destroy pathogens, so infections that are normally controlled develop.
parts.working: B1 lymphocytes make antibodies / fight pathogens; B1 weakened immune system cannot destroy pathogens.

practice.stem: In one study, about 30 % of babies born to mothers with HIV were infected when the mothers had no treatment, but only 2 % were infected when the mothers took antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of babies, out of 500, expected to be infected (i) without treatment and (ii) with treatment, and the number of infections prevented.
parts.answer: (i) 150 (ii) 10; 140 prevented

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three ways in which HIV may pass from a mother to her baby.
parts.answer: Across the placenta (during pregnancy); during birth (contact with blood and body fluids); in breast milk.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A common test for HIV detects antibodies against HIV in the blood. Explain why a person who was infected one week ago may test negative.
parts.answer: It takes time for the immune system (lymphocytes) to make enough antibodies to be detected; after one week there may not yet be enough antibodies.
parts.working: B1 antibodies take time to be produced; B1 too few to detect yet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this person should be tested again some weeks later and should take precautions in the meantime.
parts.answer: By then antibodies would be detectable, giving a reliable result; meanwhile the virus may still be present and the person could pass it on.
parts.working: B1 later test reliable once antibodies produced; B1 can still transmit HIV in the meantime.

practice.stem: In a health survey, 75 out of 12 500 people in the general population tested positive for HIV. In a separate survey of 800 people who inject drugs, 304 tested positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people testing positive (i) in the general population sample and (ii) among people who inject drugs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the percentage is among people who inject drugs. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 63 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why people who inject drugs have a much higher chance of being infected with HIV.
parts.answer: Needles and syringes are often shared; a needle used by an infected person contains blood with HIV, which is injected directly into the next person's blood.
parts.working: B1 sharing needles; B1 infected blood enters bloodstream directly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme begins the digestion of protein in the stomach?
A amylase
B lipase
C maltase
D pepsin
parts.answer: D pepsin
parts.working: Pepsin is the protease secreted in the stomach and works at acidic pH. Amylase digests starch, not protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the substrate and the products of the enzyme lipase.
parts.answer: substrate: fats (lipids); products: fatty acids and glycerol
parts.working: B1 fat; B1 fatty acids and glycerol (both).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes lipase into the duodenum.
parts.answer: pancreas

practice.stem:
Lipase is added to full-cream milk containing a few drops of an indicator that is pink above pH 8.3 and colourless below it. A little sodium carbonate solution is first added so the milk starts pink. The time taken for the pink colour to disappear is recorded at four temperatures.
temperature / °C | time for pink colour to disappear / s
15 | 420
25 | 210
35 | 110
55 | 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pink colour disappears.
parts.answer: lipase digests fat in the milk to fatty acids (and glycerol); the fatty acids lower the pH below 8.3
parts.working: B1 fats broken down to fatty acids; B1 acids lower the pH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the temperature at which lipase was most active in these results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 25 °C as 1000 ÷ time. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 4.8 (arbitrary units)

practice.stem:
Enzyme | Produced by | Substrate | Products
Amylase | salivary glands and pancreas | starch | (i)
Protease | stomach (pepsin) and pancreas | protein | (ii)
Lipase | pancreas | (iii) | fatty acids and glycerol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the table about three digestive enzymes.
parts.answer: (i) maltose; (ii) amino acids (or peptides); (iii) fats (lipids)
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) maltose from starch; (ii) amino acids or peptides from protein; (iii) fats (lipids) are the substrate of lipase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the enzyme pepsin works in the stomach, where the pH is about 2, but salivary amylase does not work well there.
parts.answer: Pepsin has its optimum pH near 2, so its active site matches its substrate best in the acidic stomach. Amylase has its optimum near pH 7; at pH 2 its active site changes shape (it is denatured), so it stops working.
parts.working: 1 mark: pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. 1 mark: amylase has an optimum near pH 7. 1 mark: at pH 2 the active site of amylase changes shape. 1 mark: the enzyme is denatured and stops working.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row shows the places where starch is digested and the product of amylase action?
A mouth and stomach; glucose
B mouth and small intestine; maltose
C stomach and small intestine; maltose
D mouth and small intestine; glucose
parts.answer: B mouth and small intestine; maltose
parts.working: Salivary amylase acts in the mouth and pancreatic amylase in the small intestine (duodenum); amylase produces maltose, which maltase then breaks down to glucose. Glucose is the product of maltase, not amylase; amylase does not act in the acid stomach.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.
Starch is broken down to ______ by the enzyme amylase. This sugar is then broken down to ______ by the enzyme ______, which is found on the membranes of the epithelium lining the small intestine. Proteins are broken down to ______ by proteases such as pepsin and ______.
parts.answer: maltose; glucose; maltase; amino acids; trypsin
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student mixes salivary amylase with starch solution at different pH values at 37 °C. A drop of the mixture is tested with iodine solution every 15 s until it no longer turns blue-black. The results are:
pH | time for starch to disappear / s
4 | 300
6 | 75
7 | 60
8 | 100
10 | 600
The rate of reaction can be found as 1000 ÷ time. Calculate the rate at pH 7 and at pH 4. Give each answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the optimum pH of this amylase from these results.
parts.answer: pH 7

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the starch takes 600 s to disappear at pH 10.
parts.answer: pH far from the optimum changes the shape of the active site of amylase; fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form so digestion is slow
parts.working: B1 active site changes shape / some enzyme molecules denatured; B1 starch fits less often / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

practice.stem:
A student fills a length of Visking (dialysis) tubing with a mixture of starch solution and amylase solution, ties both ends and places it in a boiling tube of distilled water at 37 °C. Every 10 minutes, samples of the water outside the tubing are tested with iodine solution and with Benedict's solution.
time / min | iodine test on water outside | Benedict's test on water outside
0 | orange-brown | blue
10 | orange-brown | green
20 | orange-brown | orange
30 | orange-brown | brick red

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results of the Benedict's test.
parts.answer: amylase digests starch to maltose / reducing sugar; maltose molecules are small enough to diffuse through the tubing; more sugar outside over time so colour goes from blue to brick red
parts.working: B1 starch digested to reducing sugar (maltose); B1 sugar is small and diffuses out through the tubing; B1 concentration outside increases with time (colour sequence).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the iodine test on the water outside stays orange-brown throughout.
parts.answer: starch molecules are too large to pass through the tubing

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this experiment.
parts.answer: repeat with boiled (denatured) amylase / with water instead of amylase

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is produced when protein is partly digested by pepsin in the stomach?
A amino acids
B fatty acids and glycerol
C glucose
D polypeptides (peptides)
parts.answer: D polypeptides (peptides)
parts.working: Pepsin is a protease that cuts protein into smaller polypeptide chains. Amino acids are only made later, when enzymes in the small intestine finish the job. Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats, and glucose from starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the digestion of starch is correct?
A It is completed by pepsin in the stomach
B Maltase converts maltose into glucose in the small intestine
C Lipase converts starch into maltose in the mouth
D Salivary amylase is made by the wall of the stomach
parts.answer: B Maltase converts maltose into glucose in the small intestine
parts.working: Amylase breaks starch into maltose, and maltase in the small intestine converts maltose into glucose. Pepsin acts on protein, lipase acts on fats, and salivary amylase is made by the salivary glands, not the stomach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of the hydrochloric acid secreted in the stomach.
parts.answer: kills pathogens / harmful microorganisms in food; gives the acidic pH that is optimum for pepsin
parts.working: B1 kills bacteria / pathogens; B1 provides optimum (low) pH for enzymes (pepsin).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pepsin stops working when the stomach contents reach the duodenum. Explain why.
parts.answer: bile (alkaline) neutralises the acid so pH rises; pepsin is far from its optimum pH; the shape of its active site changes so substrate no longer fits
parts.working: B1 bile / alkaline secretion neutralises acid, pH rises; B1 pepsin has a low optimum pH; B1 active site changes shape / enzyme denatured / no enzyme–substrate complexes form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why proteins in a meal of chicken karahi must be digested before they can be used by body cells.
parts.answer: proteins are large insoluble molecules that cannot pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; they are broken down to small soluble amino acids that can be absorbed; cells then use the amino acids to build their own proteins
parts.working: B1 proteins are large / insoluble; B1 cannot be absorbed (cannot cross the epithelium / membranes); B1 amino acids are small and soluble so can be absorbed and then used to make new proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some people with cystic fibrosis, thick mucus blocks the duct that carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum. Suggest and explain two effects of this on digestion.
parts.answer: less amylase, protease (trypsin) and lipase reach the duodenum, so starch, protein and fat are less digested; pancreatic juice is alkaline, so acid from the stomach is less neutralised and enzymes in the small intestine are not at their optimum pH
parts.working: Two effects, each with explanation (2 × 2): less fat digested because less lipase (fatty food passes out in faeces); less protein / starch digested because less trypsin / amylase; fewer nutrients absorbed so poor growth / weight loss; contents of duodenum stay acidic so intestinal enzymes work slowly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student adds protease to egg white (protein) at pH 2, 5, 7 and 9, keeping each tube at 37 °C. The time taken for the cloudy mixture to become clear is recorded. State the independent variable.
parts.answer: pH
parts.working: 1 mark: pH of the buffer solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the dependent variable.
parts.answer: The time taken for the mixture to become clear (accept rate = 1 ÷ time).
parts.working: 1 mark: time for the mixture to clear.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Volume and concentration of protease solution; amount of egg white (or temperature, kept at 37 °C)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: volume or concentration of protease, amount of egg white, temperature, volume of buffer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the test tubes should be kept at 37 °C.
parts.answer: 37 °C is close to body temperature, so the enzyme works at a rate that can be compared; the temperature must be the same in all tubes so that only pH changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature must be kept constant so that only pH is changed (37 °C is near the enzyme's optimum).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the effect of bile on fats in the small intestine?
A It breaks fats down into fatty acids and glycerol.
B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
C It absorbs fats into the lacteals.
D It produces lipase to digest fats.
parts.answer: B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
parts.working: Bile emulsifies fat, breaking large drops into small droplets and increasing their surface area for lipase. It contains no enzymes, so A is wrong: that is the action of lipase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of human tooth used for:
(i) biting off pieces of food
(ii) grinding and chewing food
parts.answer: (i) incisors (ii) molars (accept premolars)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how chewing food helps chemical digestion.
parts.answer: chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymes to act on, so digestion is faster
parts.working: B1 increases surface area; B1 for enzymes / faster chemical digestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why chewing food increases the rate at which starch is digested.
parts.answer: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, giving a larger surface area. This allows more contact between the starch and the amylase in saliva, so more starch is broken down per unit time.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area of food. 1 mark: more contact with amylase in saliva. 1 mark: more starch digested per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of molars in an adult human, including all four quadrants of the jaws. Show how you obtained your answer.
parts.answer: 12 molars
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 molars in each quadrant. 1 mark: 3 × 4 quadrants. 1 mark: 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of the tongue in digestion.
parts.answer: Mixes food with saliva; moves food around the mouth and to the back for swallowing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: mixing food with saliva; moving food for chewing; pushing food to the back of the mouth for swallowing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where bile is made and where it is stored.
parts.answer: made in the liver; stored in the gall bladder
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which bile helps the digestion of fats in the small intestine.
parts.answer: emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase; it is alkaline and neutralises stomach acid, giving a suitable pH for enzymes in the small intestine
parts.working: B1 emulsification; B1 larger surface area for lipase so faster digestion; B1 bile is alkaline / neutralises hydrochloric acid; B1 optimum pH for enzymes in the small intestine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the stomach carries out physical digestion.
parts.answer: muscles in the stomach wall contract to churn the food, mixing it with gastric juice and breaking it into smaller pieces
parts.working: B1 muscle contractions / churning; B1 breaks food up / mixes with juices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cube of boiled potato with sides of 1 cm is cut into 8 equal cubes, each with sides of 0.5 cm. Calculate the total surface area before and after cutting.
parts.answer: before 6 cm²; after 12 cm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (b) to explain why physical digestion speeds up chemical digestion.
parts.answer: the surface area doubles, so more food is exposed to enzymes at once

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which tooth is used for tearing and piercing meat?
A incisor
B canine
C premolar
D molar
parts.answer: B canine
parts.working: Canines are long and pointed and are used to tear and pierce food. Incisors are used for cutting, while premolars and molars have broad surfaces for grinding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of enamel in a tooth.
parts.answer: It is the hardest substance and protects the tooth from abrasion and acid.
parts.working: 1 mark: hard enamel protects the tooth from wear and acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the pulp in a tooth.
parts.answer: It contains blood vessels and nerves that supply the tooth.
parts.working: 1 mark: pulp contains blood vessels and nerves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how bacteria in the mouth cause tooth decay.
parts.answer: Bacteria ferment sugars in the food to form acid. The acid dissolves (demineralises) the enamel, so the tooth decays.
parts.working: 1 mark: bacteria produce acid from sugars. 1 mark: acid dissolves the enamel and damages the tooth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how bile salts emulsify fat and why this increases the rate at which lipase digests fat.
