parts.answer: Bile salts break large fat globules into many small droplets (emulsification). This gives a much larger surface area of fat, so lipase has more contact with the fat and digests it faster. Bile itself is not an enzyme and does not change the fat chemically.
parts.working: 1 mark: bile salts break large globules into small droplets. 1 mark: larger surface area for lipase. 1 mark: more contact between lipase and fat. 1 mark: bile is not an enzyme and does not chemically break fats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient has her gall bladder removed. Her liver continues to make bile, which now trickles slowly and continuously into the duodenum. Explain why the doctor advises her to avoid large fatty meals.
parts.answer: without a store there is no large release of bile when a fatty meal arrives; fat is poorly emulsified, so surface area is small; lipase digests the fat slowly / incompletely, causing discomfort or fatty faeces
parts.working: B1 bile cannot be released in large amounts at meal times; B1 less emulsification / small surface area of fat; B1 fat digestion by lipase is slow / incomplete.

practice.stem:
A student investigates the effect of bile salts on fat digestion. Two test-tubes each contain 5 cm³ of vegetable oil mixed with 5 cm³ of a dilute alkaline solution containing an indicator. Tube A also has 1 cm³ of bile salt solution; tube B has 1 cm³ of distilled water. Lipase is added to both tubes at 35 °C and the time for the indicator to change colour (showing a fall in pH) is recorded.
tube A (with bile salts): 4 min
tube B (without bile salts): 11 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in time when bile salts are present. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is faster in tube A.
parts.answer: bile salts emulsify the oil into small droplets; larger surface area for lipase so fatty acids form faster
parts.working: B1 emulsification; B1 larger surface area for lipase / more enzyme–substrate collisions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1 cm³ of distilled water was added to tube B.
parts.answer: to keep the total volume (and so concentrations) the same in both tubes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process breaks large pieces of food into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition?
A chemical digestion
B physical digestion
C egestion
D absorption
parts.answer: B physical digestion
parts.working: Physical (mechanical) digestion by the teeth and stomach churning increases the surface area for enzymes without changing the molecules. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break chemical bonds, so A is wrong; egestion and absorption are different processes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Milk fat is digested by lipase in two tubes at the same temperature. In tube A (no bile salts) the milk cleared in 3.6 min. In tube B (with bile salts) it cleared in 2.4 min. Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of digestion when bile salts are present. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time. 1 mark: rate B ÷ rate A = 3.6 ÷ 2.4 = 1.5. 1 mark: 50% increase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable and one variable that must be kept the same in both tubes.
parts.answer: Independent: presence or absence of bile salts. Controlled: temperature (or volume of milk, concentration of lipase).
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable is bile salts (present or absent). 1 mark: a correctly named controlled variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a practical method for a student to show that bile salts emulsify oil. Include how the result is observed and the control.
parts.answer: Put equal volumes of oil and water into two test tubes. Add bile salts to one tube (the control has none). Shake both tubes in the same way and time how long the oil takes to separate from the water, or how long a stable emulsion lasts.
parts.working: 1 mark: oil and water in two tubes, bile salts added to one only. 1 mark: same shaking in each tube. 1 mark: time the separation of the layers (or the emulsion lasts). 1 mark: control tube with no bile salts.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly matches a nutrient with the disease caused by its deficiency?
A vitamin C – rickets
B vitamin D – scurvy
C vitamin D – rickets
D iron – scurvy
parts.answer: C vitamin D – rickets
parts.working: Lack of vitamin D (and calcium) causes rickets; lack of vitamin C causes scurvy. A and B swap the two vitamins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a balanced diet.
parts.answer: a diet containing all the nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water) in the correct proportions
parts.working: B1 all nutrient groups; B1 in the correct amounts / proportions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the body needs water.
parts.answer: solvent for transport (e.g. in blood plasma); medium for chemical reactions; cooling by sweating; removal of waste in urine
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the deficiency disease caused by a lack of each of these: (i) vitamin D; (ii) iodine; (iii) iron; (iv) vitamin C.
parts.answer: (i) rickets; (ii) goitre; (iii) anaemia; (iv) scurvy
parts.working: 1 mark each for the correct disease: rickets, goitre, anaemia, scurvy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a diet containing enough fibre helps to prevent constipation.
parts.answer: Fibre adds bulk to the faeces and holds water, which softens them. The bulk stimulates peristalsis, so the faeces move through the gut more easily. Fibre (cellulose) is not digested by human enzymes, so it passes through the gut intact.
parts.working: 1 mark: fibre adds bulk and holds water. 1 mark: softer faeces. 1 mark: stimulates peristalsis. 1 mark: fibre cannot be digested by human enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two nutrients that provide most of the energy in the diet, and name one nutrient needed in small amounts that does not provide energy.
parts.answer: Carbohydrate and fat (protein also accepted); vitamins or minerals (e.g. vitamin C or iron)
parts.working: 1 mark for each energy nutrient named (carbohydrate, fat, protein). 1 mark for a vitamin or mineral.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why an adult woman needs more iron in her diet than an adult man.
parts.answer: She loses iron in menstrual blood; she needs iron to replace the haemoglobin in red blood cells lost during menstruation. (Iron needs also increase in pregnancy and breastfeeding.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: loss in menstrual blood; more blood/haemoglobin lost; higher need in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hostel student eats mostly white rice and bread with very little fruit, vegetables or meat. Suggest two nutrients that may be lacking in this diet and state a good source of each.
parts.answer: e.g. vitamin C – citrus fruits / guava; iron – red meat / spinach; fibre – vegetables / whole grains; protein – meat / pulses; calcium – milk
parts.working: 1 mark each for nutrient with a matching source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the body needs (i) iron and (ii) dietary fibre.
parts.answer: (i) iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells; (ii) fibre helps food move through the gut / prevents constipation
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mineral is needed to make haemoglobin, and whose deficiency causes anaemia?
A calcium
B iron
C iodine
D sodium
parts.answer: B iron
parts.working: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, so a lack reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and causes anaemia. Calcium is needed for bones, iodine for thyroxine, and sodium for nerve impulses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why iodine is needed in the diet and describe what happens in a deficiency.
parts.answer: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine, which controls the metabolic rate. In deficiency, less thyroxine is made, so the thyroid gland enlarges as it tries to make more, causing a goitre. Children can also show poor growth and development.
parts.working: 1 mark: iodine needed to make thyroxine. 1 mark: thyroxine controls metabolic rate. 1 mark: thyroid enlarges (goitre). 1 mark: poor growth or development in children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child with kwashiorkor has a swollen belly and oedema. Explain why the swelling occurs, using knowledge of plasma proteins.
parts.answer: The diet has too little protein, so the plasma protein level falls. The water potential of the blood becomes less negative and the blood loses its osmotic pull for water, so fluid leaks out of the capillaries into the tissues, causing oedema.
parts.working: 1 mark: diet has too little protein. 1 mark: plasma protein levels fall. 1 mark: lower osmotic pull of the blood. 1 mark: fluid leaks out of capillaries into tissues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For vitamin A, state one food source and one function.
parts.answer: Food source: carrots, liver or eggs (any one); function: needed for night vision (or healthy skin/ epithelial tissues).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct food source. 1 mark for a correct function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For vitamin C, state one food source and one function.
parts.answer: Food source: guava, oranges or other citrus fruits (any one); function: needed to make collagen for healthy skin, gums and blood vessels (prevents scurvy).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct food source. 1 mark for a correct function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 100 g of guava contains 228 mg of vitamin C. A teenager needs 65 mg of vitamin C each day. Calculate the mass of guava, in g, that provides the daily need. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the deficiency disease caused by a long-term lack of vitamin C.
parts.answer: scurvy

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why rickets is more common in children who rarely go outdoors and drink little milk.
parts.answer: little sunlight on skin so less vitamin D made; little calcium (from milk) and vitamin D needed to absorb calcium, so bones are soft / weak
parts.working: B1 vitamin D made in skin in sunlight / milk supplies calcium (and vitamin D); B1 calcium needed for strong bones, vitamin D helps calcium absorption.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person's diet is high in sugary drinks and white bread and low in fibre. Which problem is most likely?
A scurvy
B constipation
C rickets
D kwashiorkor
parts.answer: B constipation
parts.working: A low-fibre diet gives small, hard faeces that are difficult to move along the gut, causing constipation. Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C, rickets by lack of vitamin D, and kwashiorkor by severe protein deficiency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 150 g portion of a food contains 6.0 g of protein. Calculate the percentage of protein by mass in the food. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of protein in a 400 g portion of the same food.
parts.working: 1 mark: 6.0 × 400 ÷ 150 seen. 1 mark: 16 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student burns 1.2 g of a peanut in a spirit burner to heat 50 g of water. The temperature of the water rises by 22 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Assume all the energy from the peanut goes to the water. Calculate the energy released to the water, in J.
parts.working: 1 mark: 50 × 4.2 × 22 seen. 1 mark: 4620 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram of peanut, in J/g, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark: 4620 ÷ 1.2 seen. 1 mark: 3850 J/g.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the term for passing out of food that has not been digested or absorbed, as faeces, through the anus?
A ingestion
B digestion
C egestion
D excretion
parts.answer: C egestion
parts.working: This is egestion. Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste (e.g. urea, CO₂); undigested food was never part of body cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State one function of each organ in digestion.
(i) salivary glands
(ii) stomach
(iii) pancreas
(iv) liver
(v) large intestine (colon)
parts.answer: (i) secrete saliva containing amylase; (ii) secretes pepsin / hydrochloric acid, churns food; (iii) secretes amylase, trypsin and lipase into the duodenum; (iv) makes bile; (v) absorbs water
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three functions of the liver in digestion and in the handling of absorbed food.
parts.answer: Any three: makes bile to emulsify fat; stores glycogen; converts excess glucose to glycogen; deaminates excess amino acids to form urea; breaks down or detoxifies harmful substances; stores vitamins and minerals.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of three correct functions with a brief description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzyme in saliva, its substrate and its product.
parts.answer: Amylase; starch; maltose
parts.working: 1 mark: amylase. 1 mark: starch. 1 mark: maltose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the large intestine in the digestive system.
parts.answer: Absorbs water and some minerals from undigested food; bacteria in the colon break down some remaining material; the remaining material is compacted into faeces, which are stored in the rectum before egestion.
parts.working: 1 mark: absorption of water and minerals. 1 mark: bacteria break down some remaining material. 1 mark: faeces formed and stored in the rectum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why peristalsis is needed in the oesophagus and in the intestines.
parts.answer: Peristalsis is a wave of rhythmic contraction of circular and longitudinal muscles that pushes food along the gut. It moves food along even when the body is not upright, and it mixes the food with digestive juices.
parts.working: 1 mark: rhythmic contraction of muscles. 1 mark: pushes food along the gut. 1 mark: moves food even against gravity or mixes contents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define digestion.
parts.answer: the breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules (using mechanical and chemical processes)
parts.working: B1 large / insoluble to small / soluble; B1 so they can be absorbed (or mention of mechanical and chemical).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Write the following in the order food passes through them:
ileum, stomach, rectum, oesophagus, duodenum, colon
parts.answer: oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, ileum, colon, rectum
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair swapped.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each statement to one process: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation or egestion.
(i) amino acids are used by a muscle cell to make new proteins
(ii) a child takes a bite of a samosa
(iii) glucose moves from the ileum into the blood
(iv) fibre leaves the body through the anus
(v) starch is broken down to maltose in the mouth
parts.answer: (i) assimilation (ii) ingestion (iii) absorption (iv) egestion (v) digestion
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organ produces bile?
A gall bladder
B liver
C pancreas
D small intestine
parts.answer: B liver
parts.working: The liver makes bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. The pancreas makes pancreatic juice, and the small intestine does not make bile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the stomach secretes mucus as well as hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid and from being digested by pepsin. The acid kills most bacteria in food and gives pepsin its optimum pH. Without mucus the stomach wall could be damaged, causing ulcers.
parts.working: 1 mark: mucus protects the stomach lining. 1 mark: acid kills bacteria. 1 mark: acid gives the optimum pH for pepsin. 1 mark: without mucus the stomach wall could be damaged or ulcerated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sequence of processes that food undergoes from ingestion to egestion. Name the process at each stage.
parts.answer: Ingestion (taking food into the mouth); digestion (physical and chemical breakdown into small molecules); absorption (small molecules pass into the blood or lymph); assimilation (absorbed molecules are used by cells); egestion (undigested material is removed through the anus).
parts.working: 1 mark each for correctly named and described processes: ingestion, digestion (physical and chemical), absorption, assimilation, egestion (maximum 4 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student eats a meal of rice and daal (lentils). Rice is mainly starch and daal contains much protein. Describe what happens to the starch and protein from the meal as it passes from the mouth to the end of the ileum.
parts.answer: mouth: chewing, salivary amylase starts starch → maltose; stomach: acid stops amylase, pepsin begins protein digestion, churning; duodenum: pancreatic amylase and trypsin continue; bile neutralises acid; maltase on epithelium makes glucose; proteases make amino acids; glucose and amino acids absorbed by villi into capillaries in the ileum
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: chewing increases surface area; salivary amylase in mouth; starch to maltose; stomach acid denatures / stops amylase; pepsin digests protein in stomach; pancreatic juice into duodenum with amylase and trypsin; bile / alkaline juice neutralises acid; maltase converts maltose to glucose (on membranes of epithelium); protein digested to amino acids; absorption of glucose and amino acids in the ileum into blood capillaries of villi.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of organs both secrete enzymes that enter the small intestine?
A stomach and liver
B pancreas and salivary glands
C pancreas and small intestine wall
D liver and gall bladder
parts.answer: C pancreas and small intestine wall
parts.working: The pancreas secretes amylase, lipase and protease into the duodenum, and the wall of the small intestine produces enzymes such as maltase. The stomach produces pepsin, which acts in the stomach, and the liver and gall bladder produce bile, which is not an enzyme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place these organs in the order that food passes through them: large intestine, mouth, stomach, rectum, oesophagus, small intestine.
parts.answer: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct order of the first three. 1 mark for the correct order of the last three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the pancreatic duct opens.
parts.answer: Into the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine).
parts.working: 1 mark: duodenum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient's pancreas is damaged and produces too little pancreatic juice. Explain the effect on the digestion of starch.
parts.answer: Pancreatic amylase is missing, so starch is not fully broken down to maltose in the small intestine.
parts.working: 1 mark: less amylase in the small intestine. 1 mark: starch not fully digested to maltose and then glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect on the digestion of protein.
parts.answer: Protease from the pancreas is missing, so protein is not fully digested into amino acids in the small intestine.
parts.working: 1 mark: less protease, so protein is only partly digested.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect on the digestion of fat.
parts.answer: Lipase from the pancreas is missing, so fats are not broken down into fatty acids and glycerol.
parts.working: 1 mark: less lipase. 1 mark: fats are not digested so less energy and fewer nutrients are absorbed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of villi that increase the rate of absorption of digested food.
parts.answer: microvilli give a large surface area; wall only one cell thick (short diffusion distance); dense capillary network maintains a concentration gradient; lacteal for fat absorption
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the microvilli on the epithelial cells lining the ileum, and explain how they help absorption.
parts.answer: Function: microvilli increase the surface area of the epithelial cells for absorption. Explanation: more food molecules can pass into the cells per unit time, and the membranes carry more carrier proteins, so absorption by diffusion and active transport is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase the surface area. 1 mark: more membrane carrier proteins. 1 mark: faster absorption by diffusion or active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why each villus has a good blood supply.
parts.answer: The capillaries take away absorbed glucose and amino acids quickly, which keeps the concentration in the villus low and maintains a steep concentration gradient for diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: capillaries take absorbed molecules into the blood. 1 mark: carried away quickly. 1 mark: keeps a steep concentration gradient so diffusion continues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how glucose absorbed from the ileum is transported to, and handled by, the liver.
parts.answer: Glucose passes into the capillaries of the villus and then into the hepatic portal vein, which carries it to the liver. The liver converts excess glucose into glycogen for storage and releases glucose back into the blood when blood sugar falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose enters the hepatic portal vein. 1 mark: carried to the liver. 1 mark: excess converted to glycogen for storage. 1 mark: glucose released back into the blood when needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define absorption.
parts.answer: Movement of digested food molecules and ions through the wall of the gut into the blood or lymph.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement of digested food through the gut wall into the blood or lymph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances absorbed in the small intestine.
parts.answer: Any two of: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, vitamins, minerals.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named substances.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Into which structure in a villus are most fatty acids and glycerol absorbed?
A blood capillary
B lacteal
C hepatic portal vein
D artery
parts.answer: B lacteal
parts.working: Fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lacteal, a lymphatic vessel at the centre of the villus. Glucose and amino acids enter the blood capillaries instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In coeliac disease, eating gluten damages the lining of the small intestine and the villi become flattened. In one patient the absorptive surface area fell from 32 m² to 4 m². Calculate the percentage decrease in surface area. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why an untreated patient with coeliac disease may lose body mass even though they eat normally.
parts.answer: smaller surface area means less glucose, amino acids and fats absorbed into the blood; less energy and fewer nutrients available, so body stores are used
parts.working: B1 less absorption of digested food; B1 less energy / materials, so fat or protein stores are used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of ileum has a surface area of 0.08 m² without its folds and villi, and 0.80 m² with them. Calculate the factor by which the surface area is increased.
parts.answer: 10 times
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.80 ÷ 0.08 seen. 1 mark: 10 times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a large surface area is important for absorption.
parts.answer: A large surface area lets more molecules pass into the blood in each second, so the rate of absorption is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: more area for diffusion or transport. 1 mark: more molecules absorbed per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sodium ions help glucose to be absorbed in the ileum.
parts.answer: Sodium ions are pumped out of the epithelial cells by active transport, so their concentration inside the cell is low. Sodium ions diffuse back in down their gradient through a carrier protein that carries glucose in at the same time. The glucose then diffuses out into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: sodium pumped out by active transport. 1 mark: sodium diffuses back in down its gradient. 1 mark: glucose carried in with the sodium through a carrier protein. 1 mark: glucose diffuses from the cell into the blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into lacteals rather than into blood capillaries.
parts.answer: Fatty acids and glycerol are reformed into fats inside the villus cells, forming droplets too large and insoluble to enter the blood capillaries easily. These fat droplets pass into the lacteal, which is a lymph vessel, and are carried to the blood by the lymphatic system.
parts.working: 1 mark: fats are re-formed inside the epithelial cells. 1 mark: fat droplets are too large for the capillaries. 1 mark: lacteal is a lymph vessel that carries fat to the blood via the lymphatic system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define assimilation.
parts.answer: the movement of digested food molecules into the cells of the body where they are used, becoming part of the cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: After absorption, glucose and amino acids travel to the liver. Describe what happens to them in the body after absorption.
parts.answer: carried in the hepatic portal vein to the liver; glucose used in respiration to release energy or stored as glycogen in liver and muscles; amino acids used to make proteins (e.g. enzymes, plasma proteins); excess amino acids deaminated in the liver to form urea
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: hepatic portal vein; glucose used for respiration; excess glucose converted to glycogen (stored in liver / muscles); amino acids used to build proteins; excess amino acids deaminated / urea formed in liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where most water is absorbed in the alimentary canal.
parts.answer: small intestine

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Each day about 9.0 dm³ of water (from food, drinks and digestive juices) enters the small intestine. The small intestine absorbs 85 % of this water. The colon absorbs 90 % of the water that reaches it.
Calculate the volume of water lost in the faeces each day, in cm³.
parts.answer: 135 cm³
parts.working: M1 water reaching colon = 9.0 × 0.15 = 1.35 dm³; M1 water left = 1.35 × 0.10 = 0.135 dm³; A1 135 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of a villus increases the rate of diffusion of digested food into the blood?
A a thick muscular wall
B a single layer of thin epithelial cells
C a large number of goblet cells
D a thick cellulose wall
parts.answer: B a single layer of thin epithelial cells
parts.working: A single thin layer of epithelial cells gives a short diffusion distance between the gut lumen and the blood. Muscle and cellulose would slow diffusion, and goblet cells secrete mucus rather than absorbing food.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which combination of digested food leaves a villus in the hepatic portal vein?
A fatty acids and glycerol
B glucose and amino acids
C glucose and fatty acids
D glycerol only
parts.answer: B glucose and amino acids
parts.working: Capillaries in the villus drain into the hepatic portal vein, which carries glucose and amino acids to the liver. Fatty acids and glycerol enter a lacteal and reach the blood through the lymphatic system, so A and C are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student fills a Visking tubing bag with starch solution and glucose solution, places it in a beaker of water and tests the water after 30 minutes. Describe what the student observes with Benedict's solution and with iodine solution, and explain what this shows.
parts.answer: The water gives a positive Benedict's test (glucose has passed through the membrane) but no blue-black colour with iodine (starch stays inside). The Visking membrane is partially permeable: small glucose molecules pass through its pores, but the large starch molecules cannot.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive Benedict's test in the water. 1 mark: no blue-black colour with iodine in the water. 1 mark: membrane is partially permeable (pores). 1 mark: glucose small enough to pass, starch too large.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each part of the eye:
(i) cornea
(ii) iris
(iii) lens
(iv) retina
(v) optic nerve
parts.answer: (i) refracts (bends) light entering the eye; (ii) controls how much light enters (changes pupil size); (iii) focuses light onto the retina (fine focusing); (iv) contains light receptors (rods and cones); (v) carries nerve impulses from the retina to the brain.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare rods and cones, stating for each the light conditions in which it works best, whether it detects colour, and where it is mainly found in the retina.
parts.answer: Rods: work in dim light; black and white only (no colour); found throughout the retina but not at the fovea. Cones: work in bright light; detect colour (three types); concentrated in the fovea.
parts.working: B1 rods light / colour; B1 rods distribution; B1 cones light / colour; B1 cones concentrated at fovea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to see the colours of objects at night.
parts.answer: Cones do not work in dim light; only rods respond, and rods do not detect colour.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When the eye focuses on a close object, which structure contracts so that the lens becomes fatter?
A ciliary muscle
B suspensory ligament
C iris
D retina
parts.answer: A ciliary muscle
parts.working: Ciliary muscles contract, slackening the suspensory ligaments, so the lens becomes fatter and refracts light more strongly. Suspensory ligaments do not contract; they are pulled tight or slackened by the ciliary muscles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the layer at the back of the eye that contains light-sensitive cells.
parts.answer: retina
parts.working: retina

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two types of light-sensitive cell found in the retina.
parts.answer: rods and cones
parts.working: 1 mark each: rods (work in dim light, no colour); cones (work in bright light, detect colour).

practice.stem: A student walks from a dark cinema into bright sunlight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the radial muscles of the iris when the pupil constricts.
parts.answer: They relax.
parts.working: 1 mark: radial muscles relax (circular muscles contract).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the pupil constricts in bright light.
parts.answer: Less light enters the eye, which protects the retina from damage or overstimulation.
parts.working: 1 mark: less light enters the eye; 1 mark: protects the retina from damage/overstimulation.

practice.stem: A student leaves a dark cinema hall in Islamabad and walks out into bright sunlight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the changes in the iris when the student walks into the bright sunlight.
parts.answer: Circular muscles of the iris contract; radial muscles relax; pupil becomes smaller (constricts), so less light enters and the retina is protected from damage.
parts.working: B1 circular contract; B1 radial relax; B1 pupil smaller so less light enters / protects retina.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of response this is and why it is useful that it is automatic.
parts.answer: A reflex (involuntary) action; it is very fast and does not need thought, so the retina is protected immediately.
parts.working: B1 reflex; B1 fast / no conscious thought.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A girl looks up from a book she is reading to a bird far away. Which row shows the changes in her eyes when she focuses on the book again?
A ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments tighten; lens becomes thinner
B ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken; lens becomes fatter
C ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments tighten; lens becomes fatter
D ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments slacken; lens becomes thinner
parts.answer: B ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken; lens becomes fatter
parts.working: For a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the elastic lens becomes fatter (more convex) to refract light more. A describes focusing on a distant object.

practice.stem: A bird-watcher looks at a bird on a distant tree, then at a page of a field guide held close to the eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments change when the eye focuses on a distant tree.
parts.answer: The ciliary muscles relax; the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight; the lens becomes thinner and refracts less light.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments tighten and pull on the lens; lens becomes thinner (refracts less).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which the eye changes its focus from near to far objects.
parts.answer: accommodation
parts.working: accommodation

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person tries to see the colours of a painting in a dim room and can only see it poorly. Why?
A the lens cannot focus light in dim conditions
B only rods are stimulated in dim light, and rods do not detect colour
C the iris is fully closed, so no light reaches the retina
D the cones are damaged by low light levels
parts.answer: B only rods are stimulated in dim light, and rods do not detect colour
parts.working: Rods work in dim light but do not detect colour; cones, which detect colour, need brighter light. The iris opens (dilates) in dim light, so option C is wrong.

practice.stem: A student shines a torch into one eye of a partner in a dim room and measures the pupil diameter with a ruler. Time 0 s is when the torch is switched on. Results: 0 s 4.0 mm; 5 s 3.2 mm; 10 s 2.7 mm; 15 s 2.6 mm; 20 s 2.6 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: time after the torch is switched on (s). Dependent: pupil diameter (mm).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in pupil diameter between 0 s and 10 s.
parts.working: (4.0 − 2.7) ÷ 4.0 × 100 = 32.5 %. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one control variable the student should keep the same, and explain why.
parts.answer: Distance of the torch from the eye (or the same torch); this keeps the light intensity the same so that only time changes.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid control variable; 1 mark for a reason linked to a fair test.

practice.stem: A man on a train is reading messages on his phone, then looks out of the window at hills several kilometres away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the eye that allow the man to focus on the distant hills after looking at his phone.
parts.answer: Ciliary muscles relax; suspensory ligaments are pulled tight (tension increases); lens is pulled thinner / less convex.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lens must change shape for the image to be focused on the retina.
parts.answer: Light from a distant object needs less refraction (rays almost parallel); a thinner lens refracts light less, so the image is focused on the retina rather than in front of it.
parts.working: B1 distant object needs less refraction / bending; B1 thinner lens bends light less to focus on retina.

practice.stem:
A volunteer's pupil was photographed after two minutes at each light intensity and its diameter measured.
Light intensity / lux : pupil diameter / mm
50 : 6.4
200 : 4.8
500 : 3.6
1000 : 2.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in pupil diameter between 50 lux and 1000 lux.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between light intensity and pupil diameter.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, pupil diameter decreases (not in direct proportion).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the volunteer stayed at each light intensity for two minutes before the photograph was taken.
parts.answer: To allow time for the pupil to adjust fully / reach a steady size.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one variable, other than light intensity, that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Distance of the light from the eye / same eye measured / same volunteer / same direction of light / looking at the same object at the same distance.

practice.stem: A bird flies across a field. Light from the bird enters one eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway taken by information from light entering the eye to the brain.
parts.answer: Light is refracted by the cornea and lens onto the retina; rods and cones are stimulated; impulses pass along the optic nerve (sensory neurone) to the brain, which interprets the image.
parts.working: 1 mark each: refraction by cornea and lens focuses the image on the retina; rods/cones stimulated (receptors); impulses along the optic nerve; brain interprets the image.

practice.stem: A student measured one pupil in bright light (2.0 mm diameter) and in dim light (6.5 mm diameter).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in pupil diameter from bright light to dim light.
parts.working: (6.5 − 2.0) ÷ 2.0 × 100 = 225 %. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the radial muscles of the iris in dim light.
parts.answer: The radial muscles contract, pulling the iris open so the pupil dilates and more light enters the eye.
parts.working: 1 mark: radial muscles contract; 1 mark: pupil dilates / more light enters.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why this change in pupil diameter is an example of a reflex action.
parts.answer: It is rapid, automatic and involuntary (no conscious decision).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'When focusing on a near object, the ciliary muscles relax and the lens becomes thinner.' Identify the error and write the correct statement.
parts.answer: Error: the ciliary muscles contract (not relax), so the lens becomes fatter (not thinner). Correct: for a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes fatter.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct statement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lens must become fatter to see a near object clearly.
parts.answer: Light from a near object diverges more, so the lens must refract it more strongly to focus it on the retina.
parts.working: 1 mark: rays from a near object diverge; 1 mark: more refraction is needed to focus them on the retina.

practice.stem: A girl accidentally touches a hot tawa (griddle) and pulls her hand away before she feels pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these in the order an impulse passes along a reflex arc, starting with the receptor:
motor neurone, effector (muscle), relay neurone, receptor, sensory neurone
parts.answer: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector (muscle)
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where the relay neurone is found.
parts.answer: In the spinal cord (central nervous system).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of a reflex action.
parts.answer: It is very fast / automatic, so damage to the body is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three types of neurone and state the job of each.
parts.answer: Sensory neurone: carries impulses from a receptor to the CNS. Relay (intermediate) neurone: within the CNS, links sensory and motor neurones. Motor neurone: carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the name and function of each neurone type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two differences between a reflex action and a voluntary action.
parts.answer: Reflex: rapid and automatic, with no conscious decision, and the pathway goes through the spinal cord; voluntary: slower, involves a conscious decision and the brain. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid differences: reflex is faster / automatic; voluntary needs a conscious decision; reflex passes through the spinal cord rather than the brain; voluntary action involves the brain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a reflex action.
parts.answer: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not need conscious thought.
parts.working: 1 mark: rapid/automatic; 1 mark: response to a stimulus without conscious control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of the part of a neurone that carries impulses away from the cell body.
parts.answer: axon
parts.working: axon

practice.stem:
A student measures his reaction time. A partner drops a metre ruler between his finger and thumb, and he catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls is recorded.
Trial : distance / cm
1 : 18
2 : 15
3 : 21
4 : 16
5 : 15
reaction time (s) = √(2d ÷ 9.8), where d is the distance in metres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance fallen.
parts.answer: 17 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the formula to calculate the reaction time for the mean distance. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is not a reflex action.
parts.answer: The response involves the brain and is a conscious decision (voluntary), so it is slower than a reflex.
parts.working: B1 involves brain / conscious; B1 voluntary / not automatic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student touches a hot pan and quickly pulls the hand away. Describe the pathway of the impulses in this reflex action.
parts.answer: Heat receptors in the skin are stimulated; the sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord; a relay neurone in the spinal cord passes it to a motor neurone; the motor neurone carries the impulse to the arm muscle (effector), which contracts and pulls the hand away.
parts.working: 1 mark: receptor stimulated and sensory neurone impulse; 1 mark: relay neurone in spinal cord; 1 mark: motor neurone to muscle effector; 1 mark: muscle contracts, hand pulled away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a reflex response is much faster than a conscious response.
parts.answer: Fewer neurones and synapses are involved, and the pathway passes through the spinal cord rather than the brain; no conscious decision is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer neurones/synapses; 1 mark: spinal cord used, not the brain; 1 mark: no conscious decision needed.

practice.stem: In a ruler drop test, the ruler falls 0.20 m before the student catches it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the reaction time, using t = √(2d ÷ g) with g = 9.8 m/s², to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: √(2 × 0.20 ÷ 9.8) = √0.0408 = 0.202 s, so 0.20 s to 2 decimal places. 1 mark for method, 1 mark for answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to make this reaction time measurement more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat the test several times and calculate the mean (or use the same person and the same ruler).
parts.working: 1 mark: repeats and mean / controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe where the cell bodies of sensory and motor neurones are found.
parts.answer: The cell body of a sensory neurone lies outside the CNS (in a ganglion beside the spinal cord); the cell body of a motor neurone lies within the CNS (spinal cord or brain).
parts.working: 1 mark: sensory cell body outside the CNS; 1 mark: motor cell body within the CNS.

practice.stem: A patient has damage to the motor neurones that run from the spinal cord to the muscles of his left leg. The sensory neurones are not damaged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the patient can feel a pin prick on his foot but cannot move his foot away.
parts.answer: Receptors and sensory neurones still work, so impulses travel to the spinal cord and up to the brain (pain felt); but impulses cannot travel along the damaged motor neurones to the leg muscles (effectors), so no movement.
parts.working: B1 sensory pathway intact → brain; B1 motor neurones damaged; B1 impulse cannot reach effector / muscle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a voluntary action and a reflex action.
parts.answer: Voluntary: involves conscious thought / the brain decides, slower. Reflex: automatic, no conscious thought, faster.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person may pull their hand away from a hot object before they feel the pain.
parts.answer: The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord, so the muscle responds before the impulse reaches the brain; pain is perceived only after the brain receives impulses along a longer pathway.
parts.working: 1 mark: reflex pathway through spinal cord; 1 mark: response starts before the brain receives impulses; 1 mark: pain is felt after the brain processes the impulses.

practice.stem: Students measured reaction times with the ruler drop test. Five distances (cm) were recorded: 18.0, 21.5, 19.0, 22.5 and 20.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance of the ruler drop, in cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the reaction time using the mean distance from part (a), using t = √(2d ÷ g) with g = 9.8 m/s², to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: d = 0.202 m; t = √(2 × 0.202 ÷ 9.8) = 0.203 s. 1 mark for converting to metres and using the formula; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify one source of error in this method.
parts.answer: The ruler is not always released from the same height, and the student's reaction time varies from trial to trial (for example by anticipating the drop).
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid source of error.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Repeat with more trials and a mean; release the ruler from the same starting position each time; use an electronic timer.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid improvement.

practice.stem: An impulse takes 15 ms to travel 1.5 m along a neurone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the impulse in m/s.
parts.working: 1.5 ÷ 0.015 = 100 m/s. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the time, in ms, for the impulse to travel 4.5 m at this speed.
parts.answer: 45 ms

parts.label: a
parts.text: A relay neurone in the spinal cord is damaged so that no impulses pass from sensory neurones to motor neurones. Explain what happens when a person touches a hot object.
parts.answer: No impulse reaches the motor neurone, so the muscle does not contract and the hand is not pulled away; the reflex fails. The impulse may still reach the brain, so the heat or pain can still be felt.
parts.working: 1 mark: no impulse reaches the motor neurone/effector; 1 mark: the hand is not pulled away; 1 mark: the impulse may still reach the brain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term hormone.
parts.answer: A chemical substance produced by a gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs.
parts.working: B1 chemical made by gland; B1 carried in blood to target organ(s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gland that secretes each hormone: (i) adrenaline, (ii) testosterone, (iii) oestrogen.
parts.answer: (i) adrenal gland; (ii) testes; (iii) ovaries.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gland that secretes adrenaline and the gland that secretes insulin.
parts.answer: adrenal gland; pancreas
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between hormonal and nervous control.
parts.answer: Hormones travel in the blood and are slower to act, but their effects last longer; nervous impulses travel along neurones and act quickly over a short time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three effects of adrenaline on the body during fight or flight.
parts.answer: Heart rate increases; breathing rate increases; glycogen is converted to glucose; blood is diverted to the muscles; pupils dilate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A person's resting heart rate is 72 beats per minute. After adrenaline is released, the heart rate rises to 108 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate.
parts.working: (108 − 72) ÷ 72 × 100 = 50 %. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the organ that is the target of adrenaline's effect on heart rate.
parts.answer: heart
parts.working: heart

practice.stem: A cricket batter is about to face a very fast bowler in front of a large crowd in Lahore. His adrenal glands release adrenaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three effects of adrenaline on the body.
parts.answer: Any three of: increased heart rate (pulse); increased breathing rate; dilated pupils; increased blood glucose concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how one of these effects helps the batter to react to the ball.
parts.answer: e.g. higher heart rate / blood glucose supplies more oxygen and glucose to muscles; faster respiration releases more energy for muscle contraction.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen / glucose to muscles; B1 more respiration / energy for movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how adrenaline increases the blood glucose concentration.
parts.answer: Adrenaline acts on the liver; the liver converts glycogen to glucose; the glucose is released into the blood, raising the blood glucose concentration and providing energy for respiration in the muscles.
parts.working: 1 mark: adrenaline acts on the liver; 1 mark: glycogen converted to glucose; 1 mark: glucose released into the blood for respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the speed and duration of hormonal responses with nervous responses.
parts.answer: A nervous response is very fast and short-lived; a hormonal response starts more slowly because the hormone must travel in the blood, but it lasts much longer; hormones reach all cells but act only on target cells with specific receptors.
parts.working: 1 mark: nervous response is fast; 1 mark: hormonal response is slower to start; 1 mark: nervous response is short-lived and hormonal response lasts longer; 1 mark: hormones act only on target cells with receptors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a danger has passed, the effects of adrenaline wear off. Describe how the body returns to normal.
parts.answer: Adrenaline is broken down (mainly in the liver) and removed from the blood; release from the adrenal glands stops; heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose return to normal.
parts.working: 1 mark: adrenaline broken down/removed; 1 mark: release stops; 1 mark: heart rate, breathing and blood glucose return to normal.

practice.stem: A student counts a pulse of 25 beats in 15 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
parts.answer: 100 beats per minute
parts.working: 25 ÷ 15 × 60 = 100 beats per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one factor that would make this measurement less accurate.
parts.answer: Errors in timing or counting the pulse; movement or exercise before measuring; any valid factor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare nervous control with hormonal control. Give three differences.
parts.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses / hormonal: chemicals; nervous: along neurones / hormonal: in the blood; nervous: very fast / hormonal: slower; nervous: short-lived effect / hormonal: longer-lasting; nervous: precise target / hormonal: may affect several organs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct comparison, max 3. Both sides needed for each mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why control of blood glucose is better done by hormones than by nerves.
parts.answer: The response needs to last a long time and affect organs throughout the body (liver, muscles); speed is not essential, and hormones in the blood reach all target cells.
parts.working: B1 long-lasting / continuous; B1 widespread targets / speed not needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight. Include four effects.
parts.answer: Faster heart rate sends more blood (oxygen and glucose) to the muscles; faster breathing brings in more oxygen; glycogen is converted to glucose to provide energy for respiration; blood is diverted from the digestive system; pupils dilate to let in more light.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of four effects, each with a link to supplying oxygen or glucose, or to a faster response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hormones act only on target cells that have specific receptors. Explain why a hormone circulating in the blood affects only certain cells.
parts.answer: Hormones are carried to all cells in the blood, but only cells with complementary receptor proteins bind the hormone and respond; other cells have no receptor, so they do not respond.
parts.working: 1 mark: hormone carried to all cells; 1 mark: specific receptors bind the hormone; 1 mark: only target cells with the receptor respond.

practice.stem: After a person is frightened by a loud noise, their breathing rate is recorded: 16 breaths per minute at 0 min, 24 at 2 min and 30 at 4 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in breathing rate from 0 min to 4 min.
parts.working: (30 − 16) ÷ 16 × 100 = 87.5 %. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why breathing rate increases after adrenaline is released.
parts.answer: Adrenaline increases breathing rate, providing more oxygen for respiration in the muscles, which releases energy for fight or flight.
parts.working: 1 mark: adrenaline increases breathing rate; 1 mark: more oxygen for respiration/energy release.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the nervous system and the endocrine system work together in a fright response.
parts.answer: Receptors detect the threat and send impulses to the brain; the brain sends nerve impulses to the adrenal glands; the adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood; adrenaline acts on target organs such as the heart, liver and muscles.
parts.working: 1 mark: receptors and nerve impulses to the brain; 1 mark: brain signals the adrenal glands; 1 mark: adrenaline released into the blood; 1 mark: target organs respond.

practice.stem: A potted plant is left on a windowsill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms (i) phototropism and (ii) gravitropism.
parts.answer: (i) a growth response of a plant to the direction of light; (ii) a growth response of a plant to gravity.
parts.working: B1 each; must refer to growth response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether a shoot shows positive or negative phototropism and positive or negative gravitropism.
parts.answer: Positive phototropism (grows towards light); negative gravitropism (grows away from gravity / upwards).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shoot bends towards a light source. Which statement explains this?
A auxin accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more
B auxin accumulates on the lit side and makes those cells elongate more
C light destroys auxin on the shaded side, so those cells shrink
D auxin is made only in the roots and moves up the shoot
parts.answer: A auxin accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more
parts.working: Auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot tip; cells there elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light. Option B reverses the effect; auxin is made in shoot tips, not roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the plant hormone involved in tropic responses.
parts.answer: auxin
parts.working: auxin

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where auxin is produced in a shoot.
parts.answer: shoot tip (apex)
parts.working: accept tip of the shoot / coleoptile tip

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tropic response of a root growing downwards.
parts.answer: positive gravitropism (geotropism)
parts.working: positive gravitropism / geotropism

practice.stem: A bean seedling's shoot was 4.0 cm long on day 1 and 5.2 cm long on day 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in shoot length.
parts.working: (5.2 − 4.0) ÷ 4.0 × 100 = 30 %. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one condition that should be kept constant in this investigation.
parts.answer: Temperature (or light, water or species of seedling); any one.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student places a pot of seedlings in a box with a small hole on one side, so light enters only from that side. After 3 days the shoots bend towards the hole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the stimulus.
parts.answer: light (from the hole in the box)
parts.working: light

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the shoots bend towards the light.
parts.answer: Auxin moves to the shaded side; cells on the shaded side elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.
parts.working: 1 mark: auxin moves to the shaded side; 1 mark: greater elongation on the shaded side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to grow towards light coming from one side.
parts.answer: Auxin is made in the shoot tip; it diffuses down the shoot; auxin moves to / accumulates on the shaded side; auxin stimulates cell elongation, so cells on the shaded side grow longer and the shoot bends towards the light.
parts.working: 1 mark each: made in tip; diffuses down; more on shaded side; stimulates cell elongation on shaded side → bending.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potted bean seedling is placed on its side in the dark. Which statement explains why the shoot grows upwards?
A Auxin collects on the upper side, so cells on the upper side elongate more.
B Auxin collects on the lower side, so cells on the lower side elongate more.
C Auxin is destroyed by gravity on the lower side, so cells on the upper side elongate more.
D Auxin collects on the lower side and stops cells on the lower side from elongating.
parts.answer: B Auxin collects on the lower side, so cells on the lower side elongate more.
parts.working: In a horizontal shoot auxin accumulates on the lower side; it stimulates cell elongation there, so the lower side grows faster and the shoot curves upwards (negative gravitropism).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why roots and shoots respond differently to gravity.
parts.answer: Auxin moves to the lower side in both. In shoots, auxin stimulates elongation on the lower side, so the shoot grows upwards (negative gravitropism). In roots, auxin inhibits elongation on the lower side, so the root grows downwards (positive gravitropism).
parts.working: 1 mark: auxin moves to the lower side in both; 1 mark: shoot: stimulates elongation, bends up; 1 mark: root: inhibits elongation, bends down; 1 mark: negative (shoot) and positive (root) named.

practice.stem:
A student tests coleoptiles (shoot tips) for 24 hours.
A: intact tip, light from one side: bends towards the light by 25°
B: tip removed: no curvature (0°)
C: tip removed, agar block containing auxin placed on one side: bends away from the block by 20°
D: tip covered by an opaque cap, light from one side: no curvature (0°)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the coleoptile in result D does not curve.
parts.answer: The tip is covered by an opaque cap, so it cannot detect the light; auxin is not redistributed, so the shoot grows straight.
parts.working: 1 mark: tip is needed to detect light; 1 mark: auxin not redistributed / no unequal growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the shoot in result C curves away from the block.
parts.answer: Auxin on one side makes the cells on that side elongate more, so the shoot bends away from the block.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A gardener pinches out the tip of a plant shoot to make the plant bushier. Which explanation is correct?
A auxin from the tip inhibits side buds; removing the tip removes this inhibition, so side buds grow
B auxin from the tip is needed by side buds to grow, so removing the tip slows them down
C pinching out the tip stops auxin being made in the roots, so the shoot grows more
D removing the tip increases the water supply to the side buds
parts.answer: A auxin from the tip inhibits side buds; removing the tip removes this inhibition, so side buds grow
parts.working: This is apical dominance: auxin from the tip inhibits lateral buds. Pinching out removes the source, so more side shoots develop. Option B reverses the effect.

practice.stem: Cress seedlings were grown for 48 hours in a control solution and in a solution of auxin at the same concentration. Mean root length: control 40 mm; auxin 28 mm. Mean shoot length: control 12 mm; auxin 15 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in root length caused by auxin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why auxin at this concentration reduces root length but increases shoot length.
parts.answer: Roots are more sensitive to auxin than shoots: at this concentration auxin inhibits elongation of root cells but stimulates elongation of shoot cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: roots are more sensitive; 1 mark: inhibits roots but stimulates shoots.

practice.stem:
Three groups of five oat seedlings were lit from one side for 6 hours. In group 1 the seedlings were untreated; in group 2 the tip of each shoot was covered with a foil cap; in group 3 the tip was cut off. The angle by which each shoot bent towards the light was measured.
Group : angles / °
untreated : 32, 28, 35, 30, 25
foil cap on tip : 2, 0, 1, 0, 2
tip removed : 0, 0, 1, 0, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean angle of curvature for each group.
parts.answer: untreated 30°; foil cap 1°; tip removed 0.2°
parts.working: M1 sum ÷ 5; A1 all three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the results show about where light is detected and where auxin is made.
parts.answer: Light is detected by the tip: covering the tip stops bending although the rest of the shoot is exposed; removing the tip stops bending, so the tip produces the substance (auxin) that causes bending.
parts.working: B1 tip detects light (foil result); B1 tip produces auxin / growth substance (tip-removed result); B1 comparison with untreated control.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why each group contained five seedlings.
parts.answer: To calculate a mean / reduce the effect of individual variation / identify anomalies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe an experiment to show that light, not gravity, causes a shoot to bend towards light. Include the apparatus, the control and what you would measure.
parts.answer: Use seedlings in a box with a hole so light comes from one side. Control: seedlings with light from all sides (or the same plant orientation). Keep the species, age, water and temperature the same. Measure the angle of bending with a protractor after a set time. Repeat and calculate a mean. Show gravity is not the cause by placing a pot on its side on a rotating (horizontal) clinostat or a control with the box turned.
parts.working: 1 mark: light from one side is the independent variable with a suitable control; 1 mark: variables kept the same (species, age, water, temperature); 1 mark: angle of bending measured with a protractor after a set time; 1 mark: repeats and mean; 1 mark: control shows gravity is not the cause (light from all sides / rotated pots); 1 mark: clear apparatus and method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the bending of shoots towards light benefits a plant growing in a shaded forest.
parts.answer: The shoot grows towards a gap in the canopy, so its leaves receive more light for photosynthesis, giving more energy for growth and survival.
parts.working: 1 mark: shoot grows towards light/a gap; 1 mark: more light absorbed by leaves; 1 mark: more photosynthesis, growth and survival.

practice.stem: In one hour, a coleoptile grew 8 mm on the shaded side and 3 mm on the lit side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of growth on the shaded side to growth on the lit side, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67 (2.67 : 1). 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the answer to part (a) to explain the direction in which the shoot bends.
parts.answer: More growth on the shaded side causes the shoot to bend towards the light.
parts.working: 1 mark: more elongation on the shaded side; 1 mark: shoot bends towards the lit side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes insulin and glucagon.
parts.answer: Pancreas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of insulin when blood glucose concentration rises after a meal.
parts.answer: Insulin is secreted into the blood; it causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen (storage), so the blood glucose concentration falls.
parts.working: B1 glucose taken up by liver / muscle; B1 converted to glycogen / blood glucose falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of glucagon on the liver.
parts.answer: Liver converts (breaks down) glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone lowers the concentration of glucose in the blood?
A adrenaline
B glucagon
C insulin
D thyroxine
parts.answer: C insulin
parts.working: Insulin, made by the pancreas, makes cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen. Glucagon raises blood glucose (option B); thyroxine controls metabolic rate.

practice.stem: The pancreas contains groups of cells called the islets of Langerhans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organ that contains the islets of Langerhans.
parts.answer: pancreas
parts.working: pancreas

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of cell in the islets that secretes insulin.
parts.answer: beta cells
parts.working: beta cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the storage carbohydrate that the liver makes from excess glucose.
parts.answer: glycogen
parts.working: glycogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the main cause of Type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: The pancreas does not produce enough (or any) insulin.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the main cause of Type 2 diabetes.
parts.answer: Body cells do not respond properly to insulin (insulin resistance); it is linked to diet, obesity and lack of exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark: cells do not respond to insulin; 1 mark: linked to diet, obesity or inactivity.

practice.stem: A student's blood glucose was measured after a meal of rice. Time 0 min: 4.5 mmol/dm³; 30 min: 8.0 mmol/dm³; 90 min: 5.2 mmol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in blood glucose between 0 min and the peak value, in mmol/dm³.
parts.answer: 3.5 mmol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the time at which blood glucose was highest.
parts.answer: 30 min
parts.working: 30 min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why blood glucose fell between 30 and 90 minutes.
parts.answer: Insulin is released; glucose is taken up by cells and converted to glycogen (stored in liver and muscles) or used in respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: insulin released; 1 mark: glucose taken up and stored as glycogen or used in respiration.

practice.stem: A 12-year-old boy in Quetta is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the cause of type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: The pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin, because the insulin-secreting cells are destroyed (by the body's immune system).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two symptoms of type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: Any two of: high blood glucose; glucose in the urine; thirst; frequent urination; tiredness; weight loss; blurred vision.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how type 1 diabetes is treated.
parts.answer: Regular injections of insulin (or insulin pump); monitoring blood glucose concentration; controlling diet (carbohydrate intake) and exercise.
parts.working: B1 insulin injections; B1 any other: monitor glucose / control diet / regular meals.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person eats a large plate of rice. Which events follow?
A Glucagon is secreted and the liver converts glycogen to glucose.
B Insulin is secreted and the liver converts glucose to glycogen.
C Insulin is secreted and the liver converts glycogen to glucose.
D Glucagon is secreted and the liver converts glucose to glycogen.
parts.answer: B Insulin is secreted and the liver converts glucose to glycogen.
parts.working: Digested starch raises blood glucose, so the pancreas secretes insulin, which makes the liver store glucose as glycogen. A describes the response to low blood glucose.

practice.stem: After a meal, a person's blood glucose falls from 9.0 mmol/dm³ to 5.4 mmol/dm³ as insulin is released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in blood glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where most glycogen is stored in the body.
parts.answer: liver and muscles
parts.working: liver and muscles

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why people with Type 1 diabetes must inject insulin rather than take it as tablets, and why their blood glucose must be monitored.
parts.answer: Insulin is a protein that would be digested in the gut, so it must be injected into the blood. Blood glucose must be monitored so the right amount of insulin is given to keep it within normal limits (preventing it becoming too high or too low).
parts.working: 1 mark: insulin is a protein digested by enzymes; 1 mark: injection puts it into the blood; 1 mark: monitoring decides the amount needed; 1 mark: keeps glucose within normal limits.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone is released when blood glucose concentration falls below normal?
A insulin
B glucagon
C ADH
D thyroxine
parts.answer: B glucagon
parts.working: Glucagon, from the alpha cells of the pancreas, causes the liver to convert glycogen to glucose, raising blood glucose. Insulin would lower it further (option A).

practice.stem:
Two people drank a glucose drink after fasting overnight. Their blood glucose concentration (mmol/dm³) was measured.
Time / min : person A : person B
0 : 5.0 : 6.2
30 : 7.8 : 12.4
60 : 6.4 : 12.9
120 : 5.2 : 11.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose concentration from 0 to 30 minutes for each person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which person has type 1 diabetes. Use the data to explain your answer.
parts.answer: Person B; glucose rises much higher (to 12.4) and is still high (11.0) after 120 minutes; no / little insulin is secreted, so glucose is not taken up by liver and muscle and converted to glycogen.
parts.working: B1 B; B1 data quoted (higher peak / stays high); B1 lack of insulin so glucose not converted to glycogen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the blood glucose of person A returns to normal by 120 minutes.
parts.answer: Rise in glucose detected by the pancreas; insulin secreted, causing liver and muscles to convert glucose to glycogen; this is negative feedback.
parts.working: B1 insulin released; B1 glucose stored as glycogen / negative feedback.

practice.stem: Runners in a marathon in Lahore are running for more than three hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During a long-distance run, blood glucose concentration begins to fall. Explain how the body brings it back to normal.
parts.answer: Fall detected by the pancreas; less insulin and more glucagon secreted; glucagon travels in the blood to the liver; liver converts glycogen to glucose, which enters the blood; glucose rises back towards the set point — negative feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: pancreas detects fall; glucagon secreted (insulin reduced); liver breaks down glycogen to glucose; glucose released into blood; negative feedback / returns to set point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why adrenaline released at the start of the race also helps the runner.
parts.answer: Adrenaline raises blood glucose concentration (by glycogen breakdown) and increases heart rate, so more glucose and oxygen reach the muscles for respiration.
parts.working: B1 increases blood glucose; B1 more glucose / oxygen delivered to muscles for respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person with Type 2 diabetes may produce insulin but still have high blood glucose.
parts.answer: Body cells (such as muscle and liver cells) respond poorly to insulin, so less glucose is taken up and stored; blood glucose stays high even though insulin is present.
parts.working: 1 mark: cells do not respond to insulin properly; 1 mark: less glucose taken up by cells; 1 mark: glucose remains high despite insulin.

practice.stem:
Three people had fasting blood tests.
Person X: glucose 5.0 mmol/dm³, insulin 60 units
Person Y: glucose 9.5 mmol/dm³, insulin 220 units
Person Z: glucose 9.8 mmol/dm³, insulin 4 units

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person most likely has Type 1 diabetes? Give a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Person Z: very high blood glucose with very low insulin, so the pancreas is not producing enough insulin.
parts.working: 1 mark: Z; 1 mark: very low insulin means no insulin produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for person Y.
parts.answer: Glucose and insulin are both high: the cells are not responding well to insulin (insulin resistance), typical of Type 2 diabetes.
parts.working: 1 mark: insulin is high but glucose is high; 1 mark: cells respond poorly to insulin.

practice.stem: A person drinks a glucose drink. Blood glucose rises from 5.0 mmol/dm³ to 11.0 mmol/dm³ within 30 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why blood glucose returns to normal within 2 hours in a healthy person.
parts.answer: Insulin is released in response to the high glucose; cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen. This is negative feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark: insulin released; 1 mark: glucose taken up and stored as glycogen (or used).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways the body responds when it is too hot.
parts.answer: Sweating; vasodilation (arterioles in the skin widen); (also less shivering / hair erector muscles relax).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways the body responds when it is too cold.
parts.answer: Shivering; vasoconstriction (arterioles in the skin narrow); (also hairs raised).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the brain that controls body temperature.
parts.answer: Hypothalamus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the part of the brain that acts as the body's thermostat.
parts.answer: hypothalamus
parts.working: hypothalamus

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two responses of the body when body temperature rises above 37 °C.
parts.answer: Sweating; vasodilation (blood vessels near the skin widen).
parts.working: 1 mark each (any two): sweating; vasodilation; hair erector muscles relax.

practice.stem: On a cold morning a person's skin looks pale and the hairs on their arms stand up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in blood flow to the skin.
parts.answer: Arterioles supplying the skin constrict (vasoconstriction), so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: vasoconstriction; 1 mark: less heat lost through the skin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the standing hairs help to keep the body warm.
parts.answer: Hair erector muscles contract, raising the hairs and trapping a layer of warm air next to the skin, which acts as insulation.
parts.working: 1 mark: muscles contract; 1 mark: trapped air acts as insulation.

practice.stem: A child's body temperature rose from 37.0 °C to 38.5 °C during an illness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the part of the brain that detects this change in body temperature.
parts.answer: hypothalamus
parts.working: hypothalamus

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how vasodilation helps a person to lose heat on a hot day.
parts.answer: Arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen (dilate); more blood flows near the skin surface; more heat is lost from the blood to the surroundings by radiation.
parts.working: B1 arterioles dilate; B1 more blood to skin surface capillaries; B1 more heat lost (radiation / convection). Do not credit 'capillaries move'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the skin of a person looks pale when they are very cold.
parts.answer: Vasoconstriction: arterioles to the skin narrow, so less blood flows near the surface (reducing heat loss).
parts.working: B1 arterioles constrict; B1 less blood near skin surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sweating cools the body.
parts.answer: Water in sweat evaporates from the skin; evaporation uses heat energy from the skin, so the skin and blood are cooled.
parts.working: B1 evaporation of water; B1 takes heat (energy) from the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person feels hotter in Karachi in humid monsoon weather than in Jacobabad in dry heat at the same air temperature.
parts.answer: In humid air there is already a lot of water vapour, so sweat evaporates slowly; less heat is removed from the skin, so cooling is less effective.
parts.working: B1 less evaporation in humid air; B1 so less heat lost / less cooling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sweating cools the body.
parts.answer: Sweat evaporates from the skin surface; evaporation needs energy (latent heat), which is taken from the skin, so the body cools.
parts.working: 1 mark: sweat evaporates; 1 mark: evaporation needs energy (latent heat); 1 mark: energy is taken from the skin/body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how shivering helps to raise body temperature.
parts.answer: Muscles contract rapidly and repeatedly (involuntarily); respiration in the muscle cells releases heat energy, which is carried around the body by the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: involuntary muscle contraction; 1 mark: respiration releases heat; 1 mark: heat distributed by the blood.

practice.stem: Sweat is 99.0 % water by mass. A person loses 600 g of sweat during exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost in the sweat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who sweats a lot should drink water.
parts.answer: Water is lost in sweat; replacing it keeps the water content of the body and the blood volume at normal levels.
parts.working: 1 mark: water lost must be replaced; 1 mark: keeps body water balance / blood volume normal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how negative feedback keeps body temperature at about 37 °C when the outside temperature rises to 35 °C.
parts.answer: Temperature receptors in the skin and the hypothalamus detect the rise; the hypothalamus compares it with the set point of 37 °C and sends nerve impulses to skin arterioles (vasodilation) and sweat glands (sweating); heat is lost; temperature returns to 37 °C and the responses stop.
parts.working: 1 mark: receptors detect the rise; 1 mark: hypothalamus compares with set point; 1 mark: vasodilation and sweating; 1 mark: heat lost, temperature returns and responses switch off.

practice.stem:
Three identical test-tubes each contain 20 cm³ of water at 80 °C. One has no covering, one is wrapped in one layer of cotton wool and one in three layers. The temperature is recorded after 10 minutes.
Tube : temperature after 10 min / °C
no covering : 52
one layer of cotton wool : 60
three layers of cotton wool : 68

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of cooling, in °C per minute, for each tube.
parts.answer: no covering: 2.8 °C/min; one layer of cotton wool: 2 °C/min; three layers of cotton wool: 1.2 °C/min
parts.working: (80 − final temperature) ÷ 10 for each (M1); 2.8 and 2.0 (A1); 1.2 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these results relate to the layer of fat under the skin of a seal living in cold water.
