parts.working: The order is lag → exponential (log) → stationary → death. The stationary phase follows the exponential phase, not the lag phase, and the death phase comes last.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a population growth curve, which phase is one in which the birth rate and the death rate are equal?
A lag phase
B exponential (log) phase
C stationary phase
D there is no such phase; the population always keeps rising
parts.answer: C stationary phase
parts.working: In the stationary phase the population is roughly constant, so births equal deaths. The lag phase is slow growth at the start (A). The exponential phase has births greater than deaths (B). Option D is wrong because the curve levels off when resources run short.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the sampling method most suitable for estimating a population of fast-moving animals such as squirrels in a forest, and give one reason.
parts.answer: mark-release-recapture; the animals move around, so quadrats would not give a reliable count
parts.working: 1 mark: mark-release-recapture. 1 mark: the animals are mobile and would not stay in a quadrat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term carrying capacity.
parts.answer: the maximum population size that an environment can support indefinitely (given the available resources)
parts.working: Accept the maximum sustainable population for the habitat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the carrying capacity is shown on a population growth curve.
parts.answer: as the level (plateau) the curve levels off at
parts.working: The stationary phase levels at the carrying capacity.

practice.stem:
Yeast cells were added to a flask of glucose solution at 25 °C. Samples were counted every 2 hours.
Time (h): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14
Number of yeast cells (thousands per mm³): 2, 3, 8, 25, 60, 92, 98, 97

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in yeast numbers between 4 and 8 hours, in thousand cells per mm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 13 thousand cells per mm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the phases of growth shown between 0–2 hours and between 10–14 hours.
parts.answer: 0–2 h: lag phase; 10–14 h: stationary phase.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the population stopped increasing after 12 hours.
parts.answer: Glucose (food) was being used up; toxic waste products such as ethanol built up; the birth (reproduction) rate became equal to the death rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: limited food/glucose; accumulation of toxic waste (ethanol, CO₂); competition; reproduction rate = death rate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the population if counting continued for several more days. Give a reason.
parts.answer: The population would decrease (death phase) because food runs out and toxic waste increases, so death rate exceeds reproduction rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: decrease / death phase; 1 mark: reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four factors that affect the rate of growth of a population.
parts.answer: Food supply; competition; predation; disease (also availability of space, nesting sites, water).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The human population of the world grew slowly for thousands of years and then increased very rapidly in the last 200 years. Suggest two reasons for the rapid increase.
parts.answer: Better medical care / vaccines / antibiotics reducing death rate (especially infant mortality); improved food supply through modern agriculture; clean water and sanitation reducing disease.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a population that has reached the stationary phase, compare the birth rate with the death rate.
parts.answer: The birth rate equals the death rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a predator–prey relationship affects the number of prey in a population of rabbits.
parts.answer: When predators (e.g. foxes) increase, more rabbits are eaten, so the rabbit population falls; with fewer rabbits, predators have less food and their numbers fall; then the rabbit population can increase again (numbers rise and fall in cycles).
parts.working: 1 mark each: more predators → fewer prey; fewer prey → fewer predators; prey numbers then rise again (cycle).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by a limiting factor for a population.
parts.answer: A factor that is in short supply and so restricts the growth of the population (e.g. food, space).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student counts 3.5 mean dandelion plants in each 0.25 m² quadrat on a field of area 400 m². Which is the best estimate of the total number of plants on the field?
A 14
B 350
C 1400
D 5600
parts.working: Density = 3.5 ÷ 0.25 = 14 plants per m². Total = 14 × 400 = 5600. The value 14 is the density, not the total (A); 350 and 1400 result from dividing by the wrong area or multiplying by the wrong factor.

practice.stem: A student catches 40 ladybirds in a mango orchard in Multan, marks them and releases them. Later she catches 60 ladybirds; 12 of them are marked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the estimated population of ladybirds in the orchard.
parts.working: Estimate = (number marked in first sample × total second sample) ÷ number marked in second sample = 40 × 60 ÷ 12 = 200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two assumptions the student makes when using this method.
parts.answer: any two of: marked and unmarked ladybirds mix randomly; the marked animals do not die or leave the area; marks do not fall off or affect survival; no births or deaths between the samples
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct assumptions.

practice.stem:
A population of fruit flies was grown in a bottle. Number of flies on each day:
Day 0: 20; Day 2: 40; Day 4: 80; Day 6: 160; Day 8: 210; Day 10: 220; Day 12: 220.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the doubling time of the flies between day 2 and day 4.
parts.answer: 2 days
parts.working: The population goes from 40 to 80 in 2 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in the number of flies between day 0 and day 6, in flies per day.
parts.answer: 23.3 flies per day (to 1 d.p.)
parts.working: (160 − 20) ÷ 6 = 23.3 flies per day.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the limiting factor that causes the population to level off after day 8.
parts.answer: food or space
parts.working: Any one limiting factor: food supply, space, or waste build-up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could use random sampling with quadrats to estimate the number of plants in a field 60 m by 40 m.
parts.answer: use a grid over the field and random number pairs (or random coordinates) to choose where to place several quadrats; count the plants in each; calculate the mean number per quadrat, divide by the quadrat area to get the density per m², then multiply by the field area of 2400 m²
parts.working: 1 mark: random positions (random numbers or coordinates). 1 mark: several quadrats. 1 mark: count and calculate the mean. 1 mark: convert to density per m² and scale up by the field area of 2400 m².

practice.stem:
A student estimated the number of dandelion plants on a school field of area 1200 m². She placed ten quadrats, each 0.25 m², on the field and counted the dandelions in each.
Counts: 3, 0, 5, 2, 4, 1, 6, 2, 3, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat.
parts.answer: 3.0 dandelions per quadrat

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelions per m².
parts.answer: 12 per m²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of dandelions on the field.
parts.answer: about 14 400 dandelions

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the student should decide where to place the quadrats.
parts.answer: Place them at random, e.g. use random numbers as coordinates on a grid of measuring tapes laid along two edges of the field; this avoids bias in choosing where to sample.
parts.working: 1 mark: random placement using random numbers/coordinates; 1 mark: avoids bias / representative sample.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest two ways the estimate could be made more reliable.
parts.answer: Use more quadrats; repeat on different days; use a larger quadrat; have clear rules for counting plants on the edge of the quadrat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After heavy rains, desert locusts in Balochistan and Sindh can increase from a few thousand to millions within months. Suggest two reasons for this rapid increase.
parts.answer: Plenty of fresh plant food after rain; moist soil for egg laying; few predators relative to locust numbers; locusts reproduce quickly with many eggs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the phase of a population growth curve that describes this rapid increase and explain what is happening to birth and death rates.
parts.answer: Exponential (log) phase; the birth (reproduction) rate is much greater than the death rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: exponential/log phase; 1 mark: birth rate greatly exceeds death rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three factors that eventually cause the swarm to decline.
parts.answer: Food runs out (vegetation eaten / dries up); increased predation by birds; disease spreading in crowded conditions; competition for food; insecticide spraying.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A gerbil colony in a Cholistan burrow area had 500 gerbils at the start of the year. During the year there were 120 births, 90 deaths, 10 individuals arrived from other colonies (immigrants) and 25 left (emigrants).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net change in the gerbil population over the year.
parts.working: Net change = births − deaths + immigrants − emigrants = 120 − 90 + 10 − 25 = +15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage growth of the population over the year. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the growth rate of a population becomes slower as the population becomes larger.
parts.answer: more competition for food, space and shelter, so death rate rises and birth rate falls
parts.working: 1 mark: more competition for limited resources. 1 mark: death rate increases / birth rate falls as population grows.

practice.stem: After monsoon rain, a pond in Lahore was checked each day for mosquito larvae. The number rose quickly for 10 days, then levelled off at about 2000 larvae per litre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of a population growth curve for mosquito larvae in a pond after monsoon rain, and name its phases.
parts.answer: lag phase (slow start), exponential phase (rapid increase), stationary phase (levelling off); the curve is S-shaped (sigmoid)
parts.working: 1 mark each for naming the phases; 1 mark for describing the S-shape (or rapid growth then levelling).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of larvae levels off, and suggest one factor that could cause the population to fall later.
parts.answer: limiting factors such as food and space run short and predators and disease increase; a fall may be due to predators such as fish or to a dry spell killing the larvae
parts.working: 1 mark for limiting factors; 1 mark for food/space; 1 mark for a factor that causes a decline (predators, disease, drying).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A single neem tree supports 3000 caterpillars, which are eaten by 20 birds. What shape is the pyramid of numbers for this food chain?
A a normal pyramid, wide at the base and narrowing to the top
B narrow at the base, widest in the middle and narrower at the top
C widest at the top and narrowest at the base
D all three levels the same width
parts.answer: B narrow at the base, widest in the middle and narrower at the top
parts.working: One tree (narrow base), 3000 caterpillars (widest bar) and 20 birds (narrower). A pyramid of biomass for the same chain would have the normal shape (A), because the tree has a very large mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Grass in a field receives energy from the Sun. A herd of goats eats grass containing 18 000 kJ of energy, and 1620 kJ of this becomes goat biomass. Calculate the percentage efficiency of the transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the trophic level of the goats.
parts.answer: Second trophic level (primary consumers).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why most of the energy in the grass did not become goat biomass.
parts.answer: Lost as heat from respiration / lost in faeces (cellulose not digested) / used for movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about pyramids of energy is correct?
A they are always inverted
B they are always upright
C they are sometimes inverted
D they always have the same shape as pyramids of numbers
parts.answer: B they are always upright
parts.working: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so each level contains less energy than the one below it; pyramids of energy are always upright. They are not inverted (A or C), and they are not the same shape as pyramids of numbers (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a pyramid of energy shows about the flow of energy through a food chain.
parts.answer: it shows the amount of energy at each trophic level per unit area per unit time; energy decreases at each level along the chain
parts.working: 1 mark: energy at each trophic level per unit area and time. 1 mark: energy flows in one direction. 1 mark: energy decreases at each level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of energy is always upright.
parts.answer: energy is always lost at each level, mainly as heat, so each trophic level must contain less energy than the level below
parts.working: 1 mark: energy lost at each level. 1 mark: so the bars must get smaller up the chain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trophic level of a grasshopper that eats grass, a frog that eats grasshoppers, and a snake that eats frogs.
parts.answer: grasshopper 2; frog 3; snake 4
parts.working: Grass is level 1 (producer). The grasshopper is the primary consumer (2), frog secondary (3) and snake tertiary (4).

practice.stem:
Energy in each trophic level of a grassland in kJ per m² per year:
Producers (grasses): 25 000
Primary consumers (grasshoppers): 2500
Secondary consumers (frogs): 200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from producers to primary consumers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from primary consumers to secondary consumers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to the energy that is not passed on from the primary consumers to the secondary consumers.
parts.answer: Used in respiration and lost as heat; lost in faeces (undigested food) and excretory products such as urea; parts not eaten / dead bodies pass to decomposers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A field of maize contains 50 000 kJ of energy in parts that humans can eat. If this maize is fed to cattle, only 4 % of the energy ends up in beef that humans eat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy that reaches humans as beef.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy humans would get by eating the maize directly.
parts.answer: 25 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why so little of the energy in the maize ends up in the beef.
parts.answer: Cattle use most of the energy in respiration for movement and to keep warm, which is lost as heat; some energy is lost in faeces and urine / methane; some energy is in parts of the cow that are not eaten (bones, skin).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Producers in a lake contain 40 000 kJ of energy per m² per year. Primary consumers contain 4000 kJ per m² per year. What is the percentage efficiency of energy transfer?
A 1 %
B 10 %
C 40 %
D 90 %
parts.working: Efficiency = 4000 ÷ 40 000 × 100 = 10 %. A (1 %) is a tenfold error in the division; C (40 %) does not come from the calculation; D (90 %) is the energy lost (100 − 10), not the efficiency.

practice.stem: A pond in Karachi has the following energy values (kJ per m² per year): algae 80 000; zooplankton 6400; small fish 512.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from algae to zooplankton.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from zooplankton to small fish.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the energy that is not transferred between the two trophic levels.
parts.answer: it is lost as heat during respiration or in waste and uneaten parts
parts.working: Accept any one of these losses.

practice.stem: Maize contains 200 000 kJ of energy. Chickens convert 15 % of the energy in the maize they eat into their own body mass. Humans eat chicken meat in which 20 % of the energy from the chickens' body mass is passed on to them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy that reaches humans if they eat the poultry, in kJ.
parts.working: Poultry biomass = 15 % of 200 000 = 30 000 kJ; humans receive 20 % of that: 30 000 × 0.20 = 6000 kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is more energy-efficient for humans to eat plants than to eat animals that eat plants.
parts.answer: each trophic level passes on only about 10 % of its energy, so eating a plant-eater wastes most of the energy the plant captured
parts.working: 1 mark: energy is lost at each level. 1 mark: fewer steps means more energy reaches humans.

practice.stem: Energy in a grassland (kJ per m² per year): grass 500 000; grasshoppers 50 000; frogs 2500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from grass to frogs overall (grass to frog). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy lost between the grass and the grasshoppers, in kJ per m² per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For the food chain  rose bush → aphids → ladybirds, describe the shapes of the pyramid of numbers and the pyramid of biomass.
parts.answer: Pyramid of numbers: narrow base (one bush), very wide second bar (thousands of aphids), narrower top (ladybirds). Pyramid of biomass: normal pyramid – largest at the base (bush), smaller for aphids, smallest for ladybirds.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of biomass gives a more useful picture of the feeding relationships than a pyramid of numbers.
parts.answer: It takes account of the size (mass) of the organisms; one large producer is shown as large, so it shows how much living material is available at each level.
parts.working: 1 mark: accounts for size/mass of individuals; 1 mark: shows amount of material/energy available at each level.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of energy is never inverted.
parts.answer: Energy is lost at every transfer (respiration, heat, waste), so each level must contain less energy than the level below it.
parts.working: 1 mark: energy lost at each transfer; 1 mark: each level has less energy than the one it feeds on.

practice.stem:
Ecologists sampled a small area of grassland and measured the dry biomass at each trophic level (g per m²).
Producers: 820
Primary consumers: 74
Secondary consumers: 9.2
Tertiary consumers: 1.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the biomass of primary consumers that is present as secondary consumers. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of producer biomass that is present as primary consumers. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the samples were dried before weighing.
parts.answer: The water content of organisms varies (e.g. with recent rain or drinking), so fresh mass is unreliable; dry mass measures only the organic material / biomass.
parts.working: 1 mark: water content varies; 1 mark: dry mass gives a fair comparison of biomass.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one disadvantage of measuring dry biomass.
parts.answer: The organisms must be killed.

practice.stem:
Biomass (dry mass, g per m²) in a tidal sea-grass area of the Indus delta:
Sea grass (producers): 1500
Sea snails (primary consumers): 90
Crabs (secondary consumers): 7.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the producer biomass that is present as primary consumers (herbivores). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of biomass for this community is upright.
parts.answer: each trophic level contains less biomass than the level below because biomass (and energy) is lost at each step
parts.working: 1 mark: biomass decreases at each step. 1 mark: because material and energy are lost in respiration and waste.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of using a single sample to construct this pyramid of biomass.
parts.answer: one sample may not represent the whole area; the biomass changes with the season
parts.working: Any one limitation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of numbers can be inverted for a tree that supports thousands of aphids, but a pyramid of energy is never inverted.
parts.answer: a single tree (large individual) supports many small aphids, so the bar for consumers is larger than for the producer; energy must decrease at each level because energy is lost at each step, so the energy pyramid is always upright
parts.working: 1 mark: numbers do not account for the size of organisms, so a tree can be fewer than its consumers. 1 mark: energy is lost at each level. 1 mark: energy pyramid must always decrease upwards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two processes that release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere from living organisms.
parts.answer: any two of: respiration (by plants, animals and microorganisms); decomposition by decomposers
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct process (combustion is not a living process, so it does not count here).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one process that releases carbon dioxide from burning material.
parts.answer: combustion (burning of wood, coal, oil or gas)
parts.working: Burning fuels releases carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two carbon stores (sinks) that hold carbon for long periods.
parts.answer: any two of: fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas); limestone and chalk rocks; sediments in the oceans; peat
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct store.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process by which carbon dioxide from the air enters plants.
parts.answer: photosynthesis
parts.working: Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the form in which carbon passes from one organism to the next in a food chain.
parts.answer: carbon compounds in food (for example glucose, protein and fat)
parts.working: Carbon is passed on in organic molecules in the food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two processes by which carbon in an animal's body returns to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: any two of: respiration (carbon dioxide breathed out); decomposition of the body after death; excretion of waste containing carbon
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and two processes that add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Removes: photosynthesis. Adds: any two of respiration (by plants, animals and decomposers), combustion of fossil fuels or wood, decomposition.
parts.working: 1 mark: photosynthesis; 1 mark each for two adding processes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how carbon in a dead tree trunk can return to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Decomposers (fungi and bacteria) feed on the dead wood and respire, releasing carbon dioxide; or the wood is burnt (combustion).
parts.working: 1 mark: decomposers; 1 mark: respiration releases CO₂ (or combustion).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how carbon from plants that died millions of years ago is now being added to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: The plants were not fully decomposed and were fossilised to form coal, oil or gas; burning these fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: fossilisation into fossil fuels; 1 mark: combustion releases CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the carbon in the body of a goat that has died can return to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the body; they respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere; some carbon may be stored in the soil or in fossil fuels
parts.working: 1 mark: decomposers feed on the body. 1 mark: decomposers respire, releasing CO₂. 1 mark: carbon can be stored in the soil or as a fossil (not essential).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released when 1000 tonnes of coal, containing 80 % carbon, is burned completely. Use relative atomic mass C = 12 and relative formula mass CO₂ = 44. Give your answer to the nearest tonne.
parts.answer: 2933 tonnes
parts.working: Mass of carbon = 80 % of 1000 = 800 tonnes. Mass of CO₂ = 800 × 44 ÷ 12 = 2933.3, so 2933 tonnes to the nearest tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how marine organisms such as corals and molluscs remove carbon from seawater.
parts.answer: they take in dissolved carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate or carbonate ions) and use calcium and carbonate to make calcium carbonate shells or skeletons; the carbon is locked up in these hard structures
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon taken from water as carbonate. 1 mark: made into calcium carbonate shells or skeletons. 1 mark: carbon becomes locked into limestone when they die and sediment forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the carbon cycle is described as a cycle, whereas energy flow through an ecosystem is one-way.
parts.answer: carbon is continuously recycled between the atmosphere, living organisms and the soil, rocks and oceans; energy is lost as heat at each step and cannot be recycled, so it must be continuously supplied by the Sun
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon is recycled between stores. 1 mark: energy is lost as heat. 1 mark: energy must be replaced by sunlight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how cutting down rainforest in the Amazon increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: trees are no longer available to take in carbon dioxide by photosynthesis; carbon stored in wood is released when the trees are burned or decay; the soil's carbon store is also disturbed
parts.working: 1 mark: less photosynthesis, so less CO₂ removed. 1 mark: burning releases stored carbon. 1 mark: decay of stumps and roots releases CO₂.

practice.stem: A monitoring station in the northern hemisphere recorded the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air during one year. The highest reading, 424.6 ppm, was in May. The lowest, 418.9 ppm, was in September.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the highest and lowest carbon dioxide concentrations recorded during the year.
parts.answer: 5.7 ppm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the carbon dioxide concentration falls between May and September.
parts.answer: In the northern summer, longer days, more light and warmth mean more photosynthesis by plants (more leaves on trees); photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide faster than respiration (and decomposition) releases it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: summer conditions / more leaves; more photosynthesis; rate of CO₂ uptake exceeds release by respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The May reading in the following year was 427.1 ppm. Suggest two human activities that explain the year-on-year increase.
parts.answer: Combustion of fossil fuels (vehicles, power stations, industry); deforestation – fewer trees to photosynthesise, and burning of the cleared wood.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A forest in the foothills of the Murree hills fixes 12 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year by photosynthesis. Plant respiration releases 7 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year, and the animals and decomposers release 3.5 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net carbon stored by one hectare of the forest each year.
parts.answer: 1.5 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year
parts.working: Net storage = 12 − 7 − 3.5 = 1.5 tonnes per hectare per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the carbon stored in the forest if the trees are cut down and burned.
parts.answer: the stored carbon is released as carbon dioxide during burning, adding to the atmosphere; the forest can no longer remove carbon by photosynthesis
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon released as CO₂ by burning. 1 mark: forest stops absorbing CO₂ by photosynthesis.

practice.stem: Dissolved carbon dioxide in a pond in Lahore was 8 mg per dm³ at dawn and 3 mg per dm³ in the afternoon of the same day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved carbon dioxide between dawn and afternoon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dissolved carbon dioxide concentration falls during the day.
parts.answer: algae and aquatic plants photosynthesise in light, using carbon dioxide faster than it is released by respiration
parts.working: 1 mark: photosynthesis uses CO₂ in light. 1 mark: photosynthesis rate exceeds respiration release during daylight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃) is heated in a cement kiln and breaks down to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Write the balanced symbol equation.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
parts.working: 1 mark for correct formulas; 1 mark for the balanced equation (one carbon in each product/reactant).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this process adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, even though the limestone was formed from living organisms.
parts.answer: the carbon was stored in the limestone for millions of years; heating releases it back into the atmosphere, so it is a human-driven transfer to the atmosphere
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon was stored in rock. 1 mark: heating releases CO₂ into the air faster than natural processes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon in 300 g of dried leaves that are 45 % carbon.
parts.working: 300 × 0.45 = 135 g of carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released when all this carbon is burned. Use relative atomic mass C = 12, relative formula mass CO₂ = 44.
parts.working: 135 × 44 ÷ 12 = 495 g of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organisms in the root nodules of pea plants convert nitrogen gas into compounds the plant can use?
A nitrifying bacteria
B denitrifying bacteria
C nitrogen-fixing bacteria
D decomposing fungi
parts.answer: C nitrogen-fixing bacteria
parts.working: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium/nitrogen compounds. Nitrifying bacteria (A) live in the soil and convert ammonium ions to nitrate ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process converts ammonium compounds in the soil into nitrites and then nitrates?
A nitrogen fixation
B nitrification
C ammonification
D denitrification
parts.answer: B nitrification
parts.working: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium compounds to nitrites and then to nitrates. Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas (A); ammonification releases ammonia from dead matter (C); denitrification converts nitrates back to nitrogen gas (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen gas makes up about 78 % of the air. Explain why plants cannot use it directly.
parts.answer: the two nitrogen atoms in N₂ are joined by a very strong triple bond, so the gas is unreactive; it must first be fixed into compounds such as nitrates or ammonia
parts.working: 1 mark: very strong, unreactive triple bond. 1 mark: needs fixing into a usable form (ammonia/nitrate) first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process that converts nitrogen gas into ammonia.
parts.answer: nitrogen fixation
parts.working: Fixation changes N₂ into ammonia or nitrogen compounds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two groups of organisms that carry out this process.
parts.answer: any two of: Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of legumes; free-living bacteria (for example Azotobacter); cyanobacteria
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct group.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In waterlogged soil, which process is increased and makes the soil less fertile?
A denitrification of nitrate ions to nitrogen gas
B nitrification of ammonium ions to nitrate ions
C nitrogen fixation by lightning
D absorption of nitrate ions by root hairs
parts.answer: A denitrification of nitrate ions to nitrogen gas
parts.working: Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen; denitrifying bacteria thrive in anaerobic conditions and convert nitrate ions to nitrogen gas, which is lost from the soil. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so nitrification (B) decreases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how nitrogen in the proteins of dead leaves becomes nitrate ions in the soil. Name the types of organism involved.
parts.answer: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the proteins in dead leaves; they release ammonium ions (ammonification); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium ions into nitrite ions; and then into nitrate ions.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decomposers break down proteins / amino acids; ammonium ions released; nitrifying bacteria; ammonium → nitrite → nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how plants absorb nitrate ions and what they use them for.
parts.answer: By active transport into root hair cells; to make amino acids and then proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport through root hairs; 1 mark: amino acids / proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ploughing and aerating soil increases the concentration of nitrate ions in it.
parts.answer: Ploughing lets oxygen into the soil; nitrifying bacteria need oxygen (aerobic) to convert ammonium ions into nitrate ions; and denitrifying bacteria, which work in anaerobic conditions, are less active.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more oxygen; nitrifying bacteria aerobic, more nitrification; less denitrification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one way, other than by bacteria, in which nitrogen gas in the air is fixed.
parts.answer: Lightning (or the industrial Haber process to make fertiliser).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in a plant protein can become part of a goat's muscle and later reach the soil.
parts.answer: The goat eats the plant; the protein is digested to amino acids, which are absorbed and assimilated into goat proteins (muscle); excess amino acids are deaminated and the nitrogen leaves in urea/urine, or when the goat dies decomposers break down its proteins, releasing ammonium ions to the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark each: feeding and digestion to amino acids; assimilation into goat protein; return via urea/excretion or death and decomposition to ammonium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance can plant roots absorb from the soil and use directly to make amino acids?
A nitrogen gas (N₂)
B nitrate ions
C insoluble protein in dead leaves
D urea in animal urine
parts.answer: B nitrate ions
parts.working: Plants absorb nitrate ions (and ammonium ions) from the soil and use them to make amino acids and proteins. Nitrogen gas is unreactive and plants cannot use it (A). Insoluble protein must be decomposed first (C). Urea must be broken down by bacteria to nitrogen compounds before roots can use it (D).

practice.stem: A farmer in Sindh adds urea fertiliser to a wheat field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in urea added to a wheat field becomes protein in the wheat.
parts.answer: urea is broken down to ammonium compounds by bacteria; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate; roots absorb nitrate ions; the plant uses nitrate to make amino acids and then proteins
parts.working: 1 mark: urea → ammonium (by bacteria). 1 mark: nitrification to nitrate. 1 mark: absorbed by roots as nitrate. 1 mark: amino acids then proteins.

practice.stem: Soil nitrate concentration was 12 mg per kg before ploughing and 18 mg per kg one week after ploughing and aerating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the soil nitrate concentration after ploughing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ploughing and aerating the soil increases the nitrate concentration.
parts.answer: aerobic conditions improve, so nitrifying bacteria work faster and convert ammonium compounds to nitrates; more oxygen also reduces denitrification
parts.working: 1 mark: more oxygen supports nitrifying bacteria. 1 mark: less denitrification in aerated soil (or more nitrification).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of a compost heap rises and state the nitrogen compound released from the decomposing material.
parts.answer: decomposing bacteria and fungi respire, releasing energy as heat; the decay of protein releases ammonia (ammonium compounds) during ammonification
parts.working: 1 mark: aerobic respiration by decomposers releases heat. 1 mark: ammonia/ammonium released. 1 mark: decomposition of dead protein or urea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many farmers in Punjab grow a legume crop such as berseem clover or chickpea between wheat crops. Explain how this improves the yield of the next wheat crop.
parts.answer: Legumes have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria; these convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonium / nitrogen compounds used to make amino acids; when the legume roots and leftover plant parts are ploughed in, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria release nitrate ions into the soil; wheat absorbs the nitrate to make proteins, so it grows better.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: root nodules; nitrogen-fixing bacteria; N₂ → ammonium/nitrogen compounds; decomposition and nitrification add nitrate to soil; wheat uses nitrate for amino acids/proteins → growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of this method over using large amounts of nitrate fertiliser.
parts.answer: Cheaper; less nitrate washed (leached) into rivers, so less eutrophication; adds organic matter to the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two, or 2 marks for one fully explained point.

practice.stem:
Researchers measured the nitrate concentration in the soil of two plots at the end of a season. One plot grew chickpeas; the other grew wheat only.
Chickpea plot: 42 mg nitrate per kg soil
Wheat-only plot: 28 mg nitrate per kg soil

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the nitrate concentration in the plot that grew chickpeas was greater than in the plot that grew wheat only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: Chickpeas are legumes with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules; the nitrogen compounds from their roots and remains were converted to nitrate by decomposers and nitrifying bacteria.
parts.working: 1 mark: nitrogen-fixing bacteria in nodules; 1 mark: decomposition / nitrification adds nitrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should have been the same for both plots to make the comparison valid.
parts.answer: Soil type; amount of fertiliser added; watering / rainfall; time of year sampled; depth of soil sampling.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the researchers could make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Take several soil samples from different places in each plot (and/or use several plots of each type) and calculate a mean.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how lightning can make nitrates that reach the soil.
parts.answer: the energy of lightning makes nitrogen and oxygen in the air react to form nitrogen oxides; these dissolve in rain to form nitrate ions (nitric acid); the rain delivers the nitrates to the soil
parts.working: 1 mark: lightning supplies energy to react N₂ with O₂. 1 mark: nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain. 1 mark: nitrates reach the soil with rainfall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A legume crop fixes 80 kg of nitrogen per hectare. A wheat crop removes 60 kg of nitrogen per hectare in its grain and straw. Calculate the net gain in soil nitrogen after one season, assuming no losses.
parts.answer: 20 kg per hectare
parts.working: 80 − 60 = 20 kg of nitrogen per hectare.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two processes that would cause losses of nitrogen from the soil in reality.
parts.answer: any two of: leaching of nitrate ions by rain; denitrification by bacteria in waterlogged soil; removal by harvesting or erosion
parts.working: 1 mark for each of any two correct losses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which term describes all the populations of different species living together in one area?
A habitat
B community
C ecosystem
D population
parts.answer: B community
parts.working: A community is all of the populations of different species in an ecosystem. An ecosystem (C) is the community together with its non-living environment, interacting with each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is an abiotic factor in a pond?
A competition for food between fish
B predation of tadpoles by dragonfly larvae
C water pH
D disease spread between frogs
parts.answer: C water pH
parts.working: Abiotic factors are non-living. Water pH is a non-living factor that affects which organisms can survive. Competition, predation and disease all involve living organisms (biotic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term community.
parts.answer: all the populations of different species living together in one area
parts.working: The community is all the species living in one place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a community in a mangrove forest of the Indus delta.
parts.answer: mangrove trees, crabs, fish and birds living together in one area
parts.working: Accept any named group of different species living in the same mangrove area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two abiotic factors in a pond in Karachi that affect the survival of fish.
parts.answer: any two of: dissolved oxygen concentration; water temperature; pH; light intensity; amount of pollution
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct abiotic factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List two biotic and two abiotic components of a sand dune ecosystem in the Thar Desert.
parts.answer: biotic: desert grasses (or shrubs), lizards / beetles; abiotic: sand, wind, temperature (or water availability)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct component (two biotic, two abiotic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term habitat.
parts.answer: the place where an organism lives
parts.working: Accept the place or environment an organism lives in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two features of the habitat of a frog in a rice paddy.
parts.answer: any two of: shallow water; plants to hide in; insects to eat; damp conditions; a suitable temperature
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct feature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use examples from the Thar Desert to explain the meaning of each term: population, community, ecosystem.
parts.answer: Population: a group of organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time, e.g. all the chinkara gazelles in one part of the desert. Community: all the populations of different species there, e.g. gazelles, desert foxes, lizards, khejri trees and grasses together. Ecosystem: the community and its environment (sand, water, climate) interacting together.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct definition with a suitable example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two non-living (abiotic) factors in the desert ecosystem that affect the organisms living there.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature; rainfall / water availability; light intensity; wind; soil type / sand.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about an ecosystem is correct?
A it includes only the living organisms in an area
B it includes the living organisms and their non-living surroundings, and the interactions between them
C it is the same thing as a habitat
D it contains only one species
parts.answer: B it includes the living organisms and their non-living surroundings, and the interactions between them
parts.working: An ecosystem includes the community together with the abiotic environment and the interactions between them (B). A is a community, not an ecosystem; a habitat is only the place where an organism lives (C); an ecosystem usually contains many species (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using examples from an alpine meadow in Chitral, explain the difference between a population, a community and an ecosystem.
parts.answer: a population is all the individuals of one species in the meadow (for example one species of primula); a community is all the populations of different species in the meadow; an ecosystem is the community plus the non-living environment (soil, temperature, water) and their interactions
parts.working: 1 mark each for the correct definition with an example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Acid rain lowers the pH of a lake. Explain how this change could affect the snail population and the frogs that feed on snails.
parts.answer: snails cannot form shells properly in acidic water, so fewer snails survive; frogs that eat snails then have less food; so the frog population may also fall
parts.working: 1 mark: lower pH affects snails (shell formation or survival). 1 mark: fewer snails. 1 mark: frogs have less food and decline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one example of interdependence between two species in a savannah or a mangrove forest.
parts.answer: an example such as acacia trees and ants: the ants live in the thorns and protect the tree from herbivores in return for food; or mangrove roots provide shelter for young fish which feed on the algae in turn
parts.working: 1 mark: named pair of organisms. 1 mark: a correct description of how each depends on the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the following as biotic or abiotic: a sandstone boulder in a Murree forest; a population of earthworms; wind speed; fungi growing on a fallen log.
parts.answer: boulder: abiotic; earthworms: biotic; wind speed: abiotic; fungi: biotic
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two lakes have the same temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen, but their communities of animals are different. Explain how this can happen.
parts.answer: the lakes may have different histories: species can colonise one lake but not the other; different predators or competitors may be present; the lakes may have different food supplies or habitat structures
parts.working: Any three distinct reasons, 1 mark each (colonisation history, predators, competitors, food, habitat structure).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in sea temperature of 2 °C could change the community living on a coral reef.
parts.answer: the coral becomes stressed and expels the algae living in its tissues (bleaching); the coral loses its main food and colour and may die; fish and other animals that depend on the coral lose their habitat; the community becomes less diverse
parts.working: 1 mark: coral stressed and expels symbiotic algae. 1 mark: coral loses food and may die. 1 mark: habitat lost for fish and other animals. 1 mark: community becomes less diverse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins. Explain how a large fall in the number of sea otters could lead to the loss of a kelp forest.
parts.answer: without otters, sea urchin numbers increase; the urchins eat large amounts of kelp; the kelp forest is grazed away; the habitat and food for the other organisms in the kelp forest are lost
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in otters so urchins increase. 1 mark: urchins eat kelp. 1 mark: kelp forest lost. 1 mark: other species that depend on it are affected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process by which water vapour in clouds changes into liquid water droplets.
parts.answer: condensation
parts.working: Cooling of water vapour forms droplets, which fall as precipitation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which plants lose water vapour from their leaves.
parts.answer: transpiration
parts.working: Water vapour escapes through the stomata.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three processes that move water from the oceans to the land.
parts.answer: evaporation; condensation; precipitation
parts.working: 1 mark each: evaporation from the sea; condensation of vapour into clouds; precipitation of rain or snow over the land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between infiltration and surface runoff.
parts.answer: infiltration is water soaking into the ground; surface runoff is water flowing over the surface of the land into streams and rivers
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transpiration and state where in the leaf it occurs.
parts.answer: the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant; it occurs mainly through the stomata in the leaves
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of water vapour from the plant. 1 mark: through stomata in the leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the water cycle, naming the processes by which water moves between living organisms, the land, the sea and the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from seas, lakes and soil; plants lose water vapour by transpiration; water vapour cools and condenses to form clouds; it falls as precipitation (rain or snow); water runs off into rivers and seas or soaks into the soil, where it is absorbed by roots.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: evaporation; transpiration; condensation; precipitation; run-off / infiltration and uptake by plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how cutting down a large area of forest in the northern hills could affect local rainfall.
parts.answer: Less transpiration from trees, so less water vapour enters the air; fewer clouds form, so local rainfall decreases.
parts.working: 1 mark: less transpiration; 1 mark: less water vapour/condensation → less rainfall.

practice.stem: A catchment area in the Northern Areas of Pakistan receives 800 mm of rain in a year. Of this, 500 mm is returned to the atmosphere by evaporation and transpiration, and 200 mm runs off the surface into rivers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of water, in mm, that soaks into the ground (infiltrates) in the catchment area.
parts.answer: 100 mm
parts.working: Infiltration = rainfall − evaporation and transpiration − runoff = 800 − 500 − 200 = 100 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the rainfall that infiltrates into the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the removal of forest on a steep hillside can increase the risk of flooding in the valley below.
parts.answer: without tree roots and leaves, less rain is intercepted and infiltration falls; more water runs off the surface quickly; the rivers rise quickly and flood the valley
parts.working: 1 mark: less interception / less infiltration. 1 mark: more surface runoff. 1 mark: rapid rise in river flow and flooding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route taken by water from a glacier in the Karakoram mountains to the Arabian Sea.
parts.answer: snow melts and flows as meltwater into streams; the streams join the Indus River; the river flows across the plains; water evaporates and water flows into the Arabian Sea
parts.working: 1 mark: melting of glacier/snow. 1 mark: runoff into streams and the river. 1 mark: river flows to the sea. 1 mark: evaporation and eventual return via precipitation (accept evaporation from the sea).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how groundwater is formed.
parts.answer: rainwater soaks through the soil (infiltration) and percolates downwards through permeable rock; it collects in spaces in the rock until the rock is saturated, forming an underground water store
parts.working: 1 mark: infiltration. 1 mark: percolation through permeable rock. 1 mark: water stored in saturated rock layers (aquifer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how clouds form over the Murree hills.
parts.answer: warm moist air rises up the slopes; as it rises it cools; the water vapour condenses onto dust particles to form droplets, which form clouds
parts.working: 1 mark: air rises and cools. 1 mark: water vapour condenses. 1 mark: droplets form clouds (condensation nuclei).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how water returns from a river to the sea.
parts.answer: water flows along the river channel to the sea; it returns to the atmosphere by evaporation and then precipitation, and the river water flows back to the sea
parts.working: 1 mark: flows in the river to the sea. 1 mark: evaporation and condensation (cycle) returning water to land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that water is used up by plants and animals in the water cycle. Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: the statement is mainly incorrect: water is returned to the environment by transpiration, excretion, and respiration; it is recycled continuously through the cycle rather than used up; a small amount is used in photosynthesis and other reactions
parts.working: 1 mark: water is returned to the atmosphere or soil through transpiration and excretion. 1 mark: the water is recycled, not lost. 1 mark: a small amount is used in chemical reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how transpiration by the trees of the Amazon rainforest helps to maintain rainfall over the forest.
parts.answer: transpiration releases large amounts of water vapour into the air; this vapour condenses to form clouds that produce rain over the forest; so water is recycled locally instead of all being lost to the sea
parts.working: 1 mark: water vapour released by transpiration. 1 mark: condensation forms clouds. 1 mark: precipitation returns water to the forest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lake has a surface area of 50 km². Its water level falls by 1.5 m per year because of evaporation. Assume there is no inflow or outflow of water. Calculate the volume of water lost per year, in m³.
parts.working: Area = 50 km² = 50 × 10⁶ m²; volume = 50 × 10⁶ × 1.5 = 7.5 × 10⁷ m³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water evaporates faster from a shallow lake in a hot climate than from a deep lake in a cool climate.
parts.answer: higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules so more escape as vapour; a larger surface area of shallow water exposes more water to the air
parts.working: 1 mark: higher temperature increases evaporation. 1 mark: shallow lake has a larger area per volume (or more exposed surface).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the flow of the Indus River is highest in summer and lowest in winter.
parts.answer: in summer, the monsoon rains and the melting of snow and glaciers in the mountains add large amounts of water to the river; in winter, precipitation is low and the snow is frozen, so less water runs into the river
parts.working: 1 mark: monsoon rain in summer. 1 mark: snow and glacier melt in summer. 1 mark: frozen water in winter. 1 mark: less precipitation/runoff in winter.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both plant cells and animal cells but NOT in bacterial cells?
A cell membrane
B cell wall
C mitochondrion
D ribosome
parts.answer: C mitochondrion
parts.working: Bacteria have a cell membrane, a cell wall and ribosomes, but no mitochondria. Plant and animal cells both have mitochondria. Cell wall is wrong because animal cells lack one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the cell structure that matches each description.
(i) the site of aerobic respiration
(ii) the site of protein synthesis
(iii) controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell
(iv) contains the chromosomes
parts.answer: (i) mitochondrion (ii) ribosome (iii) cell membrane (iv) nucleus
parts.working: B1 each. Do not accept cell wall for (iii).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sentences about plant cells using suitable words.
The cell wall is made of ______ and stops the cell bursting. The large permanent vacuole contains ______. Chloroplasts absorb ______ energy for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: cellulose; cell sap; light
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure controls which substances enter and leave a cell?
A cell wall
B cell membrane
C nucleus
D ribosome
parts.answer: B cell membrane
parts.working: The cell membrane is partially permeable and controls movement in and out. The cell wall is fully permeable and gives support; the nucleus controls cell activities; ribosomes make proteins.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text: Name the organelle that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: chloroplast
parts.working: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: Name the structure, made of cellulose, that surrounds a plant cell and gives it support.
parts.answer: cell wall
parts.working: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose and support the cell.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.text: Name the jelly-like region of the cell in which most of the chemical reactions take place.
parts.answer: cytoplasm
parts.working: Most chemical reactions take place in the cytoplasm.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.text: Name the organelle that is the site of aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: mitochondrion (mitochondria)
parts.working: Aerobic respiration releases energy in the mitochondria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student views a plant cell and sees a large central sac filled with cell sap. Name this structure.
parts.answer: vacuole
parts.working: The vacuole is a sac of cell sap surrounded by a membrane (tonoplast).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of the cell sap in the vacuole.
parts.answer: Any two: keeps the cell firm (turgid) by pressing the cell membrane against the cell wall; stores sugars, amino acids, mineral ions or pigments.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two functions listed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each structure to its function. Structures: 1 cell membrane, 2 cell wall, 3 nucleus. Functions: A gives support and stops the cell bursting when it takes in water. B controls the activities of the cell, including the production of proteins. C is the site of most chemical reactions in the cell. D controls which substances enter and leave the cell.
Give the letter for each: (i) cell membrane (ii) cell wall (iii) nucleus.
parts.answer: (i) D; (ii) A; (iii) B
parts.working: 1 mark each: membrane controls entry and exit (D); cell wall gives support (A); nucleus controls activities (B). C refers to the cytoplasm, which is not asked for here.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare mitochondria and chloroplasts. State two features that they have in common.
parts.answer: Any two: both have a double membrane; both contain their own DNA and ribosomes; both are involved in energy transfer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features listed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one structural difference between a mitochondrion and a chloroplast.
parts.answer: A chloroplast contains thylakoid membranes stacked into grana and chlorophyll; a mitochondrion has inner membrane folds (cristae).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct difference (chlorophyll/grana/thylakoids versus cristae).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which features are present in a bacterial cell?
1 cell wall
2 plasmids
3 nucleus
4 ribosomes
A 1, 2 and 4
B 1 and 3 only
C 2, 3 and 4
D 1 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: Bacteria have a cell wall, plasmids, ribosomes and circular DNA that is not enclosed in a nucleus. Any option including 3 is wrong; 1 and 4 only omits plasmids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three structural differences between a palisade mesophyll cell and a liver cell.
parts.answer: palisade cell has a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole; liver cell has none of these
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: cell wall (cellulose) present / absent; chloroplasts present / absent; large permanent vacuole (with cell sap) present / absent or only small vacuoles; regular shape / irregular shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Liver cells contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
parts.answer: liver cells have a high rate of metabolism, so they need a lot of energy released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria
parts.working: B1 mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration; B1 high metabolic rate / many energy-requiring reactions (e.g. protein synthesis, active transport) so much energy must be released. Do not credit 'produce energy'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two structures that are found in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell.
parts.answer: any two of: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two. (Not nucleus, not chloroplast, not mitochondrion.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one structure found in a bacterial cell that is not found in a plant cell.
parts.answer: plasmid

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the main genetic material of a bacterial cell differs from that of a plant cell.
parts.answer: bacterial DNA is a single circular chromosome / loop free in the cytoplasm, not enclosed in a nucleus
parts.working: B1 circular DNA; B1 not in a nucleus / no nuclear membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student peels a thin layer of epidermis from the inside of an onion bulb, places it on a slide in a drop of iodine solution and adds a coverslip. State why iodine solution is added.
parts.answer: to stain the cells / make the nucleus and cell outline visible

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two structures the student would see in the onion cells with a light microscope.
parts.answer: any two of: cell wall, nucleus, cytoplasm, vacuole
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student notices that the onion cells have no chloroplasts. Explain why.
parts.answer: the bulb grows underground / receives no light, so the cells do not photosynthesise and do not need chloroplasts
parts.working: B1 no light reaches these cells; B1 chloroplasts are for photosynthesis, which they do not carry out.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the coverslip should be lowered slowly at an angle.
parts.answer: to avoid trapping air bubbles

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is present in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell, but NOT in an animal cell?
A nucleus
B cell wall
C ribosomes
D mitochondria
parts.answer: B cell wall
parts.working: Animal cells have no cell wall; bacterial cells (peptidoglycan) and plant cells (cellulose) both have one. Bacteria have no nucleus or mitochondria, and ribosomes are found in all three cell types.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion.
parts.answer: A double membrane (outer and inner membrane); the inner membrane is folded into cristae; the space inside (matrix) contains enzymes.
parts.working: 1 mark for double membrane. 1 mark for inner membrane folded into cristae (matrix with enzymes may also be credited).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a mitochondrion is adapted for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: The folds (cristae) increase the surface area for the enzymes and carrier molecules that release energy; the matrix contains enzymes for respiration, so more energy (ATP) is released.
parts.working: 1 mark: folds increase surface area. 1 mark: enzymes/carriers on the membrane and matrix allow more aerobic respiration.

practice.stem: A student scrapes the inside of her cheek with a cotton bud and spreads the cells on a slide. She adds a drop of methylene blue stain and a coverslip, then draws a few cells under the microscope. Each cell she draws has a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. She draws no cell wall, no chloroplasts and no large vacuole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one reason why the cheek cells have no chloroplasts.
parts.answer: Cheek cells are not photosynthetic: they are inside the body and do not receive light, so they do not need chloroplasts.
parts.working: 1 mark: cheek cells do not photosynthesise (no light / not a green, photosynthetic tissue).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the nucleus appears darker than the cytoplasm after staining with methylene blue.
parts.answer: The stain binds to the DNA (chromosomes) in the nucleus, so the nucleus takes up more stain and appears darker.
parts.working: 1 mark: the stain binds to DNA / chromosomes in the nucleus. 1 mark: the nucleus takes up more stain, so it looks darker than the cytoplasm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two structures that are found in both a human cheek cell and a plant cell.
parts.answer: Any two: cell membrane; cytoplasm; nucleus; mitochondria; ribosomes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct structure, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Cells in the pancreas make and secrete large quantities of digestive enzymes. Electron micrographs of these cells show very many ribosomes and many mitochondria.
Explain how each of these features helps the cells to carry out their function.
parts.answer: enzymes are proteins; ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, so many ribosomes allow enzymes to be made quickly in large amounts; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing the energy needed for protein synthesis and for secreting the enzymes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: enzymes are proteins; ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis; many ribosomes = enzymes made quickly / in large quantities; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration; respiration releases energy; energy needed to join amino acids / for protein synthesis; energy needed for secretion of the enzymes out of the cell. Do not credit 'mitochondria produce energy'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows the mean number of mitochondria in four types of human cell.
cell type | mean number of mitochondria per cell
heart muscle cell | 5000
liver cell | 2000
skin cell (outer layer) | 300
mature red blood cell | 0
Calculate how many times more mitochondria a heart muscle cell has than a skin cell. Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.answer: 17 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in the number of mitochondria between heart muscle cells and skin cells.
parts.answer: heart muscle contracts continuously, needs much energy from aerobic respiration in mitochondria; skin cells are less active and need less energy
parts.working: B1 mitochondria are where aerobic respiration releases energy; B1 heart muscle contracts continuously / never rests; B1 so heart cells need much more energy than skin cells (skin cells have low metabolic activity).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a mature red blood cell can still release some energy even though it has no mitochondria.
parts.answer: it respires anaerobically (in the cytoplasm)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sperm cell has a head, a midpiece and a long tail (flagellum). The head contains the nucleus and an acrosome. The midpiece contains many mitochondria.
Explain why the midpiece contains many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration; this energy (as ATP) is used to make the flagellum (tail) move the sperm.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy. 1 mark: the energy is needed for the tail to move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the acrosome helps the sperm to fertilise an egg.
parts.answer: The acrosome contains enzymes that digest the outer layers of the egg, allowing the sperm to enter the egg.
parts.working: 1 mark: contains digestive enzymes. 1 mark: these digest the egg's outer layer so the sperm can penetrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The nucleus of a sperm cell is haploid. Explain what this means and why it is important.
parts.answer: Haploid means the nucleus contains half the normal number of chromosomes (one set). When it fuses with the haploid nucleus of the egg, the full (diploid) number is restored in the zygote.
parts.working: 1 mark: half the normal number of chromosomes. 1 mark: fertilisation restores the full number of chromosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student says: 'All cells contain ribosomes and DNA, so bacteria and human cells are basically the same type of cell.'
Evaluate this statement. Refer to at least two ways in which a bacterial cell differs from a human cell.
parts.answer: Partly correct: both contain ribosomes and DNA. But a bacterial cell has no nucleus; its DNA is a single circular loop lying free in the cytoplasm, and it has no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria. A human cell has a nucleus containing linear chromosomes and membrane-bound organelles. So they are different types of cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: both contain ribosomes and DNA (statement partly correct). 1 mark: bacteria have no nucleus; their DNA is circular and free in the cytoplasm. 1 mark: no membrane-bound organelles in bacteria. 1 mark: overall conclusion that they are different cell types.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by the cell membrane being 'partially permeable', and explain why this is essential for the cell.
parts.answer: Partially permeable: some substances (for example small molecules or water) can pass through, but larger molecules or ions cannot pass freely. This controls what enters and leaves the cell, so useful substances are kept in and waste is removed.
parts.working: 1 mark: some substances can pass but others cannot. 1 mark: an example, or a correct statement about small molecules/water. 1 mark: the membrane controls the movement of substances, which is essential for keeping the correct conditions inside the cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A plant cell has an actual length of 0.04 mm. In a textbook photograph the image of the cell is 20 mm long. What is the magnification of the photograph?
A ×50
B ×500
C ×800
D ×5000
parts.working: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 20 ÷ 0.04 = 500 (both in mm). ×50 comes from misplacing the decimal point.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student draws a mango leaf from a photograph. On the drawing, the length of the leaf blade (line PQ, from leaf tip to the base of the blade) is 96 mm. The actual length of the leaf blade is 38 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Give your answer to two significant figures. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 magnification = length of drawing ÷ actual length; M1 96 ÷ 38 (= 2.526…); A1 ×2.5 (2 s.f., no units).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equation that links magnification, image size and actual size.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size
parts.working: B1 (any correct rearrangement accepted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 0.25 mm into micrometres (µm).
parts.answer: 250 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert 1800 µm into millimetres.
parts.answer: 1.8 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photograph of a whole water-lily leaf has a line drawn across its widest part. On the photograph the line is 82 mm long. The actual width of the leaf is 164 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mitochondrion is 42 mm long in a photomicrograph. The magnification is ×3000. What is the actual length of the mitochondrion?
A 0.014 µm
B 14 µm
C 140 µm
D 126 000 µm
parts.answer: B 14 µm
parts.working: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 42 ÷ 3000 = 0.014 mm = 14 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm). C divides by 300 instead of 3000; D multiplies instead of dividing; A gives 0.014 mm but labels it µm without converting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an electron micrograph a chloroplast is 30 mm long. The magnification is ×6000. What is the actual length of the chloroplast?
A 0.5 µm
B 5 µm
C 50 µm
D 180 µm
parts.answer: B 5 µm
parts.working: Convert the image to µm: 30 mm = 30 000 µm. Actual = 30 000 ÷ 6000 = 5 µm. 0.5 µm comes from using 3000 µm per 30 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A human red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. What is this diameter in millimetres?
A 0.075 mm
B 0.0075 mm
C 0.00075 mm
D 7500 mm
parts.working: 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 7.5 µm = 7.5 ÷ 1000 = 0.0075 mm. 0.075 mm results from dividing by 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photograph shows a transverse section of an okra (bhindi) pod at a magnification of ×1.7. The line XY drawn across the widest part of the image of the section is 68 mm long.
Calculate the actual width of the okra pod in mm. Show your working.
parts.answer: 40 mm
parts.working: M1 actual size = image size ÷ magnification; M1 68 ÷ 1.7; A1 40 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why line XY should be measured in millimetres rather than centimetres.
parts.answer: mm gives a more precise reading / fewer decimal places / ruler graduated in mm
parts.working: B1 idea that measuring to the nearest mm is more precise (cm leads to rounding errors).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photomicrograph of human cheek cells shows one cell with an image diameter of 45 mm. The actual diameter of the cell is 60 µm.
Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 convert 45 mm to 45 000 µm (or 60 µm to 0.06 mm) and divide; A1 ×750.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The nucleus of the same cell is 6 mm across in the photomicrograph. Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus in µm.
parts.answer: 8 µm
parts.working: M1 6000 µm ÷ 750 (ecf from (a)); A1 8 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student views a thin strip of onion epidermis under a microscope. The diameter of the circular field of view is 2.0 mm. Along one diameter, 8 cells fit end to end exactly.
Calculate the mean length of one cell in µm.
parts.answer: 250 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why this method gives only an estimate of cell length.
parts.answer: cells are not all the same length / cells may not fit exactly / cells may not lie exactly along the diameter
parts.working: B1 any one valid idea.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A drawing of a neem leaflet is 152 mm long. The actual leaflet is 190 mm long.
Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what a magnification less than 1 tells you about the drawing.
parts.answer: the drawing is smaller than the real leaflet

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The sizes of four structures are:
mitochondrion 1.5 µm
nucleus of a liver cell 0.008 mm
bacterium 0.003 mm
red blood cell 7 µm
Convert all the sizes to µm.
parts.answer: mitochondrion 1.5 µm; nucleus 8 µm; bacterium 3 µm; red blood cell 7 µm
parts.working: B2 both conversions (0.008 mm = 8 µm, 0.003 mm = 3 µm) correct; B1 one correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the four structures in order of size, starting with the smallest.
parts.answer: mitochondrion, bacterium, red blood cell, nucleus
parts.working: B1 (ecf from (a)).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student draws a pigeon feather. Line AB on the drawing, from the tip of the feather to the end of the shaft, is 118 mm. The drawing has a magnification of ×3.5.
Calculate the actual length of the feather. Give your answer in mm to two significant figures.
parts.answer: 34 mm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification; M1 118 ÷ 3.5 (= 33.7…); A1 34 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bacterium is 2 µm long. How long is it in a drawing made at ×5000 magnification?
A 0.0004 mm
B 0.4 mm
C 10 mm
D 10 000 mm
parts.answer: C 10 mm
parts.working: Image size = actual size × magnification. 2 µm = 0.002 mm; 0.002 × 5000 = 10 mm. A divides instead of multiplying and gives the wrong unit; B uses ×200 instead of ×5000; D is a unit error (10 mm × 1000).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a photomicrograph of root tip cells, a scale bar 25 mm long is labelled 10 µm. What is the magnification of the photomicrograph?
A ×250
B ×400
C ×2500
D ×25 000
parts.working: Scale bar image = 25 mm = 25 000 µm; actual = 10 µm. Magnification = 25 000 ÷ 10 = 2500. ×250 comes from converting 25 mm to 2500 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photograph of a green chilli has a magnification of ×0.8. On the photograph the chilli is 56 mm long, measured from the tip to the point where the stalk joins.
Calculate the actual length of the chilli in mm.
parts.answer: 70 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A student makes a large drawing of the chilli from the photograph. The same length on the drawing is 140 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the student's drawing compared with the real chilli. Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.working: M1 140 ÷ 70 (use of the actual length from (a), allow ecf); A1 ×2.0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the answer to (b) is not 140 ÷ 56.
parts.answer: 56 mm is the size of the photograph image, not the actual size; the photograph is itself magnified (×0.8)
parts.working: B1 magnification must compare the drawing with the actual object, not with another image.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rod-shaped bacterium is 2.5 µm long. It is drawn in a textbook at a magnification of ×12 000. Calculate the length of the drawing in mm.
parts.answer: 30 mm
parts.working: M1 image = actual × magnification = 2.5 × 12 000 = 30 000 µm; A1 30 mm (÷ 1000).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A yeast cell drawn at the same magnification is 96 mm long. How many times longer is the yeast cell than the bacterium?
parts.answer: 3.2 times
parts.working: M1 96 ÷ 30 (or actual 8 µm ÷ 2.5 µm); A1 3.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pollen grain from a cotton flower has an image diameter of 36 mm in a micrograph taken at ×800. Calculate its actual diameter in µm.
parts.answer: 45 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A pollen grain from a second species has an actual diameter of 40 µm. Calculate the diameter of its image, in mm, if photographed at the same magnification.
parts.answer: 32 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student traces the outline of a lotus leaf on centimetre-square grid paper. Inside the outline there are 42 complete squares and 18 squares that are partly covered. The student counts each part-covered square as half a square.
Estimate the area of the leaf in cm².
parts.answer: 51 cm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to (a) into mm².
parts.answer: 5100 mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the estimate of leaf area could be made more accurate.
parts.answer: use grid paper with smaller squares (e.g. mm squares)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student makes a photomicrograph of a pair of guard cells. A scale bar on the printed photomicrograph is labelled 20 µm and measures 36 mm long. A guard cell measures 27 mm long on the same photomicrograph. The caption says 'magnification ×1000'.
Calculate the magnification from the scale bar. Show your working.
parts.working: 1 mark: 36 mm converted to 36 000 µm. 1 mark: 36 000 ÷ 20 = 1800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the guard cell in µm, using the magnification from (a).
parts.answer: 15 µm
parts.working: 1 mark: 27 mm = 27 000 µm. 1 mark: 27 000 ÷ 1800 = 15 µm (actual = image ÷ magnification).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the scale bar gives a more reliable size than the magnification in the caption.
parts.answer: The printed photograph has been enlarged or reduced, so the caption magnification no longer applies; the scale bar is enlarged by the same amount as the cells, so it still gives the true size.
parts.working: 1 mark: the photograph was printed at a different size, so the caption magnification is no longer correct. 1 mark: the scale bar changes size in the same proportion as the image, so it gives the actual size.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
