Which sequence shows the levels of organisation from the smallest to the largest?
A cell → organ → tissue → organ system
B cell → tissue → organ → organ system
C tissue → cell → organ → organ system
D cell → tissue → organ system → organ
parts.answer: B cell → tissue → organ → organ system
parts.working: Similar cells form a tissue; tissues form an organ; organs working together form an organ system. Option A swaps tissue and organ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape. State how this helps the cell carry out its function.
parts.answer: large surface area (to volume ratio) for fast diffusion of oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other features of red blood cells that help them transport oxygen.
parts.answer: contain haemoglobin; no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin); small and flexible to pass through capillaries
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is an organ?
A xylem tissue
B heart
C red blood cell
D muscle fibre
parts.answer: B heart
parts.working: The heart is made of several tissues (muscle, nervous and epithelial tissue) working together, so it is an organ. Xylem is a tissue; the red blood cell and muscle fibre are cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fat (adipose) cells store lipid. Describe two structural features of a fat cell and explain how each feature helps it to store lipid.
parts.answer: Feature 1: a single large droplet of lipid fills most of the cell, giving a large store of energy-rich fat. Feature 2: the cytoplasm and nucleus are pushed to the edge of the cell, leaving space for the lipid droplet.
parts.working: 1 mark for each feature described (large lipid droplet; cytoplasm and nucleus pushed to the edge). 1 mark for each explanation (lipid stored as an energy reserve; space for the droplet to expand).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the level of organisation of a sperm cell.
parts.answer: cell
parts.working: A sperm cell is a single cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the level of organisation of the heart.
parts.answer: organ
parts.working: The heart is made of several tissues working together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the level of organisation of the circulatory system.
parts.answer: organ system
parts.working: The circulatory system is made of several organs (heart, blood vessels) working together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the level of organisation of a root hair cell.
parts.answer: cell
parts.working: A root hair is a single cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the level of organisation of xylem tissue.
parts.answer: tissue
parts.working: Xylem tissue is a group of similar cells (vessels, parenchyma) that work together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the level of organisation of a root.
parts.answer: organ
parts.working: The root is made of several tissues (epidermis, cortex, xylem and phloem) working together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An egg cell (ovum) is much larger than a sperm cell. Explain why the egg cell is larger.
parts.answer: The egg cell has a large cytoplasm containing a store of food (nutrients), which nourishes the early development of the embryo before it can feed itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: contains a store of food / nutrients. 1 mark: the food is used to nourish the developing embryo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A root hair cell and a palisade mesophyll cell are both plant cells. State two features that they share, and one feature that differs.
parts.answer: Shared: both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus (both have a cell wall and vacuole). Difference: the palisade cell contains many chloroplasts, whereas the root hair cell has none because it is underground and not photosynthetic.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two shared features (cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, cell wall, vacuole). 1 mark for the difference: palisade cells have many chloroplasts and root hair cells have none.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each specialised cell, state one feature and explain how it helps the cell carry out its function.
(i) root hair cell
(ii) ciliated cell lining the trachea
(iii) palisade mesophyll cell
(iv) sperm cell
parts.answer: (i) long extension – large surface area for water and ion uptake; (ii) cilia – beat to move mucus up and out of the airway; (iii) many chloroplasts – absorb light for photosynthesis; (iv) flagellum / tail – swims to the egg (or many mitochondria – energy for swimming; enzymes in acrosome – digest jelly coat)
parts.working: 1 mark each for feature linked to function.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly pairs a specialised cell with a feature and its function?
A red blood cell – has a nucleus – carries oxygen
B xylem vessel – living cytoplasm – transports water
C nerve cell – long axon – carries electrical impulses
D root hair cell – thick cell wall – absorbs water
parts.answer: C nerve cell – long axon – carries electrical impulses
parts.working: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus. Xylem vessels are dead, with no living cytoplasm. Root hair cells have a thin cell wall so water can pass through quickly.

practice.stem: Phloem tissue contains sieve tube elements and companion cells. A sieve tube element has no nucleus, few organelles and perforated end walls (sieve plates). Each sieve tube element is closely linked to a companion cell, which has a nucleus and many mitochondria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage to a sieve tube element of having few organelles and no nucleus.
parts.answer: There is more space in the tube for the sugar solution (sap) to flow through.
parts.working: 1 mark: more room for the sap to flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the companion cell has many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Companion cells carry out active transport: they load sugars into the sieve tube element against a concentration gradient. Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration to supply this energy (ATP).
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport needs energy. 1 mark: mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to release energy. 1 mark: sugars are loaded into the sieve tube against a concentration gradient (or the companion cell's nucleus and mitochondria control and power this).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a motor neurone.
parts.answer: A cell body at one end, with many short dendrites; one very long axon; the axon is covered in a fatty myelin sheath.
parts.working: 1 mark: a cell body with dendrites. 1 mark: a long axon with a myelin sheath.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the myelin sheath and the long axon adapt the neurone for carrying impulses over long distances.
parts.answer: The myelin sheath insulates the axon, so the impulse jumps between the gaps in the sheath (nodes of Ranvier), which makes the impulse travel faster. The long axon carries the impulse from the spinal cord to distant muscles without needing many cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: the myelin insulates and speeds up the impulse. 1 mark: the long axon carries the impulse over a long distance with few cells in the path.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Xylem vessels are dead at maturity. Explain why this is an advantage in the transport of water and mineral ions.
parts.answer: There is no cytoplasm or end walls to block the flow, so water and ions move through a continuous hollow column with little resistance. The lignin in the walls strengthens the vessel so it does not collapse under the pressure of the water column.
parts.working: 1 mark: no cytoplasm or end walls, so there is no obstruction to flow. 1 mark: a hollow, continuous column. 1 mark: lignin strengthens the walls and prevents collapse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'All cells in a tissue have the same structure.' Explain why this is not true for xylem tissue, naming two different cell types found in it.
parts.answer: Xylem tissue contains xylem vessels, which are dead, hollow tubes with lignified walls and no end walls, and xylem parenchyma, which are living cells that store food and support the vessels.
parts.working: 1 mark: names xylem vessels. 1 mark: names xylem parenchyma (or fibres). 1 mark: correct description of one difference in structure (dead and hollow vs living).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A root hair cell is a long, thin projection of an epidermis cell. Explain how this shape helps the cell to absorb water and mineral ions from the soil.
parts.answer: A large surface area is created by the long thin projection, increasing the area for water to enter by osmosis. The cell wall is thin, so water passes through quickly. The cell has many mitochondria to provide energy for the active uptake of mineral ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: large surface area for absorption. 1 mark: thin cell wall so water passes quickly. 1 mark: mitochondria release energy for active transport of mineral ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of these as a cell, a tissue, an organ or an organ system:
xylem; leaf; digestive system; neurone; heart
parts.answer: xylem – tissue; leaf – organ; digestive system – organ system; neurone – cell; heart – organ
parts.working: All five correct 3 marks; four correct 2 marks; two or three correct 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the stomach is described as an organ.
parts.answer: it is made of several different tissues (e.g. muscle, glandular / epithelial tissue) working together to perform a specific function (digestion)
parts.working: B1 group of different tissues; B1 working together for a specific function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Muscle cells in the leg of a cyclist contain many mitochondria. Explain why muscle cells need many mitochondria during a long ride.
parts.answer: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases a large amount of energy for muscle contraction. A large number of mitochondria allows the cell to release more energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. 1 mark: a large amount of energy is needed for continuous contraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Muscle cells also store glycogen. Explain how this helps the cyclist on a long ride.
parts.answer: Glycogen is a store of glucose; it is broken down to glucose when the energy demand is high, which is used in respiration to release energy for contraction.
parts.working: 1 mark: glycogen is a stored form of glucose. 1 mark: it is converted back to glucose for respiration when energy is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cell A has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Cell B has no cell wall, no chloroplasts and many lysosomes. State which cell is from a plant and which is from an animal.
parts.answer: Cell A is from a plant; cell B is from an animal.
parts.working: 1 mark: plant cell A; animal cell B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cell A, but not cell B, can make its own food.
parts.answer: Cell A has chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll to absorb light for photosynthesis; cell B has no chloroplasts, so it cannot photosynthesise and must obtain its food from other sources.
parts.working: 1 mark: chloroplasts contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis (cell A). 1 mark: cell B has no chloroplasts, so it cannot make food by photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a cell, a tissue, an organ and an organ system, using one example from a plant for each of the four levels.
parts.answer: Cell: a single unit, e.g. a palisade mesophyll cell. Tissue: a group of similar cells doing the same job, e.g. epidermis tissue. Organ: different tissues working together for a particular function, e.g. a leaf. Organ system: several organs working together, e.g. the shoot system (stem and leaves) or root system.
parts.working: 1 mark for correct definition of tissue. 1 mark for a correct definition of organ with example. 1 mark for a correct plant example for each level (cell and tissue or organ). 1 mark for a correct organ system and example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the advantages of cell specialisation for a multicellular organism.
parts.answer: Each specialised cell can carry out one job very efficiently; its structure can be adapted to its function; cells working together in tissues and organs allow complex processes that a single cell could not carry out; the organism can grow and survive in a wider range of conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: efficient for one job; structure adapted to function; division of labour allows complex functions; tissues and organs work together; a wider range of activities or environments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fish has a single circulation and a mammal has a double circulation. Explain the difference between these two systems.
parts.answer: Single: blood passes through the heart once for each complete circuit of the body (heart → gills → body → heart). Double: blood passes through the heart twice for each circuit (once to the lungs, once to the rest of the body).
parts.working: B1 single = once through heart per circuit; B1 double = twice (pulmonary and systemic circuits).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a double circulation.
parts.answer: Blood can be pumped to the body at a higher pressure (after returning from the lungs), so oxygenated blood reaches tissues faster.
parts.working: B1; accept keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these structures in the order in which a red blood cell passes through them, starting at the vena cava:
left atrium, aorta, right ventricle, lungs, pulmonary vein, right atrium, left ventricle, pulmonary artery
parts.answer: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta
parts.working: B3 all correct; B2 one structure out of place; B1 the right side (RA → RV → pulmonary artery) or the left side correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in this pathway the blood becomes oxygenated.
parts.answer: In the lungs (capillaries around the alveoli).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood into the left atrium?
A aorta
B pulmonary artery
C pulmonary vein
D vena cava
parts.answer: C pulmonary vein
parts.working: The pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs.

practice.stem: A doctor at a clinic in Hyderabad wants to check the heart of a patient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the activity of the heart can be monitored.
parts.answer: Measuring pulse rate (at wrist or neck); listening to the sounds of the valves closing with a stethoscope; electrocardiogram (ECG).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the part of the heart described by each statement.
(i) the chamber that pumps blood to the lungs
(ii) the chamber that receives blood from the vena cava
(iii) the wall of muscle that separates the left and right sides
(iv) the chamber with the thickest wall
parts.answer: (i) right ventricle; (ii) right atrium; (iii) septum; (iv) left ventricle
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle.
parts.answer: The left ventricle pumps blood all round the body, which needs a higher pressure; the right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs (low pressure protects lung capillaries). Thicker wall = more muscle = stronger contraction.
parts.working: B1 left pumps to whole body / further; B1 needs higher pressure / more muscle for stronger contraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the septum.
parts.answer: Separates oxygenated blood (left side) from deoxygenated blood (right side), so they do not mix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the valves between the atria and the ventricles and state their function.
parts.answer: Atrioventricular valves (bicuspid on the left, tricuspid on the right); they prevent blood flowing back into the atria when the ventricles contract.
parts.working: B1 name; B1 prevent backflow into the atria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the semilunar valves at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery help the heart to work efficiently.
parts.answer: They close when the ventricles relax, so blood in the arteries cannot flow back into the ventricles; this keeps blood moving in one direction.
parts.working: B1 close when ventricles relax / pressure in artery higher; B1 prevent backflow into ventricles / one-way flow.

practice.stem:
Five students at a school in Rawalpindi measure their pulse rate at rest and immediately after two minutes of skipping.
Student : resting / beats per min : after exercise / beats per min
1 : 72 : 128
2 : 68 : 120
3 : 75 : 134
4 : 70 : 126
5 : 65 : 117

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean resting pulse rate and the mean pulse rate after exercise.
parts.answer: Resting 70 beats/min; after exercise 125 beats/min
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean pulse rate. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: type of exercise; duration / intensity of exercise; time the pulse is counted for; time after exercise when pulse is measured; resting time before the first reading.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate increases during a game of football.
parts.answer: Muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose; faster heart rate delivers more blood (oxygen, glucose) to muscles; and removes more carbon dioxide (and heat) from them.
parts.working: B1 more respiration in muscles / more energy needed; B1 more oxygen and glucose delivered; B1 more carbon dioxide removed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the hormone that increases heart rate before the match begins.
parts.answer: Adrenaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row describes the valves while the ventricles are contracting and pumping blood out of the heart?
A atrioventricular valves open; semilunar valves open
B atrioventricular valves open; semilunar valves closed
C atrioventricular valves closed; semilunar valves open
D atrioventricular valves closed; semilunar valves closed
parts.answer: C atrioventricular valves closed; semilunar valves open
parts.working: As the ventricles contract the atrioventricular valves close to stop backflow into the atria, and the semilunar valves are pushed open so blood leaves through the arteries. B gives the opposite.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence shows the path of blood in the circulation of a fish?
A heart → gills → body → heart
B heart → body → gills → heart
C heart → gills → heart → body → heart
D heart → lungs → heart → body → heart
parts.answer: A heart → gills → body → heart
parts.working: A fish has a single circulation: blood goes from the heart to the gills, then directly to the body and back to the heart. C and D describe a double circulation.

practice.stem:
A student counts her pulse for 15 seconds at one-minute intervals after running. Her resting rate is 72 beats per minute.
Time after running / min : beats in 15 s
0 : 31
1 : 27
2 : 24
3 : 21
4 : 30
5 : 18
6 : 18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each count into a pulse rate in beats per minute.
parts.working: Multiply each 15-second count by 4 (M1); all correct (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest one reason for it.
parts.answer: 4 minutes (120 beats/min); e.g. the student miscounted / moved or talked / lost the pulse / counted for longer than 15 s.
parts.working: B1 4 min reading; B1 plausible reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the results, state how long it took for the pulse rate to return to its resting value (72 beats/min).
parts.answer: 5 minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why counting for 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 is less accurate than counting for a full minute.
parts.answer: Any counting error is multiplied by 4 (a miss of one beat gives an error of 4 beats/min).

practice.stem:
Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute.
cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume
A trained athlete from Karachi has a resting heart rate of 52 beats/min and a stroke volume of 96 cm³. A student who does not train has a resting heart rate of 75 beats/min and a stroke volume of 66 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cardiac output of each person in dm³ per minute. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Athlete: 4.99 dm³/min; other student: 4.95 dm³/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the athlete has a lower resting heart rate but almost the same cardiac output.
parts.answer: Training has made the heart muscle stronger / larger, so each beat pumps more blood (larger stroke volume); fewer beats are needed to deliver the same volume of blood.
parts.working: B1 stronger / larger heart muscle; B1 larger stroke volume so fewer beats needed.

practice.stem: Some babies are born with a hole in the septum between the left and right ventricles. In some of these babies, deoxygenated blood passes through the hole from the right ventricle into the left ventricle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this affects the oxygen concentration of the blood in the aorta.
parts.answer: Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle mixes with oxygenated blood in the left ventricle; so blood in the aorta has a lower oxygen concentration than normal.
parts.working: B1 mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood; B1 lower oxygen in aorta / to body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two symptoms a baby with this condition might show.
parts.answer: Any two of: tiredness / lack of energy; breathlessness; slow growth / poor feeding; bluish skin or lips.
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to less oxygen reaching tissues.

practice.stem:
The table shows the pressure in the left ventricle and in the aorta during one heartbeat.
Time / s : left ventricle / kPa : aorta / kPa
0.0 : 1 : 11
0.1 : 8 : 10
0.2 : 16 : 15
0.3 : 15 : 14.5
0.4 : 9 : 13
0.5 : 2 : 12
0.6 : 1 : 11.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table, state the times at which the semilunar valve in the aorta is open. Explain how you decided.
parts.answer: 0.2 s and 0.3 s; this is when the pressure in the left ventricle is higher than the pressure in the aorta.
parts.working: B1 both times; B1 ventricle pressure greater than aortic pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the maximum and minimum pressure in the aorta.
parts.answer: 5 kPa

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pressure in the aorta never falls as low as the pressure in the left ventricle.
parts.answer: The semilunar valve closes so blood cannot flow back into the ventricle; the elastic wall of the aorta recoils, keeping pressure up between beats.
parts.working: B1 valve closes / prevents backflow; B1 elastic recoil of artery wall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the length of time spent exercising affects a person's heart rate. Include what you would measure, how you would make it a fair test, how you would record the results and how you would reach a conclusion.
parts.answer: Measure resting pulse; do the same exercise (e.g. step-ups at a fixed rate) for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 minutes; measure pulse immediately afterwards for 1 minute; rest until pulse returns to resting before the next trial; repeat and calculate means; plot pulse against time.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: measure resting pulse first; independent variable – exercise times (at least 4 values); same type and intensity of exercise (e.g. step height and rate set by a metronome); measure pulse at wrist/neck for 60 s (or with a pulse monitor) immediately after; rest until pulse returns to resting rate between trials; same person / same conditions (same time of day, no food or drink); repeat each time and calculate a mean; table: exercise time / min against pulse rate / beats per min; conclusion from graph trend; safety: stop if dizzy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare arteries, veins and capillaries by stating for each: the relative thickness of the wall, the size of the lumen, and whether valves are present.
parts.answer: Arteries: thick muscular elastic wall, narrow lumen, no valves (except at base of aorta/pulmonary artery). Veins: thin wall, wide (large) lumen, valves present. Capillaries: wall one cell thick, very narrow lumen, no valves.
parts.working: B1 per vessel with all three features correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel carries blood from the small intestine to the liver?
A hepatic artery
B hepatic portal vein
C hepatic vein
D renal vein
parts.answer: B hepatic portal vein
parts.working: The hepatic portal vein carries blood rich in absorbed food from the gut to the liver. The hepatic vein carries blood away from the liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why blood flowing out of a cut artery spurts in time with the heartbeat.
parts.answer: Each contraction of the ventricles pushes blood into the aorta at high pressure. The pressure rises and falls with each heartbeat, and the elastic artery wall stretches and recoils, so the blood leaves in spurts.
parts.working: 1 mark: ventricles contract and push blood into arteries at high pressure. 1 mark: pressure rises and falls with each heartbeat. 1 mark: elastic artery wall stretches and recoils, so blood flows out in spurts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the elastic walls of the aorta help to maintain blood flow between heartbeats.
parts.answer: During ventricular contraction (systole) the aorta wall stretches to take the blood. During relaxation (diastole) the elastic wall recoils, pushing the blood forward so that the flow and pressure are maintained and the surges from the heart are smoothed out.
parts.working: 1 mark: walls stretch when blood enters during systole. 1 mark: elastic recoil during diastole. 1 mark: pushes blood forward, so flow is maintained. 1 mark: smooths out the surges of pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that: (i) carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; (ii) carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium; (iii) carries blood from the kidney to the vena cava.
parts.answer: (i) pulmonary artery; (ii) pulmonary vein; (iii) renal vein
parts.working: 1 mark each: pulmonary artery; pulmonary vein; renal vein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a capillary is related to its function.
parts.answer: Wall is one cell thick so diffusion distance is short; substances (oxygen, glucose) diffuse quickly into tissues / narrow lumen brings red cells close to tissue cells.
parts.working: B1 thin wall / one cell thick; B1 short diffusion distance / exchange of materials.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function.
parts.answer: Thick muscular and elastic wall withstands high pressure from the heart; elastic tissue stretches and recoils to maintain pressure / smooth flow.
parts.working: B1 thick wall withstands high pressure; B1 elastic recoil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why veins have valves.
parts.answer: Blood in veins is at low pressure; valves prevent backflow (keep blood moving towards the heart).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the blood vessel that:
(i) carries blood to a kidney
(ii) carries blood away from the liver
(iii) carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs
(iv) carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the body
parts.answer: (i) renal artery; (ii) hepatic vein; (iii) pulmonary artery; (iv) aorta
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel has the thickest muscular and elastic wall?
A vena cava
B pulmonary vein
C aorta
D hepatic portal vein
parts.answer: C aorta
parts.working: The aorta carries blood at high pressure from the left ventricle, so its wall has thick layers of elastic tissue and muscle. The vena cava, pulmonary vein and hepatic portal vein carry blood at lower pressure and have thinner walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Veins have a wider lumen than arteries, yet the blood pressure in veins is much lower. Explain why.
parts.answer: The blood has already passed through the capillaries, so the pressure has fallen by the time it reaches the veins. Veins have thin walls because they do not need to withstand high pressure. The wide lumen holds a large volume of blood with little resistance to flow. Valves in the veins stop blood flowing backwards, so the blood keeps moving towards the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark: pressure has already fallen after the capillaries. 1 mark: thin walls because high pressure is not needed. 1 mark: wide lumen offers little resistance. 1 mark: valves keep blood moving towards the heart.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why blood from the small intestine passes through the liver before it reaches the rest of the body.
parts.answer: Absorbed glucose, amino acids and other nutrients enter the hepatic portal vein, which takes them to the liver. The liver stores or converts excess nutrients, deaminates excess amino acids, and removes or detoxifies harmful substances before the blood reaches the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark: nutrients enter the hepatic portal vein. 1 mark: liver stores or converts excess nutrients. 1 mark: liver deaminates amino acids or detoxifies harmful substances. 1 mark: blood composition regulated before it reaches the heart.

practice.stem:
The mean blood pressure was measured in different vessels of a person at rest.
Vessel : mean pressure / kPa
aorta : 13
large arteries : 12
arterioles : 7
capillaries : 3
large veins : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in pressure between the aorta and the capillaries. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Blood pressure in large veins is very low. Explain how blood in the leg veins is still returned to the heart.
parts.answer: Valves in veins prevent backflow; contraction of skeletal muscles around the veins squeezes them and pushes blood towards the heart; wide lumen gives little resistance to flow.
parts.working: B1 valves prevent backflow; B1 skeletal muscle contraction squeezes veins; B1 wide lumen / low resistance.

practice.stem:
Rings of the same width were cut from an artery and a vein from a goat (from a butcher). Each ring was hung from a hook, its length measured, a 50 g mass hung on it, and the length measured again. The mass was then removed.
Ring : length at start / mm : length with mass / mm : length after mass removed / mm
artery : 20 : 26 : 20.5
vein : 20 : 33 : 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in length of each ring when the mass was added.
parts.answer: Artery: 30 %; vein: 65 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the results, compare the elasticity of the two rings and explain why this property of the artery wall is useful.
parts.answer: The artery ring stretched less and returned almost to its original length (20.5 mm), so its wall is elastic; the vein ring stayed stretched (30 mm), so it is much less elastic. Elastic recoil of the artery wall helps keep blood pressure up and blood flowing smoothly between heartbeats.
parts.working: B1 artery recoils almost fully / more elastic than vein, with data; B1 recoil maintains pressure / evens out flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to make this investigation more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat with several rings from each vessel (from more animals) and calculate means.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of veins helps to return blood to the heart against the force of gravity?
A thick elastic walls
B valves
C a narrow lumen
D a large number of capillaries
parts.answer: B valves
parts.working: Valves stop blood flowing backwards, and contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes the veins to push blood towards the heart. Veins have thin walls and a wide lumen, so A and C are wrong; capillaries are not part of veins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The aorta has an internal diameter of 2.4 cm. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the aorta, in cm², to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.52 cm²
parts.working: 1 mark: radius = 1.2 cm, A = πr². 1 mark: 4.52 cm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the total cross-sectional area of all the capillaries is much larger than the cross-sectional area of the aorta.
parts.answer: Capillaries branch into a huge number of vessels in parallel. Their total cross-sectional area is much larger than the aorta, so the blood flows slowly through them. This gives more time for diffusion of substances between the blood and the cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: many capillaries in parallel. 1 mark: total area is much larger, so the blood flow slows. 1 mark: slow flow gives time for exchange by diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person with high blood pressure has narrowed arterioles. Explain how this raises blood pressure, and give one effect of the higher pressure on the heart.
parts.answer: Narrower arterioles increase resistance to blood flow, so the pressure in the arteries rises. The left ventricle has to pump harder against this pressure, so its muscular wall thickens and the heart works harder.
parts.working: 1 mark: narrower arterioles increase resistance. 1 mark: pressure in the arteries rises. 1 mark: heart must pump harder. 1 mark: left ventricle wall thickens (or heart failure risk increases).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each of the following blood components: (i) red blood cells, (ii) phagocytes, (iii) lymphocytes, (iv) platelets.
parts.answer: (i) transport oxygen (using haemoglobin); (ii) engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis); (iii) produce antibodies; (iv) help blood to clot.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances transported dissolved in plasma.
parts.answer: Any two of: glucose, amino acids, carbon dioxide, urea, hormones, ions (salts), water, plasma proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which part of the blood carries carbon dioxide, urea and hormones?
A plasma
B platelets
C red blood cells
D white blood cells
parts.answer: A plasma
parts.working: These substances are carried dissolved in the plasma. Red blood cells mainly carry oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three substances that are transported in blood plasma and are not blood cells.
parts.answer: Any three of: glucose, amino acids, carbon dioxide, urea, hormones, plasma proteins (e.g. fibrinogen), mineral ions
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct substance named.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between red blood cells and white blood cells.
parts.answer: Red blood cells have no nucleus and contain haemoglobin; white blood cells have a nucleus and do not contain haemoglobin (white cells are larger and have irregular shapes).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct differences: nucleus present or absent; contains haemoglobin or not; shape; size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium.
parts.answer: The phagocyte moves towards the bacterium, surrounds it and engulfs it into a vacuole by endocytosis. Enzymes from lysosomes then digest the bacterium.
parts.working: 1 mark: phagocyte moves towards the bacterium. 1 mark: engulfs it (phagocytosis). 1 mark: lysosome enzymes digest it.

practice.stem: A boy cuts his knee while playing cricket.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens in the blood to form a clot when the skin is cut.
parts.answer: Platelets are involved; soluble fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh of fibres that traps red blood cells, forming a clot.
parts.working: B1 fibrinogen → fibrin; B1 soluble to insoluble; B1 mesh traps blood cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of blood clotting.
parts.answer: Prevents loss of blood; prevents entry of pathogens.
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
Red blood cell counts were measured for two healthy adults of the same age.
Person living in Karachi (sea level): 5.0 million per mm³
Person living in Murree (about 2300 m above sea level): 5.9 million per mm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference in red blood cell count of the person living in Murree compared with the person living in Karachi.
parts.answer: 18 % higher

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: Air at high altitude contains less oxygen (lower pressure); more red blood cells / haemoglobin carry more oxygen to the tissues.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen at altitude; B1 more red cells increase oxygen transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood cells contain haemoglobin?
A platelets
B red blood cells
C phagocytes
D lymphocytes
parts.answer: B red blood cells
parts.working: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen. Platelets are cell fragments that help clotting, and phagocytes and lymphocytes are white blood cells that defend the body; none of these contain haemoglobin.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which white blood cells produce antibodies?
A phagocytes
B lymphocytes
C platelets
D red blood cells
parts.answer: B lymphocytes
parts.working: Lymphocytes make antibodies that target specific pathogens. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens, platelets help blood to clot, and red blood cells carry oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how haemoglobin helps red blood cells to carry oxygen.
parts.answer: Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs, forming oxyhaemoglobin, so large amounts of oxygen can be carried in the blood. In tissues where oxygen concentration is low, the oxygen is released for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs. 1 mark: large amounts of oxygen carried. 1 mark: oxygen released where it is needed for respiration.

practice.stem: In a blood smear, 200 white blood cells were counted: 136 phagocytes, 56 lymphocytes and 8 other white cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of white blood cells that were lymphocytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a phagocyte and a lymphocyte can be distinguished when seen under a microscope.
parts.answer: Phagocyte: lobed (multi-lobed) nucleus and granular cytoplasm; lymphocyte: large round nucleus filling most of the cell, little cytoplasm.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A week later the person develops a bacterial infection. Suggest how the numbers of each type of white blood cell change and explain why.
parts.answer: Both increase; more phagocytes to engulf and digest the bacteria; more lymphocytes to make antibodies against the bacterial antigens.
parts.working: B1 increase; B1 phagocytes engulf/digest; B1 lymphocytes produce (specific) antibodies.

practice.stem: Dengue fever is common in Pakistan after the monsoon. In one patient the platelet count fell from 250 000 per mm³ to 40 000 per mm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in platelet count.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why doctors watch for bleeding and bruising in this patient.
parts.answer: Platelets are needed for blood clotting; with fewer platelets, blood clots slowly / less well, so small damaged vessels keep bleeding.
parts.working: B1 platelets needed for clotting; B1 so clotting is slower and bleeding continues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person with a low platelet count bruises easily and bleeds for longer than usual.
parts.answer: Platelets are needed to seal damaged blood vessels and start the clotting process. With fewer platelets, fewer plugs form and fewer clotting chemicals are released, so the blood clots more slowly and blood leaks into the tissues under the skin, causing bruises.
parts.working: 1 mark: platelets needed to seal wounds and start clotting. 1 mark: fewer platelets so fewer plugs and less clotting. 1 mark: blood leaks into tissues under the skin, causing bruises. 1 mark: bleeding continues for longer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A blood smear is counted under a microscope. Out of 2000 white blood cells, 1260 are lymphocytes, 680 are neutrophils and 60 are monocytes. Calculate the percentage of white blood cells that are neither lymphocytes nor neutrophils.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person living at high altitude has less oxygen available in the air. Explain how this can lead to an increase in the number of red blood cells.
parts.answer: Less oxygen reaches the kidneys, which release a hormone that stimulates the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. The extra red blood cells contain more haemoglobin, which carries more oxygen to the tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: less oxygen in the blood and kidneys. 1 mark: hormone released by the kidney. 1 mark: hormone stimulates bone marrow to make more red blood cells. 1 mark: more haemoglobin carries more oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two risk factors for coronary heart disease that a person can change.
parts.answer: Smoking; a diet high in saturated fat or salt; lack of exercise; obesity (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two changeable risk factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a high-salt diet may increase the risk of coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: High salt intake raises blood pressure. The high pressure damages and stretches the artery walls and can cause small tears, so fatty deposits are more likely to build up. The heart also has to work harder against the raised pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark: raises blood pressure. 1 mark: damages artery walls. 1 mark: fatty deposits (atheroma) more likely to form. 1 mark: heart works harder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how statins can reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Statins lower the level of LDL cholesterol in the blood. This slows the build-up of fatty deposits (atheroma) in the coronary arteries, so the arteries stay wider and blood flow to the heart is maintained.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower blood cholesterol (LDL). 1 mark: slow the build-up of atheroma. 1 mark: arteries stay wider. 1 mark: lower risk of a blockage or clot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A town has 48 000 adults and 15% of them have high blood pressure. Calculate the number of adults with high blood pressure.
parts.answer: 7200 adults

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the term atheroma.
parts.answer: A fatty deposit (plaque) in the wall of an artery that narrows the lumen.
parts.working: 1 mark: fatty deposit or plaque in the artery wall. 1 mark: narrows the lumen of the artery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the coronary arteries.
parts.answer: Supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood (oxygen and glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a blockage in a coronary artery can cause a heart attack.
parts.answer: Fatty deposits (cholesterol) build up in the artery wall and narrow it / a clot forms; less blood, oxygen and glucose reach part of the heart muscle; that muscle cannot respire aerobically, so it stops contracting / dies.
parts.working: B1 fatty deposit / clot blocks artery; B1 less oxygen (and glucose) to heart muscle; B1 less respiration / muscle cells die / cannot contract.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two risk factors for coronary heart disease that a person can change.
parts.answer: Any two of: diet high in saturated fat / salt; smoking; lack of exercise; stress; obesity.
parts.working: 1 mark each; not age, sex or genes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens when a coronary artery becomes blocked.
parts.answer: Less oxygen and glucose reach the heart muscle, so aerobic respiration slows and anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid. Chest pain (angina) occurs during exercise. If the blockage is complete, the heart muscle cells die, causing a heart attack.
parts.working: 1 mark: less oxygen and glucose supplied to heart muscle. 1 mark: anaerobic respiration and lactic acid. 1 mark: chest pain (angina). 1 mark: heart muscle cells die (heart attack).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a stent is used to treat a narrowed coronary artery.
parts.answer: A thin catheter with a deflated balloon is guided into the narrowed artery. The balloon is inflated to widen the artery (angioplasty), and a stent (a mesh tube) is left in place to keep the artery open, restoring blood flow to the heart muscle.
parts.working: 1 mark: catheter with balloon guided into the artery. 1 mark: balloon inflated to widen the artery. 1 mark: stent left to keep the artery open. 1 mark: blood flow to heart muscle restored.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways a doctor can diagnose a blocked coronary artery, and explain how one of them works.
parts.answer: Any two of: ECG (electrocardiogram, records the heart's electrical activity); angiogram (X-ray pictures of the arteries taken after a dye is injected). Explanation (angiogram): the dye makes the arteries visible on the X-ray, so a narrowed or blocked part shows up.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named tests (2 marks). 1 mark: the dye makes the arteries visible on the X-ray. 1 mark: a narrowing or blockage appears as a reduced width of the artery in the image.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how regular exercise reduces the risk of coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Exercise keeps the heart muscle strong and efficient, lowers blood pressure, and helps control body mass. It also raises HDL cholesterol and lowers LDL cholesterol, slowing the build-up of atheroma.
parts.working: 1 mark: strengthens the heart muscle. 1 mark: lowers blood pressure. 1 mark: helps control body mass. 1 mark: changes blood cholesterol levels (raises HDL or lowers LDL).

practice.stem:
A study followed men aged 45–60 for ten years.
Group : deaths from coronary heart disease per 100 000 men per year
non-smokers : 120
smoke 1–14 cigarettes per day : 210
smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day : 390

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for heavy smokers than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 3.25 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the data show about smoking and coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Death rate increases as the number of cigarettes smoked increases; heavy smokers have over three times the death rate of non-smokers.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 quoting figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why these data alone do not prove that smoking causes coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Other factors could be involved (diet, exercise, age, stress, genes); smokers may differ from non-smokers in these ways; correlation does not show cause.
parts.working: B1 other risk factors not controlled; B1 correlation ≠ causation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A study followed 2000 adults. Of 300 smokers, 84 developed coronary heart disease (CHD). Of 1700 non-smokers, 51 developed CHD. Calculate the percentage of smokers who developed CHD.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of non-smokers who developed CHD.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times more likely a smoker was to develop CHD than a non-smoker. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 9.33 times
parts.working: 1 mark: 28 ÷ 3 seen. 1 mark: 9.33.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this study cannot prove that smoking causes CHD.
parts.answer: Other factors, such as diet, exercise or family history, may differ between the groups (correlation is not causation).
parts.working: 1 mark: other factors could explain the difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood flows through the chambers of the heart, yet the heart muscle still needs its own blood supply from the coronary arteries. Explain why.
parts.answer: The thick heart muscle is too thick for oxygen and glucose to diffuse into it from the blood in the chambers. The muscle cells need a constant supply for aerobic respiration to release energy for contraction, and the coronary arteries deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: thick muscle too far for diffusion from the chambers. 1 mark: muscle needs constant oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration. 1 mark: energy needed for contraction. 1 mark: coronary arteries supply the wall and remove carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A man has chest pain (angina) when he climbs stairs. Explain, using oxygen supply and respiration, why the pain occurs during exercise.
parts.answer: Exercise increases the demand for oxygen and glucose by the heart muscle. The narrowed coronary arteries cannot supply enough, so the heart respires anaerobically and lactic acid builds up, causing pain. The pain eases when he rests.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: heart needs more oxygen during exercise; narrowed artery limits supply; anaerobic respiration; lactic acid builds up and causes pain; pain eases at rest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two lifestyle changes that could reduce his risk of a heart attack.
parts.answer: Stop smoking; reduce salt and saturated fat in the diet; take regular exercise; lose weight (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible lifestyle changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor recommends an artificial pacemaker for a patient whose natural sinoatrial node (SAN) is not working. Explain what the pacemaker does.
parts.answer: The SAN normally sends out electrical impulses that set the rhythm of the heartbeat. The pacemaker produces electrical impulses that stimulate the heart muscle to contract, keeping the heart beating at a regular rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: the SAN normally sets the heart rate with electrical impulses. 1 mark: the pacemaker replaces the impulses. 1 mark: keeps the heart beating regularly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is transpiration?
A the uptake of water by root hair cells
B the loss of water vapour from leaves
C the movement of sucrose through the phloem
D the evaporation of water from the soil surface
parts.answer: B the loss of water vapour from leaves
parts.working: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves (water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffuses out through the stomata). A is water uptake; C is translocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway taken by water from the soil to the air around a leaf. Name the cells or tissues it passes through.
parts.answer: Water enters root hair cells (by osmosis), passes through the root cortex cells to the xylem, moves up the xylem in the root and stem into the leaf veins, passes into mesophyll cells, evaporates from their surfaces into the air spaces and diffuses out through the stomata.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four in correct order: root hair cell; root cortex; xylem (root → stem → leaf); mesophyll cells; evaporation into air spaces; diffusion out through stomata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to the loss of water vapour from leaves.
parts.answer: Transpiration.

practice.stem:
A potted cotton plant was weighed every 2 hours during a sunny day in Faisalabad, and the rate of water loss was calculated.
Time: 06:00, 08:00, 10:00, 12:00, 14:00, 16:00, 18:00
Rate of water loss (g per hour): 0.4, 1.6, 3.2, 4.1, 3.6, 1.8, 0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time at which the rate of water loss was highest.
parts.answer: 12:00 (4.1 g per hour).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss for the seven readings. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.17 g per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the rate was low at 06:00.
parts.answer: Low temperature; low light so stomata were (partly) closed; higher humidity in early morning.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the most suitable type of graph to display these results and how the axes should be arranged.
parts.answer: A line graph with time on the x-axis and rate of water loss (g per hour) on the y-axis.
parts.working: 1 mark: line graph; 1 mark: time on x-axis, rate on y-axis with units.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a leaf, where does liquid water change into water vapour during transpiration?
A on the surfaces of the mesophyll cells, into the air spaces
B inside the xylem vessels of the leaf veins
C in the guard cells, before it passes out of the stoma
D on the outer surface of the waxy cuticle
parts.answer: A on the surfaces of the mesophyll cells, into the air spaces
parts.working: Water evaporates from the wet cell walls of mesophyll cells into the air spaces, then water vapour diffuses out through the stomata. Guard cells control the stoma but are not the main evaporating surface; the cuticle is waterproof.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Under which set of conditions will a well-watered maize plant with open stomata lose water vapour fastest?
A 15 °C, humid air, still air
B 15 °C, dry air, windy
C 35 °C, humid air, still air
D 35 °C, dry air, windy
parts.answer: D 35 °C, dry air, windy
parts.working: High temperature increases evaporation and diffusion; dry air gives a steep water vapour gradient; wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the gradient steep. C has a high temperature but humid, still air reduces the gradient.

practice.stem: A leafy shoot of a guava plant was set up in a potometer. The air bubble in the capillary tube moved 36 mm in 5 minutes in still air. A fan was then switched on and the bubble moved 62 mm in 5 minutes. The internal radius of the capillary tube is 0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water taken up in still air in 5 minutes. Use the formula volume = πr²l, where r is the internal radius of the tube and l the distance moved. Give your answer in mm³ to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 28.3 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in still air in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 5.7 mm³/min
parts.working: 28.27 ÷ 5 = 5.7 mm³/min (allow follow-through).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the distance moved when the fan was switched on. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the fan increased the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: Moving air removes water vapour from around the leaf surface, keeping a steep water vapour concentration (diffusion) gradient between the air spaces and the outside air; more water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, so more water is pulled up the xylem (transpiration pull) and taken up from the potometer.
parts.working: 1 mark each: wind removes water vapour near the leaf; steeper diffusion gradient; faster loss through stomata / more transpiration pull.

parts.label: e
parts.text: State two precautions when setting up a potometer.
parts.answer: Cut the shoot under water; make all joints airtight (e.g. with petroleum jelly); dry the leaves; let the shoot settle for a few minutes before taking readings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases when the temperature rises.
parts.answer: Water molecules gain more kinetic energy, so more water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells; water vapour diffuses faster out through the stomata; warm air can also hold more water vapour, so the diffusion gradient is steeper.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: more kinetic energy; faster evaporation from mesophyll surfaces; faster diffusion of water vapour through stomata; steeper gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration is lower on a humid day.
parts.answer: Humid air contains more water vapour, so the concentration gradient of water vapour between the air spaces in the leaf and the air outside is smaller; less water vapour diffuses out.
parts.working: 1 mark: more water vapour in the air outside; 1 mark: smaller diffusion gradient, slower diffusion out of stomata.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the feature of the leaf interior that provides a large surface for evaporation.
parts.answer: The large internal surface area of the mesophyll cells facing the interconnecting air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an investigation to find out how wind speed affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. You are provided with a potometer, an electric fan and normal laboratory apparatus.
In your plan, include: what you will vary and how; what you will measure; the variables you will keep constant; how you will make the results reliable.
parts.answer: Set up a potometer with a leafy shoot cut under water and airtight joints; vary wind speed by placing the fan at different distances (e.g. 25, 50, 75, 100 cm) or using fan speed settings, plus a no-fan control; measure the distance the bubble moves in a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) and calculate the rate; keep the same shoot, temperature, light intensity and humidity constant; allow 5 minutes to settle at each speed; repeat three times at each speed and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: independent variable – wind speed changed by fan distance/setting with at least 4 values; dependent variable – distance moved by bubble (or volume) in a stated time; rate = distance ÷ time; two controlled variables (e.g. temperature, light intensity, same shoot/leaf area, humidity); acclimatisation time before readings; reset the bubble with the reservoir; repeats and mean; safety/precaution such as airtight seals or cutting under water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On a hot afternoon in Multan the leaves of a pumpkin plant droop, even though the soil is moist. By evening they have recovered. Explain why the leaves droop.
parts.answer: The rate of transpiration is greater than the rate of water uptake by the roots; the leaf cells lose water and become flaccid (lose turgor pressure); so the leaves are no longer supported and wilt.
parts.working: 1 mark each: water loss faster than uptake; cells lose turgor / become flaccid; loss of support → wilting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to the plant of wilting.
parts.answer: The leaves hang down so less surface faces the sun / less heat absorbed, reducing further water loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the leaves recover in the evening.
parts.answer: Lower temperature and light, so transpiration falls (stomata close); water uptake now exceeds loss so cells take in water by osmosis and become turgid again.
parts.working: 1 mark: less transpiration in evening; 1 mark: cells regain water / become turgid.

practice.stem:
Blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink when it absorbs water. A student clipped one dry square of cobalt chloride paper to the upper surface and one to the lower surface of a leaf on a hibiscus plant, and timed how long each took to turn pink.
Upper surface: 240 s
Lower surface: 40 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster the paper on the lower surface changed colour than the paper on the upper surface.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the results show about the two leaf surfaces.
parts.answer: The lower surface loses water vapour faster, so it has more stomata than the upper surface.
parts.working: 1 mark: more water lost from lower surface; 1 mark: more stomata on lower surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cobalt chloride paper must be kept dry and handled with forceps.
parts.answer: Any moisture from the air or from fingers would turn the paper pink before the experiment starts, giving a false result.
parts.working: 1 mark: paper is sensitive to any water; 1 mark: fingers/air moisture would change colour → invalid result.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to improve the reliability of the results.
parts.answer: Repeat on several leaves of the same plant and calculate means.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potometer is used to estimate the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Why does it not measure the rate of transpiration exactly?
A Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells, so uptake is not exactly equal to loss.
B Water vapour lost from the leaves is absorbed back into the capillary tube.
C The potometer measures the movement of sucrose instead of water.
D Water can only enter the shoot by osmosis when the stomata are closed.
parts.answer: A Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells, so uptake is not exactly equal to loss.
parts.working: A potometer measures water uptake. A small proportion of the water absorbed is used (e.g. in photosynthesis) or stays in cells to keep them turgid, so uptake is only approximately equal to water lost. B, C and D are not true.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves up the xylem of a tall tree such as a shisham tree.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cells and diffuses out of the leaf; this creates a transpiration pull (tension) on the water in the xylem; water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion), so a continuous column of water is pulled up from the roots; the xylem vessels are narrow, continuous, hollow tubes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: evaporation/transpiration from leaf; creates transpiration pull / tension; cohesion between water molecules; continuous column of water; pulled up through xylem (continuous hollow tubes) from roots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the trunk of a tree becomes very slightly narrower in diameter at midday than at night.
parts.answer: At midday the transpiration rate is highest, so the tension in the xylem is greatest; the walls of the xylem are pulled inwards, slightly reducing the diameter.
parts.working: 1 mark: high transpiration at midday; 1 mark: greater tension/pull on xylem walls draws them inwards.

practice.stem:
Four similar leafy shoots of a bean plant were treated as follows and hung up in the same room for 48 hours.
A: no petroleum jelly; B: jelly on upper leaf surfaces; C: jelly on lower leaf surfaces; D: jelly on both surfaces.
Shoot | initial mass (g) | mass after 48 h (g)
A | 25.0 | 21.2
B | 24.6 | 21.3
C | 25.4 | 24.6
D | 24.8 | 24.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in mass for each shoot. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.working: (initial − final) ÷ initial × 100. 3 marks all four correct; 2 marks three correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What do the results suggest about where the stomata are found on these leaves? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Most stomata are on the lower surface: covering the lower surface (C) reduced mass loss far more than covering the upper surface (B), whose loss was almost the same as uncovered shoot A; the jelly blocks the stomata so water vapour cannot diffuse out.
parts.working: 1 mark: most stomata on lower surface; 1 mark: comparison using data B vs C (or A vs C); 1 mark: jelly blocks stomata / prevents diffusion of water vapour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why shoot D still lost a small amount of mass.
parts.answer: Water vapour was lost through the stem or through the jelly / cuticle, or the jelly did not cover the leaves completely.
parts.working: B1 for any valid suggestion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be made more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat with several shoots for each treatment and calculate mean percentages.

practice.stem:
A researcher measured the rate of water loss from a leafy shoot of a mulberry tree in still air and in moving air.
Still air: 2.4 g per hour
Moving air: 4.2 g per hour

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water loss in moving air compared with still air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The researcher then covered the shoot with a clear plastic bag in moving air, and the rate fell to 0.6 g per hour. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Water vapour collects inside the bag, so the air around the leaf becomes very humid / saturated; the bag also prevents wind removing water vapour; the diffusion gradient between leaf air spaces and the air is very small, so little water vapour diffuses out.
parts.working: 1 mark each: humidity in bag rises; wind cannot remove water vapour; small diffusion gradient → slow loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plants in very windy places, such as the northern mountain passes, often have small leaves.
parts.answer: Smaller leaf surface area means fewer stomata exposed and less water vapour lost, which reduces the risk of wilting when wind increases transpiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller surface area / fewer stomata; 1 mark: reduces water loss by transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Water moves up the xylem of a tall eucalyptus tree in a continuous column. Which statement best explains this?
A Loss of water vapour from the leaves pulls water up, and water molecules are attracted to each other.
B Xylem vessels contract in waves, squeezing water upwards.
C Root hair cells actively pump water molecules into the xylem using energy from respiration.
D Sucrose in the xylem draws water upwards by osmosis from cell to cell.
parts.answer: A Loss of water vapour from the leaves pulls water up, and water molecules are attracted to each other.
parts.working: Transpiration pull: evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from leaves creates a pull on the water column; cohesion (attraction between water molecules) keeps the column continuous. Xylem cells are dead and cannot contract; water enters roots by osmosis, not active transport of water; xylem carries no sucrose.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a function of xylem?
A transport of sucrose and amino acids
B transport of water and mineral ions and support
C absorption of light for photosynthesis
D gas exchange with the atmosphere
parts.answer: B transport of water and mineral ions and support
parts.working: Xylem transports water and mineral ions and its lignified walls help support the plant. Sucrose and amino acids travel in phloem (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the positions of xylem and phloem in a transverse section of a young dicotyledonous stem.
parts.answer: Vascular bundles in a ring near the outside of the stem; in each bundle the xylem is towards the inside (centre) and the phloem towards the outside.
parts.working: 1 mark: bundles in a ring; 1 mark: xylem inner, phloem outer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the positions of xylem and phloem in a transverse section of a root.
parts.answer: Xylem in the centre of the root (in a star or X shape); phloem in groups between the arms of the xylem.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem central; 1 mark: phloem between xylem arms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In a leaf vein, state which tissue is nearer the upper surface.
parts.answer: Xylem.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student cuts across a young sunflower root and looks at it under a microscope. Where is the xylem?
A in a ring of bundles just under the epidermis
B in the centre, in a star shape with phloem between its arms
C scattered evenly through the cortex
D in the outer layer, forming the root hairs
parts.answer: B in the centre, in a star shape with phloem between its arms
parts.working: In a dicotyledonous root the xylem is central (star/cross shape) with phloem between the arms. A ring of vascular bundles is the arrangement in a stem, which is the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of xylem.
parts.answer: transport of water and mineral ions; support of the plant
parts.working: 1 mark each: transport of water; transport of mineral ions; support / strength. Max 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of phloem.
parts.answer: transport of sucrose and amino acids
parts.working: B1 sucrose and amino acids (both needed).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the substance that thickens the walls of xylem vessels.
parts.answer: lignin
parts.working: B1 lignin.

practice.stem: A transverse section of a young stem of a bean plant is described: it has an outer epidermis, then a cortex, then a ring of eight vascular bundles, with a large region of pith in the centre. In each vascular bundle there are two tissues, P and Q. P is on the side nearest the epidermis; Q is on the side nearest the pith and has cells with wide, empty spaces and thick walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify tissues P and Q.
parts.answer: P = phloem; Q = xylem
parts.working: B1 P phloem; B1 Q xylem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one difference between the position of xylem in this stem and in a root of the same plant.
parts.answer: In the stem xylem is in a ring of bundles (towards the inside of each bundle); in the root it is in the centre.
parts.working: B1 stem: in bundles in a ring / root: central (star-shaped) core.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain three ways in which the structure of xylem vessels is related to their function.
parts.answer: No cross walls (end walls broken down) – a continuous tube so water flows without obstruction; no cell contents (dead, hollow) – leaves a clear lumen for water; thick walls strengthened with lignin – support the plant and stop vessels collapsing under tension; narrow tubes – help maintain a continuous water column.
parts.working: For each of three features: 1 mark feature, 1 mark explanation. Features: no cross walls; no cytoplasm / hollow / dead; lignified thick walls; narrow continuous tubes; pits allow sideways movement.

practice.stem: A celery stalk with leaves was stood in water containing red dye for 2 hours. A thin transverse slice was then cut. Red dots could be seen arranged in a ring near the outside of the slice. A student drew the slice; the width of the drawing is 84 mm and the actual width of the slice is 14 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue that was stained red and explain why.
parts.answer: Xylem; the dye solution was drawn up the stalk in the xylem with the water by transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem; 1 mark: water (and dye) carried up in xylem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
parts.working: M1: magnification = drawing size ÷ actual size = 84 ÷ 14; A1: ×6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dye moved up faster in the celery stalk that still had its leaves than in a stalk with the leaves removed.
parts.answer: Leaves carry out transpiration; the loss of water vapour from leaves creates the transpiration pull that draws water and dye up the xylem; without leaves there is little pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: leaves transpire; 1 mark: transpiration pull drives movement up xylem.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two features of a good biological drawing of this section.
parts.answer: Any two of: clear continuous outlines with no shading; correct proportions; large (uses most of the space); labelled with ruled label lines that do not cross.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of a xylem vessel helps water to flow up the stem in a continuous column?
A many chloroplasts to provide energy
B cross walls with holes between the cells
C no cross walls, forming a long hollow tube
D a thin, flexible cellulose wall
parts.answer: C no cross walls, forming a long hollow tube
parts.working: Xylem vessels are dead cells joined end to end with no cross walls and no contents, forming a continuous tube. Cross walls with holes (sieve plates) are a phloem feature; xylem walls are thickened with lignin, not thin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a leaf, the xylem in each vein is nearer the upper surface and the phloem nearer the lower surface. State why it is important that the veins branch into a dense network in the leaf blade.
parts.answer: So that every mesophyll cell is close to a vein: water reaches cells quickly for photosynthesis and keeping cells turgid, and sugars are carried away quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: short distance to each mesophyll cell; water supply for photosynthesis; water to replace that lost by transpiration / keep turgid; sucrose removed / loaded into phloem quickly; support of the leaf blade.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why xylem vessels having no cell contents is an advantage.
parts.answer: No cytoplasm or nucleus blocks the tube, so water and mineral ions can flow freely with little resistance.
parts.working: B1 nothing to block / hollow / empty lumen; B1 allows (mass) flow of water with little resistance / faster.

practice.stem:
A student stood a leafy stem of busy lizzie (balsam) in a beaker of water containing a blue dye. After 15 minutes, thin slices were cut across the stem at different heights and examined.
height above water / mm | blue dots seen?
20 | yes
40 | yes
60 | yes
80 | yes
100 | no

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the minimum speed at which the dye travelled up the stem, in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 5.3 mm per minute (80 mm in 15 min)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your answer is a minimum value.
parts.answer: The dye may have reached a height between 80 mm and 100 mm, which was not tested.
parts.working: B1 dye may have gone higher than 80 mm (but below 100 mm) / slices only every 20 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The blue dots were seen in a ring of small spots between the outer cortex and the centre of each slice. Name the tissue they show.
parts.answer: xylem
parts.working: B1 xylem (in the vascular bundles).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to measure the height reached by the dye more accurately.
parts.answer: Cut slices at smaller height intervals (e.g. every 5 mm) between 80 and 100 mm / split the stem lengthways and measure the stained length.
parts.working: B1 any valid improvement.

practice.stem: A student drew one xylem vessel seen in a longitudinal section of a pumpkin stem under a microscope. The microscope magnification was ×400. The width of the vessel on the student's drawing was 36 mm and the drawing was the same size as the image.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual width of the xylem vessel in µm.
parts.answer: 90 µm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification = 36 ÷ 400 = 0.09 mm; A1 90 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The walls of the vessel had spiral and ring-shaped thickenings. Name the substance in these thickenings and give its function.
parts.answer: lignin; makes the wall strong / waterproof so the vessel does not collapse
parts.working: B1 lignin; B1 strengthens / supports / prevents collapse under tension / waterproof.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'Xylem carries substances up and down the plant, and phloem carries substances only upwards.' Correct both parts of this statement.
parts.answer: Xylem carries water and mineral ions only upwards (from roots to leaves); phloem carries sucrose and amino acids both up and down (source to sink).
parts.working: B1 xylem: upwards only; B1 phloem: in both directions / source to sink.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cut stem of a leafy plant is stood in red dye for several hours. Explain why the red dye is found in the xylem but not in the phloem.
parts.answer: Xylem vessels carry water up the stem in the transpiration stream, and the dye travels with this water; phloem carries sucrose and amino acids in living sieve tubes, not water, so the dye is not carried in it.
parts.working: B1 xylem carries water (and dissolved dye) up the stem by transpiration pull; B1 phloem transports sugars and amino acids, not water, so dye is not carried in it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says 'xylem vessels are living cells that pump water up the stem'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Mature xylem vessels are dead – they have no cytoplasm or cell contents; they cannot pump; water is pulled up by transpiration pull (with cohesion between water molecules), not pumped.
parts.working: 1 mark each: xylem vessels are dead / hollow; no contents to do work / no pumping; water moved by transpiration pull and cohesion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lignin in xylem walls is important for a tall tree.
parts.answer: Lignin makes the walls strong and rigid, giving support to the stem/trunk and stopping the vessels collapsing inwards under the tension of the transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: support/strength for the plant; 1 mark: prevents collapse under tension.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between the contents of xylem and phloem.
parts.answer: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries sucrose and amino acids (in solution).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the structure of a xylem vessel with that of a phloem tube. Give three differences.
parts.answer: xylem: dead cells, no contents; phloem: living cells with cytoplasm. xylem: walls thickened with lignin; phloem: cellulose walls only. xylem: no cross walls; phloem: cross walls with pores (sieve plates).
parts.working: 1 mark per comparative pair, max 3: dead vs living; lignin vs no lignin; no cross walls vs perforated cross walls; empty lumen vs cytoplasm present; water/ions vs sucrose/amino acids carried (accept as one difference).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Woody stems contain many layers of xylem. Explain why trees can grow much taller than plants with soft, non-woody stems.
parts.answer: Lignified xylem (wood) is strong and rigid, so it supports a tall heavy trunk, and its vessels do not collapse when water is pulled up a long distance.
parts.working: B1 lignin gives strength / support for weight; B1 vessels withstand tension / do not collapse / carry water to great height.

practice.stem: A gardener in Islamabad ties a wire tightly around the trunk of a young apple tree and forgets it. Over two years the trunk grows wider above the wire, but the wire cuts into the outer layers of the trunk. The xylem in the centre is not damaged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue in the outer layers of the trunk that is squeezed by the wire.
parts.answer: phloem
parts.working: B1 phloem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the trunk swells just above the wire.
parts.answer: Sucrose moving down from the leaves in the phloem cannot pass the wire, so it builds up above it and is used for extra growth there.
parts.working: B1 translocation (downwards) blocked; B1 sucrose accumulates above the wire / used for growth / cell division there.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the roots of the tree may eventually die, even though the leaves stay green for a long time.
parts.answer: Roots receive no sucrose for respiration, so they cannot release energy, cannot absorb ions actively and die; the leaves stay green because xylem still carries water up.
parts.working: B1 no sucrose reaches roots / no energy from respiration; B1 xylem undamaged so water still reaches leaves (until roots die).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substances are transported in the phloem?
A water and mineral ions
B sucrose and amino acids
C starch and glucose
D oxygen and carbon dioxide
parts.answer: B sucrose and amino acids
parts.working: Phloem translocates sucrose and amino acids from sources to sinks. Water and mineral ions are carried in the xylem (A). Starch is insoluble and is not transported.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define translocation.
parts.answer: The movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources to sinks.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement of sucrose and amino acids; 1 mark: in phloem from source(s) to sink(s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a source and a sink, and give one example of each in a flowering plant.
