parts.answer: Source: a part of the plant that releases sucrose or amino acids, e.g. a photosynthesising leaf (or a storage organ when its store is used). Sink: a part that uses or stores sucrose or amino acids, e.g. root, growing shoot tip, developing fruit or seed, storage organ.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of source; 1 mark: example; 1 mark: definition of sink; 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pea plant is forming pods with developing seeds. State whether the developing seeds are a source or a sink, and explain why.
parts.answer: Sink; they receive sucrose and amino acids from the leaves through the phloem and use them for growth or store them.
parts.working: 1 mark: sink; 1 mark: receive (import) sucrose/amino acids via phloem for growth or storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the insoluble carbohydrate that the developing seeds make from sucrose for storage.
parts.answer: Starch.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When one of these seeds germinates, its stored food supplies the growing shoot and root before the new leaves can photosynthesise. Explain whether the seed's food store is now a source or a sink.
parts.answer: Source; the stored starch is broken down to sugar, which is moved as sucrose in the phloem to the growing shoot and root (the sinks).
parts.working: 1 mark: source; 1 mark: starch broken down and sucrose translocated to growing shoot/root (sinks).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which direction is sucrose translocated in a flowering plant?
A only upwards, from roots to leaves
B only downwards, from leaves to roots
C from sources to sinks, which may be up or down the plant
D from sinks to sources, against gravity
parts.answer: C from sources to sinks, which may be up or down the plant
parts.working: Translocation is movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from regions of production or release (sources) to regions of use or storage (sinks); sinks can be above or below the source. Water in xylem moves only upwards, which is the main distractor's idea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two substances that are translocated in the phloem.
parts.answer: sucrose; amino acids
parts.working: 1 mark each: sucrose; amino acids. Do not accept glucose, starch or water as the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A potato plant has green leaves and underground tubers that are growing. State which of these is the source and which is the sink, and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: Leaves are the source because they make sugar by photosynthesis; growing tubers are the sink because sugar is stored there (as starch).
parts.working: B1 leaves are the source and tubers the sink; B1 leaves make sugar (sucrose) by photosynthesis; B1 tubers store it (as starch) or use it for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In early spring, before any leaves have grown, the buds of a potato plant start to grow using food stored in the tuber. During this time, which statement is correct?
A The tuber is a source and the growing shoots are sinks.
B The tuber is a sink and the growing shoots are sources.
C The tuber and the shoots are both sinks.
D Sucrose moves from the shoots to the tuber in the xylem.
parts.answer: A The tuber is a source and the growing shoots are sinks.
parts.working: Stored starch in the tuber is converted to sucrose and sent in the phloem to the growing shoots, so the tuber is a source and the shoots are sinks. In summer the tuber becomes a sink (B describes summer, not spring). Sucrose moves in phloem, not xylem (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer removed a complete ring of bark (including the phloem) from one branch of a mango tree, without damaging the xylem. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swelled. Explain why.
parts.answer: Removing the bark removed the phloem, so sucrose made in the leaves could not be translocated past the ring down the branch; sucrose and other substances built up above the ring, causing swelling (extra growth).
parts.working: 1 mark each: phloem removed / cut; sucrose from leaves cannot pass the ring; accumulates above ring → swelling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves on the ringed branch did not wilt.
parts.answer: The xylem was not damaged, so water and mineral ions could still travel up to the leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem intact; 1 mark: water still reaches leaves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fruits on the ringed branch grew larger than fruits on other branches.
parts.answer: Sucrose made by the leaves of that branch could not move down to the roots or trunk, so more was available to the fruits (sinks) on that branch.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose kept in that branch; 1 mark: more sucrose to the fruits / fruits as sinks receive more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aphids feed by pushing a fine mouthpart (stylet) into a plant stem. The liquid they drink contains a high concentration of sugar. Name the tissue the stylet enters and the sugar it contains.
parts.answer: Phloem; sucrose.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aphid colonies on a young tomato plant cause the fruits to stay small. Explain why.
parts.answer: The aphids remove sucrose (and amino acids) from the phloem, so less reaches the fruits, which are sinks; less energy/raw material for growth.
parts.working: 1 mark: aphids take sucrose/amino acids from phloem; 1 mark: less reaches fruits (sinks) for growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why aphids are often found feeding on the young growing tips of plants.
parts.answer: The phloem there carries sucrose and amino acids towards the growing tip (a sink), so the sap is rich in nutrients / tissues are soft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In sugarcane, sucrose is stored in the stem. Describe how sucrose made in a leaf reaches the stem.
parts.answer: Glucose is made by photosynthesis in the mesophyll cells and converted to sucrose; sucrose enters the phloem in the leaf veins; it is translocated through the phloem to the stem, which acts as a sink (store).
parts.working: 1 mark each: made in leaf by photosynthesis (glucose → sucrose); loaded into phloem; translocated to stem (sink).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plants transport carbohydrate as sucrose rather than as starch.
parts.answer: Sucrose is soluble so it can be carried in solution in the phloem sap; starch is insoluble and cannot be transported.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose soluble; 1 mark: starch insoluble so cannot move in phloem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why sugarcane fields need a supply of nitrate ions as well as sunlight.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids (and proteins) for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mango trees in Multan flower in spring. Explain why the flower buds of a mango tree are sinks for sucrose.
parts.answer: Flower buds are growing and cannot photosynthesise enough, so they need sucrose for respiration and to make new cells/cell walls.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: buds are growing; have little/no chlorophyll so make little sugar; sucrose used in respiration to release energy; sucrose used to build new cells / cellulose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A fungal disease damages the phloem in the stalks of young mango fruits. Predict and explain the effect on the fruits.
parts.answer: Fruits stay small / fall off because sucrose and amino acids cannot reach them, so they lack energy and materials for growth and storing sugar.
parts.working: B1 fruits smaller / do not ripen / drop; B1 phloem can no longer translocate sucrose (and amino acids) to fruit; B1 less respiration / growth / less sugar stored, so fruit is less sweet.

practice.stem:
A scientist supplied carbon dioxide containing radioactive carbon to one leaf of a wheat plant whose grains were filling. After 6 hours she measured how much of the radioactivity had reached different parts.
part of plant | percentage of radioactivity
supplied leaf | 34
developing grains (ear) | 48
roots | 11
other leaves | 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the compound, containing radioactive carbon, that moves out of the supplied leaf.
parts.answer: sucrose
parts.working: B1 sucrose. Glucose alone is not credited.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the radioactivity that left the supplied leaf.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why most of the radioactivity that left the leaf went to the developing grains.
parts.answer: Grains are the main sink at this stage: they are growing fast and converting sucrose to starch for storage.
parts.working: B1 grains are (the largest/main) sink; B1 sucrose converted to starch / stored / used for growth of grains.

practice.stem: One mature leaf of a young bean plant was enclosed in a clear bag containing carbon dioxide made with radioactive carbon. The plant was left in light for 6 hours, then parts of the plant were tested for radioactivity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue in which the radioactive substance was found in the stem.
parts.answer: Phloem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the radioactive substance most likely to be carried in this tissue, and explain how it was formed.
parts.answer: Sucrose; the leaf used the radioactive carbon dioxide in photosynthesis to make glucose, which was converted to sucrose for transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: sucrose; 1 mark: from radioactive CO₂ fixed in photosynthesis → glucose → sucrose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Radioactivity was found both in the young leaves at the top of the plant and in the roots. Explain why the substance moved both upwards and downwards.
parts.answer: Translocation moves sucrose from a source (the mature leaf) to sinks; sinks are found both above (growing shoot tip / young leaves) and below (roots); so phloem can carry substances in either direction depending on where the sinks are.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mature leaf is a source; young leaves and roots are sinks; phloem transports in both directions, to wherever sinks are.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why no radioactivity was found in the mature leaves below the treated leaf.
parts.answer: These mature leaves are themselves sources (photosynthesising), not sinks, so they do not import sucrose.

practice.stem: Radioactive carbon dioxide was supplied to a leaf near the top of a sunflower plant. A detector found that the radioactive sugar had travelled 72 cm down the stem in 1.5 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean speed of translocation in cm per hour.
parts.answer: 48 cm per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to mm per minute.
parts.answer: 8 mm per minute
parts.working: M1: 480 mm per hour; A1: 480 ÷ 60 = 8 mm/min.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The experiment was repeated at night in darkness. The radioactivity travelled only 30 cm in 1.5 hours. Suggest why translocation was slower.
parts.answer: Less photosynthesis in darkness, so less sucrose produced in the leaf / smaller concentration difference between source and sink; lower temperature at night slows the process.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid suggestions; one must refer to less sucrose from the source.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one hazard of using radioactive substances and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: ionising radiation can damage cells / DNA. Precaution: wear gloves, use forceps, keep exposure time short, dispose of material safely.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sugar beet plant stores sucrose in its swollen root in its first year. In its second year it uses this store to grow a tall flowering shoot. Which row is correct for the root in each year?
A year 1: sink; year 2: source
B year 1: source; year 2: sink
C year 1: sink; year 2: sink
D year 1: source; year 2: source
parts.answer: A year 1: sink; year 2: source
parts.working: In year 1 sucrose arrives and is stored, so the root is a sink; in year 2 stored sugar is released and moved to the shoot, so the root is a source. The same organ can be a source or a sink at different times.

practice.stem: An aphid feeds on a stem of a cotton plant with its mouthpart (stylet) inside a phloem tube. The aphid is removed and its cut stylet is left in the stem. Sap flows out of the stylet at 2.0 mm³ per hour for 24 hours. The sap contains 150 g of sucrose per dm³. (1 dm³ = 1 000 000 mm³)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sucrose, in mg, that flows out of the stylet in 24 hours.
parts.answer: 7.2 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sap flows out of the cut stylet without the aphid sucking.
parts.answer: The phloem contents are under pressure, because sucrose is loaded at the source and moves by mass flow towards sinks.
parts.working: B1 phloem sap is under pressure; B1 sucrose is being translocated / pushed from source to sink.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why aphids rarely feed by pushing their stylet into the xylem.
parts.answer: Xylem sap contains water and mineral ions but almost no sugar or amino acids (and is under tension, not pressure).
parts.working: B1 xylem has no sucrose/amino acids, so little food / sap is pulled up, not pushed out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water enters a root hair cell from the soil.
parts.answer: By osmosis: the soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap, so water moves in through the partially permeable cell membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: osmosis; 1 mark: from higher water potential (soil) to lower (cell) through partially permeable membrane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the route taken by water from the root hair cell to the leaf.
parts.answer: Through the root cortex cells; into the xylem in the centre of the root; up the xylem in the stem to the leaf; into mesophyll cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three in order: root cortex; xylem; stem xylem to leaf; mesophyll cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the pathway taken by water from the soil to a mesophyll cell?
A root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cell
B root hair cell → phloem → xylem → mesophyll cell
C root cortex cells → root hair cell → xylem → mesophyll cell
D root hair cell → xylem → root cortex cells → mesophyll cell
parts.answer: A root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cell
parts.working: Water enters root hair cells, crosses the cortex to the xylem in the centre of the root, rises in the xylem and leaves it to reach mesophyll cells. Phloem does not carry water up from the roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two features of a root hair cell that help it to absorb water.
parts.answer: long thin extension giving a large surface area; thin cell wall / no cuticle / cell sap more concentrated than soil water
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2: long extension / large surface area; thin wall; partially permeable membrane; concentrated cell sap / vacuole; no waxy cuticle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which water enters a root hair cell.
parts.answer: osmosis
parts.working: B1 osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process by which mineral ions such as nitrate are often taken into a root hair cell.
parts.answer: active transport
parts.working: B1 active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Root hair cells do not contain chloroplasts. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They are underground with no light, so they cannot photosynthesise.
parts.working: B1 no light (underground), so chloroplasts would be no use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A gardener in Peshawar transplants a guava sapling and tears off most of the fine roots. Explain why the sapling wilts.
parts.answer: Root hairs are lost, so the surface area for water uptake falls; water uptake is less than water lost by transpiration; cells lose turgor so the plant wilts.
parts.working: B1 root hairs removed / damaged; B1 smaller surface area for absorption (osmosis); B1 uptake less than transpiration loss / cells become flaccid.

practice.stem:
A student placed a young wheat seedling with its roots in a narrow measuring cylinder of water. A thin layer of oil was put on the water surface. The volume of water was read each day.
day | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3
volume / cm³ | 250 | 238 | 226 | 214

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume of water taken up per day.
parts.answer: 12 cm³ per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a layer of oil was added.
parts.answer: to stop water evaporating from the surface of the water in the cylinder
parts.working: B1 prevents evaporation, so loss is only due to uptake by the plant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could show that the water lost from the cylinder was taken up by the plant and not lost in another way.
parts.answer: Set up a control cylinder with oil and water but no seedling.
parts.working: B1 identical cylinder with no plant (volume should stay the same).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of the tissue that water enters after it has crossed the root cortex.
parts.answer: xylem
parts.working: B1 xylem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main force that pulls water up from the roots to the leaves.
parts.answer: transpiration pull (evaporation of water from leaves)
parts.working: B1 transpiration / transpiration pull.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a plant growing in dry soil absorbs less water than one in moist soil.
parts.answer: In dry soil the soil water is scarce/more concentrated, so the concentration gradient into root hair cells is smaller and less water enters by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 less water / smaller gradient / soil solution more concentrated; B1 less osmosis into root hairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is it an advantage for a root hair cell to have a long, thin extension?
A It increases the surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions.
B It contains chloroplasts for photosynthesis in the soil.
C It reduces the distance that sucrose has to travel to the leaves.
D It lets the root hair cell take in water by active transport.
parts.answer: A It increases the surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions.
parts.working: The extension greatly increases the surface area in contact with soil water, so more water (by osmosis) and ions (by active transport) can be absorbed. Root hair cells have no chloroplasts (B), and water enters by osmosis, not active transport (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Fertiliser is spilled around the roots of a tomato plant, so the soil water becomes very concentrated. Which statement describes what happens to the root hair cells?
A They gain water by osmosis because the soil water has more water molecules.
B They lose water by osmosis because the soil solution is more concentrated than the cell sap.
C They gain water by active transport using energy from respiration.
D They are not affected because the cell wall stops water leaving.
parts.answer: B They lose water by osmosis because the soil solution is more concentrated than the cell sap.
parts.working: Water moves by osmosis from a dilute solution (higher water potential) to a concentrated solution (lower water potential) across a partially permeable membrane; here that is out of the cells into the soil, so the plant wilts. The cell wall is fully permeable and does not stop water movement.

practice.stem: A student counted root hairs on the main root of a radish seedling using a hand lens. In a 1 mm section of root she counted 55 root hairs. The root-hair zone was 16 mm long. Each root hair has a mean surface area of 0.012 mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the total number of root hairs on this root.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the root hairs. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 11 mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why this is an underestimate of the area through which the seedling absorbs water.
parts.answer: Side (lateral) roots and other parts of the root surface also absorb water / hairs may be missed when counting.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves from the root hair cell across the root to the xylem.
parts.answer: By osmosis from cell to cell across the cortex; each cell inwards has a more concentrated cell sap / lower water potential; water then enters the xylem (and is pulled up by transpiration).
parts.working: B1 osmosis; B1 through cortex cells (cell to cell); B1 down a concentration (water potential) gradient / towards xylem / pulled by transpiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a waterlogged soil, with no air in it, can reduce the uptake of mineral ions by roots.
parts.answer: No oxygen for aerobic respiration in root cells, so little energy is released for active transport of ions.
parts.working: B1 lack of oxygen / less aerobic respiration; B1 less energy (ATP) for active transport.

practice.stem:
Rice seedlings were grown in solutions of different salt (sodium chloride) concentration. After 10 days the seedlings were weighed.
salt concentration / g per dm³ | 0 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16
mean mass of seedling / g | 4.0 | 3.8 | 3.2 | 2.0 | 0.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean mass between 0 and 8 g per dm³ of salt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your knowledge of osmosis to explain why seedlings in high salt concentrations grow less.
parts.answer: The soil solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so less water (or no water) enters root hair cells by osmosis / water leaves; cells lose turgor, less water for photosynthesis and growth.
parts.working: B1 salt solution more concentrated / lower water potential than root cells; B1 less water absorbed / water lost by osmosis; B1 less turgor / less photosynthesis / less cell expansion so less growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers in parts of Sindh find salty soil after years of irrigation. Suggest one way to reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Flush salts out with good drainage / plant salt-tolerant varieties / reduce over-irrigation.
parts.working: B1 any sensible suggestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A potted spider plant has stopped growing and its soil is dry. After watering, its leaves become firm again within an hour. Explain how water absorbed by the roots makes the leaves firm.
parts.answer: Water enters root hairs by osmosis and moves up the xylem to the leaves; it enters leaf cells by osmosis; vacuoles swell and press the cytoplasm against the cell wall so cells become turgid.
parts.working: B1 osmosis into roots; B1 transported in xylem; B1 leaf cells become turgid / pressure against cell wall supports leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other use of the water absorbed by the roots, apart from support.
parts.answer: raw material for photosynthesis / cooling by evaporation / transport of mineral ions
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chilli seedlings were pulled from a nursery bed and replanted in a field. Many of them wilted for several days. Explain why.
parts.answer: Pulling up the seedlings damaged or tore off many root hairs; the surface area for water absorption was reduced; transpiration from the leaves continued, so water loss was greater than uptake and the cells lost turgor.
parts.working: 1 mark each: root hairs damaged/lost; less surface area for absorption; water loss by transpiration exceeds uptake → wilting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two things the farmer could do to reduce wilting after transplanting.
parts.answer: Lift seedlings with soil around the roots; transplant in the evening or on a cool, cloudy day; remove some leaves; water the field well; give shade for the first few days.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two, each linked to protecting root hairs or reducing transpiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seedlings recover after about a week.
parts.answer: New root hairs grow, restoring the surface area for water uptake.

practice.stem:
A student set up two similar bean seedlings with roots in nutrient solution. Air was bubbled through the solution of seedling A. Nitrogen gas (no oxygen) was bubbled through the solution of seedling B. After 6 hours the amount of potassium ions absorbed and the volume of water absorbed were measured.
seedling | potassium ions absorbed / arbitrary units | water absorbed / cm³
A (air) | 96 | 5.2
B (nitrogen) | 12 | 4.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more potassium ions were absorbed by seedling A than by seedling B.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in potassium uptake.
parts.answer: Potassium ions are absorbed by active transport, which needs energy from aerobic respiration; without oxygen root cells release little energy so uptake is low.
parts.working: B1 active transport; B1 needs energy / ATP from respiration; B1 no oxygen so (aerobic) respiration stops / much less energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the volume of water absorbed was similar in both seedlings.
parts.answer: Water enters by osmosis, a passive process that does not need energy from respiration, so lack of oxygen has little effect.
parts.working: B1 osmosis; B1 passive / no energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gardeners in Gilgit cover newly transplanted seedlings with shade cloth for the first week. Explain how this helps the seedlings survive.
parts.answer: The shade cloth reduces light and heat on the leaves, so stomata partly close and transpiration falls; water loss is reduced while the damaged roots regrow root hairs, so the seedlings do not wilt.
parts.working: B1 less light and heat reach the leaves; B1 transpiration (water loss) is reduced / stomata partly close; B1 roots have time to regrow root hairs so uptake can catch up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the seedlings should be watered thoroughly immediately after they are transplanted.
parts.answer: The water replaces water lost during transplanting and fills the soil around the roots, so root hairs are in contact with water and can absorb it.
parts.working: B1 replaces water lost from the plant and raises soil water supply; B1 water in contact with the root hairs / soil around roots allows uptake by osmosis.

practice.stem: You are given germinating seeds of mustard, Petri dishes, filter paper, a hand lens, sodium chloride solutions of different concentrations and distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of sodium chloride affects the number of root hairs that grow on mustard seedlings. Include the variables to control, how you would make your results reliable and what you would measure.
parts.answer: Grow seeds on filter paper soaked in a range of salt concentrations (0 = distilled water control) for a fixed time; count root hairs per mm of root with hand lens; keep constant temperature, light, volume of solution, number and type of seeds, time; repeat / use many seedlings per dish and calculate mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: independent variable range (at least 4 concentrations incl. distilled water); same volume of solution / same filter paper; same number of seeds of same age/size; same temperature / light / time; method of measuring (count root hairs in a fixed length, e.g. 2 mm, using hand lens) ; several seedlings per dish / repeats and mean; record in table / plot concentration against mean number; safety or prediction statement (more salt, fewer root hairs).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student finds an animal under a stone in a garden in Lahore. It has a body divided into two parts, four pairs of jointed legs and no antennae. To which group does it belong?
A arachnids
B crustaceans
C insects
D myriapods
parts.answer: A arachnids
parts.working: Arachnids have two body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen), four pairs of legs and no antennae. Insects have three pairs of legs and three body parts; crustaceans have more than four pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae.

practice.stem: A wildlife survey in the Margalla Hills records a common leopard and a rose-ringed parakeet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that all mammals have but birds do not have.
parts.answer: Fur / hair on the skin; mammary glands (produce milk); external ears (pinnae).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: fur/hair; mammary glands / feed young on milk; external ear (pinna); accept: give birth to live young (most), diaphragm, different types of teeth. Do not accept 'warm-blooded' (birds are too).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that birds have that mammals do not have.
parts.answer: Feathers; a beak (and lay hard-shelled eggs).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: feathers; beak; wings (forelimbs as wings); lay eggs with hard shells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the group of arthropods to which an organism with a body in three parts (head, thorax and abdomen), three pairs of legs and one pair of antennae belongs.
parts.answer: Insects
parts.working: B1 insects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A woodlouse has seven pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae. Name its arthropod group.
parts.answer: Crustaceans
parts.working: B1 crustaceans.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A centipede has a long body made of many similar segments, each with one pair of legs. Name its arthropod group.
parts.answer: Myriapods
parts.working: B1 myriapods.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one feature that all arthropods share.
parts.answer: Jointed legs / an exoskeleton / a segmented body.
parts.working: B1 any one of: jointed legs (limbs); exoskeleton; segmented body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the kingdom to which each organism belongs: (i) Chlorella, a single-celled organism with a nucleus and chloroplasts that lives in ponds; (ii) a bacterium that lives in soil; (iii) a mushroom.
parts.answer: (i) Protoctists; (ii) Prokaryotes; (iii) Fungi.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature found in all prokaryote cells that is not found in protoctist cells.
parts.answer: No nucleus – DNA is a circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm (plasmids may be present).
parts.working: B1 no nucleus / circular DNA / plasmids. Do not accept 'cell wall' (some protoctists have walls).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is found in protoctists but NOT in bacteria?
A a cell membrane
B ribosomes
C a nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope
D circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm
parts.answer: C a nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope
parts.working: Protoctists are eukaryotes, so their genetic material is inside a nucleus with a nuclear envelope; bacteria are prokaryotes and have no nucleus. A cell membrane and ribosomes are found in both groups. Circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm is a bacterial feature, not a protoctist one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is shared by organisms in the fungus kingdom and the prokaryote kingdom but NOT by organisms in the plant kingdom?
A cells have a cell wall
B cell walls are not made of cellulose
C cells contain a nucleus
D cells contain chloroplasts
parts.answer: B cell walls are not made of cellulose
parts.working: Fungi and prokaryotes both have cell walls, but neither wall is made of cellulose, whereas plant walls are cellulose. A is wrong because plants also have cell walls; prokaryotes have no nucleus (C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A frog and a monitor lizard are both vertebrates. Describe two differences between the skin and eggs of amphibians and reptiles.
parts.answer: Skin: amphibians have moist, smooth skin without scales; reptiles have dry skin covered in scales. Eggs: amphibians lay eggs without shells (in water / jelly); reptiles lay eggs with soft, leathery shells (on land).
parts.working: B1 amphibian skin moist / no scales; B1 reptile skin dry / scaly; B1 amphibian eggs no shell / laid in water; B1 reptile eggs leathery / rubbery shell / laid on land. Comparative pairs needed for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why amphibians usually need to return to water or very damp places to breed.
parts.answer: Their eggs have no shell, so they would dry out (lose water) on land; the eggs must be fertilised and develop in water.
parts.working: B1 eggs lack a shell / waterproof covering so dry out; accept larvae (tadpoles) live in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer in Sindh grows wheat and maize. Both are monocotyledons. State two features of the leaves or flowers that show they are monocotyledons.
parts.answer: Leaves have parallel veins; flower parts are in threes (or multiples of three).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: parallel veins; long narrow leaves; flower parts in threes/multiples of three; seed has one cotyledon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mustard and chickpea plants are dicotyledons. Give two ways their leaves or seeds differ from those of monocotyledons.
parts.answer: Dicot leaves have a branching network of veins (not parallel); dicot seeds have two cotyledons (not one).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two comparative points: net/branched veins vs parallel; two cotyledons vs one; flower parts in fours or fives vs threes; leaves usually broad vs narrow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ferns are also in the plant kingdom. State how the reproduction of ferns differs from that of flowering plants.
parts.answer: Ferns do not produce flowers or seeds; they reproduce using spores.
parts.working: B1 spores (no flowers / no seeds).

practice.stem: In a practical lesson a student is given four preserved vertebrate specimens, labelled P, Q, R and S, and the following notes about each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Specimen P has scales, gills and fins. Specimen Q has moist skin with no scales and four limbs. Name the vertebrate group of P and of Q.
parts.answer: P: fish. Q: amphibian.
parts.working: B1 P fish; B1 Q amphibian.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Specimen R has dry scaly skin and lays leathery eggs. Specimen S has feathers and a beak. Name the groups of R and S.
parts.answer: R: reptile. S: bird.
parts.working: B1 R reptile; B1 S bird.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature that the student should look for, using a hand lens, to confirm that a preserved specimen is a mammal rather than a bird.
parts.answer: Hair / fur on the skin (or external ears, mammary glands / nipples).
parts.working: B1 hair/fur; accept pinna, nipples/mammary glands.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the comparison: the number of pairs of legs in (i) an insect, (ii) an arachnid.
parts.answer: (i) 3 pairs; (ii) 4 pairs.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student observes an animal on a beach in Gwadar. It has a hard, chalky exoskeleton, ten jointed legs, two pairs of antennae and compound eyes on stalks. Identify its group and give two reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Crustacean: it has more than four pairs of legs (five pairs) and two pairs of antennae (also calcified exoskeleton).
parts.working: B1 crustacean; B1 more than 4 pairs of legs / 5 pairs; B1 two pairs of antennae; accept chalky (calcium carbonate) exoskeleton as one reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which kingdom contains organisms whose cell walls are made of chitin?
A Plantae
B Fungi
C Protoctista
D Prokaryotae (bacteria)
parts.answer: B Fungi
parts.working: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin. Plant cell walls are cellulose and bacterial cell walls are peptidoglycan. Chitin also forms insect exoskeletons, but insects are animals, not fungi.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about viruses is correct?
A They have a cell membrane surrounding a protein coat.
B They contain genetic material inside a protein coat and can only reproduce inside living cells.
C They contain ribosomes, which they use to make their protein coat outside a host cell.
D They are classified in the prokaryote kingdom because they have no nucleus.
parts.answer: B They contain genetic material inside a protein coat and can only reproduce inside living cells.
parts.working: A virus is a protein coat around genetic material (DNA or RNA); it has no cell structures, so it reproduces only inside host cells. Viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms (D) and have no ribosomes or membrane of their own.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Yeast is placed in the fungus kingdom even though it is single-celled. State two features of fungal cells that yeast shows.
parts.answer: A nucleus; a cell wall that is not made of cellulose; (stores carbohydrate as glycogen; no chloroplasts).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: has a nucleus; cell wall not made of cellulose (accept chitin); no chloroplasts / does not photosynthesise; stores glycogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Most fungi, such as bread mould, are made of thread-like structures. Name these structures.
parts.answer: Hyphae (forming a mycelium).
parts.working: B1 hyphae.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why fungi are not classified as plants, even though both have cell walls and do not move from place to place.
parts.answer: Fungi do not have chloroplasts so cannot photosynthesise; they feed by saprophytic / parasitic nutrition (secreting enzymes and absorbing the products); their cell walls are not made of cellulose; they store glycogen, not starch.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no chloroplasts/chlorophyll; cannot photosynthesise / heterotrophic, feed on organic matter (saprophytic/parasitic); cell wall not cellulose; store glycogen not starch.

practice.stem: During an outbreak of dengue fever in Karachi, a microbiology student compared the dengue virus with a bacterium that causes a skin infection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the structure of a bacterial cell with that of a virus particle.
parts.answer: Bacterium: cell with cytoplasm, cell membrane, cell wall, ribosomes, circular DNA and (often) plasmids. Virus: no cell structure – only genetic material (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat; no cytoplasm, membrane or ribosomes; much smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparative points: bacterium has cytoplasm/virus does not; cell membrane; cell wall vs protein coat; ribosomes; circular DNA + plasmids vs DNA or RNA; bacteria are cells/viruses are not cells; viruses much smaller.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.
parts.answer: They are not made of cells and do not show all the characteristics of living organisms (e.g. no respiration, nutrition or excretion) on their own; they can only reproduce inside a host cell.
parts.working: B1 not cells / no cell structure; B1 do not carry out (all) life processes, e.g. respiration / only reproduce inside other cells.

practice.stem: A student collected three arthropods from leaf litter in Murree and recorded these features.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the information to identify the group to which each animal belongs: Animal 1 – 3 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of wings, 1 pair of antennae, 3 body sections. Animal 2 – 4 pairs of legs, 0 antennae, 2 body sections. Animal 3 – about 60 segments, 2 pairs of legs on most segments, 1 pair of antennae.
parts.answer: 1: insect; 2: arachnid; 3: myriapod.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student should count legs on both sides of the body rather than on one side only and then doubling.
parts.answer: Some legs may be missing / damaged, so counting both sides gives an accurate number.
parts.working: B1 legs may be lost or damaged on preserved/live specimens; idea of accuracy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other feature, visible with a hand lens, that would help to confirm that Animal 1 is an insect.
parts.answer: Compound eyes / mouthparts / spiracles / wings attached to the thorax.
parts.working: B1 any sensible visible insect feature, e.g. wings on thorax, compound eyes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The scientific name of the domestic cat is Felis catus. Which statement is correct?
A Felis is the species name and catus is the genus.
B Felis is the genus and catus is the species.
C Felis and catus are both genus names.
D Felis catus is the name of the kingdom.
parts.answer: B Felis is the genus and catus is the species.
parts.working: In the binomial system the first name (capital letter) is the genus, the second (small letter) is the species. A reverses them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term species.
parts.answer: A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
parts.working: B1 group of organisms that can (inter)breed / reproduce; B1 to produce fertile offspring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule. Mules are infertile. Explain whether horses and donkeys belong to the same species.
parts.answer: They are different species, because although they can breed, the offspring (mule) are not fertile.
parts.working: B1 different species; B1 offspring infertile / cannot reproduce.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which taxonomic group contains both lions (Panthera leo) and domestic cats (Felis catus) but NOT dogs?
A genus
B family
C order
D class
parts.answer: B family
parts.working: Lions and domestic cats are in different genera (Panthera and Felis) but both belong to the family Felidae. The order Carnivora also contains dogs (family Canidae), and the class Mammalia is larger still, so the family is the correct group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the seven main levels of classification in order, from the largest group to the smallest group.
parts.answer: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
parts.working: 2 marks for all seven in the correct order; 1 mark for four to six in the correct order. Phylum is called division for plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how knowing an organism's genus helps a scientist predict its features.
parts.answer: Organisms in the same genus share many features because they are closely related, so features of one known species can be used to predict those of another species in the same genus.
parts.working: 1 mark: organisms in the same genus are closely related and share features; 1 mark: so a known species can be used to predict features of another.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The lion (Panthera leo), tiger (Panthera tigris) and leopard (Panthera pardus) are in the genus Panthera. The cheetah is Acinonyx jubatus. Which pair would be expected to share the MOST similar DNA base sequences?
A Panthera pardus and Acinonyx jubatus
B Panthera pardus and Panthera tigris
C Acinonyx jubatus and Felis catus
D they all have identical DNA
parts.answer: B Panthera pardus and Panthera tigris
parts.working: Organisms in the same genus share a more recent common ancestor, so their DNA base sequences are more similar. Cheetah is in a different genus (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the binomial system of naming organisms.
parts.answer: An internationally agreed system in which each species is given a two-part scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
parts.working: B1 two names / two parts; B1 genus then species; accept internationally agreed / in Latin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mango tree is Mangifera indica. Explain why scientists use this name rather than a local name such as 'aam'.
parts.answer: Local names differ between languages and regions; the scientific name is the same worldwide, so scientists everywhere know exactly which species is meant (avoids confusion).
parts.working: B1 common names vary between countries/languages; B1 binomial name is universal / avoids confusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the name correctly as it would appear in a printed textbook.
parts.answer: Mangifera indica, in italics, with a capital M for the genus and a small i for the species.
parts.working: B1 italics (or underlined if hand-written) and capital for genus only.

practice.stem: Dolphins and sharks have a similar streamlined shape with fins, but dolphins are mammals and sharks are fish.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the main purpose of classification systems.
parts.answer: To group organisms according to the features they share, so that they reflect evolutionary relationships.
parts.working: B1 group by shared features / reflect evolutionary relationships.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Traditionally organisms were classified using morphology (body form) and anatomy. Suggest one reason why classification using DNA sequences may be more reliable.
parts.answer: Organisms that look similar may not be closely related (similar features can evolve separately in different environments); DNA shows actual genetic relatedness / common ancestry.
parts.working: B1 similar appearance may be due to similar environment, not relatedness; B1 DNA directly reflects how recently species shared a common ancestor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows the order and family of four mammals.
W: order Carnivora, family Felidae
X: order Carnivora, family Canidae
Y: order Rodentia, family Muridae
Z: order Primates, family Hominidae
Which pair of organisms belongs to the same order but to different families?
A W and Y
B W and X
C X and Z
D Y and Z
parts.answer: B W and X
parts.working: W and X are both in the order Carnivora but their families (Felidae and Canidae) are different. W and Y, X and Z, and Y and Z each have different orders, so they do not match the description.

practice.stem: Four pigeon-like birds were collected near a canal in Lahore. P and R have grey bodies with two black wing bars. Q has a white body and no wing bars. S has grey bodies and two black wing bars but is much larger than P. P and R can mate and produce fertile young. P and S cannot produce young.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which two birds are most likely to belong to the same species? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: P and R; they look alike and can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
parts.working: 1 mark for P and R; 1 mark for the reason, that members of one species can breed together to produce fertile offspring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why body size alone is not enough to decide whether S is a different species from P.
parts.answer: Size varies within one species (for example with age, sex or food), so size cannot show a species boundary; P and S cannot produce young, so they are different species.
parts.working: 1 mark: size varies within a species; 1 mark: P and S cannot produce fertile young together, which is the test that shows they are different species.

practice.stem: Sweet basil is a herb grown in kitchen gardens across Pakistan. Its scientific name is Ocimum basilicum. A related species, Ocimum tenuiflorum (holy basil), is also grown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the genus name and the species name in Ocimum basilicum.
parts.answer: Genus: Ocimum; species: basilicum
parts.working: 1 mark for both names correctly identified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the first word of the binomial name tells you about sweet basil and holy basil.
parts.answer: They are closely related: they belong to the same genus and so share many features and a recent common ancestor.
parts.working: 1 mark: same genus; 1 mark: they are more closely related than species from different genera.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two rules for writing a binomial name correctly in print.
parts.answer: The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name starts with a lower-case letter; the whole name is printed in italics (or underlined when handwritten).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: genus name has a capital letter; species name has a lower-case letter; name is italic or underlined; genus is written before species.

practice.stem:
Part of the same gene was sequenced in four species of wild cat (12 bases shown):
Species A: ATGCCTAGGTCA
Species B: ATGCATAGCTGA
Species C: ATGCCTAGGTCC
Species D: TTGACTAAGTGA

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which species is most closely related to species A. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Species C; its sequence differs from A at only 1 of the 12 positions, fewer differences than any other species.
parts.working: B1 species C; B1 fewest differences in base sequence (1 difference).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of positions at which species D differs from species A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sequence of bases in DNA is useful for classifying organisms.
parts.answer: Organisms that share a more recent common ancestor have more similar base sequences, so the degree of similarity shows evolutionary relationships.
parts.working: B1 more similar sequence = more closely related; B1 shared (recent) common ancestor / reflects evolutionary relationships.

practice.stem: A sequence of 40 DNA bases from the same gene was compared in three species of freshwater fish. Species W and species X differ at 6 positions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the 40 bases that are the same in species W and species X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Species W and Y differ at 14 of the 40 positions. Calculate the percentage similarity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain which species, X or Y, shares a more recent common ancestor with W.
parts.answer: X; it has a higher percentage of identical bases (85 % against 65 %), so fewer mutations have accumulated since they separated.
parts.working: B1 X; B1 more similar sequence / fewer differences.

practice.stem: Biologists sometimes disagree about how to classify bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the biological definition of a species (a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring) is hard to apply to bacteria.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce mainly asexually by binary fission, so there is no interbreeding to test; genes can also pass between unrelated bacteria, which blurs the boundaries between groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: mainly asexual reproduction (binary fission), so no mating test; 1 mark: no way to test for fertile offspring; 1 mark: genes can pass between unrelated bacteria, so boundaries are unclear.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one method, based on molecules rather than appearance, that scientists can use to decide how closely two bacterial strains are related.
parts.answer: Compare the base sequences of the same gene (DNA) in both strains and count the differences; fewer differences means a closer relationship.
parts.working: 1 mark: compare DNA or gene base sequences; 1 mark: fewer differences means a closer relationship.

practice.stem: Bats fly using wings, as birds do. However, bats are mammals: they have fur and produce live young that feed on milk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the presence of wings does not show that bats and birds are closely related.
parts.answer: Their wings evolved separately for flight (analogous structures); bats and birds do not share a recent common ancestor for this feature.
parts.working: 1 mark: wings evolved independently (analogous, not homologous); 1 mark: bats and birds are not closely related.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that show bats belong to the mammals rather than the birds.
parts.answer: Fur or hair; give birth to live young; young are fed on milk from mammary glands.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: hair or fur; live young; milk produced by mammary glands.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A seedling bends towards light from a window. Which characteristic of living organisms does this show?
A excretion
B growth
C nutrition
D sensitivity
parts.answer: D sensitivity
parts.working: Sensitivity is the ability to detect and respond to changes in the environment (here light). Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass, which is not the main point here.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the characteristic of living organisms described by each definition: (i) the removal of waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements; (ii) the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules to release energy; (iii) a permanent increase in size and dry mass.
parts.answer: (i) Excretion; (ii) Respiration; (iii) Growth.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the meaning of the term nutrition.
parts.answer: Taking in materials for energy, growth and development.
parts.working: B1 taking in materials for energy, growth and development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each observation, name the characteristic of living organisms it shows: (i) a goat chewing grass; (ii) a cow giving birth to a calf; (iii) a person sweating removes excess salts and urea in the sweat; (iv) a child getting taller each year.
parts.answer: (i) Nutrition; (ii) Reproduction; (iii) Excretion; (iv) Growth.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A yeast culture is placed in sugar solution. Its cells release energy from glucose. Which characteristic of living organisms is this?
A excretion
B nutrition
C respiration
D sensitivity
parts.answer: C respiration
parts.working: Respiration is the release of energy from food molecules such as glucose in cells. Nutrition is taking in food; excretion is removing waste; sensitivity is detecting and responding to stimuli.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the characteristic of living organisms shown by each example.
(i) A cat hears a mouse and turns its head towards the sound.
(ii) A bacterium splits into two identical cells.
(iii) A child's bones become longer over several years.
(iv) An earthworm moves through soil by contracting its body.
parts.answer: (i) sensitivity; (ii) reproduction; (iii) growth; (iv) movement
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct characteristic.

practice.stem: Five items were compared: a sea urchin, a burning candle, a growing seedling, a crystal of salt grown in a laboratory, and a bacterium living in milk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which of the five items are living organisms?
parts.answer: Sea urchin, seedling and bacterium
parts.working: 1 mark for all three correct and no others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one characteristic of living organisms that a candle flame does not show.
parts.answer: Reproduction (it cannot make copies of itself).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid characteristic such as reproduction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the growth of a salt crystal does not show that it is alive.
parts.answer: A crystal grows by adding ions to its surface; it has no cells and does not use its own metabolism (respiration, nutrition) to grow.
parts.working: 1 mark: crystal grows by adding ions, not by cell division; 1 mark: it has no cells or metabolism.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that breathing and respiration are the same. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs; respiration is the chemical release of energy from glucose inside cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: breathing is ventilation of the lungs; 1 mark: respiration is the release of energy from glucose in cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas breathed out in a higher concentration than breathed in, and state where it is made in the body.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide; it is made in the mitochondria of cells during respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon dioxide; 1 mark: made in cells (mitochondria) during respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car engine takes in fuel and oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide and water. A student says this means the car is alive. Name two characteristics of living organisms that the car seems to show.
parts.answer: Nutrition (takes in fuel – a source of energy) and excretion-like release of waste / respiration-like release of energy; also movement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: movement; 'respiration' (releases energy from fuel with oxygen); 'nutrition' (takes in fuel); 'excretion' (gives out waste gases).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three characteristics of living organisms that the car does not show.
parts.answer: Growth; reproduction; sensitivity (cannot respond to stimuli by itself).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: growth; reproduction; sensitivity. Accept excretion/respiration only if not used in (a).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term reproduction.
parts.answer: The processes that make more of the same kind of organism.
parts.working: B1 processes that make more of the same kind of organism.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define movement as a characteristic of living organisms.
parts.answer: An action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place.
parts.working: B1 action by organism or part of organism; B1 causing change of position or place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a rose plant, which is fixed in the soil, still shows movement.
parts.answer: Parts of the plant move, e.g. leaves/flowers turn towards light, flowers open and close, or cytoplasm moves within cells.
parts.working: B1 any valid example of a part moving.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of excretion?
A removal of faeces from the rectum
B release of urea in urine by the kidneys
C scattering of seeds from a fruit
D breakdown of starch by amylase in the mouth
parts.answer: B release of urea in urine by the kidneys
parts.working: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste made by the body's cells, such as urea. Faeces are undigested food and are removed by egestion, not excretion. Seed dispersal and digestion are not excretion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define growth.
parts.answer: A permanent increase in the size or dry mass of an organism, from making new cells and new living material.
parts.working: 1 mark for a permanent increase in size or dry mass; 1 mark for the increase coming from cell division or new living material.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A dried raisin swells when placed in water. Explain why this is not growth.
parts.answer: The increase in size comes from water being absorbed; no new living material is made and no cells divide, and the increase is not permanent.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase is due to water absorption, not new living material; 1 mark: no cell division, so not permanent growth.

practice.stem: A student claims that a campfire is alive because it grows, needs fuel and gives out waste gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two characteristics of living organisms that a campfire does not show.
parts.answer: Reproduction; it does not respond to stimuli in a regulated way (or is not made of cells).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: it cannot reproduce; it is not made of cells; it does not respond to stimuli in a controlled way.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fire's spread is not the same as growth in living organisms.
parts.answer: Growth in living organisms is an increase in size from cell division and the building of new living material from food; the fire spreads by burning fuel and makes no new living material.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth is by cell division and building new living material; 1 mark: fire spreads by using up fuel with no new living material.

practice.stem: A student finds some old rice grains in a jar and wants to find out whether they are still alive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the student would need to observe to conclude that the grains are living, using three characteristics of living organisms.
parts.answer: e.g. Growth: the grains germinate and increase in size/dry mass; Respiration: they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide (detected with hydrogencarbonate indicator / limewater); Sensitivity: roots grow downwards and shoots grow towards light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three characteristics each linked to an observable sign: growth (germination, increase in size); respiration (CO₂ released / O₂ used / heat released); sensitivity (response to light or gravity); nutrition (seedling makes food / uses stored starch); excretion (CO₂ removed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why showing only one characteristic would not be enough to decide that something is alive.
parts.answer: Some non-living things show one characteristic (e.g. crystals grow, a flame 'respires' / moves); living things must show all seven.
parts.working: B1 non-living things can show some characteristics; living things show all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A virus particle outside a host cell shows none of the characteristics of living organisms. Explain why.
parts.answer: It has no cell structure and does not carry out respiration, nutrition or growth on its own; it needs the machinery of a host cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: no cells and no metabolism of its own; 1 mark: it depends on a host cell to reproduce.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the characteristic that a virus shows only inside a host cell, and explain how it does so.
parts.answer: Reproduction; the virus uses the host cell's ribosomes and enzymes to make new copies of its genetic material and protein coat.
parts.working: 1 mark: reproduction; 1 mark: uses host cell's ribosomes and enzymes to make new virus parts.

practice.stem: A scientist builds a robot that moves towards a light source. It takes in electrical energy from a battery, gives off heat as it works, and can use a 3D printer to make copies of some of its own parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the robot is alive. Refer to at least three characteristics of living organisms.
parts.answer: Not alive: it moves and responds to light (sensitivity and movement are shown), but it has no cells, does not respire or excrete waste from metabolism, takes in batteries that are not digested as food, and its copies are made by a machine rather than by living reproduction.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid point with reasoning, up to 4: sensitivity and movement are shown; no cells; no respiration (energy from a battery, not from food); no excretion or nutrition as in living organisms; copies are made by a machine, not by reproduction.

practice.stem:
A key for six insects found in a school garden:
1 wings present → 2; wings absent → 5
2 wings covered in scales → 3; wings without scales → 4
3 antennae with club at tip → butterfly; antennae feathery or thread-like → moth
4 one pair of wings → housefly; two pairs of wings → dragonfly
5 narrow waist between thorax and abdomen → ant; no narrow waist → silverfish

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify insect P, which has wings, wings with scales, and antennae with a club at the tip.
parts.answer: Butterfly
parts.working: B1 butterfly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Insect Q has wings, no scales on its wings, and two pairs of wings. Identify Q.
parts.answer: Dragonfly
parts.working: B1 dragonfly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Insect R has no wings and a narrow 'waist' between thorax and abdomen. Identify R.
parts.answer: Ant
parts.working: B1 ant.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why each step of a dichotomous key has exactly two statements.
parts.answer: 'Dichotomous' means dividing into two; each step offers two contrasting choices so that only one can be true for the organism.
parts.working: B1 two contrasting/opposite statements so only one applies.

practice.stem:
A student uses this key to identify four fruits, W to Z.
1 Peel can be removed by hand → go to 2; peel cannot be removed by hand → go to 3
2 Fruit splits into segments of juicy pulp → Fruit X; fruit does not split into segments → Fruit Y
3 Fruit contains one large stone → Fruit Z; fruit contains many small seeds → Fruit W

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the fruit whose peel can be removed by hand and which splits into segments of juicy pulp.
parts.answer: Fruit X
parts.working: Step 1 (peel removed by hand) → step 2 (splits into segments) → Fruit X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the fruit whose peel cannot be removed by hand and which contains one large stone.
parts.answer: Fruit Z
parts.working: Step 1 → step 3 (one large stone) → Fruit Z.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the fruit whose peel cannot be removed by hand and which contains many small seeds.
parts.answer: Fruit W
parts.working: Step 1 → step 3 (many small seeds) → Fruit W.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the fruit whose peel can be removed by hand and which does not split into segments.
parts.answer: Fruit Y
parts.working: Step 1 → step 2 (does not split into segments) → Fruit Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of statements forms a valid step in a dichotomous key?
A tall / short
B has flowers / does not have flowers
C large leaves / green leaves
D has petals / has flowers
parts.answer: B has flowers / does not have flowers
parts.working: Each step needs two statements that are opposites and cover every possibility. 'Has flowers / does not have flowers' does this. 'Tall / short' leaves out medium plants, and the other pairs overlap, so an organism could fit both or neither.

practice.stem:
A key for four leaves found on school grounds:
1 Leaf narrow with parallel veins → Plant 1; leaf broad → go to 2
2 Leaf palmately lobed (lobes spread from one point) → Plant 2; leaf not lobed → go to 3
3 Leaf with a smooth edge → Plant 3; leaf with a toothed edge → Plant 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify a leaf that is broad, not lobed and has a toothed edge.
parts.answer: Plant 4
parts.working: Step 1 (broad) → step 2 (not lobed) → step 3 (toothed) → Plant 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify a leaf that is narrow with parallel veins.
parts.answer: Plant 1
parts.working: Step 1 (narrow, parallel veins) → Plant 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the first step divides the leaves into narrow and broad groups.
parts.answer: It is a clear feature with two opposite states, and it splits the leaves into two groups, which makes the key quicker to use.
parts.working: 1 mark: clear opposite features; 1 mark: divides the sample into two groups, speeding up identification.

practice.stem:
A key for four pond organisms, A to D:
1 Body has tentacles around the mouth → Organism A; no tentacles → go to 2
2 Body has no fixed shape → Organism B; body has a fixed shape → go to 3
3 Body has jointed legs → Organism C; no jointed legs → Organism D

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the organism that has no tentacles, a fixed shape and jointed legs.
parts.answer: Organism C
parts.working: Step 1 (no tentacles) → step 2 (fixed shape) → step 3 (jointed legs) → Organism C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the organism that has tentacles around its mouth.
parts.answer: Organism A
parts.working: Step 1 (tentacles) → Organism A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a student might need a hand lens to use step 3.
parts.answer: Jointed legs are very small and hard to see without magnification.
parts.working: 1 mark: the legs are too small to see clearly without magnification.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A key to four leaves is shown.
1 leaf divided into leaflets → go to 2; leaf not divided into leaflets → go to 3
2 more than 10 leaflets → leaf P; 10 leaflets or fewer → leaf Q
3 leaf edge smooth → leaf R; leaf edge toothed → leaf S
A leaf is not divided into leaflets and has a toothed edge. Which leaf is it?
A P
B Q
C R
D S
parts.answer: D S
parts.working: Not divided → step 3; toothed edge → S. R is the smooth-edged undivided leaf.

practice.stem:
A student has four seeds:
Kidney bean: 15 mm long, rounded, smooth, no groove
Broad bean: 22 mm long, flat, smooth, no groove
Wheat: 6 mm long, oval, groove along one side
Mustard: 2 mm long, round, no groove

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify the four seeds. Use only features given in the table.
parts.answer: e.g. 1 seed longer than 10 mm → 2; 10 mm or shorter → 3. 2 seed flat → broad bean; seed rounded → kidney bean. 3 seed has a groove → wheat; no groove → mustard.
parts.working: B1 first step splits into two groups of two using one feature; B1 each later step uses one contrasting pair; B1 every seed ends at one name; B1 statements use features from the table (not size words like 'big'). Allow any correct logical key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why features such as colour can be unreliable in a key.
parts.answer: Colour can vary within a species / with age, ripeness or storage, so different people may judge it differently.
parts.working: B1 variation within species / subjective.

practice.stem:
Four birds visited a school garden in Rawalpindi.
Crow: mostly black feathers, large, stout beak
Pigeon: grey feathers with two black bars on each wing, round body
Sparrow: brown streaked feathers, small
Kingfisher: blue back, orange breast, long straight beak

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key with three steps that separates the four birds. Use only the features in the table.
parts.answer: Example key: 1 Mostly black → Crow; not mostly black → go to 2. 2 Orange breast → Kingfisher; no orange breast → go to 3. 3 Two black wing bars → Pigeon; no black wing bars → Sparrow.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three valid steps with two opposite statements; 1 mark for all four birds correctly placed at an end point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why 'large' and 'small' are weak features to use in a key.
parts.answer: Size is relative and there is no sharp boundary between large and small, so two people may decide differently; size can also vary within a species.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid reason: no sharp boundary, relative judgement, or variation within a species.

practice.stem: A student uses a key for flowering plants. Step 3 asks, 'Number of petals more than five?' The flower the student has collected is damaged and only some petals remain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest what the student should do.
parts.answer: Count the petals on another, undamaged flower of the same plant, or use a step that uses a feature still visible, such as the leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible action such as using another flower or a different step.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a key should use features that are present and easy to see at any time of year.
parts.answer: Some features, such as flowers, are only present for part of the year, so the key would fail at other times; features such as leaves are available for most of the year.
parts.working: 1 mark: some features are seasonal; 1 mark: a key must work for any sample, so it needs features that are always visible.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A key:
1 Animal has a backbone → go to 2; no backbone → go to 4
2 Covered in feathers → Bird; not covered in feathers → go to 3
3 Covered in scales → Lizard; not covered in scales → Frog
4 Has eight legs → Spider; has six legs → Beetle
An animal has a backbone, no feathers and no scales. Which identification does the key give?
A Lizard
B Bird
C Frog
D Spider
parts.answer: C Frog
parts.working: Step 1: backbone → step 2. Step 2: no feathers → step 3. Step 3: no scales → Frog. A lizard has scales, a bird has feathers, and a spider has no backbone.

practice.stem:
A key for three land snails:
1 Shell tall and coiled → go to 2; shell flat → go to 3
2 Shell banded → Snail P; shell unbanded → Snail Q
3 Shell banded → Snail R; shell unbanded → Snail S

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify a snail with a tall, unbanded shell.
parts.answer: Snail Q
parts.working: Step 1 (tall) → step 2 (unbanded) → Snail Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify a snail with a flat, banded shell.
parts.answer: Snail R
parts.working: Step 1 (flat) → step 3 (banded) → Snail R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why colour is not used as a feature in this key.
parts.answer: Colour can vary within the same species, for example with diet or the habitat, so it is not a reliable feature for identifying species.
parts.working: 1 mark: colour varies within a species; 1 mark: so it cannot reliably separate species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a key for 40 species needs more steps than a key for 8 species.
parts.answer: Each step divides the remaining group into only two, so more species need more steps before each one is reached.
parts.working: 1 mark: each step splits the group into two; 1 mark: more species need more steps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why keys are usually written using features that can be seen without dissecting the organism.
parts.answer: Dissection would damage or kill the organism, which is not practical for field identification; features that can be seen in living organisms let people identify them without harm.
parts.working: 1 mark: dissection destroys the specimen; 1 mark: field identification must work on living organisms.

practice.stem:
A key to five freshwater fish species, A–E, from the Indus river:
1 mouth sucker-shaped → 3; mouth not sucker-shaped → 2
2 adipose fin present → 4; adipose fin absent → species A
3 barbels present → species D; barbels absent → species E
4 body without scales → species B; body with scales → species C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify fish X, which has a sucker-shaped mouth and no barbels. Show the steps you used.
parts.answer: Species E: step 1 (mouth sucker-shaped) leads to step 3; no barbels leads to species E.
parts.working: B1 correct route 1 → 3; B1 E.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fish Y has a normal mouth, an adipose fin and scales absent. Identify Y.
parts.answer: species B
parts.working: B1 B.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says step 2 of the key would be better written as 'large fish' or 'small fish'. Explain why this would be a poor change.
parts.answer: 'Large' and 'small' are relative/subjective and size changes with age, so different users would choose differently; a key needs clear, observable contrasting features.
parts.working: B1 subjective / no fixed boundary; B1 size varies with age / individual, so fish could be misidentified.

practice.stem:
A teacher wrote this step for a key:
2 Has wings → go to 3; has a large body → go to 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two errors in step 2.
parts.answer: 1: 'has a large body' is not the opposite of 'has wings', so an animal with no wings and a small body has no route. 2: size is vague and relative, so it cannot be judged reliably.
parts.working: 1 mark per error: second statement is not the opposite of the first (gaps or overlap); size is not a clear yes/no feature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite step 2 correctly for the same two groups of animals.
parts.answer: 2 Has wings → go to 3; no wings → go to 4
parts.working: 1 mark for two opposite statements with correct destinations.

practice.stem: A key was tested on 20 insects of known identity. Four were identified wrongly. Two of the errors came from a step using 'hairy' or 'smooth' body surfaces, which was hard to judge with the naked eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the errors other than the difficulty of seeing hairs with the naked eye.
parts.answer: The student misread the step, or the specimen was damaged or unclear.
parts.working: 1 mark for any sensible reason such as misreading the key, damaged specimens or ambiguous wording.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement to the key and to the test procedure.
parts.answer: Use a hand lens or microscope to check body hairs; rewrite steps using clearer features; test the key on more specimens and with a second observer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible change to the key; 1 mark for a sensible change to the test procedure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two plants that are heterozygous for flower colour (Rr) are crossed. Red (R) is dominant to white (r). What is the expected ratio of red to white offspring?
A 1 : 1
B 3 : 1
C 1 : 3
D all red
parts.working: Rr × Rr gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr: three red to one white. 1 : 1 (A) is the result of a test cross Rr × rr.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of (i) homozygous and (ii) heterozygous.
parts.answer: (i) Having two identical alleles of a particular gene; (ii) having two different alleles of a particular gene.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why two heterozygous individuals do not 'breed true' for a characteristic.
parts.answer: Each can pass on either allele, so offspring can be homozygous dominant, heterozygous or homozygous recessive – some offspring show a different phenotype from the parents.
parts.working: B1 gametes carry different alleles; B1 offspring can be recessive / different phenotype.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two parents with the genotypes Bb and bb are crossed. What is the probability that an offspring has the genotype bb?
A 0%
B 25%
C 50%
D 75%
parts.working: A cross of Bb × bb gives Bb and bb in a 1:1 ratio, so half the offspring are bb (50%). A 25% answer would be correct for Bb × Bb, not this cross.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cross produces offspring in a 1:1 phenotypic ratio?
A Aa × Aa
B AA × aa
C Aa × aa
D AA × AA
parts.answer: C Aa × aa
parts.working: Aa × aa gives Aa and aa in a 1:1 ratio, so the phenotypes (dominant and recessive) also appear in a 1:1 ratio. Aa × Aa gives 3:1 and AA × aa gives all Aa, while AA × AA gives all AA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a recessive allele can be carried by an individual without showing in the phenotype.
parts.answer: A heterozygote has one dominant allele and one recessive allele. The dominant allele is expressed and masks the recessive allele, so the recessive trait does not show. The recessive allele can still be passed on to the next generation.
parts.working: 1 mark: heterozygote has one dominant and one recessive allele. 1 mark: dominant allele is expressed and masks the recessive. 1 mark: recessive allele can still be passed on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define genotype and phenotype, using pea seed shape as an example.
parts.answer: Genotype: the alleles an organism carries (e.g. Rr). Phenotype: the observable characteristic produced (e.g. round seeds).
parts.working: 1 mark: genotype is the allele combination. 1 mark: example Rr. 1 mark: phenotype is the observable feature. 1 mark: example round seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a farmer could use a test cross to find out whether a black-coated goat is homozygous (BB) or heterozygous (Bb). Black (B) is dominant to brown (b).
parts.answer: Cross the black goat with a brown goat (bb, homozygous recessive); if any offspring are brown, the black goat is Bb; if all offspring (in a large number) are black, it is probably BB.
parts.working: B1 cross with homozygous recessive / brown goat; B1 any brown offspring → Bb; B1 all black → BB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram for the cross if the black goat is heterozygous. State the expected ratio of offspring phenotypes.
parts.answer: Bb × bb; gametes B, b and b; offspring Bb (black), bb (brown); ratio 1 black : 1 brown.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 1 : 1 black : brown.

practice.stem: A student in Multan grew 810 pea seeds from a cross between two tall plants. 612 plants were tall and 198 were dwarf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of tall to dwarf plants, to the nearest whole number : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotypes of the parent plants. Use T for tall and t for dwarf.
parts.answer: Tt × Tt
parts.working: B1 both Tt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the ratio is not exactly the expected ratio.
parts.answer: Fertilisation is random / chance; sample is too small to give the exact ratio.
parts.working: B1 random fusion of gametes / chance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a pedigree diagram can show whether a trait is dominant or recessive.
parts.answer: If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait must be recessive, because both parents must carry the recessive allele. A dominant trait appears in every generation and an affected person has at least one affected parent. A recessive trait can skip generations.
