parts.working: 1 mark: unaffected parents with an affected child shows a recessive trait. 1 mark: dominant trait appears in every generation. 1 mark: affected child of unaffected parents must be recessive. 1 mark: recessive traits can skip a generation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Free earlobes (E) are dominant to attached earlobes (e). Two parents who are both heterozygous (Ee) have children. (i) State the genotype ratio of the children. (ii) State the phenotype ratio of the children.
parts.answer: (i) 1 EE : 2 Ee : 1 ee; (ii) 3 free : 1 attached
parts.working: (i) 2 marks: 1 mark for the three genotypes EE, Ee and ee; 1 mark for the ratio 1:2:1. (ii) 2 marks: 1 mark for the two phenotypes; 1 mark for the ratio 3:1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A plant with white flowers (rr) is crossed with a heterozygous red-flowered plant (Rr). Draw a Punnett square and state the expected phenotype ratio of the offspring.
parts.answer: Offspring: Rr and rr in equal numbers; phenotype ratio 1 red : 1 white
parts.working: 1 mark: correct gametes. 1 mark: correct Punnett square. 1 mark: genotypes Rr and rr in equal numbers. 1 mark: 1 red : 1 white.

practice.stem: A family pedigree is described: Persons 1 (father) and 2 (mother) are both unaffected. They have three children: person 3 (son, unaffected), person 4 (daughter, unaffected) and person 5 (son, has cystic fibrosis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Use the pedigree to state the genotypes of persons 1 and 2. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Both Ff. They are unaffected, so each has at least one F; their child 5 has cystic fibrosis (ff) and received one f from each parent.
parts.working: B1 both Ff; B1 unaffected so have dominant allele; B1 affected child must have received f from each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that the next child of persons 1 and 2 will have cystic fibrosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Person 4 is unaffected. Calculate the probability that person 4 is a carrier (Ff).
parts.working: M1 unaffected offspring of Ff × Ff are FF, Ff, Ff (ff excluded); A1 2/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In pea plants, round seeds (R) are dominant to wrinkled seeds (r). Two plants with round seeds and the genotype Rr are crossed. State the genotypes of the parents.
parts.answer: Rr and Rr
parts.working: 1 mark: both parents Rr.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a Punnett square for this cross and list the genotypes of the offspring.
parts.answer: RR, Rr, Rr, rr
parts.working: 1 mark: correct Punnett square with gametes R and r from each parent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the expected percentage of wrinkled seeds in the offspring.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the expected ratio of round seeds to wrinkled seeds.
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 round : 1 wrinkled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In goats, black coat (B) is dominant to white coat (b). A black goat is crossed with a white goat. The kids are 9 black and 8 white. State the genotype of the black parent, with a reason.
parts.answer: Bb, because the white kids (bb) must receive a b allele from the black parent, and the 1:1 ratio is typical of a heterozygote.
parts.working: 1 mark: Bb. 1 mark: white kids are bb so the black parent must carry b; roughly equal numbers show it is heterozygous.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of white kids. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark: 8 ÷ 17 seen. 1 mark: 47.1%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this cross is a test cross and what the result shows.
parts.answer: The white (recessive) parent is used to test the black parent. A roughly 1:1 ratio of black to white kids shows that the black parent is heterozygous (Bb).
parts.working: 1 mark: crossed with a homozygous recessive parent. 1 mark: 1:1 ratio shows heterozygous black parent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele f. Two carriers (Ff × Ff) have children. Calculate the probability that their first child has cystic fibrosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: ff from Ff × Ff = 1/4. 1 mark: 25%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that both of their first two children have cystic fibrosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1/4 for each child. 1 mark: multiply the probabilities for independent events. 1 mark: 1/16 = 6.25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where in a cell are proteins assembled from amino acids?
A nucleus
B ribosome
C cell membrane
D vacuole
parts.answer: B ribosome
parts.working: mRNA carries a copy of the gene from the nucleus to a ribosome in the cytoplasm, where amino acids are joined in order. The nucleus (A) is where the mRNA copy is made, not the protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms (i) gene and (ii) allele.
parts.answer: (i) A length of DNA that codes for a protein; (ii) an alternative form of a gene.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what a chromosome is made of.
parts.answer: DNA (carrying genetic information in the form of genes).
parts.working: B1 DNA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of chromosomes in (i) a human skin cell and (ii) a human egg cell.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the molecule that carries a copy of a gene from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
parts.answer: mRNA (messenger RNA)
parts.working: B1 mRNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the units that are joined together to make a protein.
parts.answer: Amino acids
parts.working: B1 amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what determines the order in which these units are joined.
parts.answer: The sequence of bases in the gene / mRNA.
parts.working: B1 base sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A polypeptide contains 150 amino acids. Assuming each amino acid is coded for by three bases, calculate the number of bases on the coding strand of the gene that codes for it. Ignore stop codons.
parts.answer: 450 bases
parts.working: 1 mark: 150 × 3 seen. 1 mark: 450 bases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what a stop codon does during translation.
parts.answer: It signals the end of the polypeptide; no amino acid is added for it.
parts.working: 1 mark: it marks the end of translation, so the chain is released and no amino acid is added.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the roles of ribosomes and transfer RNA (tRNA) in protein synthesis.
parts.answer: Ribosomes are the site where the mRNA codons are read and the polypeptide chain is built. Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a codon on the mRNA. Amino acids are joined in the order set by the codons.
parts.working: 1 mark: ribosomes are the site of translation. 1 mark: tRNA carries a specific amino acid. 1 mark: anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon. 1 mark: amino acids are joined in order by peptide bonds.

practice.stem: The gene for insulin is found in all human body cells but is used only in some cells of the pancreas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the information in a gene is used to make a protein.
parts.answer: The gene is a sequence of bases in DNA in the nucleus; a copy of the gene is made as an mRNA molecule; mRNA moves out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm; mRNA attaches to a ribosome; the ribosome assembles amino acids into a protein molecule; the specific order of bases in the mRNA determines the specific sequence of amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: DNA stays in nucleus; mRNA made as a copy of gene; mRNA leaves nucleus (through pores) to cytoplasm; mRNA attaches to ribosome; ribosome joins amino acids; base sequence determines amino acid sequence; amino acid sequence determines the protein's shape / function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gene contains 1 260 bases on its coding strand. Three bases code for one amino acid. Assuming every base in the gene codes for an amino acid, calculate the number of amino acids in the protein it codes for.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mutation removes one base near the start of the gene. Suggest why this usually has a large effect on the protein made.
parts.answer: The bases after the deletion are read in different groups of three, so the sequence of amino acids changes from that point; the protein has a different shape and may not function.
parts.working: B1 changes the reading of all later bases / amino acid sequence; B1 protein shape / function changed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the shape of a protein is important for its function, using an enzyme as an example.
parts.answer: The amino acid sequence determines how the protein folds; an enzyme's active site must have a specific shape complementary to its substrate.
parts.working: B1 sequence determines shape; B1 active site shape complementary to substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the statement 'a person's genotype for eye colour is homozygous recessive'.
parts.answer: Homozygous: has two identical alleles of the gene; recessive: the allele only expressed when no dominant allele is present (e.g. bb).
parts.working: B1 two identical alleles; B1 recessive alleles (only expressed when homozygous).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define (i) phenotype and (ii) genotype.
parts.answer: (i) The observable features of an organism; (ii) the genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a sample of DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine. What percentage of the bases are thymine?
A 20%
B 30%
C 40%
D 60%
parts.working: Adenine always pairs with thymine (A–T) in DNA, so the two bases are present in equal numbers. Thymine is therefore 30%. Adenine and thymine together make 60%, so A (20%) and D (60%) are incorrect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a substitution of one base in a gene may produce no change in the protein made.
parts.answer: The genetic code is degenerate: more than one codon codes for the same amino acid. A change in one base, often the third base of the codon, may give a codon that still codes for the same amino acid, so the protein sequence does not change.
parts.working: 1 mark: the genetic code is degenerate (several codons per amino acid). 1 mark: the new codon may code for the same amino acid. 1 mark: so the amino acid sequence is unchanged. 1 mark: change often in the third base of the codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A nerve cell and a white blood cell from the same person contain the same genes but make different proteins. What is the best explanation?
A The cells have different numbers of chromosomes.
B Different genes are expressed (switched on) in each type of cell.
C Each cell type has lost the genes it does not need.
D Mutations have changed the genes in one cell type.
parts.answer: B Different genes are expressed (switched on) in each type of cell.
parts.working: All body cells carry the same genes, but each specialised cell expresses only the genes for the proteins it needs. Body cells do not lose genes (C) and have the same chromosome number (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a change in the base sequence of a gene can result in a protein that does not work.
parts.answer: The base sequence determines the sequence of amino acids; a different amino acid sequence changes how the protein folds (its shape); e.g. an enzyme's active site no longer fits its substrate.
parts.working: B1 base sequence → amino acid sequence; B1 changed shape; B1 consequence for function, e.g. active site / binding site.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Most body cells do not express the gene for haemoglobin, though they contain it. Suggest one advantage of switching off unneeded genes.
parts.answer: Saves energy and materials (amino acids) by not making proteins the cell does not need.
parts.working: B1 saves energy / resources; accept prevents proteins interfering with the cell's own function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A protein is made of 285 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of bases in the mRNA that codes for it, given three bases code for one amino acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gene in the DNA is longer than this. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: Not all of the DNA of a gene codes for amino acids, e.g. start/stop signals or regions that are removed / do not code.
parts.working: B1 non-coding regions / stop signal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why DNA does not leave the nucleus to make proteins, but mRNA does.
parts.answer: DNA is very large / is the master copy, which must be protected from damage in the cytoplasm; mRNA is a small, short-lived copy of one gene that can pass through the nuclear pores.
parts.working: B1 DNA too large / kept safe; B1 mRNA small copy of a single gene that can leave nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these in order from the largest to the smallest: base, gene, chromosome, nucleus.
A base, gene, chromosome, nucleus
B nucleus, chromosome, gene, base
C chromosome, nucleus, gene, base
D gene, base, chromosome, nucleus
parts.answer: B nucleus, chromosome, gene, base
parts.working: A nucleus contains chromosomes; each chromosome carries many genes; each gene is a sequence of many bases. The order is nucleus > chromosome > gene > base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the base that pairs with cytosine in DNA.
parts.answer: Guanine (G)
parts.working: 1 mark: guanine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the base that pairs with adenine in DNA.
parts.answer: Thymine (T)
parts.working: 1 mark: thymine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the transcription of a DNA template strand with the base adenine, state which base is placed in the mRNA.
parts.answer: Uracil (U)
parts.working: 1 mark: uracil (mRNA has U in place of T).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the pentose sugar in a DNA nucleotide.
parts.answer: Deoxyribose
parts.working: 1 mark: deoxyribose.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A father has blood group AB and a mother has blood group O. Which blood groups could their children have?
A A or B only
B AB or O only
C A, B, AB or O
D A only
parts.answer: A A or B only
parts.working: Father IᴬIᴮ gives Iᴬ or Iᴮ; mother IᴼIᴼ gives Iᴼ; children are IᴬIᴼ (group A) or IᴮIᴼ (group B). No child can be AB or O.

practice.stem: A class of 40 students in Hyderabad recorded their blood groups: A – 9, B – 13, AB – 4, O – 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the 40 students with blood group O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which blood group shows that two alleles are codominant.
parts.answer: AB
parts.working: B1 AB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable way of displaying these results and give a reason.
parts.answer: A bar chart (with gaps between bars), because blood group is a discontinuous (categoric) variable.
parts.working: B1 bar chart; B1 discontinuous / categories.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A child has blood group A. Which genotype could the child have?
A IAIA or IAIO
B IBIB or IBIO
C IAIB only
D IOIO only
parts.answer: A IAIA or IAIO
parts.working: Blood group A is produced by IA IA or IA IO, because IA is dominant over IO. IAIB is group AB, and IOIO is group O. Group B genotypes (IB IB or IB IO) would be group B, not A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person with blood group O has no A or B antigens on the surface of their red blood cells.
parts.answer: The person has the genotype IOIO. The IO allele does not produce a working antigen, and it is recessive, so no A or B antigen is made. Only the IA and IB alleles produce these antigens.
parts.working: 1 mark: genotype IOIO. 1 mark: IO allele produces no functional antigen. 1 mark: IO is recessive. 1 mark: only IA or IB alleles produce A or B antigens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sex of a human child is determined.
parts.answer: The father can give either an X or a Y chromosome in sperm. The mother always gives an X chromosome in her egg. A child who receives Y from the father is male (XY); a child who receives X is female (XX).
parts.working: 1 mark: the father's sperm carries X or Y. 1 mark: the mother's egg always carries X. 1 mark: XY is male, XX is female.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A man with normal vision and a woman who is a carrier have a son. What is the probability that the son is colour blind?
A 0
B 0.25
C 0.5
D 1.0
parts.working: A son gets Y from his father and one X from his mother: Xᴮ or Xᵇ with equal chance, so 0.5. 0.25 (B) is the probability for any child (son or daughter) being colour blind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by codominance, using the ABO blood group alleles as an example.
parts.answer: Both alleles in a heterozygote are expressed in the phenotype; e.g. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant so a person with IᴬIᴮ has blood group AB.
parts.working: B1 both alleles expressed in heterozygote; B1 IᴬIᴮ gives AB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of children from a father who is IᴬIᴼ and a mother who is IᴮIᴼ. Give the probability of a child having blood group O.
parts.answer: Parental genotypes IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ; gametes Iᴬ, Iᴼ and Iᴮ, Iᴼ; offspring IᴬIᴮ (AB), IᴬIᴼ (A), IᴮIᴼ (B), IᴼIᴼ (O); probability of O = 0.25 (1 in 4).
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring genotypes (Punnett square); B1 phenotypes; B1 probability 0.25 / 25 % / 1 in 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the blood group of a person with each genotype: (i) IᴮIᴼ, (ii) IᴬIᴮ, (iii) IᴼIᴼ.
parts.answer: (i) B; (ii) AB; (iii) O.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A couple both have blood group A. Their first child has blood group O. State the genotypes of the parents and the probability that their next child will have blood group A.
parts.answer: Both parents IᴬIᴼ; probability of group A = 0.75.
parts.working: B1 both IᴬIᴼ; M1 offspring IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴼIᴼ; A1 0.75 (3/4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the sex chromosomes of (i) a human male and (ii) a human female.
parts.answer: (i) XY; (ii) XX.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a genetic diagram to show why the chance of a baby being a boy is 50 %.
parts.answer: Parents XX × XY; gametes X (egg) and X or Y (sperm); offspring XX (girl) and XY (boy) in a 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: B1 parental chromosomes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring XX : XY 1 : 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the father's sperm determines the sex of the child.
parts.answer: All eggs carry an X chromosome; half of sperm carry X and half carry Y.
parts.working: B1 eggs all X, sperm X or Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A man with blood group AB (IAIB) and a woman with blood group O (IOIO) have children. Complete a genetic diagram for their children.
parts.answer: Gametes from the father: IA and IB; gametes from the mother: IO. Offspring: IAIO and IBIO.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct gametes from both parents. 1 mark: correct genotypes IAIO and IBIO in the offspring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the blood groups of the children and the expected percentage of each.
parts.answer: 50% group A (IAIO); 50% group B (IBIO); no children with group AB or group O
parts.working: 1 mark: 50% group A and 50% group B. 1 mark: no AB or O children expected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A father has blood group A (genotype IAIO) and the mother has blood group B (genotype IBIO). Calculate the probability that a child has blood group O, and the probability that a child has blood group AB.
parts.answer: Blood group O: 25%. Blood group AB: 25%.
parts.working: 1 mark: O needs IO from each parent: 1/2 × 1/2 seen. 1 mark: O = 25%. 1 mark: AB needs IA from father and IB from mother: 1/2 × 1/2 seen. 1 mark: AB = 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why red-green colour blindness is more common in men than in women.
parts.answer: The allele is on the X chromosome (sex-linked) and the Y chromosome carries no copy of the gene; a man has only one X, so one recessive allele (XᵇY) makes him colour blind; a woman needs two recessive alleles (XᵇXᵇ), which is less likely.
parts.working: B1 gene on X chromosome / not on Y; B1 males need only one recessive allele; B1 females need two / heterozygous females are carriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A colour-blind man (XᵇY) and a woman with normal vision who is not a carrier (XᴮXᴮ) have children. Use a genetic diagram to give the probability that (i) a daughter is a carrier and (ii) a son is colour blind.
parts.answer: Gametes Xᵇ, Y and Xᴮ; daughters XᴮXᵇ, sons XᴮY. (i) 1 (all daughters carriers); (ii) 0.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 (i) 1 / 100 %; B1 (ii) 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A woman whose father was colour blind has normal vision. She has children with a man who has normal vision. Give the woman's genotype and explain how you worked it out.
parts.answer: XᴮXᵇ; she has normal vision so has at least one Xᴮ, and she must have received Xᵇ from her colour-blind father (fathers pass their X to daughters).
parts.working: B1 XᴮXᵇ; B1 reasoning – father gives his only X (Xᵇ) to daughter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first child is a colour-blind boy.
parts.working: M1 offspring XᴮXᴮ, XᴮXᵇ, XᴮY, XᵇY; A1 1/4 = 0.25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the probability that two of their children are both colour-blind boys.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a codominant system, what does a heterozygote show?
A only the dominant phenotype
B only the recessive phenotype
C both alleles expressed in the phenotype
D neither allele expressed
parts.answer: C both alleles expressed in the phenotype
parts.working: In codominance both alleles are expressed equally, as in blood group AB (IA IB). Option A describes complete dominance, B describes a recessive trait, and D is never true of a heterozygote with a functional allele.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome (Xh). A woman who is a carrier (XHXh) and a man with haemophilia (XhY) have children. Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that a daughter has haemophilia.
parts.working: 1 mark: daughters are XHXh or XhXh (mother gives XH or Xh, father gives Xh). 1 mark: half of the daughters have haemophilia, so 50%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that a child (son or daughter) has haemophilia.
parts.working: 1 mark: sons: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 are affected. 1 mark: daughters: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 are affected; 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 = 50%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the probability that a child is a female carrier.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1/2 of children are daughters. 1 mark: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 25% are carriers (XHXh).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many chromosomes are present in each cell produced when a human body cell (46 chromosomes) divides by mitosis?
A 23
B 46
C 92
D 69
parts.working: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells with the same chromosome number as the parent, 46. 23 (A) is the result of meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three roles of mitosis in the human body.
parts.answer: Growth; repair of damaged tissues; replacement of cells (e.g. skin, red blood cells).
parts.working: B1 each; accept asexual reproduction only for other organisms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of cell division that produces sperm cells.
parts.answer: Meiosis
parts.working: B1 meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define (i) a haploid nucleus and (ii) a diploid nucleus.
parts.answer: (i) A nucleus containing a single set of chromosomes; (ii) a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a haploid cell and one example of a diploid cell in a human.
parts.answer: Haploid: sperm or egg cell; diploid: any body cell, e.g. a cheek cell or zygote.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of interphase that prepare a cell for mitosis.
parts.answer: The DNA replicates so that each chromosome is made of two identical chromatids. The cell grows and increases its number of organelles, such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Protein synthesis and energy stores increase to prepare for division.
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA replicates so each chromosome has two chromatids. 1 mark: cell grows. 1 mark: organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes are duplicated. 1 mark: energy stores and proteins are built up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the cells produced by meiosis differ from each other.
parts.answer: Any two of: they carry different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes (homologous pairs are sorted randomly); they carry different combinations of alleles; they are not identical to each other.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: different chromosome combinations from random sorting of homologous pairs; different allele combinations; the cells are not identical to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how uncontrolled mitosis can lead to a tumour, and how mutations are involved.
parts.answer: A mutation in a gene that controls the cell cycle can cause cells to divide without control. The rapidly dividing cells form a mass of cells called a tumour, which may invade other tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: mutation in a gene controlling the cell cycle. 1 mark: cells divide without control. 1 mark: a mass of cells (tumour) forms. 1 mark: cells may invade other tissues.

practice.stem: A patient in a hospital in Lahore needs treatment to replace damaged blood-forming tissue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term stem cell.
parts.answer: An unspecialised cell that divides by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions.
parts.working: B1 unspecialised; B1 divides by mitosis to give cells that can become specialised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stem cells taken from a patient's own bone marrow can be used to replace damaged cells without being rejected.
parts.answer: The new cells are genetically identical to the patient's (made by mitosis), so they have the same antigens and are not recognised as foreign by the immune system.
parts.working: B1 genetically identical / same DNA; B1 same antigens / not attacked by immune system.

practice.stem: A student examined a stained squash of an onion root tip under a microscope. In one field of view 150 cells were counted and 24 of them showed chromosomes that were visible (dividing).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells that were dividing (mitotic index).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student used the tip of the root rather than a region further back.
parts.answer: Cells divide by mitosis mainly at the root tip (growth region); further back cells are elongating / specialising.
parts.working: B1 mitosis occurs at tip / growth region.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the estimate more reliable.
parts.answer: Count cells in more fields of view / from more roots and calculate a mean.
parts.working: B1 more fields / more roots / repeats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare mitosis and meiosis by giving three differences.
parts.answer: Mitosis gives 2 cells, meiosis gives 4 (cells / gametes); mitosis gives genetically identical cells, meiosis gives genetically different cells; mitosis keeps chromosome number (diploid), meiosis halves it (haploid); mitosis for growth/repair, meiosis for gamete production.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mitosis is also used in asexual reproduction. Explain why a field of potato plants grown from tubers of one plant all show the same disease susceptibility.
parts.answer: Tubers are produced by mitosis so all the plants are genetically identical (clones); none has alleles giving resistance, so all are equally affected.
parts.working: B1 mitosis → genetically identical / clones; B1 same alleles / no variation for resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell with 8 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes does each gamete produced contain?
A 2
B 4
C 8
D 16
parts.answer: B 4
parts.working: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so the gametes have 4 chromosomes. A gives 2, which is too few, and C and D are the diploid number or more, which is not produced by meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tissue culture starts with 40 cells. Each cell divides by mitosis once every 4 hours. Calculate the number of cells after 24 hours, assuming every cell keeps dividing.
parts.answer: 2560 cells
parts.working: 1 mark: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 divisions. 1 mark: 2 to the power 6 = 64 seen. 1 mark: 40 × 64 seen. 1 mark: 2560 cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to chromosomes before and during mitosis so that the two daughter cells are genetically identical.
parts.answer: Each chromosome is copied (replicated / DNA copied) before division; the two copies separate, one copy going to each end of the cell; each new nucleus receives an exact copy of every chromosome; cell then divides (cytoplasm).
parts.working: B1 chromosomes replicate before mitosis; B1 copies separate (to opposite poles); B1 each daughter nucleus gets full identical set.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that gametes are produced by meiosis, not by mitosis.
parts.answer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number (diploid 46 → haploid 23); at fertilisation two gametes fuse to restore the diploid number; otherwise the chromosome number would double every generation; meiosis also produces genetic variation.
parts.working: B1 halves chromosome number / haploid; B1 fertilisation restores diploid; B1 prevents doubling each generation / gives variation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many cells would be produced from one fertilised egg after 12 rounds of mitosis, assuming every cell divides each time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Red blood cells have no nucleus and live for only about four months. Explain why stem cells in the bone marrow must keep dividing throughout a person's life.
parts.answer: Red blood cells cannot divide (no nucleus) and are constantly being destroyed, so they must be replaced; stem cells divide by mitosis to make new cells that become specialised as red blood cells.
parts.working: B1 red blood cells cannot divide / are continually lost and need replacing; B1 stem cells divide by mitosis and the daughter cells become specialised (as red blood cells).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the chromosome number in the egg of a dog, whose body cells have 78 chromosomes, and name the division producing it.
parts.answer: 39; meiosis.
parts.working: B1 39; B1 meiosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell?
A prophase
B metaphase
C anaphase
D telophase
parts.answer: B metaphase
parts.working: In metaphase the chromosomes line up along the equator (middle) of the cell and attach to spindle fibres. In prophase they condense, in anaphase the chromatids are pulled apart, and in telophase the nuclei re-form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the chromosome number of a human gamete with that of a human body cell, and explain how fertilisation restores the chromosome number.
parts.answer: A human gamete has 23 chromosomes (haploid); a body cell has 46 (diploid). Fertilisation fuses two gametes to form a zygote with 46 chromosomes. Mitosis then keeps this number constant in the cells of the body.
parts.working: 1 mark: gamete has 23 (haploid), body cell has 46 (diploid). 1 mark: fertilisation fuses two gametes. 1 mark: zygote has 46 chromosomes. 1 mark: mitosis keeps the number constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis?
A C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
B 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
C 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
D CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂
parts.answer: B 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
parts.working: Six carbon dioxide and six water give one glucose and six oxygen, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. A is the aerobic respiration equation; D is not balanced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)
parts.working: B1 reactants carbon dioxide + water; B1 products glucose + oxygen. Condition (light/chlorophyll) above the arrow is expected but not separately credited.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of energy for photosynthesis and name the pigment that absorbs it.
parts.answer: Light (energy); chlorophyll.
parts.working: B1 light; B1 chlorophyll.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to the energy absorbed by chlorophyll.
parts.answer: It is transferred into chemical energy in glucose (and other carbohydrates).
parts.working: B1 light energy transferred to chemical energy in glucose / carbohydrates.

practice.stem: A sugarcane plant in a field in Punjab makes glucose by photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways the plant uses the glucose it makes.
parts.answer: Respiration to release energy; converted to starch for storage; converted to cellulose for cell walls; (also sucrose for transport, amino acids/proteins, fats/oils, nectar).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: respiration; starch (storage); cellulose (cell walls); sucrose (translocation in phloem); amino acids/proteins (with nitrate); fats and oils (storage in seeds); nectar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why glucose is converted to starch for storage in the leaf.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble so it does not affect water potential / osmosis in cells; it is large so does not diffuse out of cells (and is compact).
parts.working: B1 insoluble; B1 does not affect osmosis / water potential / cannot move out of cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors, other than light intensity, that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration; temperature.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide concentration; B1 temperature. Do not accept light (excluded by the question).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis is slow on a cold, sunny winter morning.
parts.answer: Low temperature means the enzymes controlling photosynthesis work slowly (molecules have less kinetic energy, fewer collisions), so temperature is limiting.
parts.working: B1 temperature is limiting; B1 enzymes slow / less kinetic energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two raw materials of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide and water.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how each raw material enters a leaf of a neem tree.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide diffuses in from the air through the stomata; water is absorbed by root hairs and carried to the leaf in the xylem.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ through stomata by diffusion; B1 water via xylem (from roots).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas released as a by-product.
parts.answer: Oxygen
parts.working: B1 oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A leaf is in bright sunlight and its rate of photosynthesis is greater than its rate of respiration. Which row describes the net movement of the two gases through the stomata?
A oxygen leaves the leaf; carbon dioxide enters the leaf
B carbon dioxide leaves the leaf; oxygen enters the leaf
C both oxygen and carbon dioxide leave the leaf
D both oxygen and carbon dioxide enter the leaf
parts.answer: A oxygen leaves the leaf; carbon dioxide enters the leaf
parts.working: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, so when it exceeds respiration the net movement is oxygen out and carbon dioxide in. B describes the reverse, which happens when respiration is greater than photosynthesis, such as at night.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potted plant is kept in a sealed glass box in bright light for six hours. What happens to the concentrations of gases in the box?
A carbon dioxide increases, oxygen decreases
B carbon dioxide decreases, oxygen increases
C both carbon dioxide and oxygen decrease
D neither changes because respiration and photosynthesis balance
parts.answer: B carbon dioxide decreases, oxygen increases
parts.working: In bright light the rate of photosynthesis is greater than the rate of respiration, so CO₂ is used up faster than it is made and O₂ is released. Option D would apply only at the compensation point (dim light).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is orange-red at atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration. A leaf is placed in a sealed tube of indicator and kept in bright light for 2 hours. What colour is the indicator at the end?
A yellow
B orange-red
C purple
D blue-black
parts.answer: C purple
parts.working: Photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so CO₂ is removed and the indicator turns purple. Yellow (A) shows a higher CO₂ concentration, e.g. in darkness.

practice.stem:
A student in Peshawar put a piece of Elodea pondweed in a test-tube of water containing sodium hydrogencarbonate. A lamp was placed at different distances. After 5 minutes at each distance, bubbles were counted for one minute, three times.
Distance / cm: 10, 20, 40
Bubbles per minute (trial 1, 2, 3): 10 cm – 47, 50, 47; 20 cm – 21, 23, 22; 40 cm – 8, 6, 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute at each distance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between distance from the lamp and the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: As distance increases, the rate (bubbles per minute) decreases; the decrease is not proportional – it falls steeply at first.
parts.working: B1 greater distance → fewer bubbles / lower rate; B1 data quote or idea that it is not linear (halving distance more than doubles the rate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student allowed the plant to stand for 5 minutes at each new distance before counting.
parts.answer: So the plant could adjust (acclimatise) to the new light intensity and the rate became steady.
parts.working: B1 allows rate to reach a steady state at new light intensity.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to the method of measuring the gas released.
parts.answer: Collect the gas in a gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder and measure its volume, since bubbles vary in size.
parts.working: B1 measure volume (gas syringe / capillary tube) as bubble size varies.

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of tomato plants at 25 °C was measured at two carbon dioxide concentrations.
Light intensity / units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Rate at 0.04 % CO₂: 0, 9, 16, 18, 18
Rate at 0.1 % CO₂: 0, 9, 17, 26, 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term limiting factor.
parts.answer: Something present in the environment in such short supply that it restricts life processes (here, the rate of photosynthesis).
parts.working: B1 factor in shortest supply that restricts / limits the rate of a process.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Between 0 and 4 units of light, name the factor limiting the rate. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the rate increases as light intensity increases, and the rates at the two CO₂ concentrations are (almost) the same, so CO₂ is not limiting.
parts.working: B1 light intensity; B1 rate rises as light rises / rates almost identical at both CO₂ concentrations so CO₂ not limiting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Above 6 units of light, the rate at 0.04 % CO₂ stays at 18 arbitrary units. State the factor limiting the rate at this point and explain the evidence.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration; increasing light no longer raises the rate, but the rate is higher (30) at 0.1 % CO₂.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ concentration; B1 rate higher at 0.1 % CO₂ at the same light intensity / plateau with more light.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate at 8 units of light when CO₂ is raised from 0.04 % to 0.1 %.

practice.stem: A student investigates whether chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis using a potted geranium plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should test a leaf for starch.
parts.answer: Boil the leaf in water (about 1 minute) to kill cells and break membranes; switch off the Bunsen burner and place the leaf in a tube of ethanol in the hot water-bath to remove chlorophyll; dip in water to soften; spread on a white tile and add iodine solution.
parts.working: B1 boil in water; B1 in ethanol, heated in a water-bath (not over a flame) to remove chlorophyll; B1 rinse in (warm) water to soften; B1 add iodine solution; blue-black = starch.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plant had been kept in the dark for 48 hours before the experiment. Explain why.
parts.answer: To destarch the leaves – the starch present is used up (converted to sugar and used in respiration / moved away), so any starch found afterwards was made during the experiment.
parts.working: B1 removes / uses up starch; B1 so starch found must be produced during the investigation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One leaf was variegated (green and white areas). After 6 hours of light, only the green areas turned blue-black. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 chlorophyll needed for photosynthesis / starch formation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the ethanol must not be heated directly over the Bunsen flame.
parts.answer: Ethanol is flammable.
parts.working: B1 flammable.

practice.stem: Leaf discs were cut from a spinach leaf with a cork borer, and the air was removed from them by suction so that they sank in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution. The time for discs to float in light was measured at different temperatures. At 25 °C the mean time for the discs to float was 180 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature of the water. Dependent: time taken for the leaf discs to float (rate of photosynthesis).
parts.working: B1 temperature; B1 time for discs to float / number of discs floating.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of photosynthesis at 25 °C as 1000 ÷ mean time (in s). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.6 (arbitrary units)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the leaf discs float.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis produces oxygen, which collects in the air spaces of the discs, making them less dense than the solution.
parts.working: B1 oxygen produced by photosynthesis; B1 gas fills air spaces, reducing density.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Light intensity (distance from lamp); concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate; number / size of discs; type and age of leaf; volume of solution.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
The volume of oxygen released by a water plant in a pond in Faisalabad was measured on a summer day.
Time: 08:00, 12:00, 16:00
Total volume of oxygen collected / cm³: 4.4, 18.4, 24.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen production in cm³ per hour between 08:00 and 12:00.
parts.answer: 3.5 cm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the rate between 12:00 and 16:00 is lower even though the light intensity at midday is high.
parts.answer: Another factor became limiting, e.g. the high temperature caused stomata to close so less CO₂ entered, or CO₂ concentration was limiting.
parts.working: B1 another limiting factor named (CO₂ / temperature too high); B1 linked explanation, e.g. stomata close to reduce water loss so CO₂ uptake falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A greenhouse grower raises the carbon dioxide concentration from 0.04% to 0.10%. Explain why this increases the yield only when light and temperature are not limiting.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is a raw material. If light and temperature are high enough, carbon dioxide is the limiting factor, so more carbon dioxide means more glucose is made per second. If light or temperature is limiting, the extra carbon dioxide has no effect because another factor sets the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: carbon dioxide is a raw material for the light-independent reactions. 1 mark: when carbon dioxide is limiting, raising it increases the rate. 1 mark: when light or temperature is limiting, extra carbon dioxide does not change the rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other factor, apart from light, temperature and carbon dioxide, that could limit the rate of photosynthesis in the greenhouse.
parts.answer: Water supply (or a shortage of mineral ions such as magnesium)
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct factor, e.g. water supply or magnesium ions for chlorophyll. 1 mark for a clear link to the process, e.g. water is a raw material; magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of an aquatic plant at 15 °C with very low carbon dioxide concentration. Increasing light intensity has no effect on the rate. Which change would increase the rate most?
A increase the light intensity further
B add sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water
C move the lamp further away
D replace the plant with a smaller piece
parts.answer: B add sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water
parts.working: The rate does not respond to light, so light is not limiting; the very low CO₂ is the limiting factor. Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases CO₂ into the water. More light (A) has already been shown to have no effect.

practice.stem: Light intensity from a small lamp is proportional to 1 ÷ (distance)².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative light intensity at 30 cm compared with 10 cm. Give your answer as a fraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 15 cm the plant produced 36 bubbles per minute. Assuming the rate is proportional to light intensity, predict the rate at 30 cm.
parts.answer: 9 bubbles per minute
parts.working: M1 intensity at 30 cm is (15/30)² = 1/4 of that at 15 cm; A1 36 × 1/4 = 9.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student found that the actual rate at 30 cm was 14 bubbles per minute. Suggest one reason why it was higher than predicted.
parts.answer: Light from the room / window also reached the plant; or the rate is not exactly proportional because another factor (e.g. CO₂) limits at higher intensity.
parts.working: B1 background light / other light sources; or rate not proportional at 15 cm because CO₂/temperature limiting.

practice.stem: A farmer near Islamabad grows cucumbers in a glasshouse in winter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the farmer burns paraffin in heaters inside the glasshouse during winter nights and early mornings.
parts.answer: Burning paraffin releases heat, raising the temperature so enzymes of photosynthesis work faster; it also releases carbon dioxide, which increases CO₂ concentration – a limiting factor; so the rate of photosynthesis increases, giving more glucose and higher yield.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: raises temperature; enzymes work faster / more kinetic energy; releases CO₂; CO₂ (or temperature) is limiting; faster photosynthesis → more growth / yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The farmer also switches on lamps in the glasshouse in the evening. Suggest why this may not increase yield on very cold nights if the heaters are switched off.
parts.answer: Temperature would then be the limiting factor, so extra light would not increase the rate; enzymes work slowly at low temperature.
parts.working: B1 temperature limiting; B1 rate cannot increase with more light / low enzyme activity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the farmer should not raise the glasshouse temperature to 45 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes would be denatured / the rate would fall / it would cost more fuel without extra yield.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured (or cost exceeds benefit).

practice.stem: Four boiling tubes contained equal volumes of orange-red hydrogencarbonate indicator. Tubes A, B and D each contained one spinach leaf; tube C had no leaf. Tube B was wrapped in aluminium foil. All tubes were sealed and placed 20 cm from a lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of the indicator expected in tubes A, B and C after 4 hours.
parts.answer: A (light): purple; B (foil-covered, dark): yellow; C (no leaf): orange-red (unchanged).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result in tube B.
parts.answer: In the dark there is no photosynthesis; the leaf respires and releases carbon dioxide, so CO₂ concentration rises and the indicator turns yellow.
parts.working: B1 no photosynthesis (no light); B1 respiration releases CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the purpose of tube C.
parts.answer: It is a control, showing that the colour change is caused by the leaf and not by light or the indicator itself.
parts.working: B1 control – change is due to leaf.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Tube D was covered with thin white tissue paper so that it received dim light. After 4 hours the indicator was still orange-red. Explain why.
parts.answer: In dim light the rates of photosynthesis and respiration are equal (compensation point), so the CO₂ taken in equals the CO₂ released and there is no net change.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis rate = respiration rate; B1 no net change in CO₂ concentration.

practice.stem: The balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the equation to state the ratio of glucose molecules made to oxygen molecules released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A plant released 0.6 mol of oxygen in one day. Use the equation to calculate how many moles of carbon dioxide it absorbed and how many moles of glucose it made.
parts.answer: 0.6 mol CO₂; 0.1 mol glucose
parts.working: B1 0.6 mol CO₂ (1 : 1); B1 0.1 mol glucose (1 : 6).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the plant's dry mass at the end of the day increases by less than the mass of glucose it made.
parts.answer: Some of the glucose is broken down in respiration (to release energy), producing CO₂ and water which are lost; so only the remainder is converted into new biomass.
parts.working: B1 glucose used in respiration; B1 products lost as gases / not stored.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student places a pondweed in a beaker of water under a lamp and counts the oxygen bubbles released per minute. The lamp is then moved closer, doubling the light intensity. Which result is most likely?
A The bubble rate stays exactly the same at every light intensity
B The bubble rate rises until another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes limiting
C The bubble rate falls because strong light damages the pondweed
D The bubble rate rises in direct proportion to light intensity without any limit
parts.answer: B The bubble rate rises until another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes limiting
parts.working: Light is limiting only at low intensities. When light stops being limiting, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature sets the rate. D is wrong because the rate levels off; A is wrong because light does change the rate at low intensity; C is wrong because the plant is not damaged at this light level.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which tissue of a leaf does most photosynthesis take place?
A upper epidermis
B palisade mesophyll
C spongy mesophyll
D xylem
parts.answer: B palisade mesophyll
parts.working: Palisade cells are tightly packed near the upper surface and contain the most chloroplasts. Spongy mesophyll cells have fewer chloroplasts and many air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue or structure described: (i) a waxy, waterproof layer on the upper surface; (ii) pores, mainly on the lower surface, surrounded by two cells that change shape; (iii) vessels that bring water to the leaf.
parts.answer: (i) Cuticle; (ii) stomata (guard cells); (iii) xylem.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the phloem in a leaf vein.
parts.answer: Transports sucrose and amino acids away from the leaf to other parts of the plant.
parts.working: B1 transports sucrose / amino acids (translocation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student draws a transverse section of a leaf from a microscope slide. State two rules the student should follow when making a biological drawing.
parts.answer: Use a sharp pencil with clear, continuous lines; no shading; draw large, filling the space; correct proportions; label lines ruled and not crossing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the tissues the student would see in order, from the upper surface to the lower surface, in a section that passes between veins.
parts.answer: Cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis (with guard cells), cuticle.
parts.working: B1 epidermis then palisade then spongy; B1 lower epidermis with guard cells/stomata at the bottom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the guard cells of a stoma change shape to open the stoma when the leaf has plenty of water.
parts.answer: Water enters the guard cells by osmosis, so they become turgid and swell. Because the inner walls are thicker and less stretchy than the outer walls, the cells bend outwards and the pore between them opens.
parts.working: 1 mark: water enters guard cells by osmosis. 1 mark: guard cells become turgid. 1 mark: the thin outer walls bulge out. 1 mark: the thick inner walls cause the cells to curve apart, opening the pore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student counts 48 stomata in one field of view of the lower epidermis. The field of view has an area of 0.25 mm². Calculate the stomatal density, in stomata per mm².
parts.answer: 192 stomata per mm²
parts.working: 1 mark: 48 ÷ 0.25 seen. 1 mark: 192 stomata per mm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of stomata expected in an area of 2.0 mm² of the same lower epidermis.
parts.answer: 384 stomata
parts.working: 1 mark: 192 × 2.0 seen (method). 1 mark: 384 stomata.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why leaves of plants growing in shade are often larger and thinner than leaves of plants growing in full sun.
parts.answer: A larger surface area captures more of the limited light. A thinner leaf lets light penetrate to the chloroplasts in the lower cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area to capture more light. 1 mark: thinner leaf so that light reaches more cells. 1 mark: shade plants need to maximise light absorption. 1 mark: a thin leaf uses less material and energy to build.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a stoma is.
parts.answer: A pore in the epidermis, mainly on the lower surface, that allows gases to pass in and out.
parts.working: 1 mark: a pore (opening) in the epidermis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the cells that surround a stoma and control its opening.
parts.answer: Guard cells
parts.working: 1 mark: guard cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two gases that pass through the stomata in a leaf.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide and oxygen (water vapour is also accepted)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: carbon dioxide, oxygen, water vapour.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which leaf adaptation increases the rate of diffusion of carbon dioxide to the palisade cells?
A a waxy cuticle
B air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
C xylem vessels in the veins
D a transparent upper epidermis
parts.answer: B air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
parts.working: Air spaces allow CO₂ to diffuse quickly from the stomata to the mesophyll cells. A transparent epidermis lets light through, not CO₂.

practice.stem: Leaves of a banana plant are broad and thin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Large surface area to absorb light; thin, so short diffusion distance for CO₂; transparent epidermis / no chloroplasts lets light reach mesophyll; palisade cells packed near upper surface with many chloroplasts; air spaces in spongy mesophyll for gas diffusion; stomata let CO₂ in and O₂ out; guard cells control stomata; xylem supplies water; phloem removes sucrose.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six feature + function pairs from the list. A feature without its function does not score.

practice.stem:
A student painted clear nail varnish on both surfaces of a hibiscus leaf, peeled it off and counted stomata in four fields of view under a microscope.
Lower surface: 24, 28, 27, 25
Upper surface: 3, 2, 4, 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of stomata per field of view on the lower surface.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The area of the field of view was 0.20 mm². Calculate the mean stomatal density on the lower surface in stomata per mm².
parts.answer: 130 stomata per mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the upper surface has far fewer stomata than the lower surface.
parts.answer: The upper surface is in direct sunlight and is warmer, so more water would be lost by transpiration; fewer stomata on top reduces water loss.
parts.working: B1 upper surface hotter / in sunlight; B1 reduces water loss (transpiration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of (i) the cuticle and (ii) the upper epidermis of a leaf.
parts.answer: (i) Reduces water loss (waterproof, waxy); (ii) protects the leaf and lets light pass through to the mesophyll (transparent).
parts.working: B1 cuticle reduces water loss / evaporation; B1 epidermis transparent – lets light through / protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage for every mesophyll cell to be close to a vein.
parts.answer: Xylem in the vein supplies water (for photosynthesis and support) over a short distance; phloem removes sucrose quickly, so products do not build up.
parts.working: B1 water supplied by xylem; B1 sucrose / products removed by phloem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the veins also help the leaf to stay flat and spread out.
parts.answer: Xylem walls are strengthened with lignin, giving support so the leaf exposes a large surface to light.
parts.working: B1 lignin / xylem support keeps large area facing light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The upper and lower epidermis of a leaf are transparent. State why this is an advantage for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Light can pass through to the palisade mesophyll cells below.
parts.working: 1 mark: light reaches the photosynthetic cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the functions of the xylem and of the phloem in a leaf.
parts.answer: Xylem carries water and mineral ions into the leaf; phloem carries sugars (sucrose) out of the leaf.
parts.working: 1 mark for xylem: carries water and mineral ions up from the roots. 1 mark for phloem: carries sugars made in photosynthesis to other parts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the function of the waxy cuticle on the upper surface.
parts.answer: It is waterproof and reduces water loss by evaporation.
parts.working: 1 mark: a waterproof layer that reduces evaporation from the epidermis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Spongy mesophyll cells have few chloroplasts and many large air spaces between them. Explain how these features help the leaf to photosynthesise.
parts.answer: The air spaces let carbon dioxide diffuse quickly to the cells and oxygen diffuse away. The spongy cells are close to the stomata, so gases travel a short distance. They have few chloroplasts because the palisade layer above absorbs most of the light.
parts.working: 1 mark: air spaces allow rapid diffusion of carbon dioxide and oxygen. 1 mark: cells lie close to the stomata. 1 mark: few chloroplasts because light is mostly absorbed by the palisade layer above. 1 mark: loose packing gives a large surface area for gas exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Most leaves have more stomata on the lower epidermis than on the upper epidermis. Explain how this helps the leaf reduce water loss.
parts.answer: The lower surface is more shaded and sheltered from wind, so the air close to its stomata is more humid and less water vapour diffuses out. The upper surface is in direct sunlight and is more exposed, so it has fewer stomata to limit water loss.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower surface is shaded/sheltered. 1 mark: humid air reduces the concentration gradient for diffusion of water vapour. 1 mark: upper surface is exposed to sun and wind. 1 mark: fewer stomata on the upper surface limit water loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to compare the number of stomata on the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf using clear nail varnish impressions. Describe the method, including how the impressions are made and how the mean number of stomata is found.
parts.answer: Paint a thin layer of clear nail varnish onto a small area of the epidermis and leave it to dry. Peel off the dried film and mount it on a microscope slide. Count the stomata in several fields of view of the same size, then calculate the mean for each surface.
parts.working: 1 mark: thin layer of clear nail varnish painted on and left to dry. 1 mark: peel off and mount on a slide. 1 mark: count stomata in several fields of view of the same area. 1 mark: calculate the mean and compare the two surfaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air to a chloroplast in a palisade cell.
parts.answer: Diffuses through an open stoma (between guard cells) into the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll; dissolves in the moist surface / water film of mesophyll cells; diffuses through the cell wall, membrane and cytoplasm into a palisade cell chloroplast.
parts.working: B1 through stoma; B1 air spaces (spongy mesophyll); B1 dissolves in water on cell surface then diffuses into palisade cell / chloroplast. Process must be diffusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why palisade mesophyll cells are found near the upper surface of the leaf and contain many chloroplasts.
parts.answer: The upper surface receives the most light; many chloroplasts absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 most light near upper surface; B1 more chlorophyll absorbs more light / higher rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the lower epidermis cells (other than guard cells) have no chloroplasts.
parts.answer: Little light reaches the lower surface, so chloroplasts there would be of little use / the epidermis is mainly protective.
parts.working: B1 little light reaches / role is protection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the arrangement of cells in the palisade mesophyll and spongy mesophyll.
parts.answer: Palisade cells are long, column-shaped and tightly packed in rows; spongy cells are irregular / rounded and loosely packed with large air spaces.
parts.working: B1 palisade tightly packed / columnar; B1 spongy loosely packed with air spaces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a leaf from a plant growing in deep shade in a forest is often thinner and larger than a leaf from a plant growing in full sun.
parts.answer: Light is limiting in shade, so a larger surface area absorbs more of the little light available; a thin leaf has fewer layers so light reaches all cells / shorter diffusion path (fewer palisade layers needed).
parts.working: B1 larger area to capture more light; B1 thinner – light penetrates to all mesophyll / fewer palisade layers needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the cells that open and close stomata, and state one advantage to the plant of closing stomata at night.
parts.answer: Guard cells; reduces water loss by transpiration when CO₂ is not needed for photosynthesis (no light).
parts.working: B1 guard cells; B1 reduce water loss (no photosynthesis at night).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of palisade mesophyll cells allows them to absorb the most light?
A They are short and round
B They are packed in tight columns and contain many chloroplasts
C They have thick cellulose walls only
D They contain large vacuoles and no chloroplasts
parts.answer: B They are packed in tight columns and contain many chloroplasts
parts.working: Palisade cells are packed in columns close to the upper surface and contain many chloroplasts, so they catch a lot of light. A is wrong because round cells would leave gaps; C is wrong because the walls do not absorb light; D is wrong because palisade cells are the main photosynthetic cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Leaf X has stomata only on its lower surface. Leaf Y, of the same size and in the same conditions, has stomata on both surfaces. Which statement is most accurate?
A Leaf X loses more water by transpiration than leaf Y
B Leaf X loses less water by transpiration than leaf Y
C Leaf X cannot exchange gases with the air
D Leaf X cannot carry out photosynthesis
parts.answer: B Leaf X loses less water by transpiration than leaf Y
parts.working: Fewer stomata means fewer routes for water vapour to diffuse out, so less transpiration. Leaf X still has stomata for gas exchange, so C and D are wrong, and A is the opposite of the expected result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thick-leaved desert plant has a thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata in pits, and a thick epidermis. Explain how each feature reduces water loss.
parts.answer: The thick cuticle is waterproof, so less water evaporates through the epidermis. Sunken stomata trap humid air in the pit, so the diffusion gradient for water vapour is smaller. A thick epidermis is a further barrier to water vapour diffusing out.
parts.working: 1 mark: thick cuticle is waterproof. 1 mark: sunken stomata trap humid air. 1 mark: this reduces the concentration gradient for water vapour. 1 mark: thick epidermis slows diffusion of water vapour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of these features for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Less carbon dioxide can enter the leaf, so the rate of photosynthesis is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark: sunken stomata and thick layers slow the entry of carbon dioxide. 1 mark: so the rate of photosynthesis is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The leaves of a pot plant turn yellow because the plant cannot make enough chlorophyll. Which mineral ion is the plant most likely to be lacking?
A calcium
B chloride
C magnesium
D sodium
parts.answer: C magnesium
parts.working: Magnesium ions are part of the chlorophyll molecule, so a shortage causes yellowing (chlorosis). Nitrate (not offered) is used for amino acids; the other ions are not used to make chlorophyll.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why plants need (i) nitrate ions and (ii) magnesium ions.
parts.answer: (i) To make amino acids (and so proteins); (ii) to make chlorophyll.
parts.working: B1 nitrate → amino acids/proteins; B1 magnesium → chlorophyll.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the appearance of a plant deficient in nitrate ions.
parts.answer: Stunted growth (small, weak plant); yellowing of (older / lower) leaves.
parts.working: B1 stunted / poor growth; B1 yellow leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why root hair cells have a large surface area, and how this helps the plant take up mineral ions.
parts.answer: Root hairs give a large surface area for the uptake of ions from the soil, so more membrane carrier proteins are in contact with the soil water and more ions are absorbed per unit time.
parts.working: 1 mark: many root hairs give a large surface area. 1 mark: more membrane carrier proteins are in contact with soil water. 1 mark: more ions are absorbed per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the leaf symptoms of magnesium deficiency, and state which leaves are affected first. Explain why.
parts.answer: The leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. The older leaves are affected first because magnesium is mobile in the phloem and moves from old leaves to young leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark: yellowing between the veins. 1 mark: veins stay green. 1 mark: older leaves affected first. 1 mark: magnesium is mobile and is moved from old leaves to new leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 25 kg bag of fertiliser is labelled as 18% nitrogen by mass. Calculate the mass of nitrogen in the bag, in kg.
parts.answer: 4.5 kg
parts.working: 1 mark: 25 × 18/100 seen. 1 mark: 4.5 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of this fertiliser needed to supply 9.0 kg of nitrogen.
parts.answer: 50 kg
parts.working: 1 mark: 9.0 ÷ 0.18 seen. 1 mark: 50 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why manure or compost must be broken down by decomposers before its nitrogen can be absorbed by plant roots.
parts.answer: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down proteins and waste in the manure, releasing ammonium compounds. Nitrifying bacteria then convert these into nitrate, which roots can absorb by active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: decomposers break down proteins and waste. 1 mark: ammonium compounds are released. 1 mark: nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate. 1 mark: roots absorb nitrate ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the element in chlorophyll that is supplied as a mineral ion.
parts.answer: Magnesium
parts.working: 1 mark: magnesium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the element found in nitrate that is needed to make amino acids.
parts.answer: Nitrogen
parts.working: 1 mark: nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a pot plant needs mineral ions from the soil. Name one ion for each reason.
parts.answer: Nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins; magnesium ions to make chlorophyll (phosphate ions for DNA and ATP also accepted).
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason with a correct ion, e.g. nitrate for proteins, magnesium for chlorophyll.

practice.stem:
Maize seedlings were grown for four weeks in water culture solutions. Mean dry mass per seedling:
Complete solution: 2.9 g
No magnesium: 1.6 g
No nitrate: 0.8 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean dry mass of the seedlings grown without nitrate compared with complete solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the seedlings grown without nitrate had the lowest dry mass.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids; amino acids are used to make proteins; proteins are needed for new cells / growth (and enzymes), so growth is reduced.
parts.working: B1 nitrate for amino acids; B1 proteins made from amino acids; B1 proteins needed for growth / new cytoplasm / enzymes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dry mass is a better measure of growth than fresh mass.
parts.answer: Water content of the seedlings varies (with time of day / watering), so fresh mass is not reliable; dry mass measures only the biomass.
parts.working: B1 water content varies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mineral ion is needed to make DNA and ATP, and whose shortage restricts root growth?
A calcium ions
B phosphate ions
C sodium ions
D chloride ions
parts.answer: B phosphate ions
parts.working: Phosphate ions are needed to make DNA, ATP and cell membranes, so a shortage restricts growth, especially of roots. Calcium, sodium and chloride are not used in this way in the plant processes described.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how mineral ions are absorbed into a root hair cell when the ion concentration in the soil water is lower than in the cell.
parts.answer: Ions are moved in by active transport, against the concentration gradient, using carrier proteins in the cell membrane. The energy comes from aerobic respiration in the mitochondria of the root hair cell, which needs oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport moves ions against the concentration gradient. 1 mark: carrier proteins in the membrane. 1 mark: energy from aerobic respiration in mitochondria. 1 mark: oxygen is needed for the aerobic respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A field is waterlogged after heavy rain. Explain why adding nitrate fertiliser to the field may not improve the growth of the crop.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so the roots cannot carry out aerobic respiration. Without enough energy, the roots cannot absorb nitrate by active transport. The nitrate may also be washed away by the water.
parts.working: 1 mark: waterlogged soil has little oxygen. 1 mark: roots cannot respire aerobically. 1 mark: less energy for active transport of nitrate. 1 mark: nitrate may be leached away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student bubbles air through a nutrient solution around the roots of one plant but not another. Explain why the aerated plant grows better.
parts.answer: Air supplies oxygen to the roots, which is used in aerobic respiration. The energy released is used for active transport of mineral ions into the root hair cells, so more ions are absorbed for growth.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen supplied to the roots. 1 mark: oxygen is used in aerobic respiration. 1 mark: energy used for active transport of mineral ions. 1 mark: more mineral ions absorbed, so better growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A poison that stops respiration is added to the water of a plant. Predict and explain the effect on the uptake of mineral ions.
parts.answer: Uptake of mineral ions slows or stops because active transport needs energy from aerobic respiration. Without this energy the root cells cannot move ions against the concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: uptake of mineral ions slows or stops. 1 mark: respiration provides energy. 1 mark: active transport needs energy to move ions against a gradient. 1 mark: ions are not absorbed even though they are present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the leaves of plants grown without magnesium became yellow and the plants grew less.
parts.answer: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; without it less chlorophyll forms (leaves yellow); less light is absorbed so less photosynthesis; less glucose is made for growth / respiration.
parts.working: B1 Mg needed for chlorophyll; B1 less light absorbed / less photosynthesis; B1 less glucose / carbohydrate for growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer in Sahiwal adds nitrogen fertiliser to a field. Explain how this can increase the yield of a wheat crop.
parts.answer: Nitrate is absorbed by root hairs (active transport) and used to make amino acids and proteins, so more new cells and larger plants / more grain protein.
parts.working: B1 nitrate absorbed by roots; B1 for protein synthesis → growth / higher yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Root hair cells take up mineral ions from dilute soil water even when the ion concentration inside the root is higher. Which process explains this, and what does it need?
A diffusion, no energy needed
B osmosis, energy from photosynthesis
C active transport, energy from respiration
D diffusion, energy from respiration
parts.answer: C active transport, energy from respiration
parts.working: Movement against a concentration gradient needs active transport, which uses energy released by aerobic respiration in the root cells. Diffusion and osmosis only move substances down a concentration gradient, so A, B and D are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer grows maize on sandy soil that has little nitrate. Describe two visible symptoms the maize would show.
parts.answer: Stunted (poor) growth; pale or yellow leaves; (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: stunted growth, pale or yellow leaves, small leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why nitrate is needed for growth.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids, which are used to make proteins for new cells and cytoplasm.
parts.working: 1 mark: nitrate is used to make amino acids. 1 mark: amino acids are used to make proteins for growth (nucleic acids also contain nitrogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student grows cress seedlings in three nutrient solutions: complete, without nitrate, and without magnesium. Name the independent variable.
parts.answer: The type of nutrient solution (which mineral ion is missing).
parts.working: 1 mark: the mineral ions present in the solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two variables that should be kept the same in all three solutions.
parts.answer: Light intensity, temperature, volume of solution, number of seedlings, species of seed, time of growth (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two controlled variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the student could make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat the experiment and calculate a mean dry mass for each solution.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeat and calculate means.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen in 1.0 dm³ of a solution containing 2.5 g dm⁻³ of potassium nitrate, KNO₃. Give your answer in g to 3 significant figures. (Ar: K = 39, N = 14, O = 16)
parts.working: 1 mark: Mr of KNO₃ = 39 + 14 + 48 = 101. 1 mark: nitrogen fraction = 14/101. 1 mark: 2.5 × 14/101 = 0.347 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen in 400 cm³ of the same solution. Give your answer in g to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrate fertiliser washes from a field into a pond. Describe and explain how this can lead to a fall in the number of fish in the pond.
parts.answer: Nitrate causes rapid growth of algae (an algal bloom) that blocks light from reaching submerged plants, which die. Decomposers break down the dead material and use up dissolved oxygen, so the fish die from lack of oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: nitrate causes an algal bloom. 1 mark: algae block light, so submerged plants die. 1 mark: decomposers break down dead plants. 1 mark: decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen. 1 mark: fish die from lack of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of discontinuous variation in humans?
A height
B body mass
C ABO blood group
D hand span
parts.answer: C ABO blood group
parts.working: ABO blood group has a few distinct categories with no intermediates and is controlled by genes only. Height, mass and hand span show a continuous range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between continuous and discontinuous variation.
parts.answer: continuous shows a range of values with intermediates, discontinuous has a few distinct categories; continuous is caused by genes and environment, discontinuous mostly by genes only
parts.working: B1 range vs distinct groups; B1 genes and environment vs genes alone (or many genes vs one/few genes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of variation in plants.
parts.answer: continuous: leaf length / plant height / mass of seeds; discontinuous: flower colour in some species / seed shape (round or wrinkled in peas)
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of continuous variation?
A the ABO blood group in humans
B the height of adults in a population
C the presence or absence of earlobes
D the colour of flowers in a pea plant
parts.answer: B the height of adults in a population
parts.working: Height varies across a range of values with no sharp categories, so it is continuous. Blood group, earlobe presence and flower colour are discrete (distinct categories).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two causes of variation between individuals of the same species.
parts.answer: Genetic differences (different alleles); environmental factors such as diet or climate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid causes.

practice.stem: A student counted the petals on 30 flowers of one plant species and measured the leaf length of the same plants. Every flower had either 5 or 6 petals. Leaf lengths ranged from 4 cm to 12 cm, with many different values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which trait is discontinuous and which is continuous.
parts.answer: Petal number is discontinuous; leaf length is continuous.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct classification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how you decided which trait is discontinuous.
