parts.text: Earthworms have no lungs. Oxygen diffuses through their skin into blood capillaries just below the surface. Suggest two features of an earthworm that allow enough oxygen to enter by diffusion.
parts.answer: Any two: long, thin body gives a large surface area to volume ratio; moist skin so oxygen dissolves; thin skin / capillaries close to surface give a short diffusion distance; blood circulation carries oxygen away, keeping a steep gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features linked to diffusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why earthworms die quickly if their skin dries out in hot sunshine.
parts.answer: Oxygen must dissolve in a film of water before it can diffuse through the skin; dry skin stops gas exchange, so not enough oxygen reaches cells for respiration.
parts.working: B1 gases must dissolve in moisture to diffuse; B1 less oxygen for respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After heavy rain, earthworms often come up to the surface of waterlogged soil. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Water fills the air spaces in the soil; water holds much less oxygen than air and oxygen diffuses very slowly through water, so the concentration gradient into the worm is reduced; at the surface they can get more oxygen.
parts.working: B1 air spaces filled with water / less oxygen in soil; B1 less oxygen diffuses into skin, so move to where there is more oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of diffusion into cubes of agar. The agar contains an alkali and a pink indicator that turns colourless when acid reaches it. Include what you would change and measure, the variables you would control, how you would make the results reliable and a safety precaution.
parts.answer: Cut cubes all exactly 1 cm side from the same block of pink agar. Prepare acid at e.g. 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mol/dm³ by diluting stock acid. Place one cube in the same volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of each concentration at the same temperature, and start a stopwatch. Record the time for the cube to become completely colourless. Repeat three times at each concentration and calculate means; calculate rate as 1 ÷ time. Wear eye protection and handle acid carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV acid concentration with ≥5 values; DV time for cube to become colourless (or depth decolourised in fixed time); same size cubes / cut accurately; same volume of acid; same temperature; same agar batch / indicator; cubes fully covered / not stirred or stirred equally; repeats and mean; rate = 1/time; safety: goggles / avoid skin contact with acid.

practice.stem: Two cubes of gelatine, of side 2 cm and 4 cm, were left in a coloured dye. After 10 minutes the dye had moved 0.3 cm into each cube from every face, leaving an uncoloured cube in the centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each cube, calculate the percentage of its volume that is still uncoloured. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2 cm cube: 34.3 %; 4 cm cube: 61.4 %
parts.working: M1 uncoloured inner cube side = side − 2 × 0.3 (1.4 cm and 3.4 cm); M1 volume = side³ (2.744 cm³ and 39.304 cm³); A1 2.744 ÷ 8 × 100 = 34.3 %; A1 39.304 ÷ 64 × 100 = 61.4 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results suggest about how far cells in a large animal could be from a supply of oxygen.
parts.answer: Diffusion only reaches a short distance in a given time, so in a large block most of the volume is not reached; cells must be close to a surface or a blood capillary (very short diffusion distance) to receive enough oxygen.
parts.working: B1 diffusion is only effective over short distances / large volume not reached; B1 cells must be near a capillary / exchange surface (need transport system).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes active transport?
A movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration using energy from respiration
B movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration using energy from respiration
C movement of water from a lower to a higher concentration of solute without using energy
D movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration without using energy
parts.answer: B movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration using energy from respiration
parts.working: Active transport moves particles against a concentration gradient (lower → higher) through a membrane, using energy released by respiration. A is down the gradient; D omits the energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process by which root hair cells take up mineral ions when the concentration in the soil is lower than in the cell.
parts.answer: Active transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this process needs energy, and where the energy comes from.
parts.answer: The ions are moved against their concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration); the energy is released by respiration in the cell (in mitochondria).
parts.working: 1 mark: against concentration gradient; 1 mark: energy from respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of protein carriers in the cell membrane in this process.
parts.answer: Carrier proteins bind the specific ions and change shape, using energy, to move them across the membrane into the cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: carrier protein binds/picks up the ion (specific); 1 mark: changes shape to move ion across membrane using energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why root hair cells contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: To carry out a lot of aerobic respiration to release the energy needed for active transport of ions.

practice.stem: A brown seaweed growing off the coast of Balochistan contains iodide ions at a much higher concentration in its cells than in the seawater around it (0.4 µmol/dm³). Over 48 hours, the iodide concentration in its cells rose from 9600 µmol/dm³ to 12 000 µmol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in iodide concentration in the seaweed cells, in µmol/dm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 50 µmol/dm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process the seaweed uses to absorb iodide ions, and state two things the process needs.
parts.answer: Active transport; it needs energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the cell membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport; 1 mark: energy (from respiration); 1 mark: (protein) carriers in the membrane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seaweed absorbs iodide ions more slowly when the seawater is very cold.
parts.answer: Respiration is slower at low temperature because enzymes work more slowly, so less energy is available for active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: slower respiration / enzyme activity; 1 mark: less energy for active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Cells that carry out a lot of active transport contain large numbers of one type of organelle. Which organelle?
A mitochondria
B chloroplasts
C vacuoles
D cell walls
parts.answer: A mitochondria
parts.working: Active transport needs energy released by respiration, which happens in mitochondria. Chloroplasts (B) carry out photosynthesis and are absent from root hair cells, which do a lot of active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define active transport.
parts.answer: The movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration (against a concentration gradient), using energy from respiration.
parts.working: B1 lower to higher concentration / against gradient; B1 using energy from respiration (through the membrane).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between active transport and diffusion.
parts.answer: Active transport needs energy from respiration but diffusion does not; active transport moves particles against a concentration gradient but diffusion moves them down a gradient; active transport uses protein carriers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: energy needed / not needed; against / down the gradient; carrier proteins needed / not needed; can be stopped by respiratory poison.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the process (diffusion, osmosis or active transport) for each movement:
(i) oxygen from alveolar air into a red blood cell
(ii) water from the soil into a root hair cell
(iii) magnesium ions from very dilute soil water into a root hair cell
(iv) glucose from the filtrate in a kidney tubule back into the blood when the filtrate glucose concentration is lower than in the blood
parts.answer: (i) diffusion (ii) osmosis (iii) active transport (iv) active transport
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.

Root hair cells absorb mineral ions such as nitrate from the soil. The concentration of nitrate is often ______ in the soil water than in the root hair cell, so the ions must move ______ their concentration gradient. This process is called ______. It uses ______ released by respiration and needs ______ proteins in the cell membrane.
parts.answer: lower; against; active transport; energy; carrier
parts.working: 1 mark for each gap.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process depends on active transport?
A uptake of nitrate ions from soil into root hair cells
B loss of water vapour through stomata
C movement of oxygen from alveoli into the blood
D entry of water into root hair cells
parts.answer: A uptake of nitrate ions from soil into root hair cells
parts.working: Nitrate ions are usually more concentrated inside root hair cells than in soil water, so they are taken up against the gradient by active transport using carrier proteins. Oxygen moves by diffusion (C) and water enters by osmosis (D).

practice.stem:
The concentrations of three ions in the cell sap of a freshwater alga and in the pond water around it were measured (in mmol/dm³).
Ion | pond water | cell sap
potassium | 0.6 | 54.0
chloride | 1.2 | 90.0
sodium | 2.4 | 30.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated potassium ions are in the cell sap than in the pond water.
parts.answer: 90 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the data show that the alga takes up potassium and chloride ions by active transport.
parts.answer: The ions are far more concentrated inside the cells than in the pond water, so they must have moved in against their concentration gradient, which requires active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentration inside much higher than outside (quote figures); 1 mark: movement against concentration gradient = active transport.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When a poison that stops respiration was added to the pond water, the concentration of potassium ions in the cells slowly fell. Explain this observation.
parts.answer: Without respiration no energy is released for active transport, so uptake stops; potassium ions then leak out / diffuse out down their concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: no energy for active transport; 1 mark: ions diffuse out down the gradient.

practice.stem:
Equal masses of carrot discs were kept in an aerated solution of potassium ions for 4 hours at different temperatures. The ions absorbed were measured in arbitrary units.
Temperature (°C): 5, 15, 25, 35, 45
Ions absorbed (units): 0.8, 2.0, 4.2, 6.0, 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: The carrot discs at 35 °C absorbed 6.0 units of ions in 4 hours. Calculate the mean rate of uptake in units per hour.
parts.answer: 1.5 units per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the results between 5 °C and 35 °C.
parts.answer: Uptake increases as temperature rises (0.8 to 6.0 units); higher temperature increases the rate of respiration (enzyme activity), so more energy is released for active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: description with data; 1 mark: more respiration / enzymes more active; 1 mark: more energy for active transport.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why uptake was much lower at 45 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes for respiration and/or the carrier proteins were denatured at high temperature, so less energy was released / carriers could not transport ions.
parts.working: 1 mark: denaturing of enzymes / carrier proteins; 1 mark: less respiration / less active transport.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables, other than time, that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: size/mass/surface area of discs; concentration of ion solution; volume of solution; oxygen supply (aeration); age/type of carrot.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a meal, glucose is absorbed into the epithelial cells of the villi even when the glucose concentration in these cells is higher than in the lumen of the small intestine. Name the process.
parts.answer: Active transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other place in the human body where glucose is moved by this process.
parts.answer: The (proximal convoluted) tubules of the kidney nephrons (reabsorption of glucose).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the epithelial cells of the villi have large numbers of mitochondria and microvilli.
parts.answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing the energy needed for active transport; microvilli increase the surface area of the membrane, so more carrier proteins / faster absorption.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria → respiration → energy; 1 mark: energy for active transport; 1 mark: microvilli give larger surface area for absorption.

practice.stem:
A farmer in Punjab measured the rate of nitrate uptake by cotton roots in two fields.
Well-drained soil: 8.4 units per hour
Waterlogged soil after heavy rain: 2.1 units per hour

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the rate of nitrate uptake in the waterlogged soil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why waterlogging reduces the uptake of nitrate ions.
parts.answer: Water fills the air spaces in the soil, so there is little oxygen for the root cells. Less aerobic respiration takes place, so less energy is released for active transport of nitrate ions against their concentration gradient.
parts.working: B1 air spaces filled with water / less oxygen reaches roots; B1 less (aerobic) respiration in root cells; B1 less energy for active transport (against gradient).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the leaves of the cotton plants in the waterlogged field turned yellow after two weeks.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and proteins (and chlorophyll); with less nitrate, less chlorophyll / protein is made, so leaves turn yellow.
parts.working: B1 nitrate needed for amino acids / proteins; B1 less chlorophyll made / poor growth so leaves yellow.

practice.stem:
Barley roots were placed in an aerated solution containing potassium ions. The total amount of potassium taken up was measured every 15 minutes. At 30 minutes a chemical that stops respiration (a respiratory inhibitor) was added.
Time / minutes: 0, 15, 30, 45, 60
Total potassium taken up / arbitrary units: 0, 12, 24, 25, 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of ion uptake in the first 30 minutes, in arbitrary units per minute.
parts.answer: 0.8 units per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of adding the inhibitor.
parts.answer: Before the inhibitor, uptake increased steadily by 12 units every 15 minutes; after the inhibitor was added at 30 minutes, uptake almost stopped (only 1 more unit by 45 minutes and none after that).
parts.working: B1 steady increase before 30 min; B1 uptake almost stops / levels off at 25 units after inhibitor, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of the inhibitor.
parts.answer: The inhibitor stops respiration, so no energy is released; the ions were being taken up by active transport, which needs energy, so uptake stops.
parts.working: B1 no respiration / no energy released; B1 active transport needs energy so stops.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant in this experiment.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature; concentration of potassium ions in the solution; mass/surface area of roots; volume of solution; aeration; type/age of plant.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The water in a lake has a much lower concentration of sodium and chloride ions than the blood of the fish living there. Explain why the fish must use active transport to take up these ions from the water through its gills.
parts.answer: The ions are more concentrated in the fish's blood than in the water, so they would not enter by diffusion; they must be moved against their concentration gradient, which needs active transport using energy.
parts.working: B1 concentration higher inside / in blood than in the water; B1 movement against the gradient needs energy / active transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the fish keep losing ions to the water, so that they must take them up continuously.
parts.answer: Ions diffuse out of the blood (e.g. across the gills) into the water, down their concentration gradient, and some are lost in urine.
parts.working: B1 diffusion out down gradient / lost in urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A factory releases a chemical into the lake that reduces respiration in gill cells. Suggest and explain the effect on the fish.
parts.answer: Less energy is released in the gill cells, so less active transport of ions; the ion concentration in the blood falls and the fish may become ill or die.
parts.working: B1 less energy for active transport / fewer ions absorbed; B1 blood ion concentration falls, so harmful to the fish.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Rice seedlings were grown in two trays of the same nutrient solution. Air was bubbled through tray P; tray Q was left still and became low in oxygen. After a week the roots in tray Q contained far fewer potassium ions. What is the best explanation?
A Less oxygen reduced aerobic respiration in the root cells, so less energy was available for active transport of potassium ions.
B Less oxygen reduced the diffusion of potassium ions because oxygen carries the ions into the cells.
C Without bubbling, the potassium ions could not move by osmosis into the roots.
D Low oxygen made the solution more concentrated, so potassium ions moved out of the roots by diffusion.
parts.answer: A Less oxygen reduced aerobic respiration in the root cells, so less energy was available for active transport of potassium ions.
parts.working: Ion uptake by roots is mainly active transport, which needs energy from aerobic respiration; low oxygen limits respiration. B is wrong because oxygen does not carry ions, C because osmosis is the movement of water, not ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the comparison of three transport processes. For each process state: (i) whether it needs energy from respiration, (ii) the direction of movement in relation to the concentration gradient, (iii) whether it needs a membrane.
Processes: diffusion, osmosis, active transport.
parts.answer: Diffusion: no energy from respiration (uses kinetic energy of particles); down the concentration gradient; no membrane needed. Osmosis: no energy from respiration; water moves from higher to lower water potential (down its gradient); needs a partially permeable membrane. Active transport: needs energy from respiration; against the concentration gradient (lower to higher); needs a membrane with carrier proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct pair of entries, six marks in total: diffusion energy + direction; diffusion membrane; osmosis energy + direction; osmosis partially permeable membrane; active transport energy; active transport against gradient + carrier proteins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A root cell takes up sodium ions by active transport. Suggest why the rate of uptake stops increasing at high external sodium ion concentrations, even with plenty of oxygen.
parts.answer: All the carrier proteins are in use (saturated), so the number of carriers limits the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: carrier proteins all occupied / limited number of carriers; 1 mark: carriers become the limiting factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The concentrations of four ions inside a root cell and in the soil water around it were measured. All four ions are still entering the cell. Which ion must be entering by active transport?
(inside the cell / soil water, in mmol/dm³) W: 5 / 10; X: 30 / 30; Y: 2 / 8; Z: 40 / 4
A ion W
B ion X
C ion Y
D ion Z
parts.answer: D ion Z
parts.working: Z is more concentrated inside (40) than outside (4), so it moves against its concentration gradient, which needs active transport. W and Y could enter by diffusion because they are more concentrated in the soil; X has no gradient.

practice.stem: In a healthy person, all the glucose filtered out of the blood in the kidney is reabsorbed into the blood from the kidney tubules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how glucose in the filtrate is moved back into the blood when its concentration in the tubule is lower than in the blood.
parts.answer: By active transport: carrier proteins in the membranes of the tubule cells move glucose against its concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.
parts.working: B1 active transport; B1 against concentration gradient using energy (from respiration) / carrier proteins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a person with untreated diabetes the blood glucose concentration is very high, and glucose appears in the urine. Suggest why, using ideas about the carrier proteins.
parts.answer: So much glucose is filtered that the carrier proteins are all working at their maximum rate (there are not enough carriers); the extra glucose cannot be reabsorbed and stays in the filtrate, so it passes into the urine.
parts.working: B1 more glucose filtered into tubule; B1 carrier proteins all in use / limited number / maximum rate reached; B1 excess glucose not reabsorbed so remains in urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cells lining this part of the tubule contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: To release the large amount of energy by aerobic respiration needed for active transport.
parts.working: B1 energy for active transport from respiration.

practice.stem:
The concentration of amino acids was measured in the fluid inside the small intestine (the lumen) and inside the epithelial cells lining the villi.
Lumen: 2.0 mmol/dm³
Epithelial cell: 12.0 mmol/dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated amino acids are inside the epithelial cells than in the lumen.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these data show that amino acids are absorbed into the cells by active transport.
parts.answer: Amino acids move from the lumen (lower concentration) into the cell (higher concentration), so they move against the concentration gradient; this needs energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the cell membrane, so it is active transport.
parts.working: B1 movement from lower to higher concentration (against the gradient); B1 needs energy from respiration and carrier proteins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the rate of absorption of amino acids if the epithelial cells are given a respiratory inhibitor. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The rate falls (almost to zero). The inhibitor stops aerobic respiration, so no energy is released for the carrier proteins to move amino acids against the gradient.
parts.working: B1 rate falls / stops; B1 no respiration, so no energy for active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether the uptake of potassium ions by carrot tissue depends on the supply of oxygen. Carrot discs can be kept in potassium chloride solution, and the concentration of potassium left in the solution can be measured with a conductivity meter (a lower reading means fewer ions left in the solution). In your plan, include what you would change, what you would measure, the variables you would keep the same, and how you would make the results reliable.
parts.answer: Use equal masses of carrot discs (same size, same carrot, rinsed) in equal volumes of the same concentration of potassium chloride. Set up flasks in which oxygen supply differs: e.g. air bubbled through with an aquarium pump, no bubbling, and nitrogen (or boiled, cooled solution with an oil layer) to give little oxygen. Keep all flasks in a water bath at e.g. 25 °C for the same time (e.g. 4 hours). Measure the conductivity at the start and the end; calculate the decrease. Include a control flask with no carrot discs. Repeat three times for each condition and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV = oxygen supply with at least 2–3 levels described; DV = change in conductivity / potassium concentration; same mass / surface area of carrot discs; same volume and concentration of KCl; same temperature (water bath) / same time; rinse discs first; control with no tissue or with boiled discs; repeat ≥3 times and calculate mean; prediction: more uptake with more oxygen because active transport needs energy from aerobic respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to test four separate food samples for (i) starch, (ii) reducing sugar, (iii) protein and (iv) fat. For each nutrient, name the reagent used and state the colour seen when the nutrient is present.
parts.answer: Starch: iodine solution → blue-black. Reducing sugar: Benedict's solution (heated) → green / yellow / orange / brick-red. Protein: biuret solution → purple (violet). Fat: ethanol (then water) → milky white emulsion.
parts.working: 1 mark per nutrient for the correct reagent AND the correct positive colour (4 × B1). Accept 'cloudy white' for the emulsion test; do not accept 'pink' for biuret.

practice.stem: A student in Multan squeezes a ripe mango to obtain some juice. She wants to find out whether the juice contains reducing sugar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should carry out the Benedict's test on a sample of the juice.
parts.answer: Put about 2 cm³ of juice in a test-tube, add an equal volume of Benedict's solution, heat in a hot water-bath (about 80 °C) for a few minutes and record the colour.
parts.working: B1 add Benedict's solution to the juice; B1 heat in a (hot / boiling) water-bath; B1 heat for a stated time (e.g. 2–5 minutes) / observe colour change. Do not credit 'heat over a Bunsen flame' alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The juice turned from blue to brick-red. State what this shows.
parts.answer: The juice contains a reducing sugar (a large amount).
parts.working: B1 reducing sugar present; accept 'high concentration of reducing sugar'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution the student should take during this test.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection (goggles) / point the test-tube away from people / use a test-tube holder.
parts.working: B1 any one sensible precaution linked to heating.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A food sample is heated with Benedict's solution. Which final colour shows that the sample contains the most reducing sugar?
A blue
B green
C yellow
D brick-red
parts.answer: D brick-red
parts.working: Brick-red shows the highest concentration of reducing sugar; blue means none. Green and yellow show smaller amounts.

practice.stem: A student places a few drops of iodine solution on each of two samples on a white tile: the cloudy water left after boiling rice, and a solution of table sugar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour the student would see if starch is present.
parts.answer: Blue-black.
parts.working: B1 blue-black; accept 'black' or 'dark blue'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student adds iodine solution to the sugar solution. State the colour seen and what this shows.
parts.answer: Stays orange-brown (yellow-brown); starch is absent.
parts.working: B1 orange / brown / yellow-brown colour; B1 no starch.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student uses a separate clean dropper for each sample.
parts.answer: To avoid contaminating one sample with another (which could give a false result).
parts.working: B1 idea of contamination / cross-contamination.

practice.stem: A breakfast in Lahore consists of a paratha fried in ghee, a boiled egg and a glass of lassi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the emulsion test could be used to show that the paratha contains fat.
parts.answer: Crush / cut the paratha and shake it with ethanol; pour the ethanol (liquid) into a tube of water; a milky white emulsion shows fat.
parts.working: B1 shake (crushed) food with ethanol; B1 add the ethanol to water (or add water); B1 cloudy / milky white = fat present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the reagent used to show that the egg contains protein and state the positive result.
parts.answer: Biuret solution; the colour changes from blue to purple.
parts.working: B1 biuret; B1 purple / violet / lilac.

practice.stem: A student mixes some grated cheese with water to make a cheese solution for a protein test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the biuret test is carried out on the cheese solution.
parts.answer: Add (a few drops of) dilute sodium hydroxide and then (dilute) copper(II) sulfate solution — or add biuret solution — and shake; no heating.
parts.working: B1 add biuret reagent / sodium hydroxide + copper sulfate; B1 shake / mix and observe (no heating needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student also sets up a tube containing distilled water instead of cheese solution, and adds the same reagents. Explain why.
parts.answer: It is a control; it shows the colour of a negative result (blue), so any purple in the test tube must be due to protein in the cheese.
parts.working: B1 control / comparison; B1 shows the colour without protein / shows the reagent alone does not turn purple.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which food test and positive result are correctly matched?
A iodine solution: orange-brown
B biuret reagent: lilac (purple)
C Benedict's solution (heated): blue
D ethanol emulsion test: clear solution
parts.answer: B biuret reagent: lilac (purple)
parts.working: Protein with biuret gives a lilac or purple colour (positive). Iodine stays orange-brown when starch is absent, so option A describes a negative result. Benedict's stays blue when no reducing sugar is present, so C is negative. The emulsion test is positive when a milky white emulsion forms, so D is wrong.

practice.stem:
A student heats 2 cm³ of each of five glucose solutions with 2 cm³ of Benedict's solution for 5 minutes in a boiling water-bath. She does the same with 2 cm³ of guava juice.
Glucose concentration / % : colour after 5 minutes
0 : blue
0.5 : green
1.0 : yellow
2.0 : orange
4.0 : brick-red
guava juice : yellow-orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table, estimate the concentration of glucose in the juice.
parts.answer: Between 1 % and 2 % (more than 1 %, less than 2 %).
parts.working: B1 range 1–2 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two variables that must be kept the same for every tube.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume of solution / volume of Benedict's solution / temperature of water-bath / heating time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two controlled variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change to the method that would give a more precise estimate.
parts.answer: Make more glucose standards at smaller intervals between 1 % and 2 % (e.g. 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8 %) / use a colorimeter instead of judging colour by eye.
parts.working: B1 any one valid improvement.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the student kept all the tubes in the same water-bath and recorded the colour after the same time.
parts.answer: Colour depends on temperature and time of heating; keeping them the same makes it a fair comparison so colour depends only on glucose concentration.
parts.working: B1 time / temperature affect the colour reached; B1 fair test / only glucose concentration varies.

practice.stem: A student wants to show that roasted groundnuts (peanuts) contain fat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the test-tube used for the emulsion test must be dry when the crushed nuts are first shaken with ethanol.
parts.answer: Fat does not dissolve in water; any water present would form the emulsion too early / stop the fat dissolving in the ethanol, so the result would be unclear.
parts.working: B1 fat dissolves in ethanol (not in water); B1 water would interfere / give a false or unclear result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a milky white colour appears when the ethanol is poured into water.
parts.answer: The fat that was dissolved in ethanol comes out of solution because fat is insoluble in water; tiny droplets of fat are suspended (an emulsion), which scatter light and look cloudy.
parts.working: B1 fat insoluble in water / comes out of solution; B1 forms tiny droplets / emulsion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the ethanol should not be heated with a Bunsen burner.
parts.answer: Ethanol is flammable.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A food is tested. Results: iodine solution stays orange-brown; Benedict's solution stays blue after heating; biuret solution turns purple; the ethanol emulsion test gives a milky white layer. Which nutrients does the food contain?
A starch and protein
B protein and fat
C reducing sugar and fat
D starch only
parts.answer: B protein and fat
parts.working: Purple biuret = protein; milky emulsion = fat. Iodine orange-brown means no starch (so A and D are wrong) and Benedict's blue means no reducing sugar (so C is wrong).

practice.stem: Two shops in Peshawar sell honey. A student wants to compare the amount of reducing sugar in each honey after diluting each with water in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Benedict's test is described as semi-quantitative. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: It gives an approximate idea of how much reducing sugar is present (by the colour reached), but not an exact concentration.
parts.working: B1 shows relative amount / range; B1 not an exact value (colours judged by eye).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the results of Benedict's tests on two honey samples could be made more quantitative.
parts.answer: Any two of: use a colorimeter to measure the colour; filter, dry and weigh the red precipitate; time how long each sample takes to change colour; compare with a range of glucose standards of known concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student compares the amount of reducing sugar in apple, orange and pomegranate juice using the Benedict's test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: type of fruit juice. Dependent: colour of the Benedict's solution after heating (amount of reducing sugar).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of juice; volume of Benedict's solution; temperature of water-bath; time of heating; dilution of juice; size of test-tube.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why each juice should be tested three times.
parts.answer: To check the results are repeatable / to identify anomalous results.

practice.stem: A student adds orange juice drop by drop from a dropping pipette to 1 cm³ of blue DCPIP solution, shaking after each drop, and counts the drops needed to decolourise it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to decide exactly when the DCPIP has been decolourised by orange juice.
parts.answer: The juice is coloured itself (orange), so the end-point colour is hard to judge / the colour fades gradually.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two other sources of error in the method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: e.g. size of drops varies → use a burette or graduated syringe; tube not shaken evenly → shake after every drop the same way; judging the colour → compare against a white background / a reference tube of decolourised DCPIP; juice left standing loses vitamin C → test immediately after squeezing.
parts.working: For each of two errors: B1 error, B1 matching improvement. Generic 'repeat it' alone scores 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A food sample is heated with Benedict's solution in a boiling water-bath for 5 minutes. The solution stays blue. Which conclusion is correct?
A the sample contains no reducing sugar
B the sample contains no sugar of any kind
C the sample contains only sucrose
D the sample contains no protein
parts.answer: A the sample contains no reducing sugar
parts.working: A blue result after heating means no reducing sugar was detected, so A is correct. Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so a blue result does not prove there is no sugar at all (B) and cannot show that only sucrose is present (C). Benedict's test says nothing about protein (D).

practice.stem:
DCPIP is a blue solution that is decolourised by vitamin C. A student finds the volume of each liquid that must be added, drop by drop, to decolourise 1.0 cm³ of DCPIP.
Vitamin C solution, 1.0 mg/cm³ : 2.5 cm³
Fresh lemon juice : 4.0 cm³
Lemon juice boiled for 10 minutes : 6.4 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of vitamin C needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of the DCPIP solution.
parts.answer: 2.5 mg
parts.working: 1.0 mg/cm³ × 2.5 cm³ = 2.5 mg (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of vitamin C, in mg/cm³, in (i) the fresh lemon juice and (ii) the boiled lemon juice. Give (ii) to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: (i) 0.625 mg/cm³; (ii) 0.39 mg/cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in vitamin C concentration caused by boiling.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why a larger volume of boiled juice was needed.
parts.answer: Boiling destroys (breaks down) some of the vitamin C, so the juice has less vitamin C per cm³.

practice.stem: A length of Visking tubing (a partially permeable membrane) is filled with a mixture of starch suspension and glucose solution. The tubing is rinsed and placed in a tube of distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the results of an iodine test and a Benedict's test on the water outside the tubing after 30 minutes. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Iodine: stays orange-brown — no starch, because starch molecules are too large to pass through the tubing. Benedict's: green/yellow/orange/red — reducing sugar present, because glucose molecules are small enough to diffuse out through the tubing.
parts.working: B1 iodine negative; B1 starch molecules too large; B1 Benedict's positive; B1 glucose small, diffuses through (partially permeable) tubing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what this model shows about digestion in the small intestine.
parts.answer: Large insoluble molecules like starch must be broken down into small soluble molecules (e.g. glucose) before they can be absorbed through the gut wall into the blood.
parts.working: B1 large molecules cannot be absorbed; B1 must be digested into small soluble molecules first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the vitamin C content of freshly squeezed orange juice with orange juice that has been kept in an open glass at room temperature for 24 hours. Include the apparatus, method, variables to control, how results are recorded and how a conclusion is reached.
parts.answer: DCPIP titration: same volume of DCPIP; add each juice drop by drop from a burette/syringe until decolourised; record volume; repeat three times; less volume = more vitamin C.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: use DCPIP (blue, decolourised by vitamin C); fixed volume of DCPIP (e.g. 1 cm³) in a test-tube; add juice from burette / graduated pipette / syringe drop by drop, shaking; record volume of juice when blue colour disappears; same oranges / same juice divided into two portions; same temperature / same concentration of DCPIP; repeat at least three times and calculate a mean; a smaller volume of juice needed means more vitamin C; table with headings 'volume of juice / cm³' for each juice; safety: eye protection.

practice.stem:
A student times how long it takes for Benedict's solution to show the first colour change (from blue to green) when heated with glucose solutions in a water-bath at 90 °C.
Glucose concentration / % : time / s
0.2 : 150
0.4 : 95
0.6 : 70
0.8 : 52
1.0 : 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in the results.
parts.answer: As glucose concentration increases, the time for the first colour change decreases (falling more slowly at higher concentrations).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of sugar-cane juice, diluted in the same way, took 80 s to show the first colour change. Assuming the change is linear between the two nearest readings, estimate the glucose concentration of the diluted juice. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why judging the 'first colour change' is a source of error and suggest how to reduce it.
parts.answer: The change is gradual and judged by eye, so it is subjective; compare against a reference tube / white background or use a colorimeter.
parts.working: B1 subjective / gradual; B1 improvement.

practice.stem:
Maize grains are soaked and left to germinate. A student crushes samples on day 0 and day 4 and tests them.
Day 0: iodine test blue-black; Benedict's test green.
Day 4: iodine test pale blue-black; Benedict's test brick-red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the results between day 0 and day 4.
parts.answer: Starch content decreases (blue-black becomes paler / orange-brown); reducing sugar increases (Benedict's goes from blue/green to orange/brick-red).
parts.working: B1 starch decreases; B1 reducing sugar increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain these changes.
parts.answer: Amylase (enzyme) becomes active in the germinating seed; it breaks down stored starch into maltose / reducing sugars; the sugars are soluble and are used in respiration to release energy for growth of the embryo.
parts.working: B1 enzyme / amylase; B1 starch → reducing sugar (maltose); B1 sugar used for respiration / energy / growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The same volume of DCPIP solution is decolourised by 2 cm³ of juice X but needs 8 cm³ of juice Y. Which statement is correct?
A Juice Y contains four times the concentration of vitamin C of juice X.
B Juice X contains four times the concentration of vitamin C of juice Y.
C Juice X contains twice the concentration of vitamin C of juice Y.
D Both juices contain the same mass of vitamin C per cm³.
parts.answer: B Juice X contains four times the concentration of vitamin C of juice Y.
parts.working: The same mass of vitamin C is needed each time. X supplies it in 2 cm³ and Y in 8 cm³, so X is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 times more concentrated. A is the common error of assuming a larger volume means more vitamin C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the chemical elements found in (i) carbohydrates, (ii) fats and (iii) proteins.
parts.answer: (i) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen; (ii) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen; (iii) carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (some also sulfur).
parts.working: B1 each; (iii) must include nitrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the smaller molecules that join to make (i) proteins and (ii) fats.
parts.answer: (i) amino acids; (ii) fatty acids and glycerol.
parts.working: B1 each; (ii) needs both.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which smaller molecules join together to form glycogen?
A amino acids
B fatty acids and glycerol
C glucose
D sucrose
parts.answer: C glucose
parts.working: Glycogen, like starch and cellulose, is a chain of glucose molecules. Sucrose is a sugar made of two units and is not the building block.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which element is present in proteins but NOT in fats or carbohydrates?
A carbon
B hydrogen
C nitrogen
D oxygen
parts.answer: C nitrogen
parts.working: Carbohydrates and fats contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Proteins also contain nitrogen (in amino groups), so C is correct. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are present in all three groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the monomer from which DNA is made.
parts.answer: nucleotides
parts.working: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two chemical elements that DNA contains in addition to carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
parts.answer: nitrogen and phosphorus
parts.working: 1 mark each for nitrogen and phosphorus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each molecule, state whether it contains nitrogen (Yes or No): glucose, amino acid, fatty acid, nucleotide.
parts.answer: glucose: No; amino acid: Yes; fatty acid: No; nucleotide: Yes
parts.working: 1 mark each. Amino acids contain an amino group; nucleotides contain a nitrogen-containing base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the smaller molecules that join together to make an enzyme.
parts.answer: amino acids
parts.working: Enzymes are proteins, which are made from amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of bond that joins amino acids together in a protein.
parts.answer: peptide bonds
parts.working: Peptide bonds link adjacent amino acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two types of molecule that combine to make a fat.
parts.answer: glycerol and fatty acids
parts.working: A fat is made from glycerol and fatty acid molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many fatty acid molecules join to one glycerol molecule to make a fat.
parts.working: One glycerol combines with three fatty acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the polymer formed when many glucose molecules are joined together in a plant.
parts.answer: starch
parts.working: Many glucose units form starch, a polysaccharide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in a potato tuber starch is stored, and why plants store starch rather than glucose.
parts.answer: in the cells of the tuber (storage organ); starch is insoluble so it does not affect the water potential of cells / is compact and does not diffuse out
parts.working: 1 mark: stored in tuber cells (storage organ). 1 mark: starch is insoluble so it can be stored without changing water potential, unlike glucose.

practice.stem: Water makes up about 60 % of the mass of an adult human body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water is important as a solvent in the human body. Give three examples.
parts.answer: Any three of: digested food molecules dissolve in water so they can be absorbed; plasma (mainly water) transports dissolved glucose, ions, hormones and CO₂; urea and other wastes are excreted dissolved in water (urine); enzyme reactions take place in solution in cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three examples linked to dissolving.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made from the same small molecule. Name it.
parts.answer: Glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each of starch, glycogen and cellulose, state whether it is found in plants or animals and give one role.
parts.answer: Starch: plants — energy store. Glycogen: animals (liver, muscles) — energy store. Cellulose: plants — forms cell walls.
parts.working: B1 each for correct location AND role.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of biological molecule and its monomer(s) is correctly matched?
A protein: glucose
B DNA: nucleotides
C starch: amino acids
D fat: nucleotides
parts.answer: B DNA: nucleotides
parts.working: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides. Protein is made from amino acids (not glucose), starch is made from glucose (not amino acids), and fats are made from glycerol and fatty acids (not nucleotides).

practice.stem:
The table gives the composition of 100 g of three foods (values are for this question only).
Food / Carbohydrate (g) / Protein (g) / Fat (g)
Cooked basmati rice / 28 / 2.7 / 0.3
Boiled egg / 1.1 / 12.6 / 9.5
Raw groundnuts / 16 / 25 / 49

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in fat content between groundnuts and boiled egg per 100 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which food contains the highest percentage of protein.
parts.answer: groundnuts (25 g)
parts.working: Groundnuts 25 g; boiled egg 12.6 g; rice 2.7 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the three elements found in all three types of nutrient in the table (carbohydrate, protein and fat).
parts.answer: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
parts.working: All three contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; proteins also contain nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms in one molecule of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), and the total number of atoms.
parts.answer: 6 C, 12 H, 6 O; total 24 atoms
parts.working: 1 mark for the three counts (6, 12, 6); 1 mark for total 24.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms in glucose in its simplest form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how glucose molecules join together to form a starch molecule.
parts.answer: glucose molecules join in a condensation reaction; a molecule of water is removed for each bond formed; many glucose units form a long chain (polymer)
parts.working: 1 mark: condensation reaction. 1 mark: water removed for each link. 1 mark: long polymer of many glucose units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one role in the body of protein other than as an enzyme.
parts.answer: any one of: structure (for example muscle, hair, skin); transport (for example haemoglobin); antibodies in defence
parts.working: Accept any correct non-enzyme protein role.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one role of fat in the body other than energy storage.
parts.answer: any one of: insulation (keeping warm); protection of organs; making cell membranes
parts.working: Accept any one of these correct roles.

practice.stem: A scientist analyses two substances taken from the cells of a cow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Substance X contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur. Suggest which group of biological molecules X belongs to. Explain.
parts.answer: Protein; only proteins (of these groups) contain nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur).
parts.working: B1 protein; B1 reason about N / S.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Substance Y contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. It is insoluble in water, is stored in liver cells, and when broken down releases glucose. Identify Y and explain why being insoluble is useful for a storage molecule.
parts.answer: Glycogen; insoluble so it does not dissolve in cytoplasm / does not affect water movement by osmosis / cannot diffuse out of the cell.
parts.working: B1 glycogen; B1 does not affect osmosis / water potential; B1 stays in the cell / does not move out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says 'proteins and carbohydrates contain exactly the same elements'. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Proteins also contain nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur); carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the order of amino acids in a protein can affect the way an enzyme works.
parts.answer: The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds and so the shape of the protein; the shape of the active site depends on this; a different order gives a different-shaped active site, so the substrate may not fit (not complementary) and the enzyme does not work.
parts.working: B1 sequence determines folding / shape; B1 active site shape; B1 substrate fits / complementary — changed order means it may not fit.

practice.stem: The energy values below are given for this question only. Fat: 37 kJ per g. Carbohydrate: 16 kJ per g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy per gram fat provides than carbohydrate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the elements in these molecules, why fats release more energy per gram than carbohydrates.
parts.answer: fats contain a higher proportion of hydrogen and fewer oxygen atoms per gram than carbohydrates do, so more energy is released when they are oxidised
parts.working: 1 mark: more C and H, fewer O per gram. 1 mark: more energy is released when these are oxidised in respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Molecule P contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and is broken down into glucose by hydrolysis. Molecule Q contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and is broken down into amino acids. Name the type of molecule P and of molecule Q, and state the bonds that are broken in each.
parts.answer: P: a polysaccharide (for example starch or glycogen); bonds between glucose units. Q: a protein (polypeptide); peptide bonds between amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each for naming P and Q as polysaccharide and protein. 1 mark each for the bonds: bonds between glucose units in P, peptide bonds in Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A polypeptide is made from 12 amino acids. Each amino acid contains one nitrogen atom. Calculate the number of nitrogen atoms in the polypeptide.
parts.working: The polypeptide contains one nitrogen per amino acid, so 12 N atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of nitrogen atoms in 5 molecules of this polypeptide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a molecule of starch contains no nitrogen atoms, although it is made from a large number of glucose units.
parts.answer: glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so joining glucose units cannot add nitrogen
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose contains no nitrogen. 1 mark: forming starch only joins glucose units with the loss of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
parts.answer: Two strands coiled together to form a double helix; each strand contains chemicals called bases; bases on the two strands are joined in pairs (A with T, C with G).
parts.working: B1 two strands; B1 double helix; B1 bases pair / bonds between bases hold strands together; accept named pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One strand of a short piece of DNA has the base sequence A T G C C T A G. Write the sequence of bases on the complementary strand.
parts.answer: T A C G G A T C
parts.working: B1 all correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pairs of bases join together in a DNA molecule?
A A with C, and G with T
B A with G, and C with T
C A with T, and C with G
D A with A, and C with C
parts.answer: C A with T, and C with G
parts.working: Adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine. B pairs bases wrongly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the two strands of a DNA double helix is correct?
A they are identical to each other
B they are complementary to each other
C they are joined by uracil bases
D each strand contains only adenine and thymine
parts.answer: B they are complementary to each other
parts.working: Each base on one strand pairs with a specific base on the other (A with T, G with C), so the two strands are complementary. They are not identical (A), uracil is not found in DNA (C), and a strand contains all four bases (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three parts that make up one nucleotide of DNA.
parts.answer: a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, a nitrogen-containing base
parts.working: 1 mark each for phosphate, deoxyribose (sugar) and a base. Accept named bases such as adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the base that is found in RNA but not in DNA.
parts.answer: uracil
parts.working: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: One strand of a short section of DNA has the base sequence C G A T T C G A. Write the base sequence of the complementary strand, in the same left-to-right order.
parts.answer: GCTAAGCT
parts.working: 1 mark for at least six bases paired correctly (C with G, A with T); 1 mark for all eight correct: GCTAAGCT.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of guanine bases in the double-stranded section.
parts.working: Strand 1 contains 2 G. The complementary strand contains 2 G (paired with the 2 C on strand 1). Total = 4.

practice.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA from a Hunza apricot tree contains 18 % guanine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the percentage of cytosine in this DNA.
parts.working: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so cytosine = guanine = 18 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of adenine in this DNA.
parts.working: G + C = 36 %, so A + T = 100 − 36 = 64 %. Adenine equals thymine, so A = 64 ÷ 2 = 32 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the two strands of a DNA molecule are held together.
parts.answer: by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases; each A pairs with a T and each G pairs with a C
parts.working: 1 mark for hydrogen bonds between bases; 1 mark for specific complementary pairing (A–T, G–C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the shape of a DNA molecule.
parts.answer: double helix
parts.working: DNA is a double helix (two strands twisted around each other).

practice.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA from the cells of a goat is analysed. 22 % of the bases are adenine (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the percentage of thymine in this DNA. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 22 %; A always pairs with T, so there is the same amount of each.
parts.working: B1 22 %; B1 A pairs with T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cytosine in this DNA.

practice.stem: One strand of a short piece of DNA has the sequence A T T G C A G C T A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the base sequence of the complementary strand.
parts.answer: T A A C G T C G A T

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the double-stranded piece, state the total number of adenine bases and the total number of guanine bases.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine in the double-stranded piece.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 15 % thymine. What percentage of the bases are guanine?
A 15
B 35
C 70
D 85
parts.working: A pairs with T, so adenine is also 15 %. A + T = 30 %, so G + C = 70 %. Guanine pairs with cytosine, so G = C = 35 %. 15 is the thymine value, not guanine; 70 is G + C together; 85 is 100 minus the thymine value and ignores A.

practice.stem:
The table shows the percentage of each base in DNA from three organisms.
Organism: A % / T % / C % / G %
X: 29 / 29 / 21 / 21
Y: 27 / 27 / 23 / 23
Z: 36 / 36 / 14 / 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which organism has the highest percentage of guanine.
parts.working: Guanine values: X 21 %, Y 23 %, Z 14 %. Y is highest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine plus cytosine in organism Z.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which two bases always have equal percentages in double-stranded DNA, and explain why.
parts.answer: adenine and thymine; they pair with each other (A with T), so each strand's A matches the other strand's T
parts.working: 1 mark for naming adenine and thymine; 1 mark for the explanation that A pairs with T by complementary base pairing.

practice.stem: One strand of a short double-stranded DNA section has the sequence A T G G C A T T C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the base sequence of the other strand, in the same left-to-right order.
parts.answer: T A C C G T A A G
parts.working: Pair each base: A–T, T–A, G–C, G–C, C–G, A–T, T–A, T–A, C–G.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total number of adenine bases in the double-stranded section.
parts.working: Strand 1 has 2 A; the other strand has 3 A (paired with the 3 T on strand 1). Total = 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the total number of adenine bases is always equal to the total number of thymine bases in a double-stranded DNA section.
parts.answer: every A on one strand pairs with a T on the other strand, and every T pairs with an A, so the numbers must match
parts.working: 1 mark for pairing rule A–T; 1 mark for the reason that every adenine has a partner thymine (and vice versa) in the other strand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'RNA and DNA follow exactly the same base pairing rules.' Explain whether the student is correct.
parts.answer: Partly correct: guanine always pairs with cytosine in both; but in RNA adenine pairs with uracil instead of thymine, so the rule for A is different.
parts.working: 1 mark: G–C pairing is the same in both. 1 mark: A pairs with U in RNA (not T). 1 mark: conclusion that the student is only partly correct.

practice.stem: A DNA molecule of 4000 base pairs contains 1400 adenine bases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of cytosine bases in the DNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the bases that are cytosine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.stem: A section of double-stranded DNA from a wheat plant contains 600 base pairs. 180 of the bases in this section are cytosine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of thymine bases in this section.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine bases in this section. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

practice.stem:
The base composition of DNA from two sources was measured.
Sample : A % : T % : C % : G %
P : 30 : 30 : 20 : 20
Q : 25 : 33 : 20 : 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, in double-stranded DNA, the percentage of adenine is always equal to the percentage of thymine.
parts.answer: Every A on one strand is paired with a T on the other strand (complementary base pairing), so the numbers must be equal.
parts.working: B1 A pairs with T; B1 one-to-one across the two strands.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which sample, P or Q, comes from a virus that has only a single strand of DNA. Give a reason using the data.
parts.answer: Q; its percentage of A (25) is not equal to T (33) and C (20) is not equal to G (22), so the bases are not paired.
parts.working: B1 Q; B1 A ≠ T / C ≠ G in Q (or A = T and C = G in P).

practice.stem: A bacterium from a yoghurt culture in Lahore has a single DNA molecule of 1 200 000 base pairs. In this DNA, 22 % of the bases are adenine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of bases in this DNA molecule.
parts.working: Each base pair contains two bases: 1 200 000 × 2 = 2 400 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of cytosine bases in this DNA molecule.
parts.working: Adenine = thymine = 22 %, so guanine = cytosine = (100 − 44) ÷ 2 = 28 %. 28 % of 2 400 000 = 672 000.

practice.stem: A researcher analysed the DNA of a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria). The base percentages were: A 33 %, T 17 %, G 26 %, C 24 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why these results show that this DNA cannot be normal double-stranded DNA.
parts.answer: In double-stranded DNA A = T and G = C, but here A (33 %) is not equal to T (17 %) and G (26 %) is not equal to C (24 %); so the DNA is single-stranded.
parts.working: 1 mark: A ≠ T and G ≠ C, so base-pairing equality is not met. 1 mark: conclusion that it is single-stranded DNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the researcher should repeat the analysis with a second sample before drawing a firm conclusion.
parts.answer: the sample could be contaminated (for example with host bacterial DNA) or the measurements could contain errors; one sample may not be representative
parts.working: Any two of: contamination with other DNA; measurement or calculation error; a single sample may not represent the whole virus population.

practice.stem: A section of double-stranded DNA from a mango tree contains 3000 base pairs. 900 of the bases in this section are cytosine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of cytosine bases in this section.
parts.working: Guanine equals cytosine, so 900 cytosine bases are paired with 900 guanine bases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of thymine bases in this section.
parts.working: Total bases = 3000 × 2 = 6000. C + G = 1800, so A + T = 4200. Adenine = thymine, so T = 4200 ÷ 2 = 2100.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the bases that are adenine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.stem: A DNA molecule has 800 base pairs. 35 % of the base pairs are G–C pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of adenine bases in this DNA. Show your working.
parts.working: G–C pairs = 35 % of 800 base pairs = 280 pairs; A–T pairs = 800 − 280 = 520 pairs. Each A–T pair contains one adenine, so adenine = 520 (and thymine = 520).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student measured the rate of an enzyme reaction at different temperatures.
temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
rate / arbitrary units: 4, 9, 17, 23, 11, 1
Which temperature is closest to the optimum temperature of this enzyme?
A 20 °C
B 30 °C
C 40 °C
D 50 °C
parts.answer: C 40 °C
parts.working: The rate is highest (23) at 40 °C, so the optimum is nearest 40 °C. 50 °C is wrong: the rate has already fallen because the enzyme is being denatured.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme from a human cell is tested at 10 °C, 25 °C and 37 °C. The rate increases as the temperature rises.
Explain why the rate increases between 10 °C and 37 °C.
parts.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate molecules move faster and collide more often, forming more enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: more kinetic energy; more (frequent / successful) collisions between enzyme and substrate; more enzyme–substrate complexes formed (per unit time) / more product per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the term used for the temperature at which an enzyme works fastest.
parts.answer: Optimum temperature
parts.working: B1 optimum (temperature).

practice.stem:
Potato contains catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. A student put 5.0 g of chopped potato into a flask with 10 cm³ of buffer solution and 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide. The oxygen was collected in an inverted measuring cylinder for 2 minutes. This was repeated with buffers of different pH.
pH: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11
volume of oxygen after 2 minutes / cm³: 4.5, 11.0, 18.5, 12.0, 3.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the pH at which catalase in potato worked best in this investigation.
parts.answer: pH 7
parts.working: B1 pH 7 (largest volume, 18.5 cm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: pH (of buffer). Dependent: volume of oxygen collected (in 2 minutes).
parts.working: B1 pH; B1 volume of oxygen (collected in 2 min) – 'amount' or 'oxygen' alone not credited.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same, and say how one of them could be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature, volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, mass/size/surface area of potato, time of collection. E.g. temperature controlled with a thermostatically controlled water-bath.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two controlled variables (B1 + B1); 1 mark for a matching method of control (e.g. thermostatically controlled water-bath; measure peroxide with a syringe; same mass of potato on a balance).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student investigates the effect of pH on the activity of amylase. Which variable must be kept constant?
A pH of the solution
B temperature of the mixture
C time taken for starch to be digested
D colour of the iodine solution
parts.answer: B temperature of the mixture
parts.working: Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it must be controlled. pH is the independent variable (A) and the time taken is the dependent variable (C).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.
'Each enzyme works best at a particular pH, called its ____ pH. If the pH is too high or too low, the shape of the ____ ____ changes. The substrate no longer ____ into it, so fewer enzyme–substrate ____ are formed. The enzyme is said to be ____.'
parts.answer: optimum; active site; fits; complexes; denatured
parts.working: 1 mark each: optimum; active site; fits (accept binds); complexes; denatured. (Active site counts as one mark.)

practice.stem:
A student placed a tube of 5 cm³ starch solution and a tube of 1 cm³ amylase solution separately in a water-bath at 37 °C for 5 minutes, then mixed them and kept the mixture in the water-bath. Every 30 s, a drop of the mixture was added to a drop of iodine solution on a spotting tile.
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180
colour: blue-black, blue-black, blue-black, dark brown-black, brown-black, orange-brown, orange-brown

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time at which the starch had been fully digested.
parts.working: B1 150 s (first time the drop stays orange-brown).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the amylase and starch were placed in the water-bath separately for 5 minutes before they were mixed.
parts.answer: So both solutions reached the test temperature (37 °C) before the reaction started; otherwise the reaction would begin at a different temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: to reach the temperature of the water-bath (equilibrate); 1 mark: so the reaction occurs at the stated temperature from the start / fair test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour that iodine solution turns when starch is present.
parts.answer: Blue-black
parts.working: B1 blue-black.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one safety precaution needed in this experiment.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection (iodine solution is an irritant) / wipe up spills.
parts.working: Any one relevant precaution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rises between 10 °C and 30 °C. Why?
A enzyme molecules become larger
B molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often
C the enzyme is being used up
D the substrate becomes more specific
parts.answer: B molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often
parts.working: A rise in temperature increases the kinetic energy of the molecules, so enzyme and substrate molecules collide and form enzyme–substrate complexes more often. Enzymes are not used up, and their size and the specificity of the substrate do not change in this range.

practice.stem: A student measured the rate of breakdown of egg-white protein by an enzyme at different pH values. Rate (arbitrary units): pH 1: 2.0; pH 2: 8.0; pH 3: 14.0; pH 4: 9.5; pH 5: 3.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the pH at which the enzyme works fastest.
parts.answer: pH 3
parts.working: 1 mark: the highest rate is at pH 3 (14 units).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the rate at pH 3 is greater than the rate at pH 5. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for (14 − 3) ÷ 3 × 100; 1 mark for 367 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate at pH 5 is lower than the rate at pH 3.
parts.answer: pH 5 is further from the optimum, so the active site changes shape and fewer substrate molecules fit; fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: 1 mark: pH 5 is further from the optimum; 1 mark: the active site shape changes, so fewer substrate molecules bind.

practice.stem: The stomach secretes a strong acid. Pepsin works best at about pH 2 in the stomach. Pancreatic amylase works best at about pH 7 to 8 in the small intestine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the acid secreted by the stomach.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid
parts.working: 1 mark for hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why pancreatic amylase would not work well if it entered the stomach without being neutralised.
parts.answer: The low pH changes the shape of the active site (denatures the enzyme), so the substrate cannot bind.
parts.working: 1 mark: pH far from the optimum; 1 mark: active site shape changes, so the enzyme is denatured.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the substance secreted by the pancreas that neutralises the acid as it enters the small intestine.
parts.answer: Sodium hydrogencarbonate
parts.working: 1 mark for sodium hydrogencarbonate (alkaline pancreatic juice).

practice.stem: An enzyme was assayed at five pH values. Rate (arbitrary units): pH 5: 12; pH 6: 30; pH 7: 45; pH 8: 30; pH 9: 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum pH shown by the data.
parts.answer: pH 7
parts.working: 1 mark: pH 7 gives the highest rate (45 units).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the rate is at pH 7 than at pH 5. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate at pH 9 is much lower than at pH 7.
parts.answer: pH 9 is far from the optimum, so the active site changes shape and fewer substrate molecules can bind.
parts.working: 1 mark: pH 9 is far from the optimum; 1 mark: active site shape changes, so fewer substrate molecules bind.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction fall when the temperature is raised well above the optimum?
A The enzyme molecules are killed by the heat.
B The substrate molecules move too fast to collide with the enzyme.
C The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.
D The enzyme is used up faster at high temperatures.
parts.answer: C The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.
parts.working: High temperature denatures the enzyme: the active site loses its shape and is no longer complementary to the substrate. Enzymes are proteins, not living things, so they cannot be 'killed' (A); faster movement actually increases collisions (B).

practice.stem:
Amylase was mixed with starch solution at five temperatures. A drop of the mixture was tested with iodine solution every 10 s until it no longer turned blue-black. The time taken was recorded.
temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
time for starch to disappear / s: 600, 300, 150, 90, 240, no end point after 900 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 40 °C and at 50 °C, using rate = 1000 ÷ time. Give each answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction shown by the results.
parts.answer: Rate increases from 10 °C to 40 °C (the time halves for each 10 °C rise from 10 °C to 30 °C); highest rate at 40 °C; rate decreases above 40 °C, to zero/no end point at 60 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: rate increases from 10 °C to 40 °C; maximum / optimum at (about) 40 °C; rate falls above 40 °C; quoting data with units (e.g. 600 s at 10 °C, 90 s at 40 °C).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the iodine never stopped turning blue-black at 60 °C.
parts.answer: The amylase was denatured; its active site changed shape so starch could no longer bind, so starch was not digested and remained.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: amylase denatured; active site shape changed / starch no longer fits / no enzyme–substrate complexes; so starch remains (iodine stays blue-black).

practice.stem:
A student added 1 cm³ of liver extract (contains catalase) to 5 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide mixed with 2 cm³ of buffer in a narrow tube, and measured the maximum height of foam produced. Each pH was tested three times.
pH 3: 4, 5, 4 mm
pH 5: 12, 14, 13 mm
pH 7: 30, 32, 31 mm
pH 9: 18, 8, 20 mm
pH 11: 6, 5, 7 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 8 mm at pH 9 (trial 2)
parts.working: B1 8 mm at pH 9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean height of foam at pH 3 (to 1 decimal place) and at pH 9 (leaving out the anomalous result).
parts.answer: pH 3: 4.3 mm; pH 9: 19.0 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the anomalous result may have occurred.
parts.answer: E.g. less liver used / hydrogen peroxide volume measured wrongly / foam height read late or early / tube not mixed.
parts.working: Any one sensible, specific reason linked to the method.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write a conclusion for this investigation.
parts.answer: Catalase activity (foam height) increases from pH 3 to pH 7, where it is greatest, and decreases from pH 7 to pH 11; optimum pH about 7.
parts.working: 1 mark for increase up to pH 7 / greatest at pH 7; 1 mark for decrease above pH 7. Must link pH to foam height / activity.

practice.stem:
Agar containing milk protein is cloudy. Paper discs were soaked in protease solution made up in buffers of different pH and placed on the milk agar. After 24 hours at 30 °C, the diameter of the clear zone around each disc was measured. Three discs were used for each pH.
pH 4: 6, 7, 8 mm
pH 6: 14, 15, 16 mm
pH 8: 11, 12, 10 mm
pH 10: 3, 4, 2 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the clear zone at each pH.
parts.answer: pH 4: 7 mm; pH 6: 15 mm; pH 8: 11 mm; pH 10: 3 mm
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mean diameter between pH 6 and pH 8. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a clear zone forms around each disc.
parts.answer: Protease diffuses out of the disc into the agar and digests the milk protein into soluble amino acids, so the cloudy protein disappears.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: protease diffuses into the agar; digests / breaks down milk protein (into amino acids), removing the cloudiness.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the measurement of the clear zones more accurate.
parts.answer: Measure the diameter at two right angles and take the mean / use a ruler with mm divisions held under the dish against a dark background.
parts.working: Any one specific improvement.

practice.stem: Biological washing powders contain enzymes, including proteases and lipases. The label on one powder says: 'Best results at 30–40 °C. Do not use above 60 °C.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the biological washing powder removes egg and blood stains well at 40 °C.
parts.answer: Stains contain protein; the protease in the powder digests the protein into soluble amino acids; 40 °C is close to the optimum temperature of the enzymes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: protease digests protein (in egg/blood) into (soluble) amino acids; 40 °C is near the optimum, so rate is high.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the powder works poorly if the clothes are washed at 90 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes are denatured at 90 °C; active site changes shape so the protein stains no longer fit / bind.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed / substrate cannot bind.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it can be cheaper for a family in Karachi to wash clothes with biological powder in cool tap water rather than with non-biological powder in hot water.
parts.answer: Less energy (electricity or gas) needed to heat the water.
parts.working: B1 saves energy / fuel for heating water.

practice.stem:
Pectinase helps to release juice from fruit. A student mixed 20 g of crushed apple with 2 cm³ of pectinase at different temperatures, then filtered the mixture for 20 minutes.
temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
volume of juice / cm³: 6.0, 9.5, 14.0, 11.0, 4.5
A control with boiled pectinase at 40 °C gave 3.0 cm³ of juice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume from 20 °C to 40 °C. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some juice was produced in the control tube with boiled pectinase.
parts.answer: Juice drains from apple pieces by gravity / from cells already broken when the apple was cut, without enzyme action.
parts.working: B1 some juice released without enzyme, e.g. from cut cells / gravity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student placed the beakers of apple pulp and pectinase in water-baths and mixed them straight away. Identify one source of error in this method and suggest an improvement.
