parts.answer: Error: the pulp and enzyme were not at the test temperature when mixed. Improvement: leave pulp and pectinase separately in the water-bath for 5–10 minutes before mixing.
parts.working: B1 error (no equilibration / temperature not reached); B1 matching improvement (equilibrate separately before mixing). Accept other matched pairs, e.g. temperature of water-bath varied – use thermostatically controlled water-bath.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the temperature range in which the optimum temperature lies, and describe how the investigation could be extended to find it more precisely.
parts.answer: Between 30 °C and 50 °C; test temperatures at smaller intervals, e.g. every 2 °C from 30 °C to 50 °C.
parts.working: B1 30–50 °C; B1 smaller intervals in this range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient with a fever has a body temperature of 40.5 °C. Suggest why a very high fever can be dangerous, in terms of enzymes.
parts.answer: Some enzymes may start to denature / active sites change shape, so metabolic reactions slow down.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes (begin to) denature / active site changes shape; 1 mark: metabolic reactions (e.g. respiration) slow / cells cannot function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage for humans to keep their body temperature close to 37 °C.
parts.answer: 37 °C is close to the optimum temperature of human enzymes, so reactions happen at a fast and constant rate; it is low enough that enzymes are not denatured.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: near optimum for enzymes; reactions fast / steady; enzymes not denatured (any two).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about enzymes are correct?
1 Extreme pH can change the shape of the active site.
2 Enzymes are denatured at low temperatures such as 5 °C.
3 Different enzymes can have different optimum pH values.
A 1, 2 and 3
B 1 and 2 only
C 1 and 3 only
D 2 and 3 only
parts.answer: C 1 and 3 only
parts.working: Statement 2 is false: at low temperatures enzymes are inactive (few collisions) but not denatured. Statements 1 and 3 are true (e.g. pepsin about pH 2, salivary amylase about pH 7). Option A is the main distractor.

practice.stem:
A student added 2 cm³ of liver extract (containing catalase) to hydrogen peroxide at five temperatures and measured the oxygen collected in 60 seconds.
Temperature (°C): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Oxygen in 60 s (cm³): 6.0, 14.5, 26.0, 32.0, 9.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen production at 40 °C in cm³ per second. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.53 cm³/s
parts.working: 1 mark for 32.0 ÷ 60 = 0.533; 1 mark for 0.53 cm³/s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the oxygen produced in 60 seconds when the temperature rises from 20 °C to 30 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the fall in oxygen produced at 50 °C.
parts.answer: The enzyme has been denatured: the heat changes the shape of the active site, so the substrate no longer fits and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzyme denatured, shape of active site changes; 1 mark: fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.

practice.stem: A student compared two samples of amylase. Sample A was kept at 0 °C for 30 minutes, then warmed to 35 °C; its activity returned to normal. Sample B was boiled for 5 minutes, cooled and then warmed to 35 °C; it showed no activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sample A regained its activity.
parts.answer: The enzyme was not denatured: low temperature only slowed the molecules, the active site kept its shape, so it worked again when warmed.
parts.working: 1 mark: not denatured, shape kept; 1 mark: low temperature only slows molecules and reduces their energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sample B did not regain its activity.
parts.answer: Boiling denatures the enzyme: the bonds holding the protein in shape break, so the active site changes shape permanently and the substrate cannot bind.
parts.working: 1 mark: the enzyme is denatured (bonds broken); 1 mark: active site shape permanently changed so substrate cannot bind.

practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the time taken for rennet (an enzyme that clots milk) to clot milk. Rennet is added to warm milk and the time for a firm curd to form is recorded at each temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature of the milk; dependent: time taken for a firm curd to form.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly named variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Volume of milk; volume of rennet (or the same type and concentration of milk).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of any two sensible controlled variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would most likely denature an enzyme?
A pH 7.0 to pH 7.5
B 37 °C to 38 °C
C pH 7.0 to pH 12.0
D 20 °C to 25 °C
parts.answer: C pH 7.0 to pH 12.0
parts.working: A large change in pH breaks the ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site changes shape. The other changes are small and within the range the enzyme tolerates; a rise from 20 °C to 25 °C only increases the rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two protein-digesting enzymes, P and Q, were tested at different pH values. Enzyme P worked best at pH 2 and enzyme Q worked best at pH 8.
Which row shows where each enzyme is most likely to act in the human alimentary canal?
A P: mouth; Q: stomach
B P: stomach; Q: small intestine
C P: small intestine; Q: stomach
D P: stomach; Q: mouth
parts.answer: B P: stomach; Q: small intestine
parts.working: The stomach is acidic (hydrochloric acid, about pH 2), so P acts there; the small intestine (duodenum) is slightly alkaline, so Q acts there. Option D is wrong because protein digestion does not take place in the mouth.

practice.stem:
A student put a protease solution in two tubes.
Tube A was kept at 2 °C for 30 minutes, then warmed to 37 °C and mixed with protein.
Tube B was kept at 80 °C for 30 minutes, then cooled to 37 °C and mixed with protein.
Tube A digested the protein normally. Tube B digested none of the protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for tube A and tube B.
parts.answer: Tube A: at 2 °C the enzyme had little kinetic energy, so there were few collisions and little activity; it was not denatured, so when warmed to 37 °C it worked normally. Tube B: at 80 °C the enzyme was denatured; the active site permanently changed shape, so substrate could not bind even after cooling.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: low temperature – low kinetic energy / few collisions (A); enzyme not denatured at low temperature, so activity returns on warming; high temperature denatures enzyme (B); active-site shape changed permanently / irreversibly, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form when cooled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seeds kept dry in a freezer in a seed bank can still germinate many years later, but seeds that have been boiled never germinate. Use your knowledge of enzymes to suggest why.
parts.answer: Freezing only makes the seeds' enzymes inactive (low kinetic energy) without denaturing them, so they work again when the seed is warmed; boiling denatures the enzymes irreversibly (active sites change shape), so the reactions needed for germination cannot take place.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: freezing slows / stops enzyme activity temporarily (not denatured, activity returns on warming); boiling denatures enzymes irreversibly / active site permanently changed, so no germination.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an investigation to find the effect of temperature on the activity of lipase.
Lipase digests fat in milk into fatty acids and glycerol. Milk mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator is pink; the pink colour disappears when enough fatty acids have been produced.
In your plan, include the apparatus and the method, the variables you will control, and how you will make your results reliable.
parts.answer: Use milk + sodium carbonate + phenolphthalein in test-tubes at five or more temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C) in thermostatically controlled water-baths; equilibrate milk and lipase separately; mix, start timer, record time for pink colour to disappear; control volumes, concentrations, pH; repeat three times and calculate a mean; wear eye protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: 1. at least five temperatures stated / range; 2. temperature controlled with thermostatically controlled water-bath; 3. equilibrate milk mixture and lipase at the temperature before mixing; 4. measure time for pink colour to disappear (dependent variable), e.g. with a stopwatch; 5. two controlled variables with method, e.g. same volume of milk/lipase measured with syringe, same lipase concentration, same volume of sodium carbonate / indicator; 6. repeat each temperature (at least) three times and calculate mean / identify anomalies; 7. control tube with boiled lipase or water instead of lipase; 8. relevant safety, e.g. eye protection with sodium carbonate or care with hot water.

practice.stem: Some bacteria live in hot springs in northern Pakistan where the water is about 75 °C. An enzyme extracted from one of these bacteria has an optimum temperature of 75 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the enzyme from the hot-spring bacterium is not denatured at 75 °C, but a human enzyme would be.
parts.answer: The bacterial enzyme has a shape (bonds holding its 3-D shape) that remains stable at high temperature, so its active site keeps its shape; the human enzyme's shape changes above about 40–45 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for: bacterial enzyme's active site / shape stays the same at 75 °C; 1 mark for: human enzyme's active site changes shape / is denatured at this temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bacterial enzyme works more slowly at 37 °C than at 75 °C.
parts.answer: At 37 °C molecules have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: less kinetic energy; fewer collisions / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using an enzyme like this in an industrial process that runs at a high temperature.
parts.answer: It is not denatured, so it keeps working at high temperatures where reactions are faster / it can be used for longer.
parts.working: Any one: works at high temperature without denaturing; faster reaction; lasts longer / reused; fewer contaminating microorganisms grow at high temperature.

practice.stem:
Yeast suspension (contains catalase) was added to hydrogen peroxide at five temperatures. The time taken to collect 10 cm³ of oxygen in a gas syringe was recorded.
temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55
time to collect 10 cm³ / s: 125, 64, 40, 52, 160

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen production at 25 °C and at 45 °C in cm³ per second. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concluded that the optimum temperature is 35 °C. Explain why this conclusion may not be correct and suggest what further work would show the optimum more precisely.
parts.answer: The optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 45 °C, because only 10 °C intervals were tested; repeat with temperatures at 2 °C (or smaller) intervals between 25 °C and 45 °C, with repeats.
parts.working: 1 mark: only 10 °C steps / large intervals; 1 mark: optimum lies between 25 °C and 45 °C; 1 mark: test more temperatures at smaller intervals in this range (with repeats).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why measuring the time to collect 10 cm³ of gas is better than collecting gas for a fixed long time, such as 10 minutes, at every temperature.
parts.answer: Over a long time the hydrogen peroxide may be used up at the faster temperatures, so the volumes would no longer show the rate / the cylinder could overflow.
parts.working: B1 substrate used up / cylinder overflows so later volumes do not reflect rate.

practice.stem:
Slices of mango were kept for 5 days at two temperatures. The mass lost because of decay was measured.
kept at 4 °C (refrigerator): mass lost 3.2 g
kept at 30 °C (kitchen in summer): mass lost 14.4 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mass loss was at 30 °C than at 4 °C.
parts.answer: 4.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in mass loss, in terms of the enzymes of decomposers on the mango.
parts.answer: At 4 °C the decomposers' enzymes have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions and slower digestion and respiration; the decomposers grow and reproduce slowly. At 30 °C enzymes are near their optimum, so decay is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: decomposers (bacteria/fungi) use enzymes to digest the mango; low temperature – less kinetic energy / fewer enzyme–substrate collisions; enzymes not denatured but activity / growth / reproduction slower at 4 °C; nearer optimum at 30 °C (any three).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the rate of decay if the mango slices kept at 4 °C were moved to 30 °C. Give a reason.
parts.answer: The rate would increase to about the same as at 30 °C, because the enzymes were not denatured at 4 °C.
parts.working: B1 rate increases; B1 enzymes not denatured (activity returns).

practice.stem: The activity of an enzyme kept at 60 °C was measured. Activity was 100 % at 0 minutes, 50 % at 5 minutes, 25 % at 10 minutes and 12.5 % at 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of activity remaining after 20 minutes. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: activity halves every 5 minutes, so 100 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2; 1 mark: 6.25 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the activity falls over time at 60 °C.
parts.answer: Heat gradually denatures the enzyme: the bonds holding its shape break, so more and more enzyme molecules lose the shape of their active site.
parts.working: 1 mark: heat denatures the enzyme over time; 1 mark: bonds break, so the active site changes shape.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the enzyme would keep its activity for longer if it were kept at 30 °C.
parts.answer: At 30 °C the bonds in the enzyme stay intact, so its active site keeps its shape for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: less denaturation at lower temperature; 1 mark: active site keeps its shape.

practice.stem: Enzymes from an Arctic fish living in water at about 2 °C have an optimum temperature of 15 °C. Human enzymes have an optimum of 37 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the temperature at which the Arctic fish enzyme works fastest.
parts.working: 1 mark for 15 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Arctic fish enzyme has a lower optimum temperature than human enzymes.
parts.answer: Its structure has evolved for cold water, so its shape is less stable and it changes shape (denatures) at lower temperatures than a human enzyme.
parts.working: 1 mark: adapted to cold conditions / structure has evolved to work at low temperatures; 1 mark: less stable at higher temperatures, so denatures earlier.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the Arctic enzyme if it were kept at 37 °C for 30 minutes.
parts.answer: It would be denatured and lose much of its activity.
parts.working: 1 mark for denatured with loss of activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which description of enzymes is correct?
A carbohydrates that act as biological catalysts
B proteins that act as biological catalysts
C proteins that are used up in the reactions they control
D fats that speed up reactions in cells
parts.answer: B proteins that act as biological catalysts
parts.working: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions and are not changed by them. C is wrong because enzymes are not used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction.
parts.working: B1 speeds up reaction AND not changed / used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product formed when amylase acts on starch.
parts.answer: Maltose
parts.working: B1 maltose (accept simple reducing sugar).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why amylase cannot digest protein.
parts.answer: Enzymes are specific; protein is not complementary in shape to the active site of amylase, so it cannot bind.
parts.working: 1 mark: active site shape; 1 mark: protein not complementary / does not fit, so no enzyme–substrate complex.

practice.stem: A student mixed starch solution with amylase and left it at 35 °C for 15 minutes. She then tested a sample of the mixture with Benedict's solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should carry out the Benedict's test on the mixture.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the sample and heat in a hot water-bath (about 80 °C) for a few minutes.
parts.working: B1 add Benedict's solution; B1 heat in a (hot) water-bath.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mixture turned brick red. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Amylase broke down starch into maltose, a reducing sugar, which gives a positive Benedict's test.
parts.working: B1 amylase digested starch; B1 into maltose / reducing sugar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour you would expect if Benedict's test was done on the starch solution before amylase was added.
parts.answer: Blue (no colour change)
parts.working: B1 blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens to an enzyme after it has catalysed a reaction?
A it is used up and destroyed
B it is permanently changed in shape
C it is released unchanged and can catalyse another reaction
D it combines with the product
parts.answer: C it is released unchanged and can catalyse another reaction
parts.working: Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up or permanently changed, so one enzyme molecule can act on many substrate molecules in turn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide in liver cells.
parts.answer: Catalase
parts.working: 1 mark for catalase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme in saliva that breaks down starch.
parts.answer: Salivary amylase
parts.working: 1 mark for salivary amylase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme in the stomach that breaks down proteins.
parts.answer: Pepsin
parts.working: 1 mark for pepsin.

practice.stem: A student wants to show that an enzyme solution contains protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the chemical test used to show that a solution contains protein.
parts.answer: Biuret test.
parts.working: 1 mark for the biuret test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change you would expect in a positive result.
parts.answer: Blue to purple (violet).
parts.working: 1 mark for blue turning purple/violet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many enzyme names end in -ase. Explain what this ending tells you.
parts.answer: That the substance is an enzyme.
parts.working: 1 mark for enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why enzyme names often include the name of the substrate they act on.
parts.answer: The name shows which substance the enzyme acts on, for example lactase acts on lactose.
parts.working: 1 mark: name identifies the substrate, e.g. lactase acts on lactose.

practice.stem: Catalase is an enzyme found in many cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction catalysed by catalase.
parts.answer: Hydrogen peroxide → (catalase) → water + oxygen
parts.working: 1 mark for hydrogen peroxide as the reactant with catalase; 1 mark for water and oxygen as products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why cells need catalase.
parts.answer: To break down hydrogen peroxide, which is a toxic by-product of metabolism.
parts.working: 1 mark: to break down a toxic substance made in the cell.

practice.stem: Mould grows on a piece of bread. The mould releases enzymes onto the bread, which digest the starch and protein. The mould then absorbs the soluble products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the substance produced by the mould digestion and absorbed by the mould.
parts.answer: Soluble products such as glucose and amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark for soluble products such as glucose or amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of digestion described.
parts.answer: Extracellular digestion.
parts.working: 1 mark for extracellular digestion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mould digests its food outside its body.
parts.answer: Starch and protein molecules are too large to be absorbed; enzymes break them into small soluble molecules outside the mould so they can be absorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark: large food molecules cannot be absorbed; 1 mark: enzymes break them into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.

practice.stem: Cellulose is a polysaccharide made of glucose units. Humans can digest starch but cannot digest cellulose, even though both are made of glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why humans cannot digest cellulose.
parts.answer: Humans do not produce an enzyme (cellulase) with an active site that fits the bonds in cellulose; enzymes are specific to their substrate.
parts.working: 1 mark: no suitable enzyme produced (cellulase absent); 1 mark: enzymes are specific, so the active site does not fit cellulose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the indigestible plant material that passes through the gut.
parts.answer: Dietary fibre (roughage).
parts.working: 1 mark for dietary fibre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the pancreatic enzymes (amylase, protease and lipase) are made.
parts.answer: The pancreas.
parts.working: 1 mark for pancreas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where these pancreatic enzymes act.
parts.answer: The small intestine.
parts.working: 1 mark for small intestine.

practice.stem: The time for a glucose test strip to change colour was measured for three lactase concentrations in milk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the rate values using rate = 1000 ÷ time for each enzyme concentration: 1 unit (40 s), 2 units (20 s), 4 units (10 s).
parts.working: 1 mark for 25 and 50; 1 mark for 100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the relationship between enzyme concentration and rate shown by these values.
parts.answer: Rate doubles when enzyme concentration doubles, so rate is directly proportional to enzyme concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate is directly proportional to enzyme concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme acts on only one substrate. Which feature explains this?
A The substrate has a shape complementary to the active site of the enzyme.
B The enzyme is denatured by all other substrates.
C The enzyme has many active sites of different shapes.
D The product has the same shape as the active site.
parts.answer: A The substrate has a shape complementary to the active site of the enzyme.
parts.working: Specificity: only a substrate whose shape is complementary to the active site can bind and form an enzyme–substrate complex. B is wrong: other molecules simply do not fit; they do not denature the enzyme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an enzyme molecule catalyses the breakdown of a substrate molecule. Use the terms active site and enzyme–substrate complex in your answer.
parts.answer: Enzyme and substrate collide; substrate fits into the complementary active site; an enzyme–substrate complex forms; substrate is broken into products; products leave the active site; enzyme is unchanged and can be used again.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: collision / random movement; substrate binds to active site (complementary shape); enzyme–substrate complex forms; products formed and released; enzyme unchanged / reused.

practice.stem:
Four tubes each contained 5 cm³ of starch solution at 35 °C:
A: + 1 cm³ amylase
B: + 1 cm³ protease
C: + 1 cm³ amylase that had been boiled and cooled
D: + 1 cm³ water
After 15 minutes a drop from each tube was tested with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the result expected for each tube.
parts.answer: A: orange-brown (no starch); B: blue-black; C: blue-black; D: blue-black
parts.working: 2 marks for all four; 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results show about enzymes.
parts.answer: Only amylase digests starch, so enzymes are specific; boiled amylase does not work because it is denatured.
parts.working: B1 specificity – protease cannot digest starch; B1 boiling denatures amylase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why tube D is included.
parts.answer: Control: shows that starch does not break down without enzyme / that any change is due to the enzyme.
parts.working: B1 control idea, comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the table by naming the missing substances.
Enzyme | substrate | product(s)
amylase | starch | (i) ____
protease | (ii) ____ | amino acids
lipase | fats and oils | (iii) ____
catalase | (iv) ____ | water and oxygen
parts.answer: (i) maltose / simple reducing sugars; (ii) protein; (iii) fatty acids and glycerol; (iv) hydrogen peroxide
parts.working: 1 mark each; (iii) needs both fatty acids and glycerol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why enzymes are important to living organisms.
parts.answer: They speed up metabolic reactions (such as respiration and digestion) so that they happen fast enough at body temperature to keep the organism alive.
parts.working: 1 mark: speed up (metabolic) reactions / catalysts; 1 mark: fast enough at body temperature (low temperatures) to sustain life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A liver cell contains hundreds of different enzymes. Suggest why so many different enzymes are needed.
parts.answer: Each enzyme is specific to one substrate / reaction, and the cell carries out many different reactions.
parts.working: B1 enzymes specific / one substrate each; B1 many different reactions in the cell.

practice.stem:
A student measured the rate of an enzyme reaction at different substrate concentrations, keeping the enzyme concentration constant.
Substrate concentration (mmol/dm³): 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0
Rate (arbitrary units): 5.0, 9.0, 14.0, 16.0, 16.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate when the substrate concentration is increased from 1.0 to 2.0 mmol/dm³. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for (14 − 9) ÷ 9 × 100; 1 mark for 55.6 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate does not increase between 4.0 and 8.0 mmol/dm³.
parts.answer: All the enzyme's active sites are occupied (saturated), so the enzyme is now the limiting factor; extra substrate cannot increase the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: active sites are full (saturated); 1 mark: enzyme is limiting, so more substrate does not help.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate increases from 0.5 to 2.0 mmol/dm³.
parts.answer: More substrate molecules collide with the active sites more often, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: 1 mark: more substrate, more collisions with active sites; 1 mark: more enzyme–substrate complexes form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one enzyme that acts inside cells and one enzyme that is secreted out of cells.
parts.answer: Inside: catalase; secreted: amylase (or pepsin).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct intracellular enzyme; 1 mark for a correct secreted enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term extracellular.
parts.answer: Acting outside the cell, after the enzyme has been secreted.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct definition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an enzyme that acts outside a cell must be made by the cell and then released.
parts.answer: It is made inside the cell on ribosomes and then secreted, so it can act on food outside the cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: made inside the cell and then secreted to act outside.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Maltase is added to a solution of maltose. What are the products?
A two molecules of glucose
B one glucose and one fructose
C amino acids
D fatty acids and glycerol
parts.answer: A two molecules of glucose
parts.working: Maltase breaks the bond between the two glucose units in maltose, giving two glucose molecules. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose; amino acids come from protein; fatty acids and glycerol come from fats.

practice.stem:
Liver extract was added to hydrogen peroxide solution. The volume of hydrogen peroxide solution remaining was measured at intervals.
Time (min): 0, 1, 2, 3
Hydrogen peroxide remaining (cm³ of solution): 10.0, 7.2, 5.1, 3.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the hydrogen peroxide used up in the first 2 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the amount of hydrogen peroxide used per minute falls over time.
parts.answer: Less substrate remains, so fewer substrate molecules collide with the enzyme's active sites and the rate falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: less substrate remains; 1 mark: fewer collisions with active sites, so slower rate.

practice.stem: Yeast enzymes convert glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide during fermentation. In one experiment, 180 g of glucose produced 92 g of ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ethanol produced from 500 g of glucose. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for 92 ÷ 180 × 500; 1 mark for 256 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process the yeast uses to produce ethanol.
parts.answer: Anaerobic respiration (fermentation).
parts.working: 1 mark for anaerobic respiration or fermentation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the yeast enzymes if the flask is heated to 90 °C.
parts.answer: They are denatured and fermentation stops.
parts.working: 1 mark for denaturation.

practice.stem: Pepsin is a protease that digests protein. The cells of the stomach wall are made of protein, yet they are not digested by pepsin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one way in which the stomach wall is protected from its own enzymes.
parts.answer: A layer of mucus lines the stomach; or pepsin is released in an inactive form.
parts.working: 1 mark for mucus lining or an inactive form of the enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the protective layer prevents digestion of the stomach wall.
parts.answer: The mucus coats the wall so pepsin cannot reach and act on the protein of the wall cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: mucus coats the wall; 1 mark: pepsin cannot reach the protein of the cells.

practice.stem: An enzyme was tested with four substrates. Rate (arbitrary units): A: 40; B: 2; C: 38; D: 0. Substrates A and C have similar shapes; B and D have very different shapes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which substrate is most likely to be the enzyme's natural substrate?
parts.answer: A
parts.working: 1 mark: A gives the highest rate and the best fit of shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for substrates B and D.
parts.answer: Their shapes do not fit the active site, so few or no enzyme–substrate complexes form and the rate is very low.
parts.working: 1 mark: shape does not fit the active site; 1 mark: few or no enzyme–substrate complexes form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why substrate C also gives a high rate.
parts.answer: Its shape is complementary to the active site, so it fits and forms enzyme–substrate complexes.
parts.working: 1 mark: shape complementary to active site; 1 mark: enzyme–substrate complexes form.

practice.stem: Some people cannot digest lactose, the sugar in milk. A dairy company in Lahore makes lactose-free milk by adding the enzyme lactase, which breaks lactose into glucose and galactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why lactase breaks down lactose but not sucrose, even though both are disaccharides.
parts.answer: Lactase's active site is complementary only to lactose; sucrose has a different shape so cannot bind / form an enzyme–substrate complex.
parts.working: B1 active site complementary to lactose (specific); B1 sucrose different shape, does not fit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company adds a small amount of lactase to a large tank of milk. Explain why only a small amount of enzyme is needed.
parts.answer: Enzymes are not used up / are unchanged at the end of the reaction, so each enzyme molecule can break down many lactose molecules.
parts.working: B1 not used up / unchanged; B1 reused many times.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mutation in the gene for lactase changes one amino acid in the active site. Suggest how this could affect the enzyme.
parts.answer: The active site may change shape so lactose no longer fits; fewer or no enzyme–substrate complexes; lactose not broken down.
parts.working: 1 mark: active site shape changed; 1 mark: lactose no longer binds / enzyme does not work (or works more slowly).

practice.stem:
An enzyme was mixed with a fixed quantity of substrate at its optimum temperature. The mass of product was measured every minute.
time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
mass of product / mg: 0, 8, 16, 22, 26, 28, 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of reaction over the first 2 minutes in mg per minute.
parts.answer: 8 mg per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why no more product forms after 5 minutes.
parts.answer: All the substrate has been used up / converted to product, so there is nothing left for the enzyme to act on; the enzyme is not used up.
parts.working: B1 substrate used up; B1 enzyme still active / not used up (no enzyme–substrate complexes can form).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The experiment is repeated with twice the concentration of enzyme and the same amount of substrate. Predict the effect on the initial rate and on the final mass of product. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Initial rate higher (about double) because more active sites are available; final mass the same, 28 mg, because the amount of substrate is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: initial rate increases; 1 mark: more active sites / more enzyme–substrate complexes; 1 mark: final mass still 28 mg because same quantity of substrate.

practice.stem:
A fixed, large amount of substrate was mixed with different amounts of enzyme at 35 °C.
Enzyme (arbitrary units): 1, 2, 3, 4
Rate (arbitrary units): 5, 10, 15, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between enzyme concentration and rate.
parts.answer: Directly proportional: the rate doubles when the enzyme concentration doubles.
parts.working: 1 mark for directly proportional, with a valid example from the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the rate at 5 units of enzyme. Show your working.
parts.answer: 25 arbitrary units
parts.working: 1 mark for 5 units of enzyme × 5 arbitrary units per unit; 1 mark for 25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate would stop increasing at very high enzyme concentrations if the substrate were limited.
parts.answer: The substrate would be used up, so there are not enough substrate molecules to occupy all the active sites; the substrate is then the limiting factor.
parts.working: 1 mark: substrate becomes used up / limiting; 1 mark: not enough substrate molecules for all the active sites.

practice.stem: A mutation changes one amino acid in an enzyme at a point far away from its active site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the enzyme might still work normally after the mutation.
parts.answer: The active site and its shape are unchanged, so the substrate still fits; a change far away from the active site does not alter the shape of the active site.
parts.working: 1 mark: active site shape unchanged; 1 mark: change far away does not affect the active site.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a mutation that changes an amino acid inside the active site would affect the enzyme more strongly.
parts.answer: The active site's shape and charges decide which substrate fits; a changed amino acid can change this shape so the substrate no longer binds.
parts.working: 1 mark: active site determines which substrate binds; 1 mark: changing its amino acid can change shape so the substrate does not fit.

practice.stem: A student compares a protease and a lipase for removing stains from cloth. Blood stains contain protein and oil stains contain fat. Each stained cloth is placed in warm water with an enzyme solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable.
parts.answer: Type of enzyme (protease or lipase).
parts.working: 1 mark for type of enzyme (or type of stain as the variable being compared).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one dependent variable and how it could be measured.
parts.answer: Time taken for the stain to disappear, measured by timing or by comparing the colour of the cloth with a standard scale.
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable dependent variable (e.g. time for stain removal); 1 mark for a valid measurement method.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one control for the investigation.
parts.answer: A stained cloth in warm water with no enzyme (or with boiled enzyme), to show the enzyme is responsible for stain removal.
parts.working: 1 mark for a control with no active enzyme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the products of the reaction are released from the active site.
parts.answer: The products have a shape that no longer fits the active site, so they leave, and the active site is free to bind another substrate molecule.
parts.working: 1 mark: products no longer complementary to the active site; 1 mark: active site then free for another substrate molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row shows the approximate percentages of oxygen and carbon dioxide in expired air?
A oxygen 21 %, carbon dioxide 0.04 %
B oxygen 16 %, carbon dioxide 4 %
C oxygen 4 %, carbon dioxide 16 %
D oxygen 0.04 %, carbon dioxide 21 %
parts.answer: B oxygen 16 %, carbon dioxide 4 %
parts.working: Expired air still contains about 16 % oxygen; carbon dioxide rises to about 4 %. A gives inspired air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences, other than gas percentages, between inspired and expired air.
parts.answer: Expired air is warmer; expired air contains more water vapour (is saturated).
parts.working: B1 temperature higher in expired; B1 more water vapour in expired.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why expired air contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inspired air.
parts.answer: Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood and is used in aerobic respiration in cells; carbon dioxide is produced by respiration and carried to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out.
parts.working: B1 O₂ diffuses into blood (at alveoli); B1 O₂ used in respiration / CO₂ made by respiration; B1 CO₂ diffuses from blood into alveoli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas that makes up about 78 % of both inspired and expired air.
parts.answer: Nitrogen
parts.working: B1 nitrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the percentage of nitrogen hardly changes between inspired and expired air.
parts.answer: Nitrogen is not used (or produced) by the body in respiration, so it is breathed out unchanged.
parts.working: B1 not used / not absorbed by the body.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the percentage of carbon dioxide in inspired air.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens during quiet expiration (breathing out at rest)?
A The diaphragm contracts and flattens.
B The ribs move upwards and outwards.
C The volume of the thorax decreases and the pressure inside it increases.
D The external intercostal muscles contract.
parts.answer: C The volume of the thorax decreases and the pressure inside it increases.
parts.working: In quiet expiration the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax, the ribs move down and in and the diaphragm domes up, so thorax volume falls and pressure rises above atmospheric, pushing air out. A, B and D describe inspiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The statements describe inspiration but are in the wrong order. Write the letters in the correct order.
P  Air moves into the lungs.
Q  The diaphragm muscles and external intercostal muscles contract.
R  The pressure inside the thorax falls below atmospheric pressure.
S  The diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out.
T  The volume of the thorax increases.
parts.answer: Q, S, T, R, P
parts.working: 3 marks for fully correct order; 2 marks if one pair swapped; 1 mark if Q is first and P is last.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the approximate percentage of carbon dioxide in inspired air and in expired air.
parts.answer: Inspired air: about 0.04 %; expired air: about 4 %.
parts.working: B1 inspired air about 0.04 %; B1 expired air about 4 % (accept 3.5–4.0 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test you could use to show that expired air contains water. Give the result.
parts.answer: Breathe onto blue cobalt chloride paper (it turns pink) or onto anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (it turns from white to blue).
parts.working: B1 named test; B1 correct colour change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the approximate percentage of nitrogen in expired air.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens during inspiration?
A The diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped.
B The external intercostal muscles contract and the ribs move up and out.
C The volume of the thorax decreases and the pressure increases.
D The internal intercostal muscles contract and the ribs move down.
parts.answer: B The external intercostal muscles contract and the ribs move up and out.
parts.working: Contraction of the external intercostals raises the ribcage while the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing thoracic volume and lowering pressure. D describes forced expiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the roles of the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles in inspiration.
parts.answer: The diaphragm muscle contracts and the diaphragm flattens (moves down); the external intercostal muscles contract; the ribs move up and out; the volume of the thorax increases, so pressure falls below atmospheric and air enters.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm contracts / flattens; B1 external intercostals contract; B1 ribcage up and out; B1 volume increases and pressure decreases (air moves in).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how forced expiration, for example when blowing up a balloon, differs from quiet expiration.
parts.answer: In forced expiration the internal intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs down and in; abdominal muscles contract pushing the diaphragm up – in quiet expiration the muscles simply relax (elastic recoil).
parts.working: B1 internal intercostals contract (ribs down and in); B1 quiet expiration is passive / muscles relax / elastic recoil.

practice.stem: A student breathes in and out gently through a mouthpiece connected to two boiling tubes of limewater, X and Y. Valves make air breathed in pass through tube X and air breathed out pass through tube Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the colour change expected in tube Y (breathed out into) and explain it.
parts.answer: Limewater turns milky / cloudy quickly, because expired air contains a high concentration (about 4 %) of carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 milky / cloudy; B1 more CO₂ in expired air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tube X (air breathed in through) also turned slightly cloudy after a much longer time. Explain why.
parts.answer: Inspired (atmospheric) air contains a small amount of carbon dioxide (0.04 %).
parts.working: B1 atmosphere has a little CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be controlled to make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Volume of limewater; concentration of limewater; number of breaths / time of breathing; size of tubes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a safer and more sensitive indicator that could replace limewater, and state its colour in expired air.
parts.answer: Hydrogencarbonate indicator; turns yellow.
parts.working: B1 hydrogencarbonate indicator; B1 yellow (from red/orange).

practice.stem: A model of the thorax is made from a glass bell jar with a rubber sheet across the open bottom. Two balloons are attached to a Y-shaped glass tube passing through a stopper at the top.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the volume and the pressure inside the bell jar (representing the thorax) when the rubber sheet is pulled down.
parts.answer: Volume increases; pressure decreases.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the balloons and explain why.
parts.answer: The balloons inflate; air at higher (atmospheric) pressure outside moves in through the tube to the lower pressure inside the balloons.
parts.working: B1 balloons inflate; B1 air moves from higher to lower pressure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the body represented by (i) the rubber sheet, (ii) the balloons, (iii) the glass tube.
parts.answer: (i) diaphragm; (ii) lungs; (iii) trachea.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one way in which the model does not show breathing accurately.
parts.answer: The bell jar walls cannot move like the ribs / no intercostal muscles; the diaphragm is pulled down rather than contracting and flattening from a dome; the space between balloon and jar is large (pleural cavity is tiny).
parts.working: B1 any one valid limitation.

practice.stem:
A student's lung volume was recorded every second while resting.
Time / s: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Lung volume / dm³: 2.5, 2.8, 3.0, 2.7, 2.5, 2.8, 3.0, 2.7, 2.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed in with each breath (the tidal volume).
parts.answer: 0.5 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the breathing rate in breaths per minute.
parts.answer: 15 breaths per minute
parts.working: M1 one breath takes 4 s; A1 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed in per minute.
parts.answer: 7.5 dm³ per minute

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether the diaphragm is contracting or relaxing between 0 s and 2 s. Give a reason using the data.
parts.answer: Contracting: the lung volume is increasing (2.5 to 3.0 dm³), which is inspiration.
parts.working: B1 contracting; B1 volume increasing / breathing in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of food blocks the trachea of a man eating at a wedding. A first-aider stands behind him and makes a sudden, strong upward push just below his ribs, under the diaphragm. Explain, in terms of volume and pressure, how this can force the food out.
parts.answer: The push forces the diaphragm upwards, which suddenly reduces the volume of the thorax (lungs); the pressure of the air in the lungs rises sharply above atmospheric; the air rushes out through the trachea and pushes the food out.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm pushed up; B1 thorax / lung volume decreases; B1 pressure increases so air forced out carrying the food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the man cannot breathe in while the food completely blocks his trachea, even though his diaphragm still contracts.
parts.answer: The volume of the thorax increases and the pressure falls, but no air can flow in through the blocked trachea, so the lungs cannot fill; the trachea is the only route for air to the lungs.
parts.working: B1 pressure falls but air cannot enter; B1 trachea is the only pathway to the lungs / no air reaches alveoli.

practice.stem:
The percentage of oxygen was measured in three samples of air from one person at rest.
Inspired air: 20.9 %
Air from deep in the alveoli: 14.0 %
Expired air: 16.0 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in oxygen percentage between expired air and alveolar air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why expired air contains more oxygen than the air in the alveoli.
parts.answer: Expired air is a mixture of alveolar air and air from the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles; this air did not reach the alveoli, so no oxygen was removed from it.
parts.working: B1 expired air mixes with air in the airways; B1 no gas exchange in trachea / bronchi so this air still has about 20.9 % oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the alveolar air always contains a much higher percentage of carbon dioxide than inspired air.
parts.answer: Blood arriving at the lungs carries carbon dioxide from respiration in body cells; it diffuses from the blood into the alveolar air, where its concentration builds up between breaths.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide from respiration carried in blood; B1 diffuses from blood into alveoli.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Air moves into the lungs during inspiration because
A the lungs expand by themselves and suck air in.
B the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.
C the alveoli actively pump air inwards.
D oxygen diffuses down a concentration gradient into the trachea.
parts.answer: B the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.
parts.working: Increasing thoracic volume lowers the pressure in the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in down the pressure gradient. Lungs have no muscle of their own (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen taken into the blood each minute, in cm³, when the person breathes 12 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 cm³. Use inspired air 21 % oxygen and expired air 16 % oxygen.
parts.answer: 300 cm³ per minute
parts.working: M1 volume breathed per minute 12 × 500 = 6000 cm³; M1 oxygen removed 21 − 16 = 5 % of it; A1 6000 × 0.05 = 300 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the oxygen percentage of expired air is not close to 0 %, even though the blood leaving the lungs is almost saturated with oxygen.
parts.answer: Some air (in the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles – dead space) never reaches the alveoli and is exhaled unchanged; air in the alveoli is not fully replaced in each breath, and exchange stops when the blood is saturated.
parts.working: B1 dead space / air in airways does not take part in exchange; B1 mixes with alveolar air / haemoglobin becomes saturated.

practice.stem: A student analysed samples of air with a gas analyser. Mean results: inspired air – oxygen 21.0 %, carbon dioxide 0.04 %; expired air – oxygen 16.0 %, carbon dioxide 4.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the inspired oxygen that was absorbed by the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the carbon dioxide concentration was in expired air than in inspired air.
parts.answer: 100 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student analysed three samples of each and calculated a mean.
parts.answer: To identify anomalies and give a more reliable result.
parts.working: B1 reliability / spot anomalies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens to breathing if the external intercostal muscles were paralysed but the diaphragm still worked.
parts.answer: Breathing in would still occur, by contraction of the diaphragm, but the ribs would not move up and out, so the increase in thoracic volume (and the volume of air inhaled) would be smaller.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm alone can still increase volume; B1 smaller volume change / shallower breaths.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a puncture wound through the chest wall into the space around one lung (pleural cavity) can cause that lung to collapse.
parts.answer: Air enters the pleural cavity, so the pressure around the lung becomes equal to atmospheric pressure; when the thorax expands the pressure in the lung no longer falls below atmospheric, so the lung does not inflate and collapses (elastic recoil).
parts.working: B1 air enters / pressure equalises; B1 pressure in the lung cannot be reduced so no air enters / lung recoils.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The air pressure inside the lungs was compared with atmospheric pressure at four moments during breathing. At which moment is air flowing into the lungs?
A lung pressure 0.2 kPa above atmospheric
B lung pressure 0.3 kPa below atmospheric
C lung pressure equal to atmospheric
D lung pressure 0.1 kPa above atmospheric
parts.answer: B lung pressure 0.3 kPa below atmospheric
parts.working: Air flows from higher to lower pressure, so it enters only when lung pressure is below atmospheric (during inspiration). When the pressures are equal (C) there is no air flow; A and D are during expiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In normal breathing, describe how air is made to enter the lungs.
parts.answer: The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, increasing the volume of the thorax, so the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric and air is drawn in.
parts.working: B1 muscles contract / thorax volume increases; B1 pressure falls below atmospheric so air enters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient whose breathing muscles are paralysed is put on a ventilator. The machine pushes air into the trachea through a tube at a pressure higher than atmospheric. Compare how air enters the lungs with the ventilator and in normal breathing.
parts.answer: Ventilator: pressure in the airway is raised above atmospheric so air is pushed in and the lungs and chest expand as a result. Normal breathing: the chest expands first and the pressure in the lungs is lowered below atmospheric, so air is pulled in. In both, air moves from higher to lower pressure.
parts.working: B1 ventilator raises pressure (positive pressure) / pushes air in; B1 normal breathing lowers pressure in thorax (air drawn in); B1 in both, air flows from higher to lower pressure / volume change of lungs in both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the patient breathes out when the ventilator stops pushing air in.
parts.answer: The stretched lungs and chest wall recoil (elastic recoil), reducing the volume and raising the pressure, so air leaves.
parts.working: B1 elastic recoil of lungs/chest decreases volume and raises pressure.

practice.stem:
Two students each took the deepest possible breath and then breathed out as far as possible through a tube into an upturned, calibrated bottle full of water. The volume of water pushed out was recorded.
Student P: 3.1, 3.3, 3.2 dm³
Student Q: 4.7, 4.5, 4.6 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume of air breathed out by each student.
parts.answer: P 3.2 dm³; Q 4.6 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much larger Q's mean volume is than P's, as a percentage of P's mean. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the students were able to breathe out more air in this test than in a normal breath at rest.
parts.answer: In forced expiration the internal intercostal muscles contract to pull the ribs down and in, and the abdominal muscles push the diaphragm further up, so the thorax volume becomes smaller than in quiet expiration.
parts.working: B1 internal intercostal muscles contract; B1 abdominal muscles push diaphragm up / volume reduced more.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the volume collected may be less than the true volume of air breathed out.
parts.answer: Any two: some air escapes round the mouthpiece or nose not closed; some carbon dioxide dissolves in the water; the student did not breathe in fully first; the water level was read inaccurately / bottle not calibrated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid sources of error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence shows the correct pathway of air into the lungs?
A larynx → trachea → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
B larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
C trachea → larynx → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
D larynx → bronchi → trachea → bronchioles → alveoli
parts.answer: B larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
parts.working: Air passes the larynx, then the trachea, which divides into two bronchi, which branch into bronchioles ending in alveoli. A puts bronchioles before bronchi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of gas exchange surfaces in animals.
parts.answer: Large surface area; thin surface (short diffusion distance); good blood supply; good ventilation with air.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For one of these features, explain how it is achieved in human lungs.
parts.answer: e.g. millions of alveoli give a large surface area / alveolus wall and capillary wall are each one cell thick / dense network of capillaries around each alveolus / breathing replaces air.
parts.working: B1 feature correctly linked to lung structure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the structure described: (i) the box-shaped organ at the top of the trachea that contains the vocal cords; (ii) the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs; (iii) the narrow tubes that branch from the bronchi.
parts.answer: (i) Larynx; (ii) alveoli; (iii) bronchioles.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the blood vessels that surround each alveolus.
parts.answer: Capillaries
parts.working: B1 capillaries.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of the lungs does NOT help gas exchange in the alveoli?
A thin walls of the alveoli
B a good supply of blood capillaries
C a large total surface area
D a thick layer of mucus lining the alveoli
parts.answer: D a thick layer of mucus lining the alveoli
parts.working: A thick layer would increase the diffusion distance and slow gas exchange; alveoli have only a thin film of moisture. A, B and C all increase the rate of diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the structure described.
(i) the tube that carries air from the larynx to the chest and is held open by rings of cartilage
(ii) one of the two tubes that branch from the trachea, each leading to one lung
(iii) the narrow tubes that branch many times inside each lung
(iv) the tiny air sacs where gas exchange takes place
parts.answer: (i) trachea (ii) bronchus (iii) bronchioles (iv) alveoli
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) The trachea divides into two bronchi.
(ii) Most gas exchange happens in the bronchi.
(iii) The walls of the alveoli are only one cell thick.
(iv) Oxygen diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
parts.answer: (i) true (ii) false (iii) true (iv) false
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Correct one of the false statements.
parts.answer: Most gas exchange happens in the alveoli; or oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood.
parts.working: B1 either correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During an asthma attack, the muscle in the walls of the bronchioles contracts, making them narrower. Name the tubes that lead from the trachea to the bronchioles.
parts.answer: bronchi
parts.working: B1 bronchi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person having an asthma attack feels short of breath.
parts.answer: Narrower bronchioles let less air reach the alveoli each breath, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood (and less carbon dioxide is removed).
parts.working: B1 less air reaches alveoli; B1 less oxygen into blood / less gas exchange.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Extra mucus is also made during an asthma attack. Name the cells that make mucus.
parts.answer: goblet cells
parts.working: B1 goblet cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of the C-shaped rings of cartilage in the trachea?
A They trap dust and pathogens.
B They keep the trachea open during changes in pressure.
C They produce mucus.
D They allow gas exchange with the blood.
parts.answer: B They keep the trachea open during changes in pressure.
parts.working: Cartilage supports the trachea so it does not collapse when air pressure falls during inspiration. Mucus is produced by goblet cells (C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of (i) goblet cells and (ii) ciliated cells in the trachea.
parts.answer: (i) Make mucus, which traps dust and pathogens; (ii) cilia beat (waft) to move mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed.
parts.working: B1 goblet – mucus traps particles / pathogens; B1 ciliated – cilia beat to move mucus upwards / away from lungs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tobacco smoke paralyses cilia. Explain why smokers are more likely to suffer from chest infections.
parts.answer: Cilia stop beating, so mucus is not removed; mucus containing bacteria / pathogens collects in the airways and lungs; pathogens multiply and cause infection (bronchitis / coughing to remove mucus).
parts.working: B1 cilia do not move mucus; B1 mucus builds up / trapped pathogens remain; B1 pathogens multiply in lungs → infection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a single spherical alveolus of radius 0.1 mm. Use surface area = 4πr² and volume = 4/3πr³. Give your answer in mm⁻¹.
parts.answer: 30 mm⁻¹ (ratio 30 : 1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lungs made of millions of small alveoli are more efficient than lungs made of one large sac of the same total volume.
parts.answer: Small alveoli have a much larger surface area to volume ratio, so the total surface area for diffusion is far greater.
parts.working: B1 larger SA:V / larger total surface area; B1 faster / more diffusion of gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the gas exchange surface in the lungs must be kept moist.
parts.answer: Oxygen must dissolve in water before it can diffuse across the cell membranes.
parts.working: B1 gases dissolve before diffusing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how carbon dioxide moves from the blood plasma into the alveolus.
parts.answer: By diffusion, from a high concentration in the blood (capillary) to a low concentration in alveolar air, across the capillary and alveolus walls.
parts.working: B1 diffusion; B1 down concentration gradient from blood to alveolus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the concentration gradient for oxygen between alveolar air and the blood is maintained.
parts.answer: Breathing (ventilation) keeps bringing fresh air with high oxygen; blood flow constantly carries oxygenated blood away and brings deoxygenated blood.
parts.working: B1 ventilation; B1 blood circulation / flow.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly describes the cells lining the trachea?
A goblet cells beat to move mucus down into the lungs; ciliated cells make mucus
B goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; ciliated cells beat to move the mucus up towards the throat
C goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; ciliated cells beat to move the mucus down into the lungs
D goblet cells engulf pathogens; ciliated cells make mucus
parts.answer: B goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; ciliated cells beat to move the mucus up towards the throat
parts.working: Goblet cells secrete mucus, which traps particles and pathogens; cilia beat to sweep the mucus up and away from the lungs to the throat, where it is swallowed. C has the direction wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway of an oxygen molecule from the air in an alveolus to the inside of a red blood cell. Name the structures it passes through.
parts.answer: It dissolves in the moisture lining the alveolus, diffuses through the thin wall of the alveolus (one cell thick), then through the wall of the capillary (one cell thick), into the blood plasma and then across the membrane of the red blood cell.
parts.working: B1 dissolves in moisture / film of water; B1 through alveolus wall and capillary wall; B1 through plasma into red blood cell (membrane).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oxygen continues to diffuse in this direction.
parts.answer: Breathing keeps bringing fresh air with a high oxygen concentration into the alveoli, and the blood flow carries oxygenated blood away and brings deoxygenated blood, so a concentration gradient is maintained.
parts.working: B1 ventilation keeps alveolar oxygen high; B1 blood flow removes oxygen / brings blood low in oxygen.

practice.stem: A student viewed a prepared slide of lung tissue with a microscope and drew one alveolus. The image of the alveolus measured 25 mm across at a magnification of ×100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the alveolus in µm.
parts.answer: 250 µm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mm; A1 × 1000 = 250 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student says that the alveoli look like empty spaces separated by very thin walls. State how this structure helps gas exchange.
parts.answer: The thin walls give a short diffusion distance; many small alveoli give a very large surface area.
parts.working: B1 thin walls / short distance; B1 large surface area.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature, other than thin walls and large surface area, that the student would expect to see close to each alveolus if the tissue was stained to show blood.
parts.answer: Many blood capillaries (containing red blood cells) surrounding each alveolus.
parts.working: B1 capillaries / rich blood supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of an alveolus and its capillary make diffusion of oxygen into the blood rapid.
parts.answer: Alveolus wall and capillary wall are each one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance; moist lining – oxygen dissolves; huge total surface area of millions of alveoli; blood flow carries oxygen away, and breathing replaces alveolar air, maintaining a steep concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: thin walls / short distance; moist surface; large surface area (many alveoli); rich capillary network; blood flow maintains gradient; ventilation maintains gradient; red cells pressed close to wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In emphysema the walls between neighbouring alveoli break down, forming fewer, larger air sacs. Explain why people with emphysema become breathless during mild exercise.
parts.answer: The surface area for gas exchange is reduced, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood per minute; not enough oxygen reaches the muscles for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 reduced surface area; B1 less oxygen absorbed / less oxygen for respiration.

practice.stem: A student examines fresh sheep lungs, attached to the trachea, obtained from a butcher's shop in Rawalpindi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how the student would show that the trachea is held open by cartilage.
parts.answer: Squeeze the trachea – it springs back into shape; or cut a section and observe C-shaped rings that are firm and do not collapse.
parts.working: B1 press / squeeze trachea; B1 it returns to shape / does not collapse (rings visible).

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the student pumps air into the lungs through the trachea with a bellows, the lungs inflate, then deflate when the bellows are removed. Explain why they deflate.
parts.answer: Lung tissue is elastic and recoils.
parts.working: B1 elastic tissue recoils.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety or hygiene precaution when handling fresh animal tissue.
parts.answer: Wear gloves / wash hands afterwards / use a sharp scalpel cutting away from the body / disinfect surfaces.
parts.working: B1 any one sensible precaution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An adult's lungs contain about 480 million alveoli, each with a surface area of 0.15 mm². Calculate the total surface area in m². (1 m² = 1 000 000 mm²)
parts.answer: 72 m²

parts.label: b
parts.text: In cystic fibrosis the mucus in the airways is very thick and sticky. Suggest and explain two effects this has on gas exchange and health.
parts.answer: Mucus blocks bronchioles, so less air reaches some alveoli – less oxygen diffuses into blood / lower effective surface area; cilia cannot move the thick mucus, so trapped bacteria stay in the lungs and cause frequent infections; a thicker layer increases diffusion distance.
parts.working: Two effects, each B1 effect + B1 explanation: blocked airways → less ventilation / less O₂ uptake; mucus not cleared by cilia → pathogens remain → infections; increased diffusion distance → slower diffusion.

practice.stem: In a healthy lung the distance between the air in an alveolus and the blood is about 0.5 µm. In a patient with pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue thickens the walls so that the distance becomes about 2.5 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the diffusion distance is in the patient.
parts.answer: 5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient becomes breathless when walking upstairs.
parts.answer: The longer diffusion distance means oxygen diffuses into the blood more slowly; less oxygen is supplied to the muscles for aerobic respiration during exercise; the brain detects the build-up of carbon dioxide, so the person breathes faster and deeper / feels breathless.
parts.working: B1 slower diffusion of oxygen (and CO₂); B1 less oxygen for respiration in muscles; B1 carbon dioxide builds up / breathing rate increases / breathless.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the patient's lungs also have a smaller volume than a healthy person's lungs.
parts.answer: The scarred / stiff walls cannot stretch as much, so the alveoli do not inflate fully.
parts.working: B1 stiff tissue cannot expand / alveoli do not fill.

practice.stem: The trachea of an adult is about 120 mm long. In a healthy person, the cilia move mucus up the trachea at about 5 mm per minute. Scientists found that after several days of breathing heavy winter smog, the rate fell to 1.5 mm per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for mucus to travel the length of the trachea (i) in a healthy person and (ii) after breathing heavily polluted smog.
parts.answer: (i) 24 minutes (ii) 80 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the cells lining the trachea normally protect the gas exchange surfaces.
parts.answer: Goblet cells secrete mucus, which traps dust particles and pathogens; ciliated cells have cilia that beat to move the mucus up the trachea to the throat, where it is swallowed, so the particles and pathogens do not reach the alveoli.
parts.working: B1 goblet cells make mucus; B1 mucus traps particles / pathogens; B1 cilia beat / sweep mucus up to throat away from lungs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why people living in a city during winter smog are more likely to suffer from chest infections.
parts.answer: Mucus is moved more slowly so it stays longer in the airways; trapped pathogens have more time to multiply and reach the lungs / bronchi and cause infection.
parts.working: B1 slower clearance / mucus builds up; B1 pathogens remain longer / reach lungs / breed in mucus.

practice.stem:
Lung surface areas and body masses of two mammals:
Mouse: lung surface area 0.07 m², body mass 0.025 kg
Human: lung surface area 70 m², body mass 70 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the lungs per kg of body mass for each mammal.
parts.answer: mouse 2.8 m² per kg; human 1.0 m² per kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mouse needs a larger lung surface area per kg of body mass than the human.
parts.answer: A mouse has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat faster; it must respire faster per kg to keep its body temperature constant, so it needs more oxygen per kg each minute.
parts.working: B1 mouse loses heat faster (large SA:V); B1 higher rate of respiration per kg / more oxygen needed per kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two features, other than a large surface area, that both mammals' gas exchange surfaces must have.
parts.answer: Any two: thin (short diffusion distance); moist; good blood supply; good ventilation with air.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change in the blood is detected by the brain and causes an increase in the rate and depth of breathing during exercise?
A an increase in glucose concentration
B an increase in carbon dioxide concentration
C a decrease in carbon dioxide concentration
D an increase in oxygen concentration
parts.answer: B an increase in carbon dioxide concentration
parts.working: More respiration in muscles releases more CO₂ into the blood; the brain detects the rise and increases breathing. A rise in oxygen (D) would not occur during exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the breathing changes during exercise.
parts.answer: Breathing rate increases; depth of breathing (volume per breath) increases.
parts.working: B1 rate increases; B1 depth increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these changes are needed.
parts.answer: Muscles contract more so they need more energy; more aerobic respiration requires more oxygen; more carbon dioxide must be removed.
parts.working: B1 more energy / respiration in muscles; B1 more oxygen supplied; B1 more carbon dioxide removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which part of the body detects an increase in carbon dioxide concentration in the blood and controls breathing.
parts.answer: The brain
parts.working: B1 brain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two effects on breathing when the carbon dioxide concentration in the blood rises.
parts.answer: Breathing rate increases and depth of breathing increases.
parts.working: B1 rate; B1 depth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is dangerous to allow carbon dioxide to build up in the blood.
parts.answer: It forms an acid / lowers blood pH, which can denature enzymes (and is toxic).
parts.working: B1 lowers pH / acidic / affects enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How does breathing change when a person starts to run?
A The rate increases but the depth stays the same.
B The rate and the depth both increase.
C The depth increases but the rate decreases.
D The rate and depth both stay the same but more oxygen is absorbed per breath.
parts.answer: B The rate and the depth both increase.
parts.working: During physical activity both the breathing rate and the depth of each breath increase, so more air is exchanged per minute. A misses the increase in depth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student holds her breath for 30 seconds. Name the gas that builds up in her blood.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which organ detects this change.
parts.answer: the brain
parts.working: B1 brain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When she starts breathing again, she breathes faster and more deeply for a short time. Explain why.
parts.answer: The higher carbon dioxide concentration in the blood is detected by the brain, which increases the rate and depth of breathing to remove the extra carbon dioxide (and take in oxygen).
parts.working: B1 high CO₂ detected / brain sends impulses to breathing muscles; B1 faster deeper breathing removes CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the flow chart using suitable words.

exercise starts → muscle cells need more ______ → rate of ______ in muscles increases → more ______ is produced and passes into the blood → this is detected by the ______ → rate and ______ of breathing increase
parts.answer: energy; respiration; carbon dioxide; brain; depth
parts.working: 1 mark per gap.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A runner's breathing rate stays high for several minutes after finishing a race. What is the main reason?
A The muscles are still contracting strongly.
B Extra oxygen is needed to break down lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration.
C The lungs need time to fill with carbon dioxide.
D Glucose must be absorbed from the gut.
parts.answer: B Extra oxygen is needed to break down lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration.
parts.working: Lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration is broken down in the liver using oxygen (the oxygen debt), so breathing stays high. The muscles have stopped working hard (A).

practice.stem:
A student in Quetta measured her breathing rate three times at rest and three times immediately after 2 minutes of skipping.
At rest (breaths per minute): 14, 16, 15
After exercise: 30, 33, 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean breathing rate at rest and after exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 15 breaths per minute; after exercise: 31 breaths per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean breathing rate. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student should measure the breathing rate.
parts.answer: Count the number of breaths (rises of the chest) in one minute using a stopwatch; repeat and take a mean.
parts.working: B1 count breaths / chest movements; B1 for a timed period (60 s) with a stopwatch.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Type / intensity of exercise (e.g. step-ups at a set rate); duration of exercise; same person; time of resting before measuring.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A football player in Lahore wore a mask attached to a breathing monitor.
At rest: rate 14 breaths per minute, tidal volume 0.5 dm³
After 6 minutes of exercise: rate 28 breaths per minute, tidal volume 2.1 dm³
Breathing rate 2, 4, 6 and 8 minutes after exercise stopped: 24, 20, 16, 14 breaths per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in tidal volume between rest and 6 minutes of exercise.
parts.answer: 1.6 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the changes in breathing rate after the exercise stopped.
parts.answer: Breathing rate falls gradually from 28 to 14 breaths per minute over about 8 minutes; it did not return to rest at once.
parts.working: B1 decreases; B1 gradual / slowly / data quote showing it takes several minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the breathing rate did not return to the resting value immediately after exercise.
parts.answer: During exercise some anaerobic respiration produced lactic acid (oxygen debt); after exercise extra oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration in liver cells to break down the lactic acid; high carbon dioxide levels take time to fall.
parts.working: B1 lactic acid built up / anaerobic respiration; B1 oxygen debt – oxygen needed to remove lactic acid (in the liver); B1 CO₂ still high / lactic acid carried in blood to liver.

practice.stem:
A student ran on a treadmill at different speeds. Her breathing was measured after 3 minutes at each speed.
Speed / km per hour: 0, 4, 8, 12
Volume per breath / dm³: 0.5, 1.0, 1.8, 2.4
Breathing rate / breaths per minute: 12, 16, 24, 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at each speed.
parts.answer: 0 km/h: 6.0 dm³, 4 km/h: 16.0 dm³, 8 km/h: 43.2 dm³, 12 km/h: 76.8 dm³
parts.working: M1 tidal volume × rate; A1 all four correct (6.0, 16.0, 43.2, 76.8).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the volume per minute is at 12 km/h than at rest.
parts.answer: 12.8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the volume of air breathed per minute increases with running speed.
parts.answer: Faster running needs more energy, so the muscles respire faster; they need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide; the increase in blood carbon dioxide is detected by the brain, which increases the rate and depth of breathing.
parts.working: B1 more (aerobic) respiration in muscles; B1 more oxygen needed / more CO₂ produced; B1 CO₂ detected by brain → rate and depth increase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Climbers who go to high mountain base camps in Gilgit-Baltistan breathe air that still contains 21 % oxygen, but the air is much less dense, so each breath contains fewer oxygen molecules. Suggest why climbers breathe faster and deeper than normal even when resting at base camp.
