parts.answer: Less oxygen enters the blood with each breath, so less oxygen reaches respiring cells; the body responds by increasing the rate and depth of breathing to take in more air per minute, so that enough oxygen is absorbed.
parts.working: B1 fewer oxygen molecules per breath / less oxygen diffuses into blood; B1 cells need oxygen for aerobic respiration; B1 faster, deeper breathing increases volume of air per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why climbing a slope at high altitude makes climbers more breathless than the same climb at sea level.
parts.answer: Exercise increases the demand for oxygen and carbon dioxide production, but each breath supplies less oxygen; breathing has to increase even more to meet the demand.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen needed for muscle respiration; B1 less available per breath so breathing must increase further / breathless.

practice.stem:
A student did step-ups for different lengths of time. After each exercise period she recorded how long it took for her breathing rate to return to its resting value.
Duration of exercise / minutes: 1, 2, 3, 4
Recovery time / minutes: 1.5, 2.5, 4.0, 6.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the duration of exercise and the recovery time.
parts.answer: The longer the exercise, the longer the recovery time; the recovery time increases more steeply for longer exercise (+1.0, +1.5, +2.0 minutes).
parts.working: B1 positive relationship; B1 increases more steeply / not proportional, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in recovery time between 1 minute and 4 minutes of exercise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the breathing rate stays high after the exercise stops.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide (and lactic acid) built up during exercise must be removed; extra oxygen is needed to break down lactic acid (repay the oxygen debt), so breathing stays fast until the blood carbon dioxide concentration returns to normal.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ still high in blood / detected by brain; B1 oxygen needed to remove lactic acid / oxygen debt.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: the same student; type / intensity of exercise (e.g. same step height and stepping rate); starting from rest each time with time to recover; same temperature; same method of counting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Two swimmers at a club in Karachi swam 200 m at the same speed. One trains every day; the other rarely exercises.
Trained: breathing rate 26 breaths per minute, volume per breath 1.8 dm³
Untrained: breathing rate 40 breaths per minute, volume per breath 1.1 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between the breathing of the two swimmers during the swim.
parts.answer: The trained swimmer's breathing rate rose less (to 26 compared with 40 breaths per minute) and each breath was deeper (1.8 dm³ compared with 1.1 dm³).
parts.working: B1 rate lower in trained swimmer with data; B1 depth greater in trained swimmer with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the trained swimmer can take deeper breaths.
parts.answer: Any two: stronger diaphragm and intercostal muscles; larger lung volume / chest expands more after training; better control of breathing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible suggestions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute by each swimmer during the swim.
parts.answer: trained 46.8 dm³; untrained 44.0 dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how physical activity leads to an increase in the rate and depth of breathing.
parts.answer: Muscles respire faster to release more energy; more carbon dioxide is produced and enters the blood; the increase in carbon dioxide concentration (fall in pH) is detected by the brain; the brain sends impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm to contract faster and more strongly.
parts.working: B1 increased respiration in muscles; B1 more CO₂ in blood; B1 detected by brain; B1 nerve impulses to breathing muscles (diaphragm / intercostals).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at rest (12 breaths per minute, 0.5 dm³ per breath) and during exercise (30 breaths per minute, 2.4 dm³ per breath). State how many times greater the exercise value is.
parts.answer: Rest 6 dm³/min; exercise 72 dm³/min; 12 times greater.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of the duration of exercise on breathing rate in students. Include the variables, the method and how you would make the results reliable.
parts.answer: Independent: duration of exercise (e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 minutes of step-ups); dependent: breaths per minute measured immediately after; control: type and rate of exercise (metronome), same step height, same students / similar age and fitness, rest until resting rate returns between trials; measure resting rate first; count chest movements for 1 minute with stopwatch; repeat 3 times per duration or use several students and calculate means; safety: stop if dizzy, students with asthma excluded.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: independent variable with at least 5 values; dependent measured correctly (count breaths for 1 min, stopwatch); two controlled variables (B1 each, max 2); return to resting rate between trials; repeats / means; relevant safety precaution.

practice.stem:
Two students did the same 3-minute exercise. Breathing rates / breaths per minute:
Resting (3 readings): A – 16, 15, 17; B – 12, 14, 22
Minutes after exercise 2, 4, 6, 8: A – 30, 22, 16, 16; B – 20, 13, 13, 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean resting breathing rate of student B without it.
parts.answer: Anomaly: 22 (third resting reading of B); mean 13 breaths per minute.
parts.working: B1 22 identified; B1 (12 + 14)/2 = 13.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many minutes after exercise each student's breathing rate first returned to within 1 breath per minute of their resting mean (A resting mean 16).
parts.answer: A: 6 minutes; B: 4 minutes.
parts.working: B1 A: 6 min (22 at 4 min is too high; 16 at 6 min); B1 B: 4 min (13 equals resting mean of 13).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which student is fitter and give one reason.
parts.answer: Student B; lower resting breathing rate and faster return to resting rate after exercise (smaller oxygen debt).
parts.working: B1 B; B1 lower resting rate or quicker recovery.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four athletes had their breathing measured during a training session. Which athlete breathed the largest volume of air per minute?
A 30 breaths per minute, 0.4 dm³ per breath
B 20 breaths per minute, 0.8 dm³ per breath
C 40 breaths per minute, 0.3 dm³ per breath
D 16 breaths per minute, 0.9 dm³ per breath
parts.answer: B 20 breaths per minute, 0.8 dm³ per breath
parts.working: Volume per minute = rate × depth: A 12.0, B 16.0, C 12.0, D 14.4 dm³ per minute. C has the fastest rate but shallow breaths, so a smaller volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the intensity of exercise affects the breathing rate of students. Use step-ups on a bench: intensity can be changed by changing the number of steps per minute (use a metronome). Include what you would change and measure, the variables you would control, how you would make the results reliable and one safety consideration.
parts.answer: Use stepping rates of e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 steps per minute set by a metronome. Before each trial the student rests until the breathing rate is at its resting value; count breaths for 1 minute at rest. Step for a fixed time (e.g. 2 minutes) on the same bench, then immediately count breaths for 1 minute (or count for 30 s and double). Keep the same student(s), bench height and duration. Repeat each intensity three times (or use several students) and calculate means. Stop if the student feels unwell; students with asthma or heart problems should not take part.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV stepping rate with ≥4 values; DV breaths per minute counted for a fixed time immediately after; measure resting rate first / rest between trials until back to resting rate; same duration of exercise; same bench height; same person / similar age, sex, fitness; repeat and calculate mean; safety (stop if dizzy; exclude those with medical conditions).

parts.label: a
parts.text: During hard exercise the athlete absorbs 3.0 dm³ of oxygen per minute. Each dm³ of air breathed in gives 0.05 dm³ of oxygen to the blood. Calculate the volume of air the athlete must breathe each minute.
parts.answer: 60 dm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each breath has a volume of 2.0 dm³. Calculate the breathing rate needed.
parts.answer: 30 breaths per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: At rest the athlete absorbs 0.25 dm³ of oxygen per minute. Calculate how many times more oxygen is absorbed per minute during hard exercise.
parts.answer: 12 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the muscles need so much more oxygen during hard exercise.
parts.answer: The muscles contract more and need much more energy; this is released by aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen.
parts.working: B1 more energy needed for muscle contraction; B1 aerobic respiration uses oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student breathes in and out of a paper bag for one minute while sitting still. The percentage of carbon dioxide in the air in the bag rises. Explain why the student's breathing rate and depth increase, even though the student is not exercising.
parts.answer: The air breathed in from the bag has a higher carbon dioxide concentration, so the concentration gradient between the blood and the alveoli is smaller; less carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood, so its concentration in the blood rises; this is detected by the brain, which sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to increase the rate and depth of breathing.
parts.working: B1 more CO₂ in inspired air; B1 smaller gradient / less CO₂ diffuses out of blood; B1 blood CO₂ rises and is detected by brain; B1 brain stimulates breathing muscles (diaphragm/intercostals) → faster, deeper breathing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this experiment should be stopped after a short time.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide would keep rising and oxygen falling in the bag, which could make the student dizzy or ill.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ builds up / O₂ falls → unsafe.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A lactic acid only
B carbon dioxide and water
C ethanol and carbon dioxide
D lactic acid and carbon dioxide
parts.answer: C ethanol and carbon dioxide
parts.working: Yeast respires anaerobically to ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is the product in human muscle; carbon dioxide and water are the products of aerobic respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.
parts.answer: glucose → lactic acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which anaerobic respiration in yeast differs from anaerobic respiration in muscle.
parts.answer: yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle produces lactic acid (no carbon dioxide)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.
parts.answer: aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not; aerobic releases much more energy per glucose; aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water, anaerobic produces lactic acid
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two, both sides stated or clearly implied.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each type of respiration, state whether each substance is used or produced, or is not involved.
Type: aerobic (human); anaerobic (human muscle); anaerobic (yeast).
Substances: oxygen; carbon dioxide; lactic acid; ethanol.
parts.answer: aerobic: oxygen used, CO₂ produced, no lactic acid, no ethanol; anaerobic muscle: no oxygen, no CO₂, lactic acid produced, no ethanol; anaerobic yeast: no oxygen, CO₂ produced, no lactic acid, ethanol produced
parts.working: B1 for each correct substance across all three types (oxygen; carbon dioxide; lactic acid; ethanol).

practice.stem:
A student puts 50 cm³ of warm sugar solution and 5 g of dried yeast into a conical flask and stretches a balloon over its neck. The circumference of the balloon is measured every 10 minutes.
time / min | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40
circumference / cm | 8.0 | 9.5 | 13.0 | 17.5 | 21.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in circumference between 0 and 40 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas that inflates the balloon and the process that produces it.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide; (anaerobic) respiration by yeast
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that should be kept constant if the experiment is repeated with different sugars.
parts.answer: temperature / mass of yeast / volume or concentration of sugar solution / size of flask
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Lactic acid bacteria, used to make yoghurt, respire anaerobically on the sugar in milk. Which product is made?
A ethanol and carbon dioxide
B lactic acid
C oxygen
D glucose
parts.answer: B lactic acid
parts.working: These bacteria produce lactic acid by anaerobic respiration; the acid lowers the pH and makes the milk protein set. Ethanol is made by yeast, not by these bacteria (A). Oxygen is not produced (C); glucose is a substrate, not a product (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sprinter runs at top speed for 15 seconds. Her muscles do not receive enough oxygen. Explain why her muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration.
parts.answer: the oxygen supply to the muscles cannot meet the demand for aerobic respiration, so glucose is broken down anaerobically to release energy more quickly
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen supply is too slow to meet demand. 1 mark: anaerobic respiration can still release some energy without oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the substance produced by anaerobic respiration in yeast, other than carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: ethanol
parts.working: Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas that makes bread dough rise when yeast respires anaerobically.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide
parts.working: Carbon dioxide forms bubbles in the dough.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After vigorous exercise, what happens to the lactic acid that has built up in the muscles?
A It is converted to glucose in the muscles and stored.
B It is carried in the blood to the liver and broken down by aerobic respiration.
C It is excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
D It is converted to ethanol in the liver.
parts.answer: B It is carried in the blood to the liver and broken down by aerobic respiration.
parts.working: Lactic acid is transported in the blood to the liver, where it is broken down by aerobic respiration, using the extra oxygen taken in (the oxygen debt). It is not mainly excreted by the kidneys.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement correctly compares anaerobic respiration with aerobic respiration?
A Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule.
B Anaerobic respiration takes place only in mitochondria.
C Anaerobic respiration releases more energy per glucose molecule.
D Anaerobic respiration uses oxygen but produces no carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: A Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule.
parts.working: Glucose is only partly broken down in anaerobic respiration, so much less energy is released per glucose molecule. It takes place in the cytoplasm, not mitochondria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After running up four flights of stairs, a student continues to breathe deeply and quickly for several minutes. Explain why.
parts.answer: during the run muscles respired anaerobically and made lactic acid; an oxygen debt built up; deep, fast breathing supplies extra oxygen; oxygen is used for aerobic respiration of the lactic acid in the liver; fast heart rate carries lactic acid to the liver
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: anaerobic respiration during exercise (not enough oxygen supplied); lactic acid produced / builds up; oxygen debt; extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid; by aerobic respiration in the liver; high heart rate transports lactic acid in the blood to the liver.

practice.stem:
A student investigates the effect of glucose concentration on anaerobic respiration in yeast. Yeast suspension and glucose solution are placed in a test-tube with a delivery tube dipping into water, and the number of gas bubbles released in 2 minutes is counted. Each concentration is tested three times.
glucose concentration / % | bubbles: trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3
0 | 0 | 0 | 0
2 | 8 | 10 | 9
4 | 17 | 16 | 31
6 | 24 | 25 | 26
8 | 26 | 25 | 27

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean number of bubbles for 4 % glucose, ignoring the anomalous result.
parts.answer: anomaly: 31 (trial 3 at 4 %); mean 16.5 (accept 17)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas in the bubbles.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of glucose concentration on the rate of respiration shown by these results.
parts.answer: rate increases as glucose increases from 0 to 6 %, then levels off; glucose is the substrate for respiration, so more glucose gives more CO₂; above 6 % something else (e.g. amount of yeast / enzymes / temperature) limits the rate
parts.working: B1 increases then levels off (6–8 %); B1 glucose is used / respired to release CO₂; B1 another factor limits / yeast enzymes working at maximum rate.

practice.stem: A student boils some glucose solution, cools it and then adds yeast. The mixture is put in a test-tube and covered with a layer of vegetable oil. A delivery tube leads from the test-tube into a second tube containing limewater.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the glucose solution was boiled and then cooled before the yeast was added.
parts.answer: boiling removes dissolved oxygen (and kills microorganisms); cooling so the yeast is not killed / enzymes not denatured
parts.working: B1 remove oxygen; B1 cool to avoid killing yeast.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the layer of oil.
parts.answer: stops oxygen (air) dissolving in the mixture

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe and explain the change seen in the limewater.
parts.answer: turns milky / cloudy because carbon dioxide is released by anaerobic respiration of the yeast
parts.working: B1 milky; B1 carbon dioxide from respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A baker in Lahore mixes yeast, sugar and flour with warm water to make naan dough and leaves it in a warm place. The dough doubles in size. Explain why.
parts.answer: yeast respires anaerobically, using sugar; carbon dioxide gas is produced; bubbles of gas are trapped in the dough so it rises; warmth gives a suitable temperature for the yeast enzymes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ethanol made by the yeast is not present in the cooked naan.
parts.answer: it evaporates during baking (high temperature)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sprinter in a 100 m race relies largely on anaerobic respiration in the leg muscles, while a marathon runner relies mainly on aerobic respiration. Explain why.
parts.answer: a sprint needs a lot of energy very quickly; the heart and lungs cannot supply oxygen fast enough; anaerobic respiration releases energy without oxygen for a short time; in a marathon the pace is slower so enough oxygen is delivered for aerobic respiration
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a sprinter cannot keep running at top speed for 10 minutes.
parts.answer: lactic acid builds up in muscles causing fatigue / pain; anaerobic respiration releases little energy per glucose
parts.working: B1 lactic acid build-up; B1 causes muscle fatigue / cramp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During 5 minutes of hard exercise, a cyclist's muscles needed 3.0 dm³ of oxygen per minute, but her lungs and heart supplied only 2.4 dm³ per minute. Calculate the total oxygen shortfall during the exercise.
parts.answer: 3.0 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the shortfall is repaid after the exercise.
parts.answer: breathing remains deep and fast so extra oxygen is taken in above the resting rate (oxygen debt); the oxygen is used to break down lactic acid by aerobic respiration in the liver; heart rate stays high to transport lactic acid to the liver
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When a field of maize is flooded for several days, the soil becomes waterlogged and the roots run short of oxygen. State the products of anaerobic respiration in the root cells.
parts.answer: ethanol and carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 (both).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the plants absorb fewer mineral ions from waterlogged soil.
parts.answer: anaerobic respiration releases much less energy; mineral ions are taken up by active transport, which needs energy; so less uptake (ethanol may also damage root cells)
parts.working: B1 less energy released; B1 ion uptake by active transport; B1 active transport needs energy from respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In anaerobic respiration in yeast, 1 mol of glucose produces 2 mol of carbon dioxide. How many moles of carbon dioxide are produced from 0.5 mol of glucose?
A 0.5
B 1
C 2
D 4
parts.answer: B 1
parts.working: 0.5 mol glucose × 2 = 1 mol carbon dioxide. A is the amount of glucose; C is the amount for 1 mol of glucose; D multiplies by 8.

practice.stem: During 8 minutes of jogging, a student's body built up an oxygen debt of 6.0 dm³. After she stopped, her breathing used 1.5 dm³ of oxygen per minute more than it did at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of minutes she needs to repay her oxygen debt.
parts.working: Oxygen debt ÷ extra oxygen per minute = 6.0 ÷ 1.5 = 4 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the oxygen debt has to be repaid after exercise.
parts.answer: the extra oxygen is needed to convert the lactic acid back into glucose (mainly in the liver) and to resynthesise / restore the stores used during exercise, ending the anaerobic respiration
parts.working: 1 mark: lactic acid is broken down aerobically or converted to glucose. 1 mark: oxygen restores the body's energy stores and reduces lactic acid levels.

practice.stem:
A student mixed yeast suspension with 5 % solutions of different sugars in identical tubes at 30 °C. The volume of gas produced in 20 minutes was measured:
Glucose 42 cm³; Fructose 39 cm³; Sucrose 36 cm³; Starch 0 cm³; Water (control) 0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of gas production for glucose, in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 2.1 cm³/min
parts.working: 42 cm³ ÷ 20 min = 2.1 cm³/min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there was no gas produced in the starch tube.
parts.answer: yeast does not produce the enzyme needed to break starch into sugars (glucose), so it cannot respire the starch
parts.working: 1 mark: yeast cannot digest starch. 1 mark: no enzyme to hydrolyse starch to glucose, so no substrate for fermentation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of the tube containing only water and yeast.
parts.answer: a control to show that gas is not produced without a sugar source (or that the yeast itself does not make gas)
parts.working: It is a control for the sugar variable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why waterlogging can kill the roots of a plant.
parts.answer: waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so root cells respire anaerobically; this releases much less energy per glucose and produces ethanol that is toxic to the root cells
parts.working: 1 mark: little oxygen in soil so anaerobic respiration. 1 mark: less energy released. 1 mark: ethanol (toxic) or lactic acid damages cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the lactic acid produced in muscles after exercise.
parts.answer: it is carried in the blood to the liver; it is converted back to glucose (or respired aerobically once oxygen is available); this uses oxygen from the oxygen debt
parts.working: 1 mark: transported in blood to the liver. 1 mark: converted to glucose or broken down in aerobic respiration. 1 mark: uses extra oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the balanced chemical equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₂H₅OH + CO₂
B C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
C C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
D C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃
parts.answer: B C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
parts.working: One glucose gives two ethanol and two carbon dioxide: atoms balance (C 6, H 12, O 6). Option A is unbalanced; C is aerobic respiration; D is lactic acid in muscle (not yeast).

practice.stem:
The concentration of lactic acid in the blood of an athlete was measured before, during and after a 400 m race.
time / min | 0 (start) | 1 (end of race) | 5 | 15 | 30 | 45
lactic acid / mmol per dm³ | 1.2 | 12.6 | 11.0 | 6.4 | 2.9 | 1.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in lactic acid concentration from the start to the end of the race.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the changes in lactic acid concentration after the race.
parts.answer: falls (quickly at first, then more slowly) from 12.6 to 1.3 mmol per dm³ over 45 minutes, almost back to the resting value
parts.working: B1 decreases over time with data quoted; B1 nearly back to starting value by 45 min / fastest fall between 5 and 15 min.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why lactic acid concentration rose during the race.
parts.answer: muscles needed energy faster than oxygen could be supplied for aerobic respiration, so they also respired anaerobically, producing lactic acid
parts.working: B1 not enough oxygen reaching muscles; B1 anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.

practice.stem:
Yeast and sugar-cane juice were kept at 30 °C in a sealed fermentation vessel. The total volume of carbon dioxide released was measured every hour.
time / h | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7
total CO₂ / dm³ | 0 | 12 | 30 | 52 | 70 | 80 | 84 | 85

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of carbon dioxide production between 1 h and 3 h, in dm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 20 dm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the rate of carbon dioxide production falls after 4 hours.
parts.answer: sugar (substrate) is being used up; ethanol concentration rises and becomes toxic to / kills the yeast
parts.working: B1 sugar runs out; B1 ethanol builds up and inhibits / kills yeast.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the useful product, other than carbon dioxide, that a sugar mill distillery obtains from this process.
parts.answer: ethanol (for fuel / industrial alcohol)

practice.stem:
Equal masses of bread dough containing yeast were placed in 100 cm³ measuring cylinders at different temperatures. The increase in volume of the dough after 20 minutes was recorded.
temperature / °C | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
increase in volume / cm³ | 8 | 22 | 40 | 26 | 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of increase in volume at 40 °C in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 2.0 cm³ per min
parts.working: M1 40 ÷ 20; A1 2.0 cm³ per min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result at 60 °C.
parts.answer: high temperature denatures the yeast enzymes (active site changes shape) so very little respiration / CO₂ is produced
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured; B1 little or no carbon dioxide made so dough barely rises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find the optimum temperature more precisely.
parts.answer: repeat with smaller temperature intervals between 30 °C and 50 °C (e.g. every 2 °C)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ethanol produced when yeast respires anaerobically can be burned as a fuel, releasing a large amount of energy. Use this fact to explain why anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: in anaerobic respiration glucose is only partly broken down; much of the chemical energy stays in the product (ethanol), which is why ethanol can still be burned as a fuel; in aerobic respiration glucose is broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water, so far more of its energy is released
parts.working: B1 glucose only partly broken down / incomplete breakdown in anaerobic respiration; B1 energy remains in ethanol (shown by it burning as a fuel); B1 aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing more energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why human muscle cells can respire anaerobically for only a short time.
parts.answer: lactic acid builds up in the muscles; this causes fatigue / cramp, so the oxygen debt must be repaid before more intense activity
parts.working: B1 lactic acid accumulates; B1 causes muscle fatigue / cramp / pain (or lowers pH and affects enzymes).

practice.stem:
Two students ran on a treadmill for 6 minutes. Their heart rates (beats per minute) were then recorded every minute until they returned to resting values.
time after exercise / min | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8
student P (trained athlete) | 150 | 120 | 98 | 80 | 66 | 64 | 64 | 64 | 64
student Q (untrained) | 172 | 158 | 140 | 122 | 108 | 96 | 88 | 80 | 74
Resting heart rate: P 64, Q 74.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how long each student took to return to their resting heart rate.
parts.answer: P: 5 minutes; Q: 8 minutes
parts.working: B1 P; B1 Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in Q's heart rate during the first 4 minutes after exercise. Give your answer to two significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why heart rate remains above resting level for several minutes after exercise and why it falls faster in the trained athlete.
parts.answer: heart continues to pump fast to carry lactic acid to the liver (repay oxygen debt); trained athlete builds up less lactic acid / smaller oxygen debt because more oxygen reaches muscles (stronger heart / larger stroke volume), so recovers sooner
parts.working: B1 lactic acid transported to liver / oxygen debt being repaid; B1 trained person respires less anaerobically / smaller debt; B1 better oxygen delivery (e.g. larger, stronger heart).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why yeast stops producing ethanol when the ethanol concentration in the fermenting mixture reaches about 14 %.
parts.answer: ethanol is toxic to yeast cells; high ethanol concentration denatures the yeast's enzymes, so respiration stops
parts.working: 1 mark: ethanol is toxic. 1 mark: it denatures enzymes. 1 mark: so yeast can no longer respire/ferment.

practice.stem:
Lactate concentration in the blood of a runner was measured after a race.
Time after race (min): 0 / 5 / 10 / 15 / 20
Lactate (mmol/dm³): 8.0 / 6.0 / 4.5 / 3.4 / 2.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in lactate concentration between 0 and 10 minutes after exercise. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: (8.0 − 4.5) ÷ 8.0 × 100 = 43.75 %, which is 44 % to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the lactate concentration falls after exercise.
parts.answer: oxygen is available again, so lactate is oxidised / converted back to glucose (mainly in the liver) and used in aerobic respiration
parts.working: Any two of: oxygen supply has returned; lactate is removed by the blood; lactate is converted to glucose in the liver; it is respired aerobically.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
A glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
B carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
C glucose → lactic acid
D glucose + oxygen → ethanol + carbon dioxide
parts.answer: A glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
parts.working: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose to carbon dioxide and water. B is photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: the chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules (glucose) to release energy
parts.working: B1 chemical reactions in cells using oxygen; B1 break down nutrients / glucose to release energy. Do not credit 'produce energy'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the cell structure where most aerobic respiration takes place.
parts.answer: mitochondrion

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three uses of the energy released by respiration in the human body.
parts.answer: muscle contraction; protein synthesis; cell division; active transport; growth; passage of nerve impulses; maintaining a constant body temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about aerobic respiration is correct?
A it produces oxygen
B it uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water
C it needs light to take place
D it removes water from the cell
parts.answer: B it uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water
parts.working: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and glucose and releases carbon dioxide and water. Producing oxygen is photosynthesis (A); respiration does not need light (C); water is produced, not removed (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
parts.working: 1 mark for reactants glucose and oxygen; 1 mark for products carbon dioxide and water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the energy released in aerobic respiration that is not used to do useful work.
parts.answer: it is released as heat (thermal energy)
parts.working: Heat energy warms the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration of glucose.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for correct formulas; 1 mark for balancing (6 O₂, 6 CO₂, 6 H₂O).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the ratio of the number of oxygen molecules used to the number of carbon dioxide molecules released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration.
parts.answer: in aerobic respiration glucose is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water; in anaerobic respiration it is only partly broken down, so much energy remains in the products (ethanol or lactic acid)
parts.working: 1 mark: complete breakdown in aerobic respiration. 1 mark: incomplete breakdown and energy left in ethanol / lactic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why breathing rate increases during exercise, linked to aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: more carbon dioxide is produced by respiration in the muscles, so it must be removed faster; more oxygen is needed for the increased rate of aerobic respiration
parts.working: 1 mark for each: more CO₂ produced needs to be removed; more O₂ needed for faster respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test, using limewater, to show that germinating seeds produce carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: place germinating seeds in a flask with a tube leading to limewater; a control with dead seeds; limewater turns milky (cloudy) if carbon dioxide is produced
parts.working: 1 mark: seeds sealed with limewater (air pumped through or connected). 1 mark: milky/cloudy result. 1 mark: control with boiled seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two cell processes that use energy from aerobic respiration in a plant.
parts.answer: any two of: active transport of mineral ions; making proteins; cell division / growth; forming cell walls
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct processes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of aerobic respiration in a germinating seed increases when the temperature rises from 10 °C to 25 °C.
parts.answer: the molecules have more kinetic energy so enzyme-controlled reactions take place faster; more collisions between enzyme and substrate
parts.working: 1 mark: higher kinetic energy/faster enzyme reaction. 1 mark: more frequent successful collisions between enzyme and substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process in the human body does NOT need energy from respiration?
A contraction of muscles
B synthesis of proteins
C diffusion of oxygen from alveoli into the blood
D uptake of ions by active transport
parts.answer: C diffusion of oxygen from alveoli into the blood
parts.working: Diffusion is passive: molecules move down a concentration gradient without energy from respiration. Active transport moves ions against a gradient and does need energy.

practice.stem: A simple respirometer contains 10 germinating mung (moong) beans on a gauze above soda lime in a boiling tube. The tube is connected to a horizontal capillary tube containing a drop of coloured liquid. The tube is kept in a water-bath at 25 °C. After 12 minutes the drop has moved 36 mm towards the boiling tube. The internal cross-sectional area of the capillary is 0.8 mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the soda lime.
parts.answer: absorbs carbon dioxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the coloured drop moves towards the beans.
parts.answer: the beans take in oxygen for aerobic respiration; the carbon dioxide released is absorbed, so the gas volume / pressure in the tube falls
parts.working: B1 oxygen used up; B1 CO₂ absorbed so volume decreases / pressure falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 2.4 mm³ per min
parts.working: M1 volume = 36 × 0.8 = 28.8 mm³; A1 28.8 ÷ 12 = 2.4 mm³ per min.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this experiment.
parts.answer: same apparatus with the same mass of boiled (dead) beans or glass beads

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two substances that the blood must deliver to leg muscle cells for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: glucose and oxygen
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of aerobic respiration in leg muscle increases when a person starts running.
parts.answer: muscles contract more often, needing more energy; more glucose and oxygen are used (supplied by faster heart and breathing rates)
parts.working: B1 more contraction / more energy needed; B1 more oxygen and glucose delivered and used.

practice.stem:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red-orange in air, turns yellow when carbon dioxide concentration rises and purple when it falls. Five woodlice were placed on a gauze above the indicator in a sealed tube. The time taken for the indicator to turn yellow was recorded at three temperatures.
temperature / °C | 10 | 20 | 30
time to turn yellow / min | 24 | 12 | 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the indicator turns yellow.
parts.answer: the woodlice respire aerobically, releasing carbon dioxide; carbon dioxide dissolves in the indicator, lowering pH / increasing CO₂ concentration
parts.working: B1 respiration; B1 carbon dioxide released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate as 100 ÷ time at 10 °C and at 30 °C. Give each to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration shown.
parts.answer: rate increases with temperature because respiration is controlled by enzymes; molecules have more kinetic energy so more enzyme–substrate collisions
parts.working: B1 enzymes; B1 more kinetic energy / more frequent collisions.

practice.stem: A respirometer contains 10 earthworms and soda lime. The coloured drop in a capillary tube of internal diameter 2.0 mm moves 35 mm towards the organisms in 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake, in mm³ per minute, to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 11.0 mm³/min
parts.working: Volume of oxygen = π × r² × distance = π × 1.0² × 35 = 109.96 mm³ in 10 min; ÷ 10 = 11.0 mm³/min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this experiment.
parts.answer: a tube with the same mass of dead (boiled) or no earthworms, with the same soda lime and capillary, kept in the same conditions
parts.working: 1 mark: same apparatus without living organisms (dead ones). 1 mark: same conditions, to show the movement is caused by respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that should be kept constant in this experiment.
parts.answer: temperature
parts.working: Accept temperature, or the number of organisms, or the size of the organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cells of the heart muscle contain many more mitochondria than skin cells do.
parts.answer: heart muscle contracts continuously and needs a large supply of energy, so it respires aerobically at a high rate; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, so more are needed; skin cells use less energy
parts.working: 1 mark: heart needs a lot of energy continuously. 1 mark: mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place. 1 mark: skin cells have a lower energy demand.

practice.stem:
A goldfish was kept in water at different temperatures and its oxygen uptake was measured.
Temperature (°C): 10 / 20 / 30 / 40
Oxygen uptake (mm³ per minute): 4.2 / 8.9 / 14.1 / 12.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the rate of oxygen uptake between 10 °C and 30 °C, in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 9.9 mm³/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the fall in oxygen uptake between 30 °C and 40 °C.
parts.answer: at high temperature the enzymes involved in respiration denature, so the rate of respiration falls
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes denature. 1 mark: fewer active enzymes so the rate of respiration falls.

practice.stem: A fish farm pond near Thatta has dissolved oxygen of 8 mg/dm³ at 6 pm. At 4 am the next day it is 5 mg/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of decrease of dissolved oxygen in the pond, in mg per dm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 0.3 mg/dm³ per hour
parts.working: Decrease = 8 − 5 = 3 mg/dm³ over 10 hours; 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 mg/dm³ per hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dissolved oxygen in the pond decreases during the night.
parts.answer: the fish and other organisms continue to respire aerobically, using oxygen from the water; there is no photosynthesis at night to add oxygen
parts.working: 1 mark: aerobic respiration by fish and microorganisms uses oxygen. 1 mark: no photosynthesis (no oxygen produced) at night.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration?
A C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
B C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
C 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
D C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 12H₂O
parts.answer: B C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
parts.working: Six oxygen molecules react with one glucose to form six carbon dioxide and six water; atoms balance. C is photosynthesis; D has too many hydrogen atoms.

practice.stem:
Germinating moong beans were placed in vacuum flask A. Flask B contained the same mass of beans that had been boiled, cooled and rinsed in disinfectant. A thermometer was put into each flask, and the mouth plugged with cotton wool. Temperatures were read every day.
day | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
flask A / °C | 21.0 | 23.5 | 26.0 | 28.0 | 29.0
flask B / °C | 21.0 | 21.0 | 21.0 | 21.5 | 21.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise in flask A over the 4 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature in flask A rises.
parts.answer: germinating seeds respire aerobically; some of the energy released is lost as heat, which the vacuum flask retains
parts.working: B1 respiration in the seeds; B1 energy released as heat / insulated flask keeps heat in.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the beans in flask B were rinsed in disinfectant.
parts.answer: to kill microorganisms (bacteria / fungi) on the beans; so any temperature rise could not be due to respiration of microorganisms
parts.working: B1 kill microbes; B1 microbes would respire and release heat.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the flask was plugged with cotton wool rather than a rubber bung.
parts.answer: allows oxygen in (and carbon dioxide out) so the seeds can respire aerobically

parts.label: a
parts.text: Climbers who travel quickly from Islamabad to a base camp at 5000 m in the Karakoram often feel tired after very little effort. At this altitude each breath contains about half as much oxygen as at sea level. Explain why the climbers tire easily.
parts.answer: less oxygen enters the blood (less haemoglobin oxygenated); less oxygen reaches muscle cells; less aerobic respiration so less energy released; more anaerobic respiration, lactic acid builds up causing fatigue
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: less oxygen absorbed into blood; less delivered to muscles; less aerobic respiration in mitochondria; less energy available for contraction; muscles respire anaerobically; lactic acid builds up / oxygen debt / fatigue.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
1 mol of glucose needs 6 mol of oxygen for complete aerobic respiration. What volume of oxygen, in dm³, is needed to fully respire 0.25 mol of glucose at room temperature (molar volume 24 dm³ per mol)?
A 6
B 24
C 36
D 144
parts.working: 0.25 mol × 6 = 1.5 mol oxygen; 1.5 × 24 = 36 dm³. A (6) is the mole ratio, not a volume; B (24) is the volume of 1 mol of oxygen; D (144) is the oxygen volume needed for 1 mol of glucose, not 0.25 mol.

practice.stem: A leaf was placed in a sealed chamber in light. Net carbon dioxide uptake was 3.5 units per hour. In the dark, the same leaf released 0.8 units of carbon dioxide per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross rate of carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis in the light, in units per hour.
parts.answer: 4.3 units per hour
parts.working: 1 mark: adds the carbon dioxide released by respiration (0.8) to the net uptake (3.5). 1 mark: correct value 4.3 units per hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaf still respires in the light.
parts.answer: respiration is needed all the time to release energy for cell processes, whether or not light is available
parts.working: 1 mark: respiration releases energy continuously in all cells. 1 mark: the carbon dioxide released in respiration is taken up by photosynthesis, so net uptake is shown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why plants must respire during the night as well as during the day.
parts.answer: plant cells need energy at all times for active transport, making proteins and growth; respiration releases this energy, which is needed at night when photosynthesis does not occur
parts.working: 1 mark: respiration in all cells continuously. 1 mark: energy needed for active transport/growth/protein synthesis. 1 mark: photosynthesis does not occur at night, so respiration is the only energy source.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in dm³ (at 24 dm³ per mol), needed to fully respire 9.0 g of glucose. The relative molecular mass of glucose is 180.
parts.answer: 7.2 dm³
parts.working: Moles of glucose = 9.0 ÷ 180 = 0.05 mol. Oxygen needed = 6 × 0.05 = 0.30 mol. Volume = 0.30 × 24 = 7.2 dm³.

practice.stem:
A ground squirrel's oxygen uptake was measured at different body temperatures.
Temperature (°C): 5 / 20 / 37
Oxygen uptake (cm³ per g per hour): 0.6 / 2.0 / 4.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the oxygen uptake is at 37 °C than at 5 °C.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hibernating animals reduce their body temperature. Explain how this helps them survive winter with little food.
parts.answer: lower temperature reduces the rate of respiration, so less glucose and fat are used per hour; energy stores last longer; the enzyme-controlled reactions of respiration slow down
parts.working: 1 mark: lower temperature means slower respiration. 1 mark: less energy is used per unit time. 1 mark: stores last through the winter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe an experiment, using germinating peas and a thermos flask, to show that respiration releases heat.
parts.answer: place germinating peas in a vacuum flask with a thermometer, plug the flask and record the temperature at intervals; use a flask of boiled dead peas as a control; the living peas show a temperature rise, the control does not
parts.working: 1 mark: living germinating seeds in flask with thermometer. 1 mark: record temperature over time. 1 mark: control with dead seeds. 1 mark: temperature rise only in the living seeds shows heat from respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why body temperature rises during hard exercise.
parts.answer: muscles respire aerobically at a high rate and release heat; the heat is carried by the blood; the body's temperature rises until heat is lost by sweating
parts.working: 1 mark: aerobic respiration releases heat energy. 1 mark: heat spreads through the body. 1 mark: heat loss (sweating) only balances it at a higher temperature.

practice.stem: A cyclist's oxygen uptake rises from 0.3 dm³ per minute at rest to 3.6 dm³ per minute during hard exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the oxygen uptake is during hard exercise than at rest.
parts.answer: 12 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of oxygen, in dm³, used over 20 minutes of exercise at this rate.
parts.answer: 72 dm³
parts.working: 3.6 dm³ per minute × 20 minutes = 72 dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four reasons why bacteria are useful in biotechnology.
parts.answer: Reproduce rapidly; can make complex molecules; few ethical concerns over their use and manipulation; have plasmids (can be genetically modified easily); can be grown in fermenters cheaply.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4.

practice.stem: A baker in Peshawar mixes flour, water, sugar and yeast to make dough for naan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
parts.answer: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 ethanol; B1 carbon dioxide (with glucose as reactant).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dough rises when left in a warm place.
parts.answer: Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide gas; bubbles of gas are trapped in the dough, making it expand.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide produced; B1 gas trapped in dough.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the ethanol when the naan is baked.
parts.answer: It evaporates (because of the high temperature).

practice.stem: A factory in Swat makes apple juice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the enzyme pectinase is used in the production of fruit juice.
parts.answer: Pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls; cells break open more easily, so more juice is released; the juice is clearer (less cloudy).
parts.working: B1 breaks down pectin; B1 cell walls; B1 more juice / clearer juice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the enzyme lactase used to produce?
A biological washing powder
B clear fruit juice
C lactose-free milk
D ethanol for biofuel
parts.answer: C lactose-free milk
parts.working: Lactase breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose, so the milk can be drunk by people who are lactose intolerant. Clear fruit juice is made using pectinase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Yeast is used to produce a biofuel from sugar cane. Which product of yeast respiration is used as the fuel?
A carbon dioxide
B ethanol
C glucose
D lactic acid
parts.answer: B ethanol
parts.working: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces ethanol, which can be burned as a fuel. Lactic acid is made by anaerobic respiration in muscles, not yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a biogas digester, anaerobic bacteria break down cow dung. Which gas is the main fuel produced?
A carbon dioxide
B methane
C oxygen
D hydrogen sulphide
parts.answer: B methane
parts.working: Biogas is mainly methane, which burns as a fuel. Carbon dioxide is a minor part of biogas and is not the fuel; oxygen is absent because the digester is anaerobic; hydrogen sulphide is only a small contaminant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a biogas digester on a farm produces methane from cow dung.
parts.answer: Cow dung is put into a sealed digester with water. Anaerobic bacteria decompose the dung in the absence of oxygen, releasing methane (and carbon dioxide). The gas is collected at the top and used as a fuel for cooking or heating.
parts.working: 1 mark: anaerobic bacteria decompose the dung. 1 mark: no oxygen present (sealed digester). 1 mark: methane is collected and used as fuel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mycoprotein is a food made by growing a fungus in a fermenter on glucose syrup. State two advantages of mycoprotein compared with meat.
parts.answer: Any two: it grows rapidly in a fermenter; it needs much less land and water than farming animals; no animals are killed; it is high in protein and low in fat.
parts.working: 1 mark for each advantage, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Papaya contains the enzyme papain, a protease. Explain how papain could be used to make meat more tender.
parts.answer: Papain is a protease: it breaks down the proteins in the muscle fibres and connective tissue, so the meat becomes softer.
parts.working: 1 mark: papain is a protease that digests proteins. 1 mark: the muscle and connective tissue proteins are broken down, so the meat softens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the enzyme amylase can be used to convert starch into a maltose syrup.
parts.answer: Amylase is added to a starch solution at its optimum temperature and pH. It breaks the starch down into maltose, so the solution becomes a maltose syrup. The enzyme is then removed or inactivated, and the syrup is filtered.
parts.working: 1 mark: amylase breaks starch down into maltose. 1 mark: used at optimum temperature and pH. 1 mark: the enzyme is removed or inactivated and the syrup is purified.

practice.stem: A student leaves a slice of bread in a sealed bag at room temperature (25 °C) and another slice in a sealed bag in a fridge (4 °C). After 5 days, mould is visible on the slice at 25 °C only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the amount of mould on the two slices would compare after 5 days.
parts.answer: More mould on the slice at 25 °C; little or none on the slice at 4 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark: more mould at 25 °C than at 4 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two slices.
parts.answer: Mould grows by enzyme-controlled reactions that work faster at warm temperatures, which are closer to the optimum for the fungus; at 4 °C the enzymes work slowly, so the mould grows very little.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes work faster at 25 °C / closer to the optimum. 1 mark: at 4 °C enzyme activity and growth are very slow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sugar is added to the warm water in which dried yeast is rehydrated before being mixed into bread dough.
parts.answer: The sugar is a respiratory substrate, providing food for the yeast so that it can start to respire and produce carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: sugar is a food/respiratory substrate for the yeast.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water should be warm but not hot.
parts.answer: Warm water activates the yeast's enzymes, so it respires quickly; very hot water would denature the enzymes and kill the yeast.
parts.working: 1 mark: warm water gives an optimum temperature for enzymes. 1 mark: hot water denatures the enzymes/kills the yeast.

practice.stem:
Equal samples of bread dough were placed in measuring cylinders at different temperatures. Each started at 50 cm³. The volume was read after 30 minutes.
Temperature / °C : volume after 30 min / cm³
20 : 62
30 : 84
40 : 98
60 : 51

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in volume, in cm³ per minute, at each temperature. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result at 60 °C.
parts.answer: Yeast enzymes are denatured (or yeast cells killed) at high temperature; so little or no respiration / carbon dioxide produced.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured; B1 little respiration / CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find the optimum temperature more accurately.
parts.answer: Repeat with smaller temperature intervals between 30 °C and 60 °C (e.g. 35, 40, 45, 50, 55 °C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the enzymes in biological washing powders remove stains of curry and egg from clothes.
parts.answer: Lipases break down fats / oils in curry into fatty acids and glycerol; proteases break down proteins in egg into amino acids; the products are small and soluble, so they wash away in water.
parts.working: B1 lipase / fats; B1 protease / protein; B1 soluble products washed away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why biological washing powders are less effective in very hot water.
parts.answer: The enzymes are denatured at high temperatures; the shape of the active site changes so substrates no longer fit.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site changes shape / substrate does not fit.

practice.stem:
Pieces of cloth stained with egg yolk were placed in a biological washing powder solution at different temperatures. The time for the stain to disappear was recorded.
Temperature / °C : time / s
20 : 600
30 : 300
40 : 160
50 : 240
60 : 900

parts.label: a
parts.text: The rate of stain removal can be calculated as 1 ÷ time. Calculate the rate at 40 °C, in s⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the temperature at which the washing powder worked best and explain the result at 60 °C.
parts.answer: 40 °C; at 60 °C the enzymes are (partly) denatured so the stain takes much longer to remove.
parts.working: B1 40 °C; B1 denatured at 60 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of making the end point of this experiment easier to judge.
parts.answer: Compare each cloth with a clean, unstained piece of the same cloth / use a light sensor or colorimeter / place cloth against a white background.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain why each of the following is controlled in an industrial fermenter producing insulin from GM bacteria:
(i) temperature
(ii) pH
(iii) oxygen supply
(iv) nutrient supply
parts.answer: (i) enzymes work best at an optimum temperature / too high denatures them; (ii) enzymes have an optimum pH; (iii) for aerobic respiration of the microorganisms; (iv) provides glucose for respiration and raw materials (e.g. amino acids / nitrogen) for growth and product.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fermenter is cleaned with steam before use.
parts.answer: To kill microorganisms (aseptic conditions); contaminating microorganisms would compete with the GM bacteria / reduce yield / contaminate the product.
parts.working: B1 kills microorganisms / sterilises; B1 contamination would reduce yield or spoil product.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does a fermenter have a stirrer?
A to make the microorganisms produce more ethanol
B to sterilise the nutrient medium
C to keep the contents evenly mixed so that nutrients, oxygen and temperature are uniform
D to remove waste products from the culture
parts.answer: C to keep the contents evenly mixed so that nutrients, oxygen and temperature are uniform
parts.working: Stirring keeps the microorganisms, nutrients, oxygen and temperature evenly distributed, so all the culture grows under the same conditions. Stirring does not produce ethanol, sterilise the medium or remove waste.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Yoghurt (dahi) is made by adding a starter culture of bacteria to warm milk. Explain why the milk is heated before the bacteria are added.
parts.answer: Heating kills other microorganisms that would compete with the starter bacteria or spoil the dahi, so the desired bacteria grow alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: kills competing or contaminating microorganisms. 1 mark: the starter culture grows without competition / the product is safe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mixture is left in a warm place to set.
parts.answer: The warm temperature is close to the optimum for the bacteria's enzymes, so the bacteria grow and respire quickly, producing lactic acid that makes the milk set.
parts.working: 1 mark: warm temperature is the optimum for bacterial enzymes / growth. 1 mark: bacteria produce acid (lactic acid) that makes the milk thicken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Enzymes can be immobilised in alginate beads. State one advantage of immobilising enzymes for an industrial process, and one advantage for the product.
parts.answer: The enzymes can be reused many times, lowering cost; the product is not contaminated with enzyme, so it is easier to purify.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes can be reused (lower cost). 1 mark: product is free of enzyme / easier to separate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vinegar is made by Acetobacter bacteria in a fermenter. Explain why the vinegar must be kept with access to air.
parts.answer: Acetobacter are aerobic bacteria; they need oxygen to oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid.
parts.working: 1 mark: the bacteria are aerobic. 1 mark: oxygen is needed to oxidise the ethanol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the conversion of ethanol to ethanoic acid.
parts.answer: ethanol + oxygen → ethanoic acid + water
parts.working: 1 mark: correct reactants and products.

practice.stem: Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol in a sealed fermenter. Relative molecular mass: glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) = 180; ethanol (C₂H₅OH) = 46. Equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of glucose in 2000 g of glucose. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 11.1 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical mass of ethanol that could be produced from 2000 g of glucose (100 % yield). Give your answer to the nearest gram.
parts.working: 1 mark: 11.1 mol glucose gives 22.2 mol ethanol (2 mol per mole). 1 mark: 22.2 × 46 = 1022 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The actual yield is 85 % of the theoretical yield. Calculate the actual mass of ethanol produced. Give your answer to the nearest gram.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the enzymes in germinating barley help to make beer.
parts.answer: Amylase in the germinating barley (malt) converts the starch into maltose. Yeast then ferments the maltose to ethanol and carbon dioxide anaerobically.
parts.working: 1 mark: amylase converts starch into sugar (maltose). 1 mark: yeast can ferment maltose. 1 mark: anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

practice.stem:
Samples of 100 g of apple pulp were mixed with different volumes of pectinase and left at 40 °C for 20 minutes, then filtered.
Pectinase / cm³ : volume of juice / cm³
0.0 : 12
1.0 : 21
2.0 : 27, 29, 18, 28
3.0 : 30
4.0 : 30.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result for 2.0 cm³ of pectinase and calculate the mean volume of juice without it.
parts.answer: 18 cm³; mean = 28 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your mean, calculate the percentage increase in juice volume with 2.0 cm³ of pectinase compared with no pectinase. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the volume of juice hardly increases above 3.0 cm³ of pectinase.
parts.answer: All the pectin has already been broken down / another factor (amount of pulp or time) is now limiting.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any two of: mass of apple pulp; temperature; time; type of apple; total volume (add water to make volumes equal); filter paper / funnel type.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Penicillin is made by a fungus grown in a fermenter.
Day : penicillin concentration / g per dm³
0 : 0
2 : 0.5
4 : 4.1
6 : 8.9
8 : 10.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of penicillin production between day 2 and day 6, in g/dm³ per day.
parts.answer: 2.1 g/dm³ per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: The fermenter has a water jacket through which cold water is pumped. Explain why.
parts.answer: The fungus respires and releases heat energy; cooling stops the temperature rising above the optimum, which would denature enzymes / kill the fungus.
parts.working: B1 respiration releases heat; B1 prevents temperature rising / denaturing enzymes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the production rate between day 6 and day 8 is lower than between day 2 and day 6.
parts.answer: Nutrients (e.g. glucose) run low; waste products build up / pH changes; so fewer cells are active.
parts.working: B1 nutrients used up; B1 waste builds up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of sugar affects the rate of carbon dioxide production by yeast. Include apparatus, method, variables to control, how results are recorded and how a conclusion is reached.
parts.answer: Yeast suspension + sugar solutions of different concentrations; collect CO₂ in a gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder or count bubbles for a fixed time; constant temperature water-bath; repeats; calculate rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: at least five sugar concentrations (e.g. 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 %); same volume and concentration of yeast suspension; same volume of sugar solution; water-bath at a fixed temperature (e.g. 35 °C, thermostatically controlled); allow time to equilibrate; measure CO₂ volume in a gas syringe (or count bubbles / measure balloon) over a fixed time; repeat three times and calculate mean; rate = volume ÷ time; table of concentration against volume of CO₂; graph and describe trend for conclusion.

practice.stem: A farm grows 65 tonnes of sugar cane per hectare on 12 hectares. Each tonne of cane can yield 72 dm³ of ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of ethanol that could be produced from the farm's sugar cane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the sugar from cane is converted into ethanol.
parts.answer: Sugar solution is mixed with yeast in a fermenter without oxygen (anaerobic); yeast respires anaerobically to produce ethanol (and carbon dioxide); ethanol is separated (distilled).
parts.working: B1 yeast; B1 anaerobic respiration / fermentation produces ethanol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of using large areas of land to grow sugar cane for biofuel.
parts.answer: Less land for food crops / higher food prices / habitat destruction and loss of biodiversity / heavy water use.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The temperature inside a large fermenter rises unless it is cooled. What is the main cause of this rise?
A The stirrer rubs against the walls.
B The microorganisms release heat energy during respiration.
C Steam used to sterilise the fermenter stays inside.
D The nutrient solution reacts with the oxygen supplied.
parts.answer: B The microorganisms release heat energy during respiration.
parts.working: Respiration by the large population of microorganisms releases energy as heat, so a water jacket is needed. Steam is only used before the fermenter is filled, so C is wrong.

practice.stem: A student compares the rate of fermentation of three sugars by yeast. Each sugar solution is mixed with yeast, and the volume of gas produced in 10 minutes is measured. The sugars are glucose, sucrose and lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable.
parts.answer: The type of sugar (glucose, sucrose or lactose).
parts.working: 1 mark: the type of sugar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one variable that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any one: the concentration and volume of the sugar solution; the mass of yeast; the temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for one suitable control variable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict how the volume of gas produced from lactose would compare with glucose. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Much less gas (little or none) from lactose: yeast does not produce lactase, so it cannot break lactose down into sugars it can ferment.
parts.working: 1 mark: lactose gives much less (or no) gas than glucose. 1 mark: yeast lacks lactase, so it cannot break lactose down for fermentation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a fermenter, yeast produces ethanol from sugar, but the rate of ethanol production stops increasing once the ethanol concentration reaches a certain level. Explain why.
parts.answer: Ethanol is toxic to yeast: it denatures the yeast's enzymes and damages its cell membranes, so the yeast cells die or slow down. The sugar supply is also used up over time, so less respiration takes place. Ethanol at high concentrations therefore limits the process.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethanol is toxic to yeast. 1 mark: it denatures enzymes or damages membranes. 1 mark: yeast die or become less active. 1 mark: sugar is used up / the process slows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of biogas digesters on farms in Punjab as a source of energy, compared with burning dried cow dung directly as fuel.
parts.answer: Advantages of biogas: a cleaner, smokeless fuel that burns more efficiently; the digester produces a sludge that can be used as fertiliser; it reduces the time spent collecting fuel and reduces disease from smoke. Disadvantages: digesters cost money to build and need regular feeding with dung and water; the gas output drops in cold weather; it needs skill to maintain. Burning dung directly is cheap but produces smoke and wastes the fertiliser value of the dung.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five valid points, two advantages and two disadvantages of biogas, plus a comparison with burning dung directly (cost, smoke, fertiliser value).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term genetic modification.
parts.answer: Changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three examples of genetic modification and state the benefit of each.
parts.answer: Any three of: bacteria given the human insulin gene → produce human insulin; crops resistant to herbicides → weeds can be sprayed without killing crop; crops resistant to insect pests → less insecticide, higher yield; crops with improved nutritional quality (e.g. rice with extra vitamin A) → reduce deficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark each for example + benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme is used to join a human gene into a bacterial plasmid?
A amylase
B DNA ligase
C protease
D restriction enzyme
parts.answer: B DNA ligase
parts.working: DNA ligase joins the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid together. A restriction enzyme cuts DNA; it does not join it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rice genetically modified to contain extra vitamin A precursor could improve health in some countries.
parts.answer: In places where people eat mainly rice, the diet may lack vitamin A; GM rice provides it, reducing vitamin A deficiency (e.g. poor night vision / blindness).
parts.working: B1 rice is a staple / main food; B1 reduces deficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some people prefer to increase vitamin A intake by eating a more varied diet (for example carrots and leafy vegetables) rather than growing GM rice.
parts.answer: Any one of: concerns about the safety or environmental effects of GM crops; a varied diet also provides other vitamins and minerals; cost of GM seed / dependence on seed companies.

practice.stem: A maize variety has been genetically modified to be resistant to a herbicide (weedkiller).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing a herbicide-resistant GM crop helps a farmer.
parts.answer: The whole field can be sprayed with herbicide; weeds are killed but the crop is not, so there is less competition and a higher yield.
parts.working: B1 herbicide kills weeds but not crop; B1 less competition / higher yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two concerns people have about growing herbicide-resistant crops.
parts.answer: Any two of: the resistance gene could spread to wild plants / weeds (making 'superweeds'); more herbicide may be used; reduced biodiversity; possible effects on human health not fully known.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The steps below describe how a gene is transferred to bacteria. Put them in the correct order (write the letters).
P Recombinant plasmids are taken up by bacteria.
Q The gene and plasmid are joined using DNA ligase.
R The gene is cut out of human DNA with a restriction enzyme.
S The bacteria multiply and make the human protein.
T A plasmid is cut open with the same restriction enzyme.
parts.answer: R, T, Q, P, S
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair reversed (accept T before R).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bt cotton contains a gene taken from which organism?
A a bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis
B a mould, Penicillium
C a virus, tobacco mosaic virus
D a maize plant
parts.answer: A a bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis
parts.working: The Bt gene codes for a protein toxin from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, which kills some caterpillar pests. The other organisms are not the source of this gene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a human gene can be expressed in bacteria after it has been inserted.
parts.answer: The genetic code is universal: the same triplet codes for the same amino acid in all organisms, so the bacterial ribosomes can translate the human gene's mRNA into the same protein.
parts.working: 1 mark: the genetic code is the same in all organisms. 1 mark: bacterial ribosomes translate the gene's codons into the correct protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transgenic organism.
parts.answer: An organism that contains a gene from a different species, introduced by genetic modification.
parts.working: 1 mark: a gene from another species is inserted by genetic modification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a transgenic organism used in agriculture or medicine.
parts.answer: Any one: Bt cotton; insulin-producing bacteria; GM salmon; golden rice.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why new GM crops must be tested in field trials before they are grown commercially.
parts.answer: Field trials show whether the crop is safe for people, animals and the environment, whether it gives the expected yield in real conditions, and whether it affects other organisms (for example pollinators or non-target insects).
parts.working: 1 mark: tests safety for people and animals. 1 mark: tests effects on the environment or non-target organisms. 1 mark: tests yield under real conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
parts.answer: Human insulin gene is cut out using a restriction enzyme, leaving sticky ends; a bacterial plasmid is cut with the same restriction enzyme; the gene and plasmid are joined with DNA ligase to form a recombinant plasmid; the recombinant plasmid is inserted into a bacterium; the bacteria multiply (in a fermenter) and express the gene, making human insulin, which is extracted and purified.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: restriction enzyme cuts out gene; sticky ends; plasmid cut with same enzyme; ligase joins; recombinant plasmid put into bacteria; bacteria reproduce / grown in fermenter and make insulin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'sticky ends'.
parts.answer: Short lengths of single-stranded DNA left at the cut ends after a staggered cut by a restriction enzyme; their exposed bases can pair with complementary bases.
parts.working: B1 single-stranded overhang; B1 unpaired bases that can pair with complementary bases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut both the human DNA and the plasmid.
parts.answer: The enzyme cuts at a specific base sequence and leaves the same sticky ends; so the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid are complementary and can pair up.
parts.working: B1 same sequence cut / same sticky ends; B1 complementary so they join.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a plasmid is correct?
A It is a small circle of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main bacterial chromosome.
B It is a chromosome found in the nucleus of a human cell.
C It is an enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together.
D It is a protein coat that surrounds the genetic material of a virus.
parts.answer: A It is a small circle of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main bacterial chromosome.
parts.working: Plasmids are small circular loops of DNA in bacterial cytoplasm; they are used as vectors to carry genes into bacteria. C describes DNA ligase, and bacteria have no nucleus, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before GM bacteria were used, insulin for people with diabetes was extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs. Suggest three advantages of using insulin made by GM bacteria.
parts.answer: Any three of: identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic or immune reactions; can be made in large quantities; cheaper / quicker to produce; consistent purity; acceptable to people who avoid pig or animal products for religious or ethical reasons; no risk of disease passed from animals.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Fish have been genetically modified with an extra growth hormone gene. At a research farm the mean mass of GM fish at 12 months was 2.8 kg and of non-GM fish of the same species 1.2 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much greater, as a percentage, the mean mass of the GM fish was than the non-GM fish. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one benefit and one concern of farming such GM fish.
parts.answer: Benefit: more food produced in less time / cheaper protein. Concern: GM fish escaping and breeding with or out-competing wild fish / effects on ecosystems / unknown health effects.
parts.working: B1 benefit; B1 concern.

practice.stem: Wheat is the main crop in parts of Sindh and Balochistan where rainfall is low.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how genetically modified drought-tolerant wheat could help farmers in a region with low and unreliable rainfall.
parts.answer: Wheat survives / grows with less water, so yields are higher in dry years; more reliable food supply and income / less irrigation needed.
parts.working: B1 survives dry conditions; B1 higher / more reliable yield or less water used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why some people are against growing GM crops.
parts.answer: Any two of: genes could transfer to wild plants; possible unknown effects on health; reduced biodiversity; seeds are expensive and farmers depend on big companies; ethical objection to altering organisms.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A scientist inserts a human gene into bacteria using a plasmid. Which gene is usually included in the plasmid so that transformed bacteria can be identified?
A a gene for antibiotic resistance
B a gene for the human protein
C a gene for DNA ligase
D a gene for restriction enzyme
parts.answer: A a gene for antibiotic resistance
parts.working: A marker gene for antibiotic resistance lets only bacteria that have taken up the plasmid survive on a plate containing the antibiotic. The human gene is the target gene, not a marker; DNA ligase and restriction enzymes are enzymes used to cut and join DNA, not marker genes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bt crops make a toxin that kills some insect pests. Explain how pests can evolve resistance to the toxin by natural selection. Suggest one way farmers can slow this.
parts.answer: Some pest insects naturally vary and a few carry alleles that make them resistant to the toxin.
