These survive and breed, passing the resistance alleles on, so the proportion of resistant pests increases. Farmers can plant a refuge of non-Bt crops nearby so that non-resistant pests survive and interbreed with the resistant ones.
parts.working: 1 mark: variation, with some individuals resistant. 1 mark: resistant insects survive and reproduce, passing on the alleles. 1 mark: a sensible method, e.g. refuge planting or rotating crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A GM tomato has its softening gene made inactive so that it ripens slowly. Explain how this could be achieved by genetic modification.
parts.answer: The gene that codes for the softening enzyme is removed or switched off, so no (or less) enzyme is made and the fruit stays firm for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: the gene is removed or made inactive. 1 mark: the enzyme that softens the fruit is not made (or made less).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to farmers and one benefit to shoppers of this GM tomato.
parts.answer: Farmers: fruit can be picked later and transported over long distances without damage, so less of the crop is wasted. Shoppers: the tomatoes stay firm and fresh for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: a farmer benefit (less waste, longer transport). 1 mark: a shopper benefit (firmer, longer-lasting fruit).

practice.stem: A researcher tests a GM variety of salt-tolerant rice in a coastal area of Sindh. The GM rice is planted in several plots of equal size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two controls for this field trial.
parts.answer: Any two: a plot of a non-GM rice variety grown alongside under identical conditions (same soil, water, fertiliser); the same planting date and treatment for all plots.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct control, e.g. a non-GM comparison plot; identical conditions for all plots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researcher uses several repeat plots.
parts.answer: Repeat plots give a mean value and show whether the difference is consistent, so one unusual plot does not mislead the conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeats allow a mean to be calculated. 1 mark: repeats show whether results are reliable / reduce the effect of anomalous plots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rice has been genetically modified to contain more iron. Explain how this could help women in rural Pakistan. State one concern about this GM rice.
parts.answer: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; eating rice with more iron helps prevent iron-deficiency anaemia, improving health and energy. A concern: people may not accept GM food, or the long-term effects on health and the environment are not yet fully known.
parts.working: 1 mark: iron is needed to make haemoglobin / prevents anaemia. 1 mark: improves health or energy for women. 1 mark: a valid concern (acceptance, safety, environment).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some people are concerned about the antibiotic-resistance marker genes used in GM crops and bacteria. Explain why.
parts.answer: The marker genes could be transferred to pathogenic bacteria, which would then become resistant to the antibiotic. Antibiotics would become less effective, making infections harder to treat.
parts.working: 1 mark: the resistance gene could pass to pathogenic bacteria. 1 mark: the bacteria become resistant to the antibiotic. 1 mark: infections become harder to treat.

practice.stem: In a field trial, four plots of a GM wheat variety were harvested and the yields (tonnes per hectare) recorded: 2.4, 2.6, 2.5, 2.9. A control plot of a non-GM variety gave a yield of 2.0 tonnes per hectare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean yield of the four GM plots.
parts.answer: 2.6 tonnes per hectare

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield of the GM wheat compared with the control.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the GM plots were compared with a non-GM control plot, rather than with another GM plot.
parts.answer: The control shows the yield without the GM trait under the same field conditions, so any difference in yield can be attributed to the GM variety.
parts.working: 1 mark: the control shows the baseline yield without the GM trait, under the same conditions, so any difference is due to the GM variety.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Salt-tolerant GM rice could be grown on land in coastal Sindh that is too salty for ordinary rice. Explain two ways this could help farmers, and state one environmental concern.
parts.answer: The rice can give a harvest on land that was previously unusable, so farmers can grow food and earn an income; less land has to be cleared for farming elsewhere. A concern: the gene could spread to wild relatives or affect the natural ecosystem.
parts.working: 1 mark: can grow on previously unusable land. 1 mark: income/food security or less land clearance. 1 mark: a valid environmental concern (gene flow or ecosystem effects).

practice.stem: Many cotton farmers in Punjab grow cotton that has been genetically modified to contain a gene from a bacterium. The gene makes a protein that is toxic to caterpillars that feed on cotton.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to farmers and the environment of growing insect-resistant GM cotton.
parts.answer: Advantages: crop makes its own toxin so pests die; less insecticide sprayed (lower cost, less harm to farm workers and to non-target insects); higher yield / less damage. Disadvantages: GM seed is expensive and must be bought each season; pests may become resistant to the toxin; non-target insects may be harmed; reduced biodiversity in a monoculture; genes may spread to wild relatives.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark each, max 6, with at least 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages for full marks.

practice.stem:
A farmer near Bahawalpur grew GM insect-resistant cotton in one field and non-GM cotton in a similar field in the same season.
Cotton type : yield / kg per hectare : number of insecticide sprays
GM : 2250 : 3
non-GM : 1800 : 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield of the GM cotton compared with the non-GM cotton.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of insecticide sprays. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the farmer should not conclude from these results alone that GM cotton is better on all farms.
parts.answer: Only one farm / one season — results may not be repeatable; other factors (soil, rainfall, pests that year) may differ between fields; cost of GM seed not included.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations.

practice.stem: Under ideal conditions in a fermenter, a bacterium divides into two every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bacteria present after 4 hours, starting with one GM bacterium, if every cell divides once every 20 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the number of bacteria in a real fermenter after 4 hours is usually smaller than your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Any two of: not every cell divides every 20 minutes (some cells die); nutrients (e.g. glucose) start to run out; toxic waste products build up / pH changes; the bacteria need time to adjust to the new conditions before dividing quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why a gene taken from a human can still be used by a bacterium to make the same human protein.
parts.answer: The base sequence of the gene codes for the order of amino acids; the same base sequence codes for the same amino acids in all organisms, so the bacterium makes a protein with the same amino acid sequence.
parts.working: B1 gene / base sequence codes for amino acid sequence; B1 code is the same (universal) in bacteria and humans.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the human protein made by bacteria must be purified before it can be used as a medicine.
parts.answer: To remove bacterial cells, other bacterial proteins and toxins / nutrients from the fermenter that could cause harmful reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A restriction enzyme cuts DNA only at the base sequence GAATTC. A linear piece of DNA has this sequence on one strand:
TTGAATTCAGCCGAATTCTTAGGCTAGAATTCCGA
How many fragments are produced when this DNA is cut completely by the enzyme?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 5
parts.answer: C 4
parts.working: GAATTC occurs 3 times, and each cut in a linear molecule adds one fragment: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer B (3) counts the cut sites, not the fragments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pollen from a GM crop can cross-pollinate with a wild relative growing nearby. Explain how this could lead to 'superweeds', and suggest two ways this risk can be reduced.
parts.answer: The transferred gene (e.g. herbicide resistance) can pass into the wild relative. Plants that receive the gene survive herbicide sprays and spread, creating weeds that are hard to control. Risks can be reduced by planting buffer zones of non-GM crops, or by removing flowers before they open / isolating the GM crop from relatives.
parts.working: 1 mark: gene flow via pollen into the wild relative. 1 mark: the resistant wild plants survive herbicide and spread. 1 mark: buffer zones. 1 mark: isolation or removal of flowers/plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two similarities and three differences between genetic modification and selective breeding.
parts.answer: Similarities: both change the genetic make-up of organisms to produce desired traits; both involve choosing organisms with the wanted characteristics. Differences: GM transfers genes between different species (even bacteria to plants), while selective breeding uses variation within a species; GM is done in a laboratory and is much faster; selective breeding takes many generations and can produce unwanted combinations of genes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of the two similarities. 1 mark each for any three differences, e.g. genes from other species; laboratory versus breeding; speed; unwanted genes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cells produce antibodies?
A lymphocytes
B phagocytes
C platelets
D red blood cells
parts.answer: A lymphocytes
parts.working: Lymphocytes make antibodies. Phagocytes (B) engulf and digest pathogens; they do not make antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the human body stops pathogens from entering it.
parts.answer: Any three of: skin as a barrier; hairs in the nose trap particles; mucus traps pathogens in the airways; hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills pathogens; blood clotting seals wounds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three mechanical / chemical barriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.
parts.answer: Phagocyte
parts.working: B1 phagocyte.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between an antigen and an antibody.
parts.answer: An antigen is a molecule (on the surface of a pathogen) that triggers an immune response; an antibody is a protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
parts.working: B1 antigen – on pathogen / foreign, causes response; B1 antibody – protein made by lymphocytes / binds antigen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why an antibody against the measles virus does not protect against the cholera bacterium.
parts.answer: Antibodies are specific; the antibody's shape is complementary only to the measles antigen.
parts.working: B1 specificity / different antigen shapes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how mucus and cilia in the trachea help to protect the body from pathogens.
parts.answer: Goblet cells make mucus, which traps pathogens and dust; cilia beat / move the mucus up to the throat; where it is swallowed (and pathogens killed by stomach acid).
parts.working: 1 mark each: mucus traps pathogens; cilia beat / waft; mucus moved upwards to throat / swallowed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why people whose cilia are damaged by smoke get more chest infections.
parts.answer: Mucus and trapped pathogens are not removed, so pathogens stay in the lungs and can multiply.
parts.working: B1 mucus / pathogens not removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by active immunity.
parts.answer: Defence against a pathogen by the body making its own antibodies after infection or vaccination, with memory cells formed.
parts.working: B1 body makes its own antibodies; B1 after exposure to antigen (infection or vaccination) / memory cells formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways a person can gain active immunity.
parts.answer: By catching the disease (natural infection) and by vaccination.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using suitable words.
'Pathogens have molecules called ____ on their surface. White blood cells called ____ make antibodies that fit these molecules. Some of these cells remain in the blood as ____ cells, which give long-term immunity. Other white blood cells, called ____, engulf and digest pathogens.'
parts.answer: antigens; lymphocytes; memory; phagocytes
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of passive immunity?
A A child is given a polio vaccine by mouth.
B A baby receives antibodies in breast milk.
C A person recovers from chickenpox and does not catch it again.
D A nurse is injected with a weakened measles virus.
parts.answer: B A baby receives antibodies in breast milk.
parts.working: Passive immunity: antibodies made by another person are received. A, C and D all make the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells (active immunity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how vaccination gives a child long-term protection against measles.
parts.answer: Vaccine contains weakened / harmless measles pathogen with its antigens; antigens stimulate lymphocytes; lymphocytes produce specific antibodies; memory cells are produced; on later infection memory cells give a faster, larger antibody response, destroying the pathogen before symptoms develop.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: weakened / dead pathogen or its antigens; antigens trigger an immune response; lymphocytes make antibodies; antibodies specific / complementary to the antigen; memory cells made; secondary response faster and greater (more antibodies); pathogen destroyed before disease develops; this is active immunity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: Antibodies have a shape complementary to a specific antigen; they lock on to the antigens on the pathogen; this leads to direct destruction of the pathogen or marks it so that phagocytes engulf and digest it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: complementary / specific shape; bind / lock on to antigens; pathogen destroyed directly OR marked for phagocytes to engulf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student wrote: 'Antibodies engulf bacteria.' Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Antibodies are protein molecules, not cells; engulfing is done by phagocytes.
parts.working: B1 antibodies are molecules / phagocytes engulf.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the comparison.
(i) Source of antibodies in active immunity.
(ii) Source of antibodies in passive immunity.
(iii) Whether memory cells are made in passive immunity.
parts.answer: (i) the person's own lymphocytes; (ii) another individual, e.g. from the mother across the placenta or in breast milk, or an injection of antibodies; (iii) no
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage to a newborn baby to receive antibodies from its mother.
parts.answer: The baby's immune system has not met these pathogens; maternal antibodies give immediate protection while the baby's own immunity develops.
parts.working: B1 immediate protection / no time needed to make antibodies; B1 baby's immune system immature / not yet exposed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row describes active immunity produced by vaccination?
A antibodies made by the person: yes; memory cells made: yes
B antibodies made by the person: yes; memory cells made: no
C antibodies made by the person: no; memory cells made: yes
D antibodies made by the person: no; memory cells made: no
parts.answer: A antibodies made by the person: yes; memory cells made: yes
parts.working: In active immunity the person's own lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells, giving long-term protection. D describes passive immunity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person who has had measles rarely catches it again, but people can catch influenza (flu) many times. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: Measles memory cells remain and recognise the same antigens on reinfection; the flu virus mutates and changes its antigens often; so memory cells / antibodies from earlier infections no longer fit the new antigens.
parts.working: 1 mark each: memory cells give long-term immunity to measles; flu virus changes antigens (mutation / new strains); existing antibodies / memory cells specific to old antigen shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a new flu vaccine is often needed each year.
parts.answer: New strains have different antigens, so the vaccine must contain the new antigens.
parts.working: B1 antigens change / new strains.

practice.stem:
A student pressed a finger onto three sterile agar plates: (1) before washing, (2) after washing with water only, (3) after washing with soap and water. The plates were incubated for 3 days and the bacterial colonies were counted.
unwashed: 184 colonies
water only: 112 colonies
soap and water: 23 colonies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of colonies when hands were washed with soap and water, compared with unwashed hands. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a conclusion for this investigation.
parts.answer: Washing hands reduces the number of bacteria transferred; washing with soap and water reduces them much more (87.5 %) than water alone (39.1 %).
parts.working: B1 washing reduces colonies; B1 soap more effective than water alone (data optional).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two safety precautions the student should take with the plates after they have been touched.
parts.answer: Seal the lid with tape and do not open it; incubate at about 25 °C, not 37 °C (to avoid growing human pathogens); dispose of plates by autoclaving; wash hands afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the investigation should be repeated with several students.
parts.answer: Different people's hands carry different numbers of bacteria, so results from one person may not be representative; to find a mean / spot anomalies.
parts.working: B1 representative / identify anomalous results.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A child recovers from chickenpox. Years later the same virus enters the body. Which response is most likely to prevent illness?
A memory cells engulf the viruses by phagocytosis
B memory lymphocytes divide quickly and produce large amounts of antibody
C the body makes no antibodies, so the virus spreads freely
D platelets release antibodies that destroy the virus
parts.answer: B memory lymphocytes divide quickly and produce large amounts of antibody
parts.working: Memory lymphocytes from the first infection divide rapidly on re-infection and make antibodies quickly and in large amounts. A describes phagocytes, not memory cells; C ignores memory cells; D is wrong because platelets are involved in clotting, not antibody production.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does passive immunity give only short-term protection?
A The antibodies received are digested by phagocytes immediately.
B No memory cells are made by the person's own immune system.
C The antigens received are destroyed by the person's antibodies.
D Lymphocytes are killed by the antibodies received.
parts.answer: B No memory cells are made by the person's own immune system.
parts.working: In passive immunity the person's own lymphocytes are not stimulated, so no memory cells form; the received antibodies are gradually broken down. A is the main distractor – antibodies are not engulfed straight away, they last weeks.

practice.stem:
The concentration of antibodies against a virus was measured in a person's blood. The person was exposed to the virus on day 0 and again on day 30.
day: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 33, 37, 42, 50
antibody concentration / arbitrary units: 0, 2, 12, 20, 9, 3, 40, 160, 120, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the peak antibody concentration was after the second exposure than after the first.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to describe two differences between the responses to the first and second exposures.
parts.answer: Second response is faster: peak reached 7 days after exposure (day 37) instead of 15 days; second response is larger: peak 160 a.u. instead of 20 a.u. (also antibodies stay higher for longer).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two comparative differences, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference in the responses.
parts.answer: The first exposure produced memory cells; on second exposure memory cells recognise the antigen and divide quickly; so antibodies are produced more rapidly and in greater quantity.
parts.working: 1 mark each: memory cells formed after first exposure; memory cells recognise the (same) antigen; rapid production of many antibodies / lymphocytes divide rapidly.

practice.stem: In a polio vaccination campaign in one district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 45 120 of the 48 000 children under five years old received the vaccine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of children in the district who were vaccinated. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why vaccinating a high percentage of children also protects the children who were not vaccinated.
parts.answer: Most people are immune, so the virus cannot pass from person to person; fewer infected people to spread it; chance of an unvaccinated child meeting an infected person is very low (herd immunity).
parts.working: 1 mark each: few people can be infected / carry the virus; transmission chain broken / spread reduced; unvaccinated child unlikely to come into contact with pathogen; idea of herd / community immunity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why health workers aim to vaccinate every child, even in a district where 94 % are already vaccinated.
parts.answer: Any remaining unvaccinated group allows the virus to survive and spread / outbreaks can start among the unvaccinated; aim to eradicate the disease.
parts.working: Any one sensible suggestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how blood clotting acts as a defence against disease.
parts.answer: When skin is cut, platelets cause the soluble protein fibrinogen to be converted to insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh of fibres that traps red blood cells; the clot seals the wound and stops pathogens entering.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fibrinogen (soluble) changed to fibrin (insoluble); mesh / network traps cells; seals wound so pathogens cannot enter (also limits blood loss).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person whose blood does not clot properly is more likely to suffer infections after an injury.
parts.answer: Wound stays open for longer so more pathogens can enter.
parts.working: B1 open wound / entry point for pathogens.

practice.stem:
Country X increased the vaccination coverage for measles among young children.
2012: coverage 61 %, measles cases 8640
2022: coverage 91 %, measles cases 1210

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in measles cases between 2012 and 2022. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the rise in vaccination coverage caused the fall in cases.
parts.answer: More children have memory cells / immunity, so fewer can be infected; less transmission of the virus in the population.
parts.working: B1 more people immune (memory cells / antibodies); B1 spread reduced / herd immunity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why there were still measles cases in 2022.
parts.answer: Any two: 9 % of children unvaccinated; some children had only one dose; vaccine not effective in every child; infected travellers bring the virus in; babies too young to be vaccinated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible reasons.

practice.stem: A man in Hyderabad is bitten by a dog that may carry the rabies virus. On the first day, doctors inject him with ready-made rabies antibodies and also give the first dose of rabies vaccine. More vaccine doses are given over the next two weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the injection of ready-made antibodies is given on the first day.
parts.answer: It gives immediate (passive) protection, because the person's own lymphocytes would take days / weeks to make enough antibodies; rabies virus could reach the nervous system before that.
parts.working: B1 immediate protection / antibodies act at once; B1 own immune response too slow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the vaccine is also given.
parts.answer: The injected antibodies are broken down after a few weeks and no memory cells are made; the vaccine stimulates the person's own lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells, giving long-term (active) immunity.
parts.working: B1 passive immunity short-lived / no memory cells; B1 vaccine gives active immunity / memory cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a transmissible disease?
A cholera
B coronary heart disease
C scurvy
D type 1 diabetes
parts.answer: A cholera
parts.working: A transmissible disease is caused by a pathogen that can pass from one host to another; cholera is caused by a bacterium. Scurvy (C) is a deficiency disease and cannot be passed on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A street-food stall in Rawalpindi wants to reduce the spread of disease to customers. Suggest three hygiene practices the cook should follow.
parts.answer: Any three: wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling food; cook food (especially meat) thoroughly; cover food to keep flies away; keep raw and cooked food apart; use clean water for washing utensils; store food cool / refrigerate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why proper disposal of rubbish near the stall also reduces disease.
parts.answer: Rubbish attracts flies / rats that carry pathogens; they can transfer pathogens to food (indirect transmission).
parts.working: B1 attracts animals / vectors; B1 these carry pathogens to food.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organism causes malaria?
A a bacterium called Vibrio
B a fungus called Candida
C a protist called Plasmodium
D a virus called HIV
parts.answer: C a protist called Plasmodium
parts.working: Malaria is caused by the protist Plasmodium, which is carried between people by Anopheles mosquitoes. Vibrio is a bacterium (cholera), Candida is a fungus, and HIV is a virus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes tuberculosis.
parts.answer: bacterium
parts.working: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes athlete's foot.
parts.answer: fungus
parts.working: Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus (Tinea).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes influenza.
parts.answer: virus
parts.working: Influenza is caused by a virus.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes malaria.
parts.answer: protist
parts.working: Malaria is caused by the protist Plasmodium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a pathogen and a vector. Use malaria as an example.
parts.answer: A pathogen is the organism that causes the disease: Plasmodium. A vector carries the pathogen from one host to another without causing the disease itself: the Anopheles mosquito.
parts.working: 1 mark: pathogen causes disease (Plasmodium). 1 mark: vector transfers the pathogen between hosts (Anopheles mosquito).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three groups of microorganisms that contain species which cause disease.
parts.answer: Any three: bacteria; viruses; fungi; protists.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why viruses can reproduce only inside living cells.
parts.answer: Viruses have no cell structure and no metabolism of their own, so they cannot make new copies without the enzymes and ribosomes of a host cell. They use the host cell's machinery to make new virus particles.
parts.working: 1 mark: viruses have no cell machinery of their own (no ribosomes or enzymes). 1 mark: they use the host cell's machinery to make copies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person who shows no symptoms can still spread a pathogen.
parts.answer: The pathogen can still be present in the person's body or secretions, and it can be passed to others through contact, droplets or contaminated food before symptoms appear or while they have none.
parts.working: 1 mark: the pathogen is present in the body/secretions without symptoms. 1 mark: it can be transmitted to others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between direct and indirect transmission of a pathogen. Give one example of each.
parts.answer: Direct transmission: the pathogen passes from one host to another by contact (e.g. touching, coughing droplets, sexual contact). Indirect transmission: the pathogen passes via a carrier such as food, water, an object or a vector (e.g. cholera from water, malaria from a mosquito).
parts.working: 1 mark: direct transmission by contact. 1 mark: indirect transmission via a carrier. 1 mark: a correct example for each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term pathogen.
parts.answer: A disease-causing organism.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pathogens can be transmitted directly or indirectly. Give one example of direct transmission and two examples of indirect transmission.
parts.answer: Direct: through blood or other body fluids (e.g. sharing needles, sexual contact). Indirect: contaminated surfaces, food or water; animals such as mosquitoes or flies; through the air (droplets).
parts.working: B1 direct example (blood / body fluids); 1 mark each for two indirect routes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of indirect transmission of a pathogen?
A a person coughs droplets onto another person
B a person shakes hands with an infected person
C a person eats food handled by an infected person who did not wash their hands
D a person has sexual contact with an infected partner
parts.answer: C a person eats food handled by an infected person who did not wash their hands
parts.working: Indirect transmission happens through a carrier, such as food, water, an object or a vector. Droplets, handshakes and sexual contact are direct transmission.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why HIV is not spread by a handshake or by sharing a meal.
parts.answer: HIV is spread only through transfer of body fluids such as blood or semen; it does not survive for long outside the body and is not transferred by casual contact.
parts.working: 1 mark: needs transfer of blood or body fluids. 1 mark: it cannot survive outside the body for long.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why HIV is classed as a virus and not as a bacterium.
parts.answer: A virus is not a cell: it is genetic material in a protein coat. It can only reproduce inside host cells, using their machinery. A bacterium is a single cell that can reproduce on its own.
parts.working: 1 mark: a virus is not a cell (genetic material in a protein coat). 1 mark: viruses can only reproduce inside host cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which coughing or sneezing can spread pathogens. Suggest one way of reducing this in a classroom.
parts.answer: Droplets containing pathogens are released into the air and can be breathed in by others; they can land on surfaces and be picked up by hands. Suggest: cover the mouth with a tissue or elbow; wear a face mask; ventilate the room.
parts.working: 1 mark: droplets containing pathogens are released into the air. 1 mark: they land on surfaces or are inhaled by others. 1 mark: a sensible way to reduce spread.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a pathogen on a door handle can infect a person who touches it.
parts.answer: The pathogen is transferred from the handle to the person's hands (indirect contact); when the person touches their mouth, nose or eyes, the pathogen enters the body.
parts.working: 1 mark: transferred to the hands. 1 mark: enters the body when the hands touch the mouth, nose or eyes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one action that reduces this risk.
parts.answer: Wash hands with soap and water (or use hand sanitiser) after touching shared surfaces.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct hygiene action.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection. State how it is spread.
parts.answer: Through sexual contact with an infected person (direct transmission of body fluids).
parts.working: 1 mark: sexual contact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways to reduce the spread of gonorrhoea.
parts.answer: Any two: using a condom; having fewer sexual partners; testing and treatment of infected people; avoiding sexual contact until treatment is complete.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible method, up to 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an infected person should complete the full course of antibiotics.
parts.answer: Completing the course kills all the bacteria and reduces the chance of partial treatment selecting resistant bacteria / of the infection returning.
parts.working: 1 mark: all bacteria must be killed to prevent recurrence or resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bed nets and insect repellent reduce malaria more effectively when used by the whole community than by one family alone.
parts.answer: If most people use nets and repellent, fewer mosquitoes are infected, so there are fewer sources of the parasite; this reduces the chance that an uninfected mosquito feeds on an infected person and then bites another person.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer infected mosquitoes. 1 mark: fewer people are infected, so the reservoir of parasite is reduced. 1 mark: an individual family cannot stop mosquitoes that bite from neighbours' households.

practice.stem:
Dengue fever is caused by a virus carried from person to person by the Aedes mosquito. A city ran a campaign to remove standing water from tyres, flowerpots and water tanks.
recorded dengue cases in 2019: 3960
recorded dengue cases in 2021: 1430

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dengue cases between 2019 and 2021. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how removing standing water reduced the number of dengue cases.
parts.answer: Mosquitoes lay eggs / larvae develop in standing water; fewer breeding sites means fewer mosquitoes; the mosquito is the vector that carries the virus between people, so fewer people are bitten and infected.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mosquitoes breed in standing water; fewer mosquitoes / vectors; less transmission of virus from infected to uninfected people.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other way people can protect themselves from dengue.
parts.answer: Use mosquito nets / repellent / long sleeves / window screens.
parts.working: Any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Malaria is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito. Explain how sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets reduces the number of malaria cases in a community.
parts.answer: The nets stop mosquitoes biting people at night, so fewer people are bitten and fewer pathogens are passed into the blood. The insecticide kills mosquitoes that land on the net, so the population of infected vectors falls, reducing transmission to the whole community.
parts.working: 1 mark: nets prevent bites. 1 mark: fewer pathogens enter the blood. 1 mark: insecticide kills mosquitoes. 1 mark: fewer infected mosquitoes reduces transmission across the community.

practice.stem: In a school of 600 students, the number of students absent with flu was recorded each day: day 1: 15; day 2: 32; day 3: 60; day 4: 96.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the 600 students who were absent on day 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of absences rose so quickly.
parts.answer: Infected students pass the virus to others through droplets and contact; each new case infects more people, so the number of cases grows rapidly.
parts.working: 1 mark: infected students pass the virus to others (droplets, contact). 1 mark: the rise is exponential as each case infects more people.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one measure the school could take.
parts.answer: Any one: students with symptoms stay at home; hand washing; cleaning surfaces; good ventilation; vaccination.
parts.working: 1 mark for a sensible measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'All bacteria cause disease.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: The statement is false. Most bacteria are harmless or useful: many live in the gut and help digestion, some are used to make yoghurt, and some fix nitrogen in soil. Only a small number of species are pathogens that cause disease.
parts.working: 1 mark: states the statement is false. 1 mark: most bacteria are harmless. 1 mark: some are useful (gut flora, yoghurt, nitrogen fixation). 1 mark: only a small number are pathogens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of pathogen that causes cholera.
parts.answer: Bacterium
parts.working: B1 bacterium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how cholera is usually transmitted.
parts.answer: By drinking water (or eating food) contaminated with faeces containing the bacterium.
parts.working: B1 contaminated water / food (sewage / faeces).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two symptoms of cholera.
parts.answer: Severe watery diarrhoea and dehydration (also loss of salts / ions, vomiting).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Two bags made of Visking tubing were set up.
Bag A was filled with distilled water and placed in concentrated salt solution; bag B was filled with dilute salt solution and placed in distilled water. After 30 minutes the bags were dried and weighed.
bag A: starting mass 12.0 g, final mass 10.2 g
bag B: starting mass 12.0 g, final mass 12.4 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass for each bag. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the change in mass of bag A.
parts.answer: The salt solution outside has a lower water potential than the water inside; water moves out of the bag by osmosis through the partially permeable Visking tubing.
parts.working: B1 lower water potential outside / water potential gradient; B1 osmosis through partially permeable membrane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Bag A is used as a model of the small intestine in cholera. State what the Visking tubing and the salt solution each represent.
parts.answer: Visking tubing: the cells / cell membranes lining the intestine. Salt solution: gut contents with chloride ions secreted because of the toxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Cholera is spread mainly by
A direct contact with the skin of an infected person
B the bite of an infected mosquito
C drinking water or eating food contaminated with faeces from an infected person
D droplets in the air breathed in when an infected person coughs
parts.answer: C drinking water or eating food contaminated with faeces from an infected person
parts.working: Cholera is a waterborne and foodborne disease spread by the faecal–oral route. A and D describe direct contact or droplet spread; B describes a vector, which is not involved in cholera.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how cholera bacteria can spread through a town's drinking water supply. Give three steps.
parts.answer: 1) An infected person passes Vibrio cholerae in faeces, which reach a river or well through sewage. 2) The water is contaminated and is drunk by other people. 3) The bacteria reach the small intestine of the new host and multiply there, producing toxin.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct step in order: faeces with bacteria enter the water supply; people drink the contaminated water; bacteria multiply in the small intestine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sachet of oral rehydration solution (ORS) should be dissolved in exactly 1 litre of water. A mother accidentally uses 2 litres of water. Suggest why this could make the drink less effective.
parts.answer: The solution is too dilute: each litre contains half the salts and glucose needed, so less sodium and water is absorbed from the gut, and the patient may not be rehydrated properly.
parts.working: 1 mark: the solution is too dilute and contains less salt and glucose. 1 mark: less sodium and water is absorbed, so rehydration is less effective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two ways in which cholera bacteria from faeces can reach a person's mouth without drinking contaminated water.
parts.answer: Any two: on unwashed hands (for example after using a toilet) and then onto food or drink; carried by flies that land on food; on cooking utensils or cups that have been contaminated.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct route, up to 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one prevention method for one of the routes you named.
parts.answer: Any one matched method: wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling food; cover food to keep flies away; wash utensils with clean water.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct method linked to the route.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a severe attack of diarrhoea, a patient's blood pressure falls. Explain why losing water into the gut causes this.
parts.answer: Loss of water into the gut reduces the volume of plasma in the blood, so there is less blood volume and blood pressure falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: less water/plasma in the blood. 1 mark: lower blood volume lowers blood pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two methods used to treat drinking water to remove or kill pathogens.
parts.answer: Any two: filtration; chlorination; boiling; UV treatment; sedimentation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct method (filtration and chlorination/boiling are the expected answers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why boiling water makes it safe to drink.
parts.answer: Heat kills the bacteria by denaturing their enzymes and proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark: heat denatures the proteins/enzymes of the bacteria, killing them.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The cholera toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine. Which row describes the effect on water potential and water movement?
A water potential of gut contents: increases; water moves: into the cells lining the intestine
B water potential of gut contents: decreases; water moves: into the cells lining the intestine
C water potential of gut contents: increases; water moves: out of the cells into the gut
D water potential of gut contents: decreases; water moves: out of the cells into the gut
parts.answer: D water potential of gut contents: decreases; water moves: out of the cells into the gut
parts.working: Chloride ions lower the water potential of the gut contents, so water leaves the cells (and blood) by osmosis into the lumen, causing watery diarrhoea. B is the common error of linking low water potential with water entering the cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the toxin produced by the cholera bacterium leads to diarrhoea and dehydration.
parts.answer: Bacterium multiplies in the small intestine and releases a toxin; toxin causes secretion of chloride ions into the lumen; this lowers the water potential of the gut contents; water moves out of the cells / blood into the lumen by osmosis; large volume of watery faeces (diarrhoea); loss of water (and ions) from blood and tissues causes dehydration.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: toxin; small intestine; chloride ions secreted into lumen; water potential of lumen lowered; water moves out by osmosis; diarrhoea; loss of water and ions from blood → dehydration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cases of cholera often increase after floods, such as those in Sindh.
parts.answer: Floodwater mixes with untreated sewage, which contains the cholera bacteria; people drink or wash food with this contaminated water.
parts.working: B1 sewage / faeces mixes with drinking water; B1 people drink contaminated water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three measures that could reduce the spread of cholera in a flooded area.
parts.answer: Any three: boil drinking water; chlorinate / treat water supplies; provide bottled or tanker water; build safe toilets / proper sewage disposal; wash hands with soap; cook food thoroughly and protect it from flies; vaccination.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where in the body do cholera bacteria multiply and produce their toxin?
A the stomach
B the small intestine
C the blood plasma
D the large intestine
parts.answer: B the small intestine
parts.working: Cholera bacteria colonise the lining of the small intestine, where the toxin is made and acts on the cells. Stomach acid kills most bacteria, the bacteria do not multiply in the blood, and they do not colonise the large intestine in this way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of immunity produced by an oral cholera vaccine. Explain why a booster dose may be needed some years later.
parts.answer: Active immunity. Antibody levels and memory cells fall over time, so a booster dose is needed to stimulate the memory cells again and restore a rapid response.
parts.working: 1 mark: active immunity. 1 mark: antibody levels fall over time. 1 mark: a booster re-stimulates memory cells / restores protection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why washing hands with soap and water reduces the spread of cholera.
parts.answer: Soap removes bacteria from the skin, so fewer cholera bacteria are transferred from hands to food or water and then to the mouth. Soap also breaks down the grease and faecal material that bacteria cling to.
parts.working: 1 mark: removes bacteria from hands. 1 mark: prevents transfer to food or water. 1 mark: soap breaks down the material bacteria stick to / kills bacteria on hands.

practice.stem: A student tests samples of water for bacteria by spreading each sample on a nutrient agar plate. She also prepares one plate with no sample added, and incubates all plates in the same incubator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why she prepares a plate with no sample added.
parts.answer: It is a control: if bacteria grow on it, the agar, the plate or her technique is contaminated.
parts.working: 1 mark: checks for contamination of the agar, plate or technique.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the plates should be incubated at 37 °C rather than at room temperature.
parts.answer: 37 °C is close to human body temperature, the temperature at which pathogens that infect humans grow best (enzymes work at their optimum).
parts.working: 1 mark: 37 °C is the optimum temperature for human pathogens. 1 mark: at room temperature the pathogens grow slowly or not at all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a health worker must wear gloves and wash hands after touching a cholera patient.
parts.answer: Cholera bacteria in faeces or vomit could be transferred to the health worker's hands and then to other patients or to food, so gloves and hand washing prevent spread.
parts.working: 1 mark: bacteria are transferred from the patient to the worker's hands. 1 mark: they could then infect other people (prevention of transfer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a patient's faeces should be disinfected before it is disposed of.
parts.answer: Disinfection kills the cholera bacteria in the faeces, so they cannot contaminate water or soil and infect other people.
parts.working: 1 mark: kills the bacteria. 1 mark: prevents contamination of water or soil and further infection.

practice.stem: An adult with cholera in a hospital in Sukkur lost fluid as watery faeces at a mean rate of 450 cm³ per hour for 16 hours. He was treated with oral rehydration solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of fluid the patient lost in 16 hours. Give your answer in dm³.
parts.answer: 7.2 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oral rehydration solution contains water, salts and glucose.
parts.answer: Water replaces the water lost in diarrhoea; salts (e.g. sodium and chloride ions) replace the ions lost; glucose provides energy and helps the absorption of salts and water from the intestine.
parts.working: 1 mark each: water replaces lost water; salts / ions replace lost ions; glucose for energy / helps ion (and water) absorption.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why antibiotics alone, without rehydration, may not save a patient with severe cholera.
parts.answer: Death is caused by dehydration; antibiotics kill bacteria but do not replace the lost water and ions quickly enough.
parts.working: B1 dehydration / fluid loss must be treated.

practice.stem:
A town built a water treatment plant that filters and chlorinates its drinking water.
mean number of cholera cases per month before the plant opened: 38
mean number of cholera cases per month after the plant opened: 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the mean number of cholera cases per month. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the water treatment plant reduced the number of cases.
parts.answer: Treatment (filtration and chlorination) kills / removes the cholera bacteria; so people no longer drink water containing the pathogen.
parts.working: B1 bacteria killed / removed (chlorine); B1 drinking water no longer contaminated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some cases still occurred after the plant was opened.
parts.answer: E.g. some homes still use untreated well water; food contaminated; pipes leaking and mixing with sewage; infection from travellers.
parts.working: Any one sensible suggestion.

practice.stem: In a refugee camp after flooding, the number of new cholera cases was recorded each day: day 1: 2; day 2: 4; day 3: 8; day 4: 16; day 5: 32; day 6: 64.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the number of cases from day 2 to day 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of cases increased so quickly.
parts.answer: Each infected person passes the bacteria to others through contaminated water and food, and the bacteria multiply in the gut, so the number of cases doubles each day.
parts.working: 1 mark: infected people contaminate water or food that others consume. 1 mark: cases double each day because the bacteria spread and multiply repeatedly (exponential growth).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two measures the camp could take to slow the spread.
parts.answer: Any two: provide clean chlorinated water; separate and treat faeces (latrines); hand washing with soap; treat patients with ORS and antibiotics; isolate cases.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible measure, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient with cholera is treated with antibiotics and oral rehydration solution (ORS). Explain why both treatments are needed, and why antibiotics alone do not stop the patient's symptoms quickly.
parts.answer: Antibiotics kill the bacteria, so no more toxin is produced and the infection is shortened. But toxin already made continues to cause water loss until it is cleared, so symptoms continue. ORS replaces the water and salts already lost, which prevents dehydration and shock while the body recovers.
parts.working: 1 mark: antibiotics kill the bacteria / stop toxin production. 1 mark: toxin already made continues to act, so symptoms do not stop at once. 1 mark: ORS replaces the water and salts lost. 1 mark: ORS prevents dehydration and shock while the body recovers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substances are all present in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule of a healthy person?
A glucose, protein and urea
B glucose, salts and urea
C protein, red blood cells and water
D red blood cells, salts and water
parts.answer: B glucose, salts and urea
parts.working: Small molecules and ions (water, glucose, salts, urea) are filtered from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule. Proteins and red blood cells are too large to pass through the filter, so A, C and D are wrong; A is the main distractor because glucose and urea are filtered but protein is not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the structures that urine passes through from a kidney to the outside of the body.
parts.answer: Ureter → bladder → urethra.
parts.working: 2 marks all three in correct order; 1 mark for three names in the wrong order or two in correct order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings blood to the kidney and the vessel that takes blood away.
parts.answer: Renal artery brings blood; renal vein takes it away.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define excretion.
parts.answer: The removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements from the body.
parts.working: 1 mark: removal of waste products of metabolism (e.g. urea, CO₂); 1 mark: and substances in excess of requirements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the excretory product removed by the lungs and the process that produces it.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide; (aerobic) respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances removed from the blood by the kidneys.
parts.answer: Urea, excess water, excess (salts) ions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organ where urea is made.
parts.answer: Liver.

practice.stem:
Six students measured the total volume of urine they produced in one 24-hour period.
Student: A, B, C, D, E, F
Volume (cm³): 1450, 1620, 980, 1800, 1350, 1520

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume of urine produced per student. Give your answer to the nearest cm³.
parts.answer: 1453 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Student C produced the smallest volume. Suggest two reasons for this.
parts.answer: Drank less water; did more exercise or was in a hot place so lost more water in sweat; ate salty food.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one variable that should be controlled to compare students fairly.
parts.answer: Volume of water drunk; amount of exercise; temperature of surroundings; the 24-hour period used.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone increases the reabsorption of water in the collecting ducts of the kidney?
A insulin
B adrenaline
C antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
D thyroxine
parts.answer: C antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
parts.working: ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated. It makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed, giving a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. Insulin controls blood glucose, adrenaline prepares the body for action and thyroxine controls the metabolic rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two treatments for kidney failure.
parts.answer: Dialysis; kidney transplant.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two correct treatments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one disadvantage of dialysis compared with a kidney transplant.
parts.answer: The patient must attend a dialysis machine several times a week for several hours each time, which limits daily life; dialysis does not do all the work of a healthy kidney (for example, it does not make hormones).
parts.working: 1 mark for the disadvantage; 1 mark for developing it, such as the time needed for sessions or dialysis not doing all kidney functions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process by which plasma moves from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: Ultrafiltration.
parts.working: 1 mark for ultrafiltration (or filtration under pressure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which water moves from the filtrate into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule.
parts.answer: Osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark for osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process by which glucose is taken from the filtrate back into the blood.
parts.answer: Active transport (co-transport with sodium ions).
parts.working: 1 mark for active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a transplanted kidney may be rejected.
parts.answer: The recipient's immune system detects the donor tissue as foreign (different antigens) and attacks it.
parts.working: 1 mark: immune system recognises the donor tissue as foreign; 1 mark: white blood cells attack the transplanted kidney.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where in the kidney does filtration of blood take place?
A from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule
B from the loop of Henle into the collecting duct
C from the collecting duct into the ureter
D from the renal vein into the renal artery
parts.answer: A from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule
parts.working: Blood at high pressure in the glomerulus is filtered into the Bowman's capsule. The collecting duct carries urine towards the ureter (C) but no filtration occurs there.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is completely reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule of a healthy person?
A urea
B glucose
C protein
D water
parts.answer: B glucose
parts.working: All the filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (by active transport). Protein is not filtered at all, so it cannot be reabsorbed (C); water is reabsorbed in several regions and not completely (D).

practice.stem:
The table shows the concentrations of some substances in the blood plasma, in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule and in the urine of a healthy person (g/dm³).
Substance | plasma | filtrate | urine
protein | 80.0 | 0.0 | 0.0
glucose | 1.0 | 1.0 | 0.0
urea | 0.3 | 0.3 | 20.0
salts | 7.2 | 7.2 | 15.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is no protein in the filtrate.
parts.answer: Protein molecules are too large to pass through the filter (the walls of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule), so they stay in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: protein molecules too large; 1 mark: cannot pass through glomerulus / capsule wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why glucose is present in the filtrate but absent from the urine.
parts.answer: Glucose molecules are small enough to be filtered; all of the glucose is reabsorbed into the blood (in the proximal convoluted tubule).
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose filtered (small molecule); 1 mark: all reabsorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the filtrate. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 67 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of urea increases as the filtrate passes along the nephron.
parts.answer: Most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed into the blood, but urea is not (or only a little), so the same amount of urea is in a much smaller volume.
parts.working: 1 mark: water reabsorbed; 1 mark: urea not reabsorbed / stays in tubule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the parts of a nephron that filtrate passes through after leaving the Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: Proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct.
parts.working: 3 marks all four in correct order; 2 marks three in order; 1 mark two in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the part of the nephron where all the glucose is reabsorbed.
parts.answer: Proximal convoluted tubule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two substances, other than glucose, that are reabsorbed from the filtrate.
parts.answer: Water and salts (ions); also amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A teacher prepared three samples of artificial 'urine' (1, 2 and 3) to represent samples from three patients. A student tested each with Benedict's solution and with biuret solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student would test each sample for glucose and what a positive result would look like.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the sample; heat in a water-bath at about 80 °C for a few minutes; a positive result is a colour change from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red.
parts.working: 1 mark: Benedict's solution; 1 mark: heat in water-bath; 1 mark: blue → green/yellow/orange/brick-red.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sample 2 gave an orange-red colour with Benedict's solution. Suggest what this indicates about the person.
parts.answer: Glucose is present in the urine, which suggests the person may have diabetes (type 1) – blood glucose is too high and not all is reabsorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose present; 1 mark: possible diabetes / high blood glucose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sample 3 gave a purple colour with biuret solution. Suggest what this shows and why it is a cause for concern.
parts.answer: Protein is present in the urine; protein is normally too large to be filtered, so the filter in the kidneys may be damaged (kidney disease).
parts.working: 1 mark: protein present; 1 mark: suggests damage to glomeruli/kidney filtration.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one safety precaution when carrying out these tests.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection / gloves; use a water-bath not a direct flame; handle hot tubes with a holder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why red blood cells and plasma proteins are not found in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: They are too large to pass through the walls of the glomerulus capillaries and the Bowman's capsule, so they remain in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: too large; 1 mark: cannot pass through glomerulus/capsule walls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why blood in the glomerulus is at high pressure and why this is important.
parts.answer: The vessel leaving the glomerulus is narrower than the one entering it (and the renal artery comes directly from the aorta); the high pressure forces small molecules and water out of the blood into the capsule (filtration).
parts.working: 1 mark: cause – narrower exit vessel / close to aorta; 1 mark: pressure forces fluid out → filtration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region of the kidney in which the glomeruli are found.
parts.answer: Cortex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A longitudinal section of a kidney shows an outer region, an inner region and a hollow space that leads into a tube. Name these three parts.
parts.answer: Cortex (outer); medulla (inner); pelvis leading to the ureter.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cortex; medulla; ureter (accept renal pelvis/ureter for the space and tube).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which parts of the nephrons lie in the medulla.
parts.answer: The loops of Henle (and collecting ducts).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each kidney contains about one million nephrons. Suggest why so many are needed.
parts.answer: To give a very large surface area / capacity for filtering the large volume of blood (about 180 dm³ filtrate per day) and for reabsorption.
parts.working: 1 mark: large total area for filtration/reabsorption; 1 mark: large volume of blood processed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria. Explain why.
parts.answer: These cells reabsorb glucose (and some ions) by active transport, against a concentration gradient; active transport needs energy; the energy is released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reabsorption of glucose/ions by active transport; requires energy; mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: These cells also have microvilli on the surface facing the filtrate. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Microvilli increase the surface area for reabsorption.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what would happen to the glucose content of urine if a poison stopped respiration in these cells.
parts.answer: Glucose would appear in the urine, because without energy it could not be reabsorbed by active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose in urine; 1 mark: no energy → no active transport.

practice.stem: Plasma flows into the kidneys' glomeruli at 650 cm³ per minute. Each minute, 125 cm³ of this plasma is filtered into the Bowman's capsules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the plasma that is filtered. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 125 ÷ 650 × 100; 1 mark for 19.2 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of filtrate formed in 24 hours. Give your answer in dm³.
parts.answer: 180 dm³
parts.working: 1 mark for 125 × 60 × 24 = 180 000 cm³; 1 mark for 180 dm³.

practice.stem: A healthy adult produces 1.5 dm³ of urine per day, containing urea at 25 g/dm³. The filtrate formed in one day is 180 dm³, containing urea at 0.25 g/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of urea excreted in one day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of urea filtered in one day.
parts.working: 1 mark for 180 × 0.25; 1 mark for 45 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the filtered urea that is excreted. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 37.5 ÷ 45 × 100; 1 mark for 83.3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is NOT a function of the kidneys?
A removing urea from the blood
B controlling the water and salt content of the blood
C producing bile
D helping to regulate blood pH by excreting hydrogen ions
parts.answer: C producing bile
parts.working: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder, not made by the kidneys. The kidneys remove urea, control the water and salt content of the blood, and help regulate blood pH by excreting hydrogen ions.

practice.stem: A healthy person's kidneys filter 40 g of salt (sodium chloride) from the plasma each day. The urine contains 6 g of salt per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the filtered salt that is reabsorbed. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: 1 mark for (40 − 6) ÷ 40 × 100; 1 mark for 85 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where most of this salt reabsorption takes place.
parts.answer: Proximal convoluted tubule.
parts.working: 1 mark for the proximal convoluted tubule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the process by which salt is mainly reabsorbed.
parts.answer: Active transport.
parts.working: 1 mark for active transport.

practice.stem: Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH from the pituitary gland.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person who has drunk alcohol produces a large volume of dilute urine.
parts.answer: Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH, so less ADH reaches the kidneys; the collecting ducts are less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed and a larger volume of dilute urine is produced.
parts.working: 1 mark: less ADH released; 1 mark: collecting ducts less permeable to water; 1 mark: less water reabsorbed, so more dilute urine.

practice.stem: A woman takes in 2.4 dm³ of water each day (1.6 dm³ drunk and 0.8 dm³ in food). She loses 0.3 dm³ in sweat, 0.5 dm³ from her lungs and skin, and 0.1 dm³ in faeces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: If her water balance is level (water taken in equals water lost), calculate the volume of water lost in her urine per day.
parts.answer: 1.5 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person must drink more water in hot weather.
parts.answer: More water is lost as sweat, so more water is needed to keep the water balance level and the blood's water potential steady.
parts.working: 1 mark: more water lost in sweat; 1 mark: extra intake needed to keep water balance and blood water potential steady.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The concentration of urea in a person's blood plasma is 0.25 g/dm³ and in their urine is 18.0 g/dm³. How many times more concentrated is urea in the urine than in the plasma?
A 4.5
B 17.75
C 72
D 450
parts.working: 18.0 ÷ 0.25 = 72. The urea is concentrated because most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed while urea is not. 17.75 is the difference, not the ratio.

practice.stem: In an adult, about 180 dm³ of filtrate is formed in the kidneys each day, but only about 1.5 dm³ of urine is produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the filtered water that is reabsorbed into the blood. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that so much of the filtered water is reabsorbed.
parts.answer: Otherwise the body would lose huge volumes of water each day and quickly become dehydrated; reabsorption keeps the water content (water potential) of the blood constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: prevents dehydration / huge water loss; 1 mark: keeps blood water content/water potential constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: On a very hot day a farm worker in Jacobabad sweats heavily and drinks little water. Describe and explain how the volume and concentration of the worker's urine change.
parts.answer: Smaller volume of urine; more concentrated (darker); because water is lost in sweat, the kidneys reabsorb more water from the filtrate back into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller volume; 1 mark: more concentrated; 1 mark: more water reabsorbed in the kidney to conserve water.

practice.stem:
A volunteer emptied their bladder and then drank 1 dm³ of water. Urine was collected every 30 minutes for 3 hours. On another day the same volunteer drank 1 dm³ of salt solution and the experiment was repeated.
Time period (min) | urine after water (cm³) | urine after salt solution (cm³)
0–30 | 40 | 40
30–60 | 250 | 55
60–90 | 310 | 60
90–120 | 140 | 50
120–150 | 60 | 45
150–180 | 45 | 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of urine produced in 3 hours after drinking (i) water and (ii) salt solution.
parts.answer: (i) 845 cm³; (ii) 290 cm³
parts.working: 1 mark each: sum of the six readings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the differences between the two sets of results.
parts.answer: After water, urine output rose to a peak of 310 cm³ at 60–90 min then fell; after salt solution the output stayed low (40–60 cm³) throughout; total volume about three times greater after water.
parts.working: 1 mark: water gives much larger volume / peak at 60–90 min; 1 mark: salt gives small, steady volume, with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the results after drinking water.
parts.answer: Water absorbed from the gut raised the water content (water potential) of the blood; the kidneys reabsorbed less water from the filtrate; so a large volume of dilute urine was produced, returning blood water content to normal.
parts.working: 1 mark each: blood water content/water potential increased; less water reabsorbed in kidney; large volume of dilute urine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the volunteer emptied their bladder at the start of the experiment.
parts.answer: So that only urine produced during the experiment was collected and measured.

practice.stem:
The table shows whether glucose was found in the urine of a person at different blood glucose concentrations.
Blood glucose (mmol/dm³): 5, 8, 10, 12, 15
Glucose in urine: none, none, none, small amount, large amount

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between blood glucose concentration and glucose in the urine.
parts.answer: No glucose appears in the urine until the blood glucose concentration rises above about 10 mmol/dm³; above this, the amount of glucose in the urine increases as blood glucose increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: none up to 10 mmol/dm³; 1 mark: increasing glucose in urine above 10 / at 12 and 15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for these results in terms of how the nephron handles glucose.
parts.answer: All glucose in the blood is filtered into the nephron; reabsorption of glucose is by active transport with carrier proteins, which have a maximum rate; above about 10 mmol/dm³ more glucose is filtered than can be reabsorbed, so the excess stays in the filtrate and appears in urine.
parts.working: 1 mark each: glucose filtered in proportion to blood concentration; reabsorption by active transport / carriers limited; excess not reabsorbed → in urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person with untreated type 1 diabetes often produces large volumes of urine and feels very thirsty.
parts.answer: Glucose left in the filtrate lowers its water potential, so less water is reabsorbed by osmosis; large volumes of urine lose water, so the person becomes dehydrated and thirsty.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose in filtrate reduces water reabsorption (osmosis); 1 mark: more water lost → thirst.

practice.stem: In a healthy adult, the kidneys produce filtrate at a rate of about 125 cm³ per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of filtrate produced in one day, in dm³.
parts.answer: 180 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The filtrate contains glucose at 1.0 g/dm³. Calculate the mass of glucose filtered each day and state how much of it is normally lost in the urine.
parts.answer: 180 g filtered; none (0 g) is lost in urine
parts.working: 1 mark: 180 × 1.0 = 180 g; 1 mark: 0 g – all reabsorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the body must reabsorb this glucose.
parts.answer: Glucose is needed for respiration to release energy; losing 180 g a day would waste a large energy source / blood glucose would fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose used in respiration / energy; 1 mark: loss would be wasteful / would lower blood glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain two differences between the composition of blood in the renal artery and in the renal vein of a healthy person.
parts.answer: Urea concentration is lower in the renal vein, because urea is filtered out and not reabsorbed (removed in urine). Oxygen concentration is lower (and carbon dioxide higher) in the renal vein, because kidney cells use oxygen in respiration, especially for active transport. (Also: less water / fewer excess ions in the renal vein because they are removed in urine.)
parts.working: For each of two differences: 1 mark for the difference with direction, 1 mark for the explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the kidneys receive about a fifth of the blood pumped by the heart at rest, although they make up less than 1 % of body mass.
parts.answer: The whole blood volume must be filtered many times a day to remove urea and keep water and ion content constant; a large blood flow keeps filtration and removal of waste fast.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood needs to be filtered frequently / large volume processed; 1 mark: to keep removing urea / regulate water and ions.

practice.stem: A dialysis machine uses a partially permeable membrane. Blood flows on one side and dialysis fluid on the other. The fluid contains the same concentrations of glucose and salts as healthy blood plasma, but no urea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why urea diffuses from the blood into the dialysis fluid.
parts.answer: The urea concentration is higher in the blood than in the fluid, so urea moves down its concentration gradient through the membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher urea concentration in blood; 1 mark: moves down the concentration gradient through the membrane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why glucose and useful salts do not leave the blood.
parts.answer: They have the same concentration in the blood and in the dialysis fluid, so there is no concentration gradient and no net movement.
parts.working: 1 mark: same concentration on both sides; 1 mark: no concentration gradient, so no net movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why red blood cells and large plasma proteins stay in the blood.
parts.answer: They are too large to pass through the pores of the membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: too large to pass through the membrane.

practice.stem: During dialysis, a patient's blood urea concentration fell from 40 mmol/dm³ to 12 mmol/dm³ in four hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of blood urea removed during dialysis. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: 1 mark for (40 − 12) ÷ 40 × 100; 1 mark for 70 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a patient with kidney failure needs dialysis regularly rather than once.
parts.answer: Urea and other wastes build up again between sessions because the kidneys cannot remove them; dialysis removes only part of the waste each time, so regular sessions are needed to keep blood urea at a safe level.
parts.working: 1 mark: wastes build up between sessions as kidneys do not work; 1 mark: dialysis removes only part of the waste each session; 1 mark: regular sessions keep levels safe.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which organ is urea formed?
A kidney
B liver
C bladder
D pancreas
parts.answer: B liver
parts.working: Urea is made in the liver from the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids (deamination). The kidney removes urea from the blood but does not make it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why excess amino acids cannot be kept in the body for later use.
parts.answer: Amino acids cannot be stored in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the liver.
parts.answer: They are deaminated: the nitrogen-containing part is removed and converted into urea; the remaining part can be used in respiration for energy (or converted to carbohydrate / glycogen or fat).
parts.working: 1 mark: deamination; 1 mark: nitrogen-containing part → urea; 1 mark: rest used for respiration / energy / converted and stored.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how urea leaves the liver.
parts.answer: Dissolved in the blood plasma (in the hepatic vein).

parts.label: a
parts.text: After digestion, amino acids are taken to the liver in the hepatic portal vein. State two uses of these amino acids in the liver or the body, other than forming urea.
parts.answer: Making proteins, e.g. plasma proteins such as fibrinogen; making enzymes; growth and repair of cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the term used for the movement of digested food molecules into cells, where they are used and become part of the cells.
parts.answer: Assimilation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the liver does with excess glucose after a meal.
parts.answer: Converts it into glycogen and stores it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lion eats mainly meat. A goat eats mainly grass and leaves. Suggest which animal produces more urea per kilogram of body mass. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The lion; meat is rich in protein, so it absorbs more amino acids than it needs; the excess is deaminated in the liver, forming more urea.
parts.working: 1 mark: lion; 1 mark: high-protein diet / more excess amino acids; 1 mark: deamination → more urea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that removes urea from the blood in both animals.
parts.answer: Kidney.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Deamination removes the nitrogen-containing amino group from amino acids. Which two products are formed?
A urea and carbon dioxide
B ammonia and a compound that can be used in respiration
C glucose and glycerol
D carbon dioxide and fatty acids
parts.answer: B ammonia and a compound that can be used in respiration
