parts.working: Deamination produces ammonia, which is toxic and is converted to urea in the liver, and a carbon-containing compound that can enter respiration or be stored. Urea is made from ammonia, not directly from amino acids; glucose and glycerol are not products of amino acid breakdown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three functions of the liver other than urea production.
parts.answer: Storage of glycogen; breakdown of alcohol and other toxins (detoxification); production of bile; production of plasma proteins; storage of vitamins.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of any three valid functions.

practice.stem: After a long period of exercise, the body's blood glucose falls and the hormone glucagon is released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where glucagon acts to raise blood glucose.
parts.answer: The liver.
parts.working: 1 mark for the liver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the carbohydrate stored in the liver that is converted to glucose.
parts.answer: Glycogen.
parts.working: 1 mark for glycogen.

practice.stem: A person's liver produces 30 g of urea each day, and all of it is excreted by the kidneys in 1.4 dm³ of urine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of urea in the urine, in g/dm³. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 21.4 g/dm³
parts.working: 1 mark for 30 ÷ 1.4; 1 mark for 21.4 g/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two effects on the liver of drinking too much alcohol.
parts.answer: Liver cells are damaged; fat builds up in the liver; scarring (cirrhosis) develops; the liver cannot process toxins as well.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of any two valid effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define deamination.
parts.answer: The removal of the nitrogen-containing amino group from amino acids, in the liver.
parts.working: 1 mark for removal of the amino group from amino acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is deamination?
A the breakdown of proteins into amino acids in the small intestine
B the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea
C the filtration of urea from the blood in the kidney
D the joining of amino acids to make proteins in the liver
parts.answer: B the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea
parts.working: Deamination occurs in the liver: the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids is removed and converted to urea. A describes digestion; D describes protein synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route taken by a urea molecule from the liver to the kidney. Name the blood vessels and the chambers of the heart it passes through.
parts.answer: Hepatic vein → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → renal artery → kidney.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: hepatic vein and vena cava; right side of heart and pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary vein and left side of heart; aorta and renal artery. Order must be correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the vessel that carries urea out of the kidney to the bladder.
parts.answer: Ureter (urea dissolved in urine).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why urea must be removed from the body.
parts.answer: Urea is toxic; if it builds up in the blood it can damage cells / tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: toxic; 1 mark: build-up would harm cells / change water potential of blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some people with kidney failure have to limit the amount of protein they eat. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Less protein means fewer excess amino acids to deaminate, so less urea is made, which the damaged kidneys cannot remove properly.
parts.working: 1 mark: less protein → less deamination → less urea; 1 mark: kidneys cannot remove urea efficiently, so it would build up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the concentrations of glucose and urea in the blood of the hepatic portal vein and of the hepatic vein one hour after a meal of rice and chicken.
parts.answer: Glucose: higher in the hepatic portal vein than in the hepatic vein. Urea: lower in the hepatic portal vein than in the hepatic vein.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a).
parts.answer: The hepatic portal vein brings glucose and amino acids absorbed from the small intestine; the liver removes excess glucose and stores it as glycogen; the liver deaminates excess amino acids and adds urea to the blood leaving in the hepatic vein.
parts.working: 1 mark each: portal vein carries absorbed food; excess glucose stored as glycogen; urea produced by deamination added to hepatic vein blood.

practice.stem: Each gram of nitrogen from excess amino acids is converted in the liver into 2.14 g of urea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person has an excess of 12.0 g of nitrogen from amino acids in one day. Calculate the mass of urea produced. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why urea is produced rather than ammonia being released into the blood.
parts.answer: Ammonia is very toxic; urea is much less toxic, can be carried in the blood and is excreted by the kidneys.
parts.working: 1 mark: ammonia is very toxic; 1 mark: urea is less toxic and can be transported and excreted.

practice.stem: Blood samples were taken from the hepatic portal vein and the hepatic vein of a person. Urea concentration (mmol/dm³): hepatic portal vein 0.20; hepatic vein 0.62.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in urea concentration from the hepatic portal vein to the hepatic vein. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the urea concentration is higher in the hepatic vein.
parts.answer: Urea is made in the liver cells and passes into the blood of the hepatic vein; the blood in the hepatic portal vein has little urea.
parts.working: 1 mark: urea is made in liver cells; 1 mark: it passes into the blood leaving the liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why liver cells contain many mitochondria, in relation to deamination and urea production.
parts.answer: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration; the conversion of ammonia to urea needs energy (ATP), so many mitochondria are needed to supply it.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to release energy; 1 mark: converting ammonia to urea needs energy; 1 mark: many mitochondria supply enough energy for this.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about urea is correct?
A urea is made in the kidneys from ammonia
B urea is made in the liver from ammonia
C urea is removed from the body in faeces
D urea is more toxic than ammonia
parts.answer: B urea is made in the liver from ammonia
parts.working: Ammonia from deamination is converted to urea in the liver. Urea is removed by the kidneys in urine, not in faeces, and it is far less toxic than ammonia.

practice.stem: In one day a person takes in 16 g of nitrogen in food. 13.6 g of this is excreted in urine and 1.6 g in faeces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the nitrogen intake that is excreted in urine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 13.6 ÷ 16 × 100; 1 mark for 85.0 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why some nitrogen is retained in the body.
parts.answer: It is used to make new body proteins for growth and repair.
parts.working: 1 mark for growth, repair or protein synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the process by which excess amino acids are changed in the liver.
parts.answer: Deamination removes the amino group, forming ammonia and a keto acid; the ammonia is converted into urea using energy from respiration; the urea is released into the blood, and the rest of the molecule is used in respiration or stored.
parts.working: 1 mark for deamination removing the amino group; 1 mark for ammonia converted to urea; 1 mark for urea released into the blood (or the remainder used or stored).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the urine of a person who has eaten very little protein for several days contains less urea.
parts.answer: Less protein means fewer amino acids are deaminated, so less urea is made in the liver and excreted by the kidneys.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer amino acids deaminated; 1 mark: less urea made and excreted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the liver converts excess glucose after a meal into glycogen.
parts.answer: Glucose would otherwise raise blood glucose too high; insulin stimulates the liver to convert glucose to glycogen, which is stored and can be converted back to glucose when needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: prevents blood glucose rising too high; 1 mark: insulin stimulates conversion to glycogen; 1 mark: glycogen stored and released again when needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person eats a meal rich in protein. One hour later, in which blood vessel will the concentration of urea be highest?
A hepatic portal vein
B hepatic vein
C renal vein
D pulmonary artery
parts.answer: B hepatic vein
parts.working: Urea is made in the liver and released into the blood leaving it, so the hepatic vein carries blood with the highest urea concentration. The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut to the liver, before urea is added; the renal vein has had urea removed.

practice.stem:
A dietitian measured the mass of urea excreted per day by one adult on three different diets.
Protein eaten (g per day): 40, 80, 120
Urea excreted (g per day): 9.5, 18.8, 28.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in urea excreted when protein intake rose from 40 g to 120 g per day. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of urea excreted per gram of protein eaten on the 120 g diet. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.24 g urea per g protein

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the relationship shown in the table.
parts.answer: More protein eaten → more amino acids absorbed than the body needs; the excess amino acids cannot be stored and are deaminated in the liver; so more urea is formed and excreted by the kidneys.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more amino acids absorbed than needed; excess deaminated in liver; more urea made → more excreted (urea roughly proportional to protein).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why some urea is still excreted on a diet with very little protein.
parts.answer: Body proteins are continually broken down / some amino acids are always deaminated, e.g. from the turnover of cells.

practice.stem:
The enzyme urease breaks down urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. A student mixed 5 cm³ of three urine samples (A, B and C) each with 1 cm³ of urease solution and three drops of phenol red indicator at 30 °C. Phenol red is yellow in acidic or neutral solution and turns pink in alkaline solution. The time for each mixture to turn pink was recorded.
Sample A: 45 s; sample B: 120 s; sample C: 80 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction for each sample, using rate = 1000 ÷ time. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: A: 22.2; B: 8.3; C: 12.5 (arbitrary units)
parts.working: 2 marks all three correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which sample contained the most urea and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Sample A; it changed colour fastest, so ammonia (alkali) was produced fastest because there was most urea for the enzyme to act on.
parts.working: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: shortest time / fastest rate because more substrate (urea) → more ammonia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the indicator changed colour.
parts.answer: Urease breaks down urea into ammonia (and carbon dioxide); ammonia makes the solution alkaline, turning phenol red from yellow to pink.
parts.working: 1 mark: urea → ammonia; 1 mark: alkaline → colour change.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State three variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of urine sample; volume/concentration of urease; volume of indicator; temperature; pH at start.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient has severe liver damage. Tests show that the concentration of urea in their blood is lower than normal but the concentration of amino acids is higher than normal. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: The damaged liver cannot deaminate amino acids efficiently; so amino acids build up in the blood; and less urea is formed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reduced deamination by liver; amino acids accumulate; less urea produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the patient's urine contains less urea than normal even though their kidneys are healthy.
parts.answer: Less urea is made by the liver, so less is filtered into the urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Doctors advise this patient to eat only a moderate amount of protein. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Excess amino acids cannot be dealt with properly by the damaged liver, so eating less protein reduces the amount of excess amino acids (and nitrogenous waste) building up.
parts.working: 1 mark: liver cannot process excess amino acids; 1 mark: less protein reduces the build-up.

practice.stem: In severe liver failure the liver cannot convert ammonia into urea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of ammonia in the blood rises.
parts.answer: Ammonia from deamination is no longer converted to urea by the damaged liver, so it builds up in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: liver cannot convert ammonia to urea; 1 mark: ammonia accumulates in the blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a build-up of ammonia is dangerous.
parts.answer: Ammonia is toxic; it can damage the brain and nervous system and disrupt the chemistry of cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: ammonia is toxic; 1 mark: it damages the brain/nervous system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the roles of the liver and the kidneys in removing nitrogen-containing waste. Give two similarities and two differences.
parts.answer: Similarities: both deal with nitrogen-containing waste; both help to keep the blood's composition constant. Differences: the liver makes urea from ammonia, while the kidneys filter urea out of the blood and excrete it; the liver releases urea into the blood, but the kidneys remove it from the body.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid similarity or difference (up to 4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a patient with liver disease might be advised to eat less protein.
parts.answer: Less protein means fewer amino acids to deaminate, so less ammonia is produced; the damaged liver cannot convert all the ammonia to urea, so less protein reduces the build-up of ammonia in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: less protein means fewer amino acids to deaminate; 1 mark: less ammonia is produced; 1 mark: the damaged liver cannot cope, so less build-up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that because the liver makes urea, it removes urea from the body. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: The claim is wrong: the liver makes urea and releases it into the blood, but the urea is removed from the body by the kidneys in urine. The liver does not excrete urea.
parts.working: 1 mark: the liver makes urea; 1 mark: urea is released into the blood; 1 mark: the kidneys remove urea from the body, not the liver.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For which disease would a doctor prescribe an antibiotic?
A influenza
B measles
C cholera
D the common cold
parts.answer: C cholera
parts.working: Cholera is caused by a bacterium, and antibiotics act on bacteria. Influenza, measles and colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not affect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what an antibiotic is used for.
parts.answer: To treat bacterial infections (kill bacteria or stop them growing) in the body.
parts.working: B1 treat bacterial infection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student with a bad cold asks a doctor for antibiotics. Explain why the doctor refuses.
parts.answer: Colds are caused by viruses; antibiotics have no effect on viruses (and unnecessary use encourages resistant bacteria).
parts.working: B1 cold caused by virus; B1 antibiotics do not kill viruses / encourage resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one disease, caused by bacteria, that can be treated with antibiotics.
parts.answer: e.g. cholera, tuberculosis, typhoid, bacterial pneumonia, strep throat.
parts.working: B1 any bacterial disease. Do not accept viral diseases (e.g. HIV, flu, COVID-19).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why some bacterial infections are now difficult to treat with antibiotics.
parts.answer: Some bacteria are resistant to antibiotics, which reduces the effectiveness of the antibiotics.
parts.working: B1 resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one example of a strain of bacteria that is resistant to several antibiotics.
parts.answer: MRSA
parts.working: B1 MRSA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Antibiotics affect bacteria but do not affect viruses. Name one structure found in bacteria that is not found in viruses.
parts.answer: Cell wall / cell membrane / ribosomes / cytoplasm.
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether each disease can be treated with antibiotics: (i) tuberculosis; (ii) HIV/AIDS; (iii) cholera; (iv) influenza.
parts.answer: (i) yes; (ii) no; (iii) yes; (iv) no.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each statement about antibiotics is true or false: (i) Antibiotics kill bacteria. (ii) Antibiotics are effective against all pathogens. (iii) Antibiotics should be taken until the course is finished. (iv) Antibiotics can be used to treat the common cold.
parts.answer: (i) true; (ii) false; (iii) true; (iv) false.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Antibodies and antibiotics are often confused. State one difference between them.
parts.answer: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes in the body; antibiotics are drugs (often made by microorganisms) taken to kill bacteria.
parts.working: B1 antibodies made by lymphocytes / white blood cells vs antibiotics are drugs taken into the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person should not take antibiotics left over from a previous illness, or share them with a family member.
parts.answer: The illness may be viral, so the antibiotic will not work; it may be the wrong antibiotic / not enough for a full course / wrong dose; this exposes bacteria to low doses so resistant bacteria survive and multiply.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: illness may be viral; wrong antibiotic for that bacterium; incomplete course / wrong dose; increases resistance; may cause allergy / side effects (not the prescribed patient).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why antibiotics are sometimes called 'a precious resource'.
parts.answer: As resistance increases, fewer antibiotics work and very few new antibiotics are being developed.
parts.working: B1 resistance making them ineffective / few new ones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first antibiotic, penicillin, was obtained from a mould. State the kingdom to which moulds belong.
parts.answer: Fungi
parts.working: B1 fungi / fungus kingdom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to bacteria when they are exposed to an antibiotic to which they are not resistant.
parts.answer: They are killed or their growth (reproduction) is stopped.
parts.working: B1 killed / growth prevented.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a doctor may change to a different antibiotic if a patient's infection does not improve.
parts.answer: The bacteria may be resistant to the first antibiotic.
parts.working: B1 resistance.

practice.stem: Equal volumes of a culture of a harmless bacterium were spread on agar plates with and without an antibiotic and incubated at 25 °C. Number of colonies: without antibiotic – mean 180; with antibiotic – 17, 20, 17.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of colonies on plates with antibiotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of colonies that survived on antibiotic plates compared with plates without antibiotic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the colonies growing on the antibiotic plates show about those bacteria.
parts.answer: They are resistant to the antibiotic.
parts.working: B1 resistant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A course of antibiotics would kill which of these organisms in a patient?
A HIV
B the influenza virus
C Salmonella, a bacterium that causes food poisoning
D the measles virus
parts.answer: C Salmonella, a bacterium that causes food poisoning
parts.working: Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect viruses. A, B and D are all viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why do antibiotics not cure diseases caused by viruses?
A Viruses are too small to be seen by the immune system.
B Viruses lack the structures and processes, such as cell walls, that antibiotics act on.
C Viruses are always resistant to antibiotics because of mutations.
D Antibiotics only work in the gut, and viruses live in the lungs.
parts.answer: B Viruses lack the structures and processes, such as cell walls, that antibiotics act on.
parts.working: Antibiotics damage bacterial structures or processes (e.g. cell wall formation); viruses have no cell wall or cell processes of their own and reproduce inside host cells. Resistance (C) is a property of some bacteria, not the reason viruses are unaffected.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is MRSA?
A a virus that causes pneumonia
B a strain of bacteria resistant to several commonly used antibiotics
C an antibiotic used in hospitals
D a fungus that produces penicillin
parts.answer: B a strain of bacteria resistant to several commonly used antibiotics
parts.working: MRSA is a strain of Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to methicillin and several other antibiotics, making infections hard to treat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the development of resistant bacteria, such as MRSA, can be minimised.
parts.answer: Use antibiotics only when essential (not for viral infections); doctors prescribe only when needed / avoid unnecessary prescriptions; patients complete the full course so all bacteria are killed; do not use antibiotics routinely in farm animals; good hygiene in hospitals reduces spread of resistant strains.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: only use when essential; not for viral infections; complete the course; do not share / keep leftover; limit use in livestock; hospital hygiene / hand washing / isolate infected patients; use the correct antibiotic (after testing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why patients are told to finish the full course of antibiotics even when they feel better.
parts.answer: Some bacteria may still be alive (the more resistant ones survive longest); if the course is stopped they can multiply, causing the infection to return and spreading resistance.
parts.working: B1 not all bacteria killed / surviving bacteria; B1 they multiply / infection returns / resistant bacteria increase.

practice.stem: The number of antibiotic prescriptions per 1000 people per day in one district was 5.2 in 2021 and 3.9 in 2024, after a campaign to reduce unnecessary use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in antibiotic prescriptions between 2021 and 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why health authorities wanted to reduce the number of prescriptions.
parts.answer: To slow the development / spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria; many prescriptions were for viral infections where antibiotics have no effect; to save money / reduce side effects.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Over the same period, the percentage of infections caused by resistant bacteria in the district did not fall. Suggest one reason.
parts.answer: Resistant bacteria already present continue to spread (e.g. in hospitals); antibiotics still used in livestock / bought without prescription; resistance takes many years to decline.
parts.working: B1 any sensible reason.

practice.stem:
A student placed discs soaked in antibiotics A and B on agar plates spread with a harmless bacterium and incubated them at 25 °C for 2 days. Diameter of clear zone / mm:
A: 26, 24, 25
B: 14, 15, 31, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the clear zone for antibiotic A.
parts.answer: 25 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result for antibiotic B and calculate the mean without it.
parts.answer: Anomaly 31 mm; mean 14 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which antibiotic would be most effective against this bacterium. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Antibiotic A; it has the largest clear zone, showing the most bacteria were killed / prevented from growing.
parts.working: B1 A; B1 largest zone / more inhibition.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the plates were incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C.
parts.answer: To reduce the chance of growing bacteria that are pathogenic to humans (which grow best at body temperature).
parts.working: B1 avoids growth of human pathogens.

practice.stem: A student prepared an agar plate to test the effect of penicillin on a harmless bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student flamed the inoculating loop until it glowed red before use.
parts.answer: To kill any microorganisms on the loop (sterilise it), so the plate is not contaminated.
parts.working: B1 sterilise / kill microorganisms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lid was held with two pieces of tape but not sealed all the way round.
parts.answer: Tape stops the lid being opened accidentally (safety); not sealing allows oxygen in, preventing the growth of harmful anaerobic bacteria.
parts.working: B1 prevents lid being lifted / contamination; B1 oxygen can enter so anaerobic (pathogenic) bacteria do not grow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the plate was stored upside down during incubation.
parts.answer: Prevents condensation dripping onto the agar surface and spreading colonies.
parts.working: B1 condensation does not drip onto agar.

parts.label: d
parts.text: After incubation a clear zone appeared around a disc containing penicillin. Explain what this shows.
parts.answer: The penicillin diffused into the agar and killed the bacteria / stopped them growing near the disc.
parts.working: B1 antibiotic diffused out and prevented bacterial growth.

practice.stem: A survey in a city found that many people bought antibiotics for coughs and fevers without seeing a doctor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some places antibiotics can be bought from a pharmacy without a doctor's prescription. Explain two ways this can increase antibiotic resistance.
parts.answer: People take antibiotics for viral illnesses where they have no benefit, exposing their bacteria to antibiotics unnecessarily; people buy only a few tablets / do not complete a full course, so some bacteria survive; wrong antibiotic or dose may be chosen, so bacteria are not killed. In each case resistant bacteria are favoured and multiply.
parts.working: Two ways, each B1 practice + B1 link to resistance (surviving / selected resistant bacteria multiply).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of a doctor testing a sample of bacteria from the patient before choosing an antibiotic.
parts.answer: The doctor can choose an antibiotic that the bacteria are not resistant to, so it will work and unnecessary antibiotics are avoided.
parts.working: B1 choose effective antibiotic / avoid ineffective use.

practice.stem: A doctor in Peshawar prescribed amoxicillin capsules of 500 mg, one capsule three times a day for 7 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of antibiotic taken during the full course and the number of capsules needed.
parts.answer: 10 500 mg (10.5 g); 21 capsules

parts.label: b
parts.text: After 3 days the patient feels better and stops taking the capsules. Calculate the number of capsules not taken.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the risk of stopping the course early.
parts.answer: Not all the bacteria have been killed; the surviving ones (often the least sensitive / resistant) multiply, so the infection can return and is harder to treat.
parts.working: B1 bacteria survive; B1 infection returns / resistant bacteria increase.

practice.stem: The number of bacteria in samples from a patient with a throat infection (arbitrary units): day 0 – 48; day 3 – 12; day 5 – 25; day 7 – 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in bacteria between day 0 and day 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The patient stopped taking the antibiotic on day 3. Describe and explain the change in the number of bacteria from day 3 to day 7.
parts.answer: The number rose from 12 to 40 (arbitrary units); the bacteria that survived were not killed by the antibiotic (more resistant) and multiplied once the antibiotic was no longer present.
parts.working: B1 increase with data; B1 surviving bacteria multiply; B1 survivors likely more resistant / antibiotic no longer present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is treated with antibiotics for at least six months. Suggest why the treatment takes so long.
parts.answer: TB bacteria grow / reproduce slowly and some are hidden inside cells / tissues, so antibiotics take a long time to kill them all.
parts.working: B1 slow-growing bacteria / hard to reach.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Patients with TB are usually given three or four different antibiotics at the same time. Explain how this reduces the chance of resistant TB bacteria developing.
parts.answer: A bacterium is unlikely to be resistant to all the antibiotics at once; any bacterium resistant to one antibiotic is killed by another, so resistant strains do not survive to multiply.
parts.working: B1 unlikely to have resistance to all; B1 bacteria resistant to one killed by another.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Typhoid is caused by a bacterium carried in contaminated water and food. Since 2016, a strain resistant to most commonly used antibiotics has spread in parts of Sindh. Explain why infections with this strain are more dangerous than infections with non-resistant strains.
parts.answer: Most antibiotics no longer kill the bacteria, so the infection is harder to treat; patients may need expensive drugs given in hospital and are more likely to suffer complications or die.
parts.working: B1 usual antibiotics ineffective; B1 longer / more serious illness, fewer treatment options.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing the number of people infected with this strain.
parts.answer: Any two: provide clean drinking water and good sanitation; good hygiene / hand washing and safe food preparation; vaccinate children against typhoid; use antibiotics only when prescribed and complete the course.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why doctors were told to use the remaining effective antibiotics only for confirmed cases.
parts.answer: Unnecessary use of these antibiotics would select for bacteria resistant to them too; keeping their use to essential cases slows the development of resistance so they stay effective.
parts.working: B1 overuse selects for resistance; B1 keeps antibiotics effective for longer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which action is most likely to reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a community?
A taking antibiotics at the first sign of any sore throat
B stopping a course of antibiotics as soon as symptoms disappear
C using antibiotics only when essential and finishing the full course
D giving leftover antibiotics to family members with similar symptoms
parts.answer: C using antibiotics only when essential and finishing the full course
parts.working: Using antibiotics only when needed reduces the chance of selecting resistant bacteria, and finishing the course kills as many bacteria as possible so fewer survive to multiply. Stopping early (B) leaves the less susceptible bacteria alive.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Paper discs soaked in four antibiotics, P, Q, R and S, were placed on agar spread with one type of bacterium. After incubation the diameters of the clear zones were P 6 mm, Q 21 mm, R 0 mm, S 14 mm (all discs 6 mm wide). Which conclusion is correct?
A P is the most effective antibiotic.
B The bacteria are resistant to R, and Q is the most effective.
C S is more effective than Q.
D All four antibiotics killed the bacteria.
parts.answer: B The bacteria are resistant to R, and Q is the most effective.
parts.working: The largest clear zone (Q, 21 mm) shows the most bacteria killed or prevented from growing. A zone no wider than the disc (P 6 mm) or none at all (R) means no effect, i.e. resistance.

practice.stem: In one country, 202 tonnes of antibiotics were used in a year: 71 tonnes in human medicine and 131 tonnes in farm animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total antibiotics used that were given to farm animals. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why giving antibiotics routinely to healthy farm animals can affect human health.
parts.answer: Bacteria in animals are exposed to antibiotics, so resistant bacteria survive and multiply; resistant bacteria (or their resistance) can pass to humans through meat, contact or the environment; antibiotics may then not work against human infections.
parts.working: B1 routine use selects for resistant bacteria; B1 resistant bacteria spread to humans (food / contact / manure); B1 infections in humans harder to treat.

practice.stem: Clear zones around two antibiotic discs on a bacterial lawn had diameters of 2.2 cm (antibiotic X) and 1.1 cm (antibiotic Y).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of each clear zone. Use area = πr² and give your answers to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Antibiotic X: 3.8 cm²; antibiotic Y: 0.95 cm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the clear zone area is for X than for Y.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is better to compare areas rather than diameters.
parts.answer: The area shows the actual region where bacteria failed to grow; doubling the diameter gives four times the area, so diameters underestimate the difference.
parts.working: B1 area represents amount of agar cleared / area ∝ diameter².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of an antibiotic affects the growth of a harmless bacterium on agar plates.
parts.answer: Prepare at least five concentrations of antibiotic by dilution (e.g. 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 %); spread bacteria evenly on agar plates using aseptic technique (sterile spreader, flame neck of bottle, lift lid only slightly); soak equal-sized filter paper discs in each concentration for the same time; place on plates at equal spacing; tape the lid with two strips (not sealed), incubate upside down at 25 °C for 48 hours; measure diameter of clear zone with a ruler; repeat three times and calculate means; control: disc soaked in sterile water; controlled variables: same bacterium, same agar volume, disc size, temperature, time; safety: do not open plates after incubation, dispose by autoclaving, wash hands.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of ≥5 concentrations with how made; aseptic technique (one detail); same-size discs soaked for equal time; incubate at 25 °C for stated time; measure diameter / area of clear zone; two controlled variables; control disc (water); repeats and mean; safety (taped lid not sealed / do not open / autoclave).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the use of an antibiotic leads to an increase in the proportion of resistant bacteria in a population.
parts.answer: There is variation in a bacterial population; some bacteria have (by random mutation) an allele giving resistance; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance allele; over many generations most of the population is resistant.
parts.working: B1 variation / random mutation already present (not caused by antibiotic); B1 non-resistant killed; B1 resistant survive and reproduce; B1 pass on allele / proportion increases over generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student writes 'the antibiotic makes the bacteria become immune'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Bacteria do not have an immune system / immunity refers to the body's response to pathogens; the antibiotic does not cause the resistance – it selects bacteria that were already resistant.
parts.working: B1 'immune' is wrong term (immunity is in the host); B1 resistance pre-exists, selected not caused.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for one resistant bacterium to produce over 4000 bacteria if it divides every 20 minutes. Show your working.
parts.answer: 4 hours (12 divisions give 2¹² = 4096)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why resistance can spread through a bacterial population very quickly when an antibiotic is used.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce very rapidly (asexually, by binary fission), so a single surviving resistant bacterium can give rise to a large resistant population in hours; each offspring inherits the resistance allele.
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction / many generations quickly; B1 all offspring inherit resistance.

practice.stem: A hospital introduced compulsory hand cleaning with alcohol gel and stricter rules on prescribing antibiotics. MRSA infections per 10 000 patients: 2020 – 6.8; 2024 – 1.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in MRSA infections between 2020 and 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each of the two measures could have contributed to the decrease.
parts.answer: Hand washing / alcohol gel kills or removes MRSA from hands, so fewer bacteria are passed between patients; reduced prescribing lowers selection pressure, so resistant strains have less advantage and become less common.
parts.working: B1 hygiene removes / kills bacteria on hands; B1 so less transmission between patients; B1 fewer antibiotics → less selection for resistant bacteria; B1 resistant bacteria do not increase in proportion.

practice.stem: Data for four countries – antibiotic doses per 1000 people per day and % of E. coli infections resistant to one antibiotic: Q – 10, 9 %; R – 18, 20 %; S – 25, 29 %; T – 32, 41 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown in the data.
parts.answer: Countries with higher antibiotic use have a higher percentage of resistant E. coli; e.g. country T (32 doses) 41 % against country Q (10 doses) 9 % – a positive correlation.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 data quote with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that 'antibiotic use is the only cause of resistance'. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The data show a correlation but do not prove cause; other factors could affect resistance, e.g. use in farm animals, hospital hygiene, sanitation, travel; only four countries were studied; but it is consistent with selection of resistant bacteria by antibiotic use.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: correlation not proof of causation; other factors named (livestock use / hygiene / sanitation / spread between countries); small sample of countries; supported by mechanism of selection.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A patient stopped taking an antibiotic after 2 days of a 7-day course. A week later the infection returned and the same antibiotic no longer worked. What is the best explanation?
A The patient's body became immune to the antibiotic.
B The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate so that they became resistant.
C The bacteria that survived the short course were the most resistant ones, and they multiplied.
D The antibiotic had been broken down by the patient's white blood cells.
parts.answer: C The bacteria that survived the short course were the most resistant ones, and they multiplied.
parts.working: A short course kills the most susceptible bacteria; the more resistant ones survive and reproduce, so the new population is mostly resistant. B is the common error: the antibiotic does not cause the mutation; it selects resistant bacteria that already exist. A is wrong because resistance belongs to the bacteria, not the patient.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best definition of a drug?
A any substance that kills bacteria
B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
C any substance made by a doctor
D any substance that is addictive
parts.answer: B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
parts.working: This is the general definition; antibiotics (A) are only one type of drug, and many drugs are neither prescribed nor addictive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term drug.
parts.answer: Any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into the body; B1 modifies / affects chemical reactions in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a drug used as a medicine and one example of a drug that people take for other reasons.
parts.answer: Medicine: any one, e.g. paracetamol, an antibiotic such as penicillin, insulin. Other: any one, e.g. caffeine, nicotine, alcohol.
parts.working: B1 medicinal drug; B1 non-medicinal drug.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these drugs could be used to treat a bacterial infection?
paracetamol; penicillin; caffeine; insulin; nicotine
parts.answer: penicillin
parts.working: B1 penicillin only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Insulin is a hormone made in the pancreas. Explain why insulin injected by a person with type 1 diabetes is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into the body that modifies chemical reactions in the body – it causes glucose to be converted to glycogen in the liver (lowering blood glucose).
parts.working: B1 taken into the body; B1 affects reactions / lowers blood glucose / glucose → glycogen.

practice.stem:
A student measured her reaction time by catching a falling ruler. The distance the ruler fell before she caught it was recorded five times before, and five times 30 minutes after, drinking a cup of coffee.
Before / cm: 18, 20, 19, 21, 17
After / cm: 15, 16, 14, 17, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance before and after drinking the coffee.
parts.answer: before 19 cm; after 15 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shorter distance means a faster reaction. State the effect of the coffee on the student's reaction time.
parts.answer: The reaction became faster (reaction time decreased).
parts.working: B1 faster reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the drug in coffee that probably caused this effect.
parts.answer: caffeine
parts.working: B1 caffeine.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the results from one student do not prove that coffee speeds up reactions for everyone.
parts.answer: Only one person was tested; the student may also have improved with practice.
parts.working: B1 one person / practice effect / no control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tobacco contains nicotine. Explain why nicotine is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into the body (absorbed into the blood from the lungs) and it affects chemical reactions / the nervous system in the body.
parts.working: B1 taken into body; B1 affects body reactions / nervous system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one property of nicotine that makes it difficult for smokers to stop.
parts.answer: It is addictive.
parts.working: B1 addictive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two other harmful substances in tobacco smoke.
parts.answer: Any two: tar; carbon monoxide; smoke particles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Caffeine content of some drinks:
Cup of tea: 40 mg
Cup of coffee: 95 mg
Can of cola: 35 mg
Can of energy drink: 80 mg
In one day, a student in Karachi drank two cups of tea, one can of energy drink and one can of cola.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of caffeine the student drank in one day.
parts.answer: 195 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate by how much the student exceeded the guideline of 100 mg per day used in this question.
parts.answer: 95 mg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Caffeine is a stimulant. Suggest why drinking an energy drink late in the evening may affect a student's sleep.
parts.answer: Caffeine increases the activity of the nervous system / keeps the student alert, so it is harder to fall asleep.
parts.working: B1 keeps alert / stimulates nervous system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dentist injects a local anaesthetic into a patient's gum before filling a tooth. The patient cannot feel pain in that area for about two hours. State why the anaesthetic is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance put into the body that changes how the body works – it stops nerve impulses from the gum (affects body reactions).
parts.working: B1 substance taken into body; B1 affects body processes / stops pain impulses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the effect wears off after about two hours.
parts.answer: The drug is carried away in the blood and broken down / removed.
parts.working: B1 drug removed / broken down.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Stimulants speed up the activity of the nervous system and depressants slow it down. Classify each drug as a stimulant or a depressant.
(i) caffeine (ii) alcohol (iii) nicotine (iv) heroin
parts.answer: (i) stimulant (ii) depressant (iii) stimulant (iv) depressant
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Medicine labels state the dose and how often to take it. Explain why a patient should not take more than the stated dose.
parts.answer: Too much of a drug can be harmful / poisonous (toxic) and may damage organs such as the liver; a larger dose does not make the treatment work faster.
parts.working: B1 overdose harmful / toxic; B1 example of harm or no extra benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why medicines should be kept out of reach of young children.
parts.answer: Children may swallow them; their small body mass means even a small amount could be a dangerous dose.
parts.working: B1 accidental overdose / small body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Athlete's foot is a skin infection caused by a fungus. It is treated with an antifungal cream. Explain why the antifungal cream is a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into (applied to and absorbed by) the body that affects chemical reactions – it kills the fungus / stops it growing.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into the body; B1 modifies chemical reactions / kills fungus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of drug used to treat infections caused by bacteria.
parts.answer: antibiotics
parts.working: B1 antibiotic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one type of pathogen that is not affected by antibiotics.
parts.answer: viruses
parts.working: B1 virus (accept fungi).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why both a painkiller such as paracetamol and an antibiotic such as amoxicillin are drugs.
parts.answer: Both are substances taken into the body that modify or affect chemical reactions in the body.
parts.working: B1 taken into the body; B1 modify / affect chemical reactions in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference in what these two drugs are used for.
parts.answer: Paracetamol relieves symptoms (pain / fever) but does not kill the pathogen; amoxicillin kills bacteria, treating the cause of a bacterial infection.
parts.working: B1 painkiller relieves symptoms; B1 antibiotic kills bacteria / treats bacterial infection.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which drug relieves the symptoms of an infection, such as pain and fever, but does not kill the pathogen?
A paracetamol
B penicillin
C amoxicillin
D streptomycin
parts.answer: A paracetamol
parts.working: Paracetamol is a painkiller that reduces pain and fever but does not kill pathogens. B, C and D are antibiotics, which kill bacteria.

practice.stem:
Daphnia (water fleas) are tiny transparent animals whose heart can be seen beating under a microscope. A student placed a Daphnia in pond water containing different concentrations of caffeine and counted the heart beats in 15 seconds.
Caffeine concentration / %: 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04
Beats in 15 s: 50, 56, 63, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute at each concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate between 0 % and 0.04 % caffeine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Caffeine is a drug. Use the results to explain why.
parts.answer: Caffeine was taken into the Daphnia's body and changed the rate of its heart beat, showing that it affects chemical reactions / processes in the body.
parts.working: B1 taken into body; B1 changed heart rate / body reactions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature of the water; size / age of Daphnia; time in the solution before counting; volume of solution; light intensity under the microscope.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A study in Australia measured the reaction time of volunteers in a driving simulator after drinking different amounts of alcohol.
Blood alcohol concentration / %: 0, 0.05, 0.08, 0.12
Reaction time / s: 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in reaction time at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 % compared with no alcohol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car travels at 25 m per second. Calculate the extra distance it travels before the driver reacts, at 0.08 % blood alcohol compared with no alcohol.
parts.working: M1 extra time 0.10 s; A1 25 × 0.10 = 2.5 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why alcohol is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is taken into the body and affects chemical reactions / the nervous system (slows reactions).
parts.working: B1 substance taken in that modifies body reactions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why many countries set a legal limit for blood alcohol when driving.
parts.answer: Slower reactions make accidents more likely / drivers cannot stop in time.
parts.working: B1 slower reactions → more accidents.

practice.stem: In this question, a doctor tells a parent to give paracetamol syrup at a dose of 15 mg per kg of body mass. The child has a mass of 18 kg. The syrup contains 120 mg of paracetamol in every 5 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dose of paracetamol for the child, in mg.
parts.answer: 270 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of syrup that contains this dose. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dose of a drug for children is calculated from body mass.
parts.answer: A smaller body has less blood / tissue, so the same amount of drug would give a higher concentration in the body; too high a concentration can be harmful (e.g. paracetamol can damage the liver).
parts.working: B1 smaller body → higher concentration from same dose; B1 risk of harm / overdose (liver damage).

practice.stem: In a trial of a new drug for influenza, 400 patients were given the drug and 400 were given a placebo. The mean time to recover was 4.2 days for the drug group and 5.6 days for the placebo group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the mean time to recover in the group given the drug.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the trial included patients of different ages and of both sexes.
parts.answer: So that the results apply to the whole population, and so that any effect that depends on age or sex is detected.
parts.working: B1 results can be generalised to the wider population; B1 shows whether the drug works differently for different groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the new drug is described as an antiviral drug rather than an antibiotic.
parts.answer: It acts against viruses (influenza is caused by a virus); antibiotics only work against bacteria.
parts.working: B1 acts on virus / antibiotics only work on bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tobacco smoke contains carbon monoxide. Explain how carbon monoxide reduces the amount of oxygen carried by the blood.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells (very strongly, and does not easily leave), so less haemoglobin is available to carry oxygen.
parts.working: B1 combines with haemoglobin; B1 less haemoglobin available for oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a smoker becomes breathless during exercise more quickly than a non-smoker.
parts.answer: Less oxygen reaches the muscles, so less aerobic respiration and more anaerobic respiration occur; carbon dioxide / lactic acid build up faster, so breathing has to increase more.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen to muscles; B1 more anaerobic respiration / faster build-up of CO₂ → breathless.

practice.stem: Salbutamol is a drug in an inhaler. It is used to treat asthma and relaxes the muscles in the walls of the bronchioles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why salbutamol is described as a drug.
parts.answer: It is a substance taken into the body that affects chemical processes in the body: it changes the activity of the muscle in the walls of the bronchioles, making it relax.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into the body; B1 modifies body processes (relaxes bronchiole muscle).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how relaxing these muscles helps a person with asthma to breathe.
parts.answer: The bronchioles become wider, so more air reaches the alveoli in each breath and more oxygen can diffuse into the blood.
parts.working: B1 bronchioles wider / less constricted; B1 more air (and oxygen) reaches the alveoli for gas exchange.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the drug is inhaled straight into the lungs rather than swallowed as a tablet.
parts.answer: It acts directly on the bronchioles, so it works quickly and less of it reaches the rest of the body, reducing side effects.
parts.working: B1 acts directly where needed (quick action) and fewer side effects elsewhere in the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person who drinks large amounts of alcohol over many years may develop liver damage. Name the organ that breaks down alcohol in the body.
parts.answer: the liver
parts.working: B1 liver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why heavy, long-term drinking damages this organ.
parts.answer: The liver has to break down large amounts of alcohol (a toxin) continuously; its cells are damaged and replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), so it cannot carry out its other functions.
parts.working: B1 liver cells break down alcohol / toxin; B1 cells damaged / scar tissue / cirrhosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying that a person is addicted to a drug.
parts.answer: The person feels a strong need to keep taking the drug and suffers unpleasant withdrawal symptoms if they stop.
parts.working: B1 need / craving to keep taking it; B1 withdrawal symptoms when stopped.

practice.stem: In a survey at a college, 240 students were asked about their drinks. 96 said they drank at least one drink containing caffeine every day. Of these 96, 29 reported having trouble falling asleep.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of students who drank at least one caffeinated drink every day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of these daily drinkers who reported trouble sleeping. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what extra information would be needed to decide whether caffeine causes the trouble sleeping.
parts.answer: The percentage of students who do not drink caffeine who also have trouble sleeping (a comparison group); and information on other causes, e.g. screen use or exam stress / the time of day they drink caffeine.
parts.working: B1 compare with non-drinkers; B1 other factors / timing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A herbal tea is advertised as a cure for influenza. Using the definition of a drug, explain what would need to be true for the tea to be classed as a drug.
parts.answer: A substance in the tea would need to be taken into the body and modify or affect chemical reactions in the body.
parts.working: B1 substance taken into body; B1 affects / modifies chemical reactions in the body.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it would not be useful for a patient with influenza to take an antibiotic instead.
parts.answer: Influenza is caused by a virus; antibiotics only act on bacteria, so they would not help (and could encourage resistance in bacteria in the body).
parts.working: B1 influenza is viral; B1 antibiotics do not affect viruses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how scientists could test fairly whether the tea reduces the length of the illness.
parts.answer: Compare two large groups of similar patients – one given the tea and one given a similar-tasting tea without the herb (placebo), without knowing which they get; record the number of days of illness and compare means.
parts.working: B1 large groups with a control / placebo group; B1 measure length of illness / compare means; accept blind trial.

practice.stem:
A student counted the heart beats of Daphnia in 15 seconds in different concentrations of ethanol. A new Daphnia was used for each concentration, and three counts were made for each.
Ethanol / %: 0 – 66, 64, 65; 1 – 58, 60, 59; 2 – 52, 51, 36; 3 – 44, 45, 46; 4 – 38, 37, 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean for that concentration without it.
parts.answer: 36 at 2 % ethanol; mean 51.5 beats

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean heart rate between 0 % and 4 % ethanol. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ethanol (alcohol) is described as a depressant drug. Explain how these results support this description.
parts.answer: As the ethanol concentration increased, the heart rate decreased; ethanol slows down body processes, which is what a depressant does.
parts.working: B1 heart rate falls as concentration rises, with data; B1 depressant slows body activity.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the student used a different Daphnia for each concentration, and one problem this causes.
parts.answer: Reason: ethanol from one test could still affect the animal in the next test. Problem: different Daphnia may have different natural heart rates (size, age), so the comparison is less fair.
parts.working: B1 avoids carry-over effect / harm to one animal; B1 individual variation in heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A company has developed a new drug to lower blood pressure. Before it can be sold it is tested on volunteers. Explain why each of these features of the trial is used.
(i) One group of volunteers is given a placebo (a tablet that looks the same but contains no drug).
(ii) Neither the volunteers nor the doctors know who is given the drug and who is given the placebo.
(iii) Several thousand volunteers take part.
(iv) The drug is first tested at very low doses on a small number of healthy volunteers.
parts.answer: (i) To compare with the drug group, so any effect caused just by taking a tablet / believing you are treated can be separated from the effect of the drug. (ii) So that expectations cannot affect the results or how they are recorded (double-blind; removes bias). (iii) To make the results reliable / reduce the effect of individual variation and to detect rare side effects. (iv) To check that the drug is safe / find side effects before larger doses and patients are used.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a drug that works well in a trial may not be approved for use.
parts.answer: It may have serious side effects / be no better than existing drugs.
parts.working: B1 harmful side effects or not better than existing treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many medicines first came from plants: aspirin was developed from a chemical in willow bark, and quinine, used to treat malaria, comes from the bark of the cinchona tree. Suggest why scientists want to protect large areas of tropical forest, even where no medicines have yet been found.
parts.answer: Forests contain huge numbers of plant species, many not yet studied; some may contain chemicals that could be developed into new drugs; if the forest is destroyed these species may become extinct before they are tested, and the potential medicines are lost.
parts.working: B1 high biodiversity / many unstudied species; B1 may contain useful drug chemicals; B1 extinction would lose them permanently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Malaria is caused by a single-celled organism, not a bacterium. Suggest why quinine is not described as an antibiotic.
parts.answer: Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria; quinine acts against the malaria parasite, which is not a bacterium.
parts.working: B1 antibiotics act on bacteria only.

practice.stem:
Deaths from lung cancer per 100 000 men per year, by number of cigarettes smoked per day:
Non-smokers: 10
1–14 per day: 78
15–24 per day: 127
25 or more per day: 251

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for those who smoked 25 or more cigarettes a day than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 25.1 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: The more cigarettes smoked per day, the higher the death rate from lung cancer; even light smokers (1–14 a day) have a death rate about 8 times that of non-smokers.
parts.working: B1 positive relationship; B1 data quote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says that these data prove that smoking causes lung cancer. Explain why the data alone do not prove this, and suggest what other evidence would help.
parts.answer: The data show a correlation; another factor (for example, working with harmful dust or air pollution) could be linked with both smoking and cancer. Evidence that would help: the cancer rate falls in people who stop smoking; laboratory evidence that chemicals in tar cause cancer in cells; the pattern is the same in many different countries and groups.
parts.working: B1 correlation is not proof of cause; B1 other factors could be involved; B1 any one valid extra evidence.

practice.stem: In this question, the concentration of a drug in the blood halves every 4 hours. Just after one dose, the concentration is 80 mg/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the drug in the blood 12 hours after the dose.
parts.answer: 10 mg/dm³
parts.working: M1 three half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10; A1 10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The drug is effective only when its concentration is above 15 mg/dm³. Calculate the concentration at 8 hours and state whether the drug is still effective at 8 hours and at 12 hours.
parts.answer: 20 mg/dm³ at 8 hours; effective at 8 hours (20 > 15) but not at 12 hours (10 < 15)
parts.working: B1 80 → 40 → 20 at 8 h; B1 effective at 8 h, not at 12 h.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the label tells the patient to take the drug at regular intervals rather than taking the whole day's dose at once.
parts.answer: The drug is broken down / removed from the body over time; regular doses keep the concentration above the effective level but below a harmful (toxic) level all day.
parts.working: B1 concentration falls as drug is broken down / excreted; B1 regular doses keep it within the effective, safe range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some athletes illegally take anabolic steroids, drugs similar to the hormone testosterone, to build muscle. Explain why these substances are drugs.
parts.answer: They are taken into the body and modify chemical reactions (increase protein synthesis / muscle growth).
parts.working: B1 taken in and modify body reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why sports organisations ban anabolic steroids.
parts.answer: Any two: gives an unfair advantage; harmful side effects (e.g. damage to the liver or heart); athletes may feel pressured to take them to compete.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Testosterone normally controls the production of sperm. Suggest why male athletes who take large doses of steroids may produce fewer sperm.
parts.answer: The high level of steroid in the blood causes the body to reduce its own hormone signals (negative feedback), so the testes make less testosterone and fewer sperm.
parts.working: B1 body detects high hormone level / reduces own production; B1 testes produce less / fewer sperm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether drinking a caffeinated drink affects the reaction time of students. Use the ruler-drop test. Include what you would change and measure, how you would make it a fair test, how you would make the results reliable and one ethical or safety consideration.
parts.answer: Use a group of e.g. 20 volunteer students. Measure each student's reaction time with the ruler-drop test (catch distance), 5 times, and calculate a mean. Then give half the students a drink containing caffeine and the other half an identical-tasting drink without caffeine (decaffeinated – a placebo), without telling them which. After 30 minutes repeat the ruler test 5 times. Keep the same ruler, same dropping height, same hand, same person dropping, no warning before dropping. Compare the change in mean distance for the two groups. Practise beforehand so learning does not affect results. Use a small, safe amount of caffeine; students with heart conditions or who avoid caffeine should not take part; get consent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV caffeine / no caffeine (or caffeine dose); DV distance ruler falls / reaction time; measured before and after a fixed time; placebo / decaffeinated drink for control group; volunteers do not know which drink (blind); same hand, ruler, starting position, dropper; practice trials to reduce learning effect; repeats and means / large group; ethics: consent, small safe dose, exclude those with health conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many drugs work by affecting enzymes. Penicillin stops an enzyme that bacteria use to build their cell walls. Explain why penicillin kills bacteria but does not harm human cells.
parts.answer: Without the enzyme, bacteria cannot build cell walls properly, so the growing bacteria burst / die; human cells have no cell wall and do not use this enzyme, so they are not affected.
parts.working: B1 bacterial cell wall not made / weak; B1 bacteria burst / die; B1 human cells have no cell wall / no such enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the definition of a drug to explain why a substance that inhibits an enzyme is a drug.
parts.answer: Enzymes control chemical reactions in the body, so inhibiting one modifies / affects chemical reactions.
parts.working: B1 link enzyme → chemical reactions modified.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why penicillin has no effect on a viral infection.
parts.answer: Viruses have no cell walls and do not have their own enzymes for making them (they reproduce inside host cells).
parts.working: B1 viruses have no cell wall / not cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: People are advised not to flush unused medicines down the toilet but to return them to a pharmacy. Suggest two harmful effects of medicines entering rivers.
parts.answer: Any two: antibiotics in the water may lead to resistant bacteria developing in the environment; hormones from medicines can affect the development / reproduction of fish; drugs may be taken in by other organisms and affect their body reactions / be passed along food chains.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics in river water could make it harder to treat human infections in future.
parts.answer: Low concentrations of antibiotic kill sensitive bacteria but allow resistant ones to survive and multiply (selection); resistant bacteria can then infect people.
parts.working: B1 selects for resistant bacteria; B1 resistant bacteria may infect humans / spread resistance.
